#6334. Teenage boys are spending less time outside, but what has changed?

U.S. teenage boys’ outdoor time fell from over an hour a day around 2010 to under 40 minutes by 2023, while girls’ outdoor time changed little.

Teenage boys in the United States once spent considerably more time outdoors than teenage girls. Around 2010, that gap was still clear. Since then, boys’ outdoor time has fallen sharply.

American boys aged 15 to 19 averaged more than 60 minutes a day outdoors around 2010. By 2023 they were under 40 minutes.

Girls initially spent less time outdoors, and their average changed little. By 2023, boys and girls were spending similarly limited amounts of time outside.

The analysis was led by Ewa Jarosz in the Department of Psychology at the University of Oslo.

Her co-authors were Vidar Ulset of the Norwegian School of Sport Sciences and Vegard Skirbekk, who also works at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health.

Time outdoors is where teenagers get their daylight and a large share of their physical activity, and the study can’t say what caused the drop, only what moved alongside it.

The numbers come from the American Time Use Survey, which the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has run since 2003.

Each person in it walks an interviewer through one full day, activity by activity, with where they were and who was with them.

The team pulled every diary from someone aged 15 to 19 between 2003 and 2023, which came to 14,235 days.

Time counted as outdoors when the diary placed the person outside away from home, or walking or cycling somewhere.

It also counted when the activity only happens outside, such as mowing a lawn, hunting or playing an outdoor sport.

Some outdoor time was missed on purpose. The survey lumps home and yard together, and it doesn’t say whether time at school was in a classroom or on a field, so neither was counted.

The team applied the same rule to every year, allowing consistent comparisons while leaving some outdoor time unmeasured.

Outdoor time for all teenagers fell over the 20 years, and the decline was concentrated among boys.

Girls’ time changed little, and the sex difference that was clear in 2010 was no longer detectable in recent years.

The steepest part of the drop for boys came after the pandemic, in both whether they went out at all and how long they stayed.

The year 2020 itself was left out of the trend lines because the survey was disrupted that year.

Some things went with more outdoor time for both sexes.

Teenagers under 16 spent more time outside than older ones, as did those in the Northeast and West and those from higher-income households.

Weekends brought longer stretches outside. Black teenagers were more likely to go out on a given day but stayed out for less time.

The team then set outdoor time beside three other ways of spending leisure: computer use and gaming, indoor exercise, and time with friends.

Smartphones were left out, because the survey didn’t measure them the same way every year and because a phone can be used outside.

Boys in the top quarter for computer leisure were less likely to go outside at all, and spent less time there when they did.

Girls showed a similar pattern, but the association was not statistically significant.

Boys who were heavy computer users spent about as much time outdoors as girls.

Time with friends ran the other way. Teenagers who spent more than the typical amount of time with a friend were more likely to be outside, boys and girls alike.

The quarter who spent the most time with friends also stayed out longest. Over the same 20 years, time with friends fell sharply for both.

In an interview with Earth.com, Jarosz said hanging out itself is in decline. It used to be low-cost and easy to arrange, she said, and now “it is crowded out by other activities.”

Could more indoor exercise have offset the loss of outdoor time? The study found no increase in indoor physical activity over the period.

Teenagers who exercised indoors were also more likely to spend time outdoors.

One kind of activity went with the other rather than replacing it.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Jarosz said the decline among boys, which worries her.

Men need more physical activity than women to get the same heart benefits, she said.

Jarosz suggested that less outdoor time could also leave boys fewer opportunities for rough-and-tumble play.

The researchers noted that indoor exercise is also selective, with cost a common barrier, and that a recent pooled analysis found people enjoy it less than activity outdoors.

Each teenager appears once, on one day, so the study tracks a population rather than following any person as they grow.

The diaries also say nothing about what the outdoors looked like, so a wooded park and a parking lot count the same.

Asked what parents can do, Jarosz said habits are mostly set earlier in childhood, and that for 15- to 19-year-olds the peer group matters more than parents do.

She was careful to call that her view rather than a study finding. She pointed instead at where teenagers live.

“We know this is highly stratified, which means that it depends on your socioeconomic status what type of outdoor environment you have nearby,” Jarosz noted.

Whether the decline has bottomed out is an open question. Jarosz said outdoor time ticked up slightly in 2021 compared with 2020, by too little to count, and that she expects some recovery now that the pandemic is over.

“The decline started already around 2010 and I think the likelihood of returning to 2010 levels of outdoor time without some intervention is probably low,” she told Earth.com.

The next diaries will show whether she is right, one day at a time.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6333. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

#6332. ADHD is linked to higher death rates from suicide, injury and illness

People diagnosed with ADHD died at a 70% higher rate across 19 studies, and those on ADHD medication died at a lower rate, a new review finds.

Most people think of ADHD as a childhood problem, the kind of thing a kid grows out of as they become adults. But a new pooled analysis of 19 studies says it is also linked to shockingly higher death rates

Across those studies and nearly 16 million people, those diagnosed with ADHD died at a 70 percent higher rate than those without it.

The extra deaths came from suicide, from injuries and from ordinary illness alike. And in the three studies that looked, people with ADHD who took medication for it died at a lower rate than those who didn’t.

Researchers at University College London and the University of Liverpool pooled the studies on ADHD and death. Every one of them was observational. The review can show that ADHD and earlier death go together, not that one causes the other.

In an interview with Earth.com, senior author Joshua Stott, a professor in UCL’s Psychology and Language Sciences division, said doctors should take the range of causes seriously.

“Clinicians should be aware that ADHD is associated with higher mortality risk via a variety of routes including accidental death and suicide and causes likely to do with co-occurring health problems,” Stott said.

The team investigated six research databases and found 19 studies published between 2012 and 2025. Each followed people with and without ADHD, some for more than 20 years.

The studies came from the United States, Canada, Sweden, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, Finland and Denmark, and about a third of the participants were female.

Twelve of the studies reported numbers that could be combined. In that pool, the rate of death by suicide was 90 percent higher among people with ADHD.

The rate of death from injury, intentional or not, was 55 percent higher. The rate of death from natural causes was 27 percent higher.

The size of the gap varied a lot from study to study. The direction did not. Every study found more deaths in the ADHD group, which the authors read as disagreement about how much, not whether.

The authors point to several paths. Differences in impulse control, emotional regulation and risk-taking can raise the chance of injury.

ADHD often comes with depression and other mental health conditions that raise the risk of suicide. Earlier work has tied ADHD to serious transport accidents.

The deaths from illness have their own explanations. People with ADHD have higher rates of heart disease and metabolic disorders. They smoke more, have more sleep disorders, and can find it harder to keep up with treatment plans and appointments.

The authors also note that people with ADHD face more exclusion, disadvantage and stigma. Substance use, they write, can be a response to environments that offer little support.

Stott said the condition itself does not have to shorten a life. “ADHD is not by definition a life-limiting condition as the right support and treatment can help people with ADHD to live long and healthy lives.”

Three of the studies, from Taiwan, Quebec and Sweden, compared people with ADHD who took medication for it against those who did not. Pooled together, the medicated group had a 25 percent lower rate of death from any cause.

The authors treat that number with care. People who get prescriptions may differ from people who don’t in how severe their ADHD is, how easily they reach health care, and what other conditions they have.

Three studies can’t untangle that. The paper says the result should not be read as proof that ADHD medication protects against death.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him most, Stott named the potential role of medication. The team doesn’t know whether the finding is causal, he told Earth.com. But some risks, such as accidental death, may be tied to traits like impulsivity that medication can help with.

“Our findings provide early evidence to suggest that medication may play an important role in supporting the health of people with ADHD,” said first author Lucy Corrigan of the University of Liverpool.

However, she cautioned that this is based on a small number of studies so the findings are preliminary. Further research is needed to clarify this link.

Seven of the 19 studies could not be pooled. They reported their results differently or measured outcomes, such as deaths from COVID-19, that nothing else matched.

Most of the studies had more men than women, which may hide risks specific to women, who are diagnosed less often. The studies also adjusted for different things, so the pooled figures are averages across very different populations.

An earlier review of ADHD and mortality found no clear rise in deaths from natural causes. This one did, which the authors attribute to newer studies and to differences in which studies were included.

The review builds on the group’s earlier finding that adults with diagnosed ADHD have a shorter life expectancy. The authors also note that autism, which often occurs alongside ADHD, may account for part of the risk.

Whether treatment lowers the death rate, or whether treated people were simply healthier to begin with, is the open question.

Asked what it would take to answer it, Stott said the ideal would be a randomized trial with long-term follow-up. Such trials are expensive and hard to run over long time frames, he said.

The authors call for studies of women, of minoritized racial and ethnic groups, and of people who were maltreated as children, to find out who carries the highest risk. For now, Stott said, the deaths come by several routes, and the support will have to as well.

“I think it is useful to highlight that [for] people with ADHD, mortality risk was apparent across a variety of routes so it is likely that support will be needed in a number of areas to reduce this,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#6331. A Viking Couple’s Grave May Reveal Who Really Settled This Strategic Island 1,100 Years Ago

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man were surprised to find not one but two of the island’s most significant Viking finds.

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man received double the surprise when they uncovered a 1,100-year-old double grave. It contained rare brooches typically worn by Scandinavian women and a sword that, according to one expert, would once have gleamed with a “bright silver” pommel. The site also produced intricately decorated trading weights, a Viking axe head, balance scales, and a ceremonial bronze ladle.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” Allison Fox said in a statement. Fox is curator for archaeology at Manx National Heritage, a museum and heritage trust on the Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland. “What makes it particularly exciting is the combination of finds, which gives us a rare opportunity to explore the lives of some of the island’s earliest Scandinavian settlers.”

Experts believe the metal detectorists, Daniel Crowe and Rhett Britton, came upon the double grave of a man and a woman who were buried with some of their finest possessions: three brooches for her and a sword for him. Fox said the date of the brooches suggests the grave may be the “earliest known female Viking Age burial” on the island. Together with the other finds, she said, the objects “help us build a picture of the people who lived here more than a thousand years ago, how they traded, and the connections they maintained across the Viking world.”

The find dates to around 900 C.E. That places it at the early end of the Viking Age on the Isle of Man, just as Scandinavian communities were becoming established there. Some of the objects are also the first of their kind found on the island.

Museum experts believe the Vikings first arrived on the island during the ninth century. Recognizing the strategic importance of its location in the Irish Sea, they established trading links before settling there. A rich Viking heritage remains across the island, and burials found in the past show evidence of pagan traditions. Viking influence still runs through Manx culture today. Tynwald, the island’s parliament, was founded during the Viking Age and is known as one of the world’s oldest continuous parliaments.

After making their discovery, Crowe and Britton didn’t try to clean the objects. Fox says this has allowed experts to fully appreciate the objects’ intricate details. She added that the brooches still have soil inside them, and the team is carefully excavating it in hopes of finding traces of textile.

Two of the brooches are a matching pair of oval “tortoise” brooches, the kind Scandinavian women wore to fasten their dresses at the shoulders. Both are covered in intricate interlocking animals, a hallmark of Viking art. According to Manx National Heritage, only one other pair like them has ever been found on the Isle of Man, and that was found by Daniel Crowe’s own father, John Crowe, along with fellow metal detectorist Craig Evans. The new pair is likely about 50 years older, which is why experts think this grave may be the island’s earliest known female Viking burial. The third brooch, decorated with spirals and a glass center, is the first of its kind found on the island.

The sword is the type a man would have carried, and it’s the 13th Viking sword found on the Isle of Man. Although the blade is badly corroded and parts of it are missing entirely, Fox said in a video from the heritage group that the pommel still shows “signs of the really intricate decorating that would have been on the pommel when it was buried.” X-ray analysis revealed traces of silver and copper wire inlaid into the iron, which makes it one of only three swords found on the island with such decoration.

“When this sword was buried,” she said, “this top part of the sword would have been really bright silver, a really high-status object.” In addition, traces of wood show that the sword’s handle was covered in wood rather than thread or horn.

Although 1,100 years in the ground caused much of the sword’s damage, experts believe the Vikings broke it on purpose as part of a burial ritual.

Because the brooches were found alongside the sword (items linked to a woman and a man, respectively), a double burial seems likely. Experts said, however, that they can’t be sure whether the grave goods came from one grave or from two graves placed close together.

Beyond the burial itself, the decorated lead weights and bronze balance scales found at the site highlight the Isle of Man’s role in Irish Sea trade. The weights are the first of their kind found on the island. One of them has a decorative bronze fitting, with artwork typical of Britain and Ireland, that may have been taken from another object.

The bronze ladle, another first for the island, was likely used in ceremonies.

Despite all the experts have gleaned from the discovery, there’s still much to be learned. “Although the original burial site has been disturbed,” Fox said, “further research may reveal much more about these objects and the people who owned them.”

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#6329. Uranus and Neptune look alike, but their chemistry hints at different pasts

Models of the deep chemistry of Uranus and Neptune find far more oxygen inside Neptune, a sign the two grew from different parts of the disk.

Uranus and Neptune are similar in size and are both known as ice giants. But new model estimates suggest Neptune’s deep atmosphere contains a much higher proportion of oxygen than Uranus’s.

The researchers calculate that the two planets’ carbon-to-oxygen ratios differ enough that each may have grown from a different part of the disk that built the solar system.

Tom Briand of Aix-Marseille Université in France led the work.

His co-authors include Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute in Boulder, Colorado, who served as a co-advisor on Briand’s doctorate.

“Uranus and Neptune may resemble twins today, but their chemistry is telling us that they are more like cousins with very different histories,” Mousis said.

Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, and no spacecraft has been back. Telescopes see only the top of each atmosphere.

Most of the oxygen on both ice giants is in water, and water condenses into clouds at pressures hundreds of times higher than sea level on Earth.

Even the probe NASA is planning for Uranus would likely sample the atmosphere down to about ten times sea-level pressure.

So the team used a stand-in. Carbon monoxide forms in the hot depths, where it stays in balance with water, and rising gas carries it upward faster than chemistry can destroy it.

The amount near the top is therefore a record of how much oxygen there is far below, a method also used on Jupiter.

On Neptune, that carbon monoxide has been known since the 1990s and measured at about 0.2 parts per million.

On Uranus, the ALMA telescope array in Chile only confirmed it in the lower atmosphere in observations from 2022 and 2024.

The team’s own reading of the 2022 data gives about 5.6 parts per billion, roughly 35 times less than Neptune.

Briand’s team extended a model of the deep chemistry so that it changes with latitude, because a fast-spinning planet mixes its atmosphere more vigorously at the equator than near the poles.

They then asked how much oxygen each planet needs down deep to produce the carbon monoxide seen at the top.

For Uranus, the answer came out at roughly 60 to 180 times the Sun’s proportion of oxygen, depending on latitude. For Neptune it was about 220 to 340 times.

Uncertainty in the chemical reaction rates shifted those ranges by about a tenth at most.

Both figures are estimates from a model, and the biggest unknown is how vigorously each atmosphere mixes.

The team wrote that the equator, where mixing is strongest, is probably the best guide to the planet as a whole.

Carbon is easier to estimate. Methane carries most of it, and methane has been measured in the upper atmosphere of both planets.

Divide carbon by oxygen, and Uranus’s ratio runs from 0.06 to 0.52, while Neptune’s runs from 0.02 to 0.12.

At the top of its range, Uranus’s ratio is close to the Sun’s. Neptune’s falls well below the Sun’s at every latitude.

The two ranges overlap between 0.06 and 0.12, so the team can’t rule out that both planets share one value.

Uranus and Neptune probably never grew into gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn, the authors wrote.

So the heavy elements each planet is made of came mostly from icy pebbles rather than from gas. That makes the ice’s carbon-to-oxygen ratio the number to match.

Mousis’s disk model follows gas and ice through the first million years of the solar system.

As the disk cooled, each compound froze at its own distance from the young Sun: carbon dioxide first, then methane, then carbon monoxide farthest out.

Where each one froze set how much carbon the local ice carried compared with water.

Both planets now orbit at about 20 to 30 times Earth’s distance from the Sun, and in the model the ice out there has close to the Sun’s carbon-to-oxygen ratio. That fits Uranus. It doesn’t fit Neptune.

Neptune’s low ratio does fit ice that formed much closer in, near the distance where water froze but carbon stayed as gas.

The authors suggest Neptune grew there and migrated outward.

“Neptune’s chemistry is difficult to reconcile with the idea that it formed where we see it today, pulling from the same reservoir of cosmic materials as Uranus,” Mousis said.

The disk model carries assumptions of its own, including how carbon was split among its molecules at the start and how turbulent the disk was. Either one moves the freezing lines. It also assumes that nothing after formation changed the planets’ carbon relative to oxygen.

The result depends on the equator being the right guide, too. If Uranus mixes less than Neptune, its ratio drops toward the shared range, and the two planets could have formed from similar material after all.

Further atmospheric measurements could help narrow the possibilities. Briand’s team wrote that its latitude maps could help choose where a Uranus probe should enter the atmosphere.

NASA’s Uranus Orbiter and Probe is a mission concept that the 2023 to 2032 planetary science decadal survey ranked as a high priority.

Mousis said it is expected to launch sometime in the next decade. Even then, estimating the oxygen hidden far below the clouds would still require models.

The full study was published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

#6328. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#6327. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

#6326. Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by turning into giants

Cancer cells that survive chemo swell into giant senescent cells that summon immune repair, and drugs that block their IAP proteins kill them.

Chemotherapy can kill a cancer cell, but some survivors enter an unusual state. After a near-lethal dose, they stop dividing and swell to many times their normal size.

Then they start pumping out the chemical signals a wound uses to call in the immune system’s repair crew. These surviving cells may help tumors return.

A team in Dublin has identified a mechanism that keeps them alive after the damage, along with experimental drugs that kill them in laboratory tests.

Seamus Martin, the Smurfit Professor of Medical Genetics at Trinity College Dublin, led the work from his lab with postdoctoral fellow Gokhan Gunay at the university’s Smurfit Institute of Genetics.

Collaborators at the University of Cologne and the Olivia Newton-John Cancer Research Institute in Melbourne took part.

Nearly all of it was done in human cancer cells grown in the lab, with some experiments in mice, and none of it involved patients.

In an interview with Earth.com, Martin was asked what surprised him most. He pointed to the cells themselves.

“These are really bizarre-looking cells,” he said.

“They are truly gigantic when compared with normal cells (approx. 10X normal size) and this is highly unusual behavior for cells, even cancer cells.”

The team gave cervical, bowel and lung cancer cells a three-hour pulse of cisplatin or etoposide, two common chemotherapy drugs that work by damaging DNA.

The dose killed about 40% of the cells within two days. The rest stopped dividing and were still alive a week later, flattened and enormous.

Biologists call this state senescence, and cells in it are often nicknamed zombie cells. They stop dividing but remain alive, secreting a stream of inflammatory proteins.

In a tumor, those signals can attract immune cells that promote new blood vessel growth and help create conditions that support tumor growth.

Martin’s lab studies the machinery that makes cells self-destruct, and the team wanted to know why these cells hadn’t.

The chemotherapy had switched on the cells’ own self-destruct receptors.

Two of them, known as Fas and DR5, rose sharply on the surface of the damaged cells, in every cell type tested and in mouse tumors treated with cisplatin.

Inside the cells, those receptors had assembled the protein complex that normally triggers death. It was fully assembled, and something was holding it back.

One of the restraints turned out to be a family of proteins called inhibitors of apoptosis, or IAPs. The senescent cells were making more of one of them than untreated cells do.

“IAPs act as the antidote to the killing effects of Death Receptors that enable the senescent cells to survive,” Martin told Earth.com.

“However, this now leaves the senescent cells in a state of addiction to the IAPs for their continued survival, which now makes them extremely vulnerable to IAP antagonists.”

Drugs that destroy IAPs already exist, and several have entered clinical trials. The team tested two of them, BV6 and birinapant, which wiped out the IAP proteins inside cells within eight hours.

Given alongside chemotherapy, the drugs killed more cancer cells outright and left far fewer survivors to enter the zombie state.

Given afterward, to cells that had already turned senescent, they killed those cells at doses that did little to normal cells.

Cells engineered to lack the self-destruct receptors, or the enzyme they activate, were largely protected from the drugs, which is how the team knew the receptors were doing the killing.

A widely studied senolytic drug, navitoclax, kills senescent cells by a different route, and it worked just as well without those receptors.

The team also went the other way. Mice bred without caspase-8, the enzyme the receptors activate, built up senescent cells in the lining of the small intestine and showed more inflammatory signaling in the liver.

In cells, deleting the same enzyme let more survivors enter senescence and kept them alive longer.

Old mice told a similar story. In lung, kidney and heart tissue from 24-month-old animals, the two death receptors were higher than in three-month-olds.

There was one living test of the drugs. Mice with an inherited retinal disease, which produces leaky new blood vessels and senescent cells in the retina, got injections of BV6 into the eye.

Their lesions shrank, and the count of senescent cells in the retina fell.

Professor Martin described the strategy as a one-two punch.

The first punch is a standard DNA-damaging drug such as cisplatin, and the second, delivered days later, is a drug that kills the senescent cells the first punch created.

In the paper, the team suggested giving an IAP-blocking drug 5 to 7 days after each round of chemotherapy.

Given ahead of chemotherapy instead, it would push more cells toward death in the first place.

The timing is the hard part, Martin noted. The second punch has to land while the tumor is vulnerable, and he said several trials of IAP-blocking drugs have been run or are under way.

The one-two punch has not been tested against a tumor in an animal in this study.

The chemotherapy-plus-drug experiments were in dishes, and the tumor experiments in mice measured the receptors rather than survival.

The one animal test of the drugs’ zombie-killing power was in a diseased eye, not a cancer.

Whether a human tumor’s survivors depend on IAPs the way these lab cells did is the open question.

Answering it means the trial the team proposes: chemotherapy paired with an IAP-blocking drug, timed to the days when the giant cells appear.

Martin said getting that timing right may decide whether the second punch connects.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6325. A NASA Veteran Claims to Have Used Mind-Bending Physics to Conquer Gravity

Charles Buhler’s claim could change how spacecraft fly. But experiments show how much work it takes to establish that a mysterious push is real.

In April 2024, Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist who helped establish a laboratory at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, made a remarkable claim. His company, Exodus Propulsion Technologies, had built a device that could produce thrust without expelling propellant. He attributed the push to what he called a “New Force.”

As we reported in our earlier coverage, Buhler’s claim would have big consequences for spaceflight. That promise depends on whether researchers outside Exodus can reproduce the push and rule out an ordinary explanation.

One physicist has spent years investigating similar claims. Martin Tajmar, a professor and chair of space systems at Dresden University of Technology in Germany, has spent two decades measuring the forces produced by charged capacitors, including lopsided ones like the designs Buhler describes.

“It’s all negative,” he tells Popular Mechanics. Meaning, his tests found no evidence of that force within the limits of his equipment. He hasn’t tested Exodus’s hardware, but his experiments show what an independent test would need to account for.

A capacitor stores electric charge. Apply a high enough voltage to certain designs, and they can set the surrounding air moving, producing a push on the device itself. Tajmar calls this corona wind, “a discharge in air that drags air molecules with it.” In those cases, the device moves by pushing air backward, much as a fan does.

Tajmar’s team wanted to see whether a capacitor would still produce a push with almost all the air removed. For their 2024 study in Scientific Reports, they put the capacitor and its battery-powered electrical equipment together on a sensitive balance inside a vacuum chamber. At 10,000 volts, an asymmetric capacitor produced no clear sign of an unexplained force, even with instruments sensitive enough to detect a push measured in billionths of a newton.

Exodus hasn’t sent Tajmar a device, so he built his own capacitors for those experiments. He says his asymmetric design follows the principles in the company’s patent, though he doesn’t know the exact dimensions of its hardware.

“It’s Exodus who have to say why my asymmetric capacitor does not produce any thrust,” he says.

He believes his results challenge the company’s explanation, but he’d need its hardware to put its particular device through the same checks.

Keeping the battery and high-voltage equipment on the balance removes outside power cables that could interfere with the reading. Researchers also have to watch for electromagnetic forces or parts shifting as they heat up, either of which could look like thrust.

Tajmar also recommends swapping the device for an electrical dummy that draws power but should produce no thrust. If the balance still registers a push, something else in the setup is causing it. Researchers would need to track that down before treating the reading as evidence of a working drive.

Buhler has also said the devices can keep producing thrust after the power is switched off. Electrical charge can linger in insulating materials, leaving an electric field even after the supply is disconnected. Researchers would need to work out whether that leftover charge explains the reading and, if there really is a push, where it comes from.

In a short white paper, Exodus says other experimenters have reproduced the effect and argues that the device pushes against the vacuum itself, allowing momentum to be conserved. But it doesn’t include their laboratory reports. Without those details, readers can’t tell how the experiments were done or whether the researchers ruled out other causes of the push.

What leaving the propellant behind could change

Spacecraft have to bring along the propellant they’ll use to speed up, slow down or change course. That adds weight, which takes more propellant to move. The rocket equation puts numbers to that trade-off, showing how much a spacecraft can change its speed with the supply it carries.

If a drive could produce useful thrust without using up propellant, engineers could plan missions differently. A spacecraft could keep changing course as long as it had enough power and the drive kept working. Some of the weight now devoted to propellant tanks and their contents could go toward other equipment.

But the drive would bring its own baggage. It would need a power source and a way to get rid of waste heat, and all of that would have to travel with it. Engineers would need to find out whether the thrust was worth the weight of the complete system. Getting a reliable push in the lab would give them a reason to start working that out.

Light can give a spacecraft a push, too. When a laser sends light in one direction, the laser gets a tiny push in the other, because light carries momentum. Tajmar points out that this already offers a way to produce thrust without using up material propellant.

“If you just power a laser with the power that we use in our experiments, the thrust is also propellantless and actually already exists,” he says.

The catch is how much power it takes. To hold up a 1.2-ounce object, roughly the weight of the devices Buhler described, a laser would need to send about 100 million watts of light downward. A drive that produced a useful push with much less power would be worth engineers’ attention. Researchers would also have to explain what carries momentum in the opposite direction, as the light does for a laser.

“You have to test it in an independent laboratory. And then with a different method,” Tajmar says. He wants the results published so other experts can examine the work, including the equipment itself. Getting the same push on a different instrument would help show that the device deserves the credit.

Nobody needs to make the whole apparatus float. Even a small sideways push would warrant attention if it survived those checks and other researchers could reliably reproduce it. Then engineers could start asking whether it was strong enough to put to work aboard a spacecraft.

Buhler’s claim promises freedom from the propellant tank, which would change how we travel through space. The next move is closer to home. Put the drive in another lab, let someone else take the controls, and see whether the promise still has any push behind it.

#6324. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 12: An open cluster in Perseus

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

The constellation Perseus is famous for its bright Double Cluster, but these two open clusters aren’t the only groups of young stars in the Hero worth viewing. Today, let’s shift our gaze to the western portion of this constellation, near its border with Andromeda, to check out M34, a mid-5th-magnitude open cluster containing about 100 stars.

Sitting 5.2° west-northwest of 2nd-magnitude Algol (Beta [β] Persei), M34 spans about half a degree, roughly the size of the Full Moon. In physical space, astronomers believe the group spans about 14 light-years and sits 1,400 light-years away. It’s best seen under lower magnifications, such as in binoculars or small amateur scopes (4 inches or so). You’ll spot several dozen stars brighter than 12th magnitude, with its brightest suns spread throughout the cluster.

#6323. Tourists carved their names in a Spanish cave for 60 years before someone noticed 280 Ice Age drawings hiding on the walls

A Catalan cave open since 1957 holds 280 engravings, 55 of them animals, probably from the Ice Age and found among modern graffiti in 2019.

On Oct. 30, 2019, during the first excavation campaign of a new project, one of the study’s authors, visiting the Cova de la Font Major in Catalonia, noticed what looked like Ice Age engravings among the modern graffiti on a passage wall.

The find was a surprise to the team. The cave had been open since January 1957, and that passage had been part of a tourist route since 1993.

Researchers have now counted 280 motifs there, including 55 animal figures. The authors attribute them to the Ice Age, but no engraving has been dated directly, so that age rests on archaeological context and drawing style.

The cave lies under the village of L’Espluga de Francolí, in the Conca de Barberà district of Tarragona province. It belongs to a limestone system with 11,780 feet (3,590 meters) of mapped galleries, where the Francolí River rises.

Its entrance probably collapsed in Roman times. In 1853 people got in through the Pou del Palletes, a private well in the courtyard of a town house, and members of the Centre Excursionista Pirinenc surveyed the cave in 1956.

The town council cleared the blocked entrance in January 1957, using machinery and no archaeological supervision. Those works destroyed a large part of the deposit at the entrance. A hoard of bronze objects then drew visitors, cavers and treasure hunters.

In 1993 the cave became a museum, and the passage known as the Gatoneres de Cal Palletes joined a tourist circuit called the Adventure Route.

The Coves de l’Espluga website now lists that route as a caving-style visit along the underground river, running from April or May 2027.

For more than six decades, thousands of people walked past the engraved panels, and some cut names and dates over them.

They did so “without the Palaeolithic origin of the figures being recognised,” wrote Josep Maria Vergès Bosch and Míriam Salas-Altès, of the IPHES-CERCA institute in Tarragona and Rovira i Virgili University.

The engravings sit about 820 feet (250 meters) from the entrance, in an enclosed space next to the underground river. Three narrow passages connect these small galleries to the main gallery.

Ceilings there run from under 3 feet (1 meter) to about 10 feet (3 meters). The galleries average about 6.5 feet (2 meters) across.

Most of the cave’s walls are conglomerate, a lumpy rock generally considered a poor surface for prehistoric art. The engravers worked only on layers of marl, a soft limy mudstone, set between the conglomerate beds.

Any reasonably hard tool could cut a line in that marl. High-resolution 3D models show that most grooves measure 0.1 to 0.3 inches (3 to 7 millimeters) wide and are shallow. About 80 percent of the figures run 6 to 18 inches (150 to 450 millimeters) long.

The same softness left the panels exposed to fingers, modern graffiti and accidental knocks. Every sector except the last stretch of sector 5 shows that damage, and the authors suspect the original total was higher than 280.

Ramon Viñas helped the two authors prospect and record the walls, with logistical support from the cave’s guides and the L’Espluga tourism office. Most of what they logged is not figurative, mainly parallel lines in groups of two, three or four, and sets of 15 to 40 strokes.

Sector 5 has 33 of the 55 animals. The list includes horses, caprines, female deer, bovids and one bear, with its ears drawn from the front and its mouth slightly open.

The authors could not name a species group for 30 percent of the animals, and they list another 15 percent as one of two options, such as caprine or deer. Eyes, nostrils and hooves are mostly missing from the outlines, and a few bellies look pregnant.

A horse in sector 5 has its feet on the boundary between conglomerate and marl. In sector 3, a deer’s muzzle touches a horizontal fissure, and the paper proposes it as ground or water, while saying that intent cannot be demonstrated.

Panel 2 of sector 2 holds hundreds of loop-shaped marks that have no clear parallels at other Paleolithic sites. An inscription dated 1199 sits on top of them, and a piece of charcoal from one groove gave a date no later than the 17th century, so the authors leave their origin open.

Radiocarbon dates from the inner galleries fall into two groups. One spans roughly 41,000 to 26,000 years ago, and the other runs from the eighth to the second century BCE.

Most of the older dates come from charcoal found near the Sala del Llac and downstream, with an apparent gap from 35,400 to 26,300 years ago.

A layer dated to about 26,000 years ago in the Galeria del Pessebre also yielded a flint backed bladelet. None of this charcoal comes from the engravings, so the dates show that people were in the galleries, not when the walls were cut.

The later group belongs to an Iron Age sanctuary in the Sala del Llac, where people left hundreds of ceramic vessels, metal objects, goat or sheep limbs and grain. One vessel held wine residue.

The drawings give a second clue. Hind legs shaped like a double Y and heads made of three lines also turn up at Mediterranean sites of the pre-Magdalenian phases, about 43,000 to 19,000 years ago.

Recent digs at sites such as Cova Foradada have also filled in the early Upper Paleolithic of southern Catalonia, a territory once treated as marginal for that period.

Until this find, only two wall images from the Upper Paleolithic were known in all of Catalonia. A black bovid at Cova del Tendo was stolen shortly after its discovery and survives in photographs and a tracing, while a possible deer at Cova de la Taverna has an uncertain human origin.

About 75 percent of known sites along Iberia’s Mediterranean side hold five animal figures or fewer, and more than 90 percent hold no more than 20. With 55, Font Major ranks third on that coast, behind Ardales and La Pileta in the far south.

The find sent researchers to check other caves, and a survey at Cova Simanya also turned up Paleolithic marks. Elsewhere in Spain, the cave of Cova Dones has yielded at least 120 Latin inscriptions in a single chamber.

The authors concluded that “no cave should be dismissed a priori,” whatever the quality of its walls or the number of its visitors.

At least one animal lies under a calcite crust that could allow uranium-series dating, which the team plans for a later stage.

Similar crusts were used to argue that Neanderthals made paintings in three Spanish caves more than 64,000 years ago, a reading other specialists rejected, and a natural varnish on the horse paintings at Chauvet Cave was recently detected under ultraviolet light.

The authors caution that one date would not fix the age of the whole collection. They also say it is too early to rule out engravings from the Magdalenian or later periods, and a full study of the panels is under way.

More than 62 years passed between the day the town council cleared the entrance and the day a member of the research team stopped at those walls.

The full study was published in the journal Antiquity.
