Mitochondria can become compromised in a number of medical conditions. What if they could be replaced like batteries?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newborn baby's heart is roughly the size of a walnut — which makes open-heart surgery challenging.

Each year, about 10,000 babies in the United States are born with critical heart defects that may require surgery to fix, often fairly soon after birth. In these infants, the two major arteries of the heart could have swapped positions or the left side of the heart may be far too small to pump properly.

Even if their surgeries go well, these babies face perilous recoveries. A complication can arise when blood flows back into the repaired heart, triggering what's known as an ischemia-reperfusion injury. This can stun the organ, triggering extensive damage that requires doctors to place the baby on a life-support machine that pumps and infuses oxygen into blood to sub in for the hampered heart and lungs. Only about 40% of newborns make it off the machine, because often, their tiny hearts don't recover.

Doctors and scientists at Boston Children's Hospital have been working to improve those odds using a creative idea: replacing the fuel source in damaged heart cells to help them bounce back from injury. That fuel source is mitochondria, the "batteries" found in most cells in the body. In this case, the mitochondria are isolated from an abdominal muscle and then injected directly into the heart.

As of April, 17 babies have undergone this procedure, and 80% made it off ECMO. It's too soon to say if the treatment improves overall survival rates, but the early data hints that it might. A clinical trial is currently underway.

James McCully (left) and his colleague Dr. Sitaram Emani of Boston Children's Hospital have developed a technique to transplant mitochondria into the hearts of children recovering from surgery.

"The first one or two for me were pretty nerve-wracking," said James McCully, a research associate at Boston Children's Hospital and associate professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School whose pioneering work paved the way for these procedures. His team isolates and purifies the mitochondria that a surgical team then transplants into patients.

"But you know, the heart comes back — you can actually almost see it coming back" in real time, he told Live Science. A heart deprived of energy looks pallid, while a freshly rejuvenated heart blushes a healthy pink.

Baby heart infusions are just one example of the promise of "mitochondrial transplantation." Following McCully's lead, other scientists have started investigating whether infusions of mitochondria could revitalize donated organs destined for transplantation, help stroke patients recover, and treat kids with devastating diseases. This work is still highly experimental, and its route to regulatory approval remains unclear.

But at its core is a straightforward idea: When a battery dies, you replace it.

The human body contains tens of trillions of cells, most of which contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria. Following some back-of-the-envelope math, that means the total potential energy in each person "is the equivalent of a lightning bolt," Douglas Wallace, director of the Center for Mitochondrial and Epigenomic Medicine at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told attendees last year at a symposium on mitochondrial medicine.

Mitochondria, in a word, are powerful. They produce most of the chemical energy used by complex cells by churning out a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The idea of transferring these fuel factories from one cell to another as a medical treatment emerged less than two decades ago — but cells have been doing such swaps on their own for eons.

A leading theory posits that mitochondria evolved from simple microbes. And today, they still retain distinctly microbial features.

Dr. Jon Brestoff, an associate professor of pathology and immunology and director of the Immunometabolism Initiative at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, describes this ability to move from cell to cell as a relic of mitochondria's bacterial past. "It is hypothesized that mitochondria transfer has likely been retained throughout evolution of eukaryotic life," the huge domain of life that includes all plants, fungi, protists and animals, Brestoff told Live Science.

Mitochondria are the powerhouses of nearly all complex cells on Earth, and there are a few theories as to how they adopted that ubiquitous role. A leading idea posits that, some 1.5 billion to 2 billion years ago, one simple cell engulfed another. The bacterial cell that got swallowed carried a circular loop of DNA inside its membrane, and that captured cell later became what we now know as the mitochondrion. The new organelle enabled cells to take advantage of the abundance of oxygen on our planet by converting it into usable fuel.

Mitochondria retained bacteria-like features, such as having their own DNA and membranes. But in 2006, researchers reported that mitochondria can also exit their "host" and survive the journey into a totally different cell — a phenomenon known as mitochondrial transfer.

"That was a complete revolution in thinking," said Dr. Lance Becker, professor and Chair of the Department of Emergency Medicine at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research. "With that notion that mitochondria might be mobile, that they might cross boundaries, that they might go from one cell to another cell, came the possibility that maybe that was something we could use to help people."

The 2006 study showed that cells that had been depleted of their own mitochondrial DNA could obtain healthy mitochondria from neighboring cells. After receiving other cells' powerhouses, the once-depleted cells were able to conduct energetically costly processes, such as cell division.

This research provided the first evidence that one cell can "donate" metabolic properties to its neighbor by sending over a fresh batch of mitochondria. Scientists once thought cells had to make all of their own mitochondria, but now, "I think cells have the ability to 'put their hand up' when they need mitochondria," Becker told Live Science.

Jon Brestoff is studying the use of mitochondrial transplantation for genetic diseases that impair the function of these cellular powerhouses.

Because those first experiments were done in lab dishes, initially, "it was unclear whether or not it was really biologically meaningful or relevant," Brestoff said. But within the past five to six years, improved tools and techniques have enabled scientists to watch mitochondrial transfer unfold within living organisms, he noted. It's been shown that cells of the same type can exchange mitochondria, as can cells of different types.

As scientists' fundamental understanding of mitochondrial transfer grew, the notion of doing the same thing therapeutically gained more traction.

"That procedure," Brestoff said, "is rooted in the biology of mitochondria transfer."

Just two years after the landmark 2006 paper, McCully's research group released data that hinted at the medicinal potential of mitochondrial transplantation.

Since then, these complementary lines of research — the foundational biology and the preclinical investigation — have continued in parallel. McCully's preclinical work helped to inspire other labs to explore the use of mitochondrial transplantation for a range of medical applications, including organ transplants and treatments for stroke and genetic disease.

McCully is "the pioneer — the guru of the field," said Dr. Giuseppe Orlando, a professor of surgery and regenerative medicine at Wake Forest University School of Medicine who is exploring mitochondrial transplantation as a way to maintain the integrity of transplant organs.

McCully's road to mitochondrial transplantation started in the 1980s. As a molecular biologist, he wanted to uncover mechanisms that protect the heart from damage, particularly when the organ's oxygen supply is compromised — such as during ischemia, or low blood flow. With an eye on older adults, he wanted to spare patients' heart tissue from the damage and cell death that can occur before and during heart surgery.

It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going.

McCully and his collaborators initially "didn't care about the mitochondria one iota," he said. They were more focused on the nucleus, the control center that houses most of a cell's DNA, and its influence on cellular pathways that might boost the heart's resilience to ischemia. But "what we found was that everything we did started coming back to the mitochondria," he said.

They found that ischemia triggers damage and dysfunction in mitochondria that persists even after the heart's oxygen supply is restored; this dysfunction ultimately kills cells. The damaged mitochondria swell up, leak their innards, and set off a chain reaction that causes a cell to self-destruct.

McCully and colleagues observed that biological pathways that seemed to reduce this cell death often centered on the mitochondria. "We were looking around at either pathways upstream of the mitochondria or downstream of the mitochondria," he said.

So, logically, they started looking directly at mitochondria, studying what the organelle looks like before, during and after ischemia. One day, while isolating mitochondria from a laboratory pig, the animal developed fibrillation, meaning its heart began beating very quickly, with an uncoordinated and rapid rhythm. The team tried to reset the heart's rhythm with electric shocks and medications, to no avail. But McCully had an idea.

"At that point in time, the heart's kind of [got a] gray pallor, and it looks dead," he said. "And I said, 'Go upstairs; grab some of those mitochondria that we've isolated from the non-ischemic type. Just bring them down.'" They'd previously gathered some healthy mitochondria from the same pig, in hopes of generating a "before-and-after" picture of ischemia. Instead, McCully suspended those healthy mitochondria in a solution and then injected them directly into the pig's fibrillating heart.

"And the heart came back — started beating normally. It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going," he said.

Surgeons sample a small piece of muscle from the patient. That muscle will serve as the source of healthy mitochondria.

After mitochondria have been isolated from the muscle sample, they are prepared in a syringe and injected into the heart tissue.

That serendipitous experiment led to a formal test of the technique in rabbit hearts, the results of which were published in 2008. In the study, they introduced healthy mitochondria to the rabbits' hearts during ischemia, just before reperfusion — when blood is reintroduced into the oxygen-starved tissue. They found that the mitochondria improved the organs' recovery and reduced tissue death. Further research in animals suggested that mitochondria that originated from one type of tissue, like liver tissue or skeletal muscle, could be introduced to other tissue types, such as cardiac muscle.

After seeing McCully's results in various animal experiments, including more with pigs, Dr. Pedro del Nido, chair of cardiac surgery at Boston Children's and a professor of child surgery at Harvard Medical School, approached him about testing the technique in human patients — namely, in babies on a life-support machine known as ECMO.

"He saw it in the animals; he saw what was going on," McCully said. "And he deemed it as being a possible intervention to save these kids."

They sought permission from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to test the procedure and cleared the required regulatory hurdles. The process was made slightly easier because the mitochondria were coming from the patients' own bodies, not from a donor, McCully noted. Once given the go-ahead, they set forth with the help of Dr. Sitaram Emani, a heart surgeon at Boston Children's. The first procedure took place in 2014.

During each procedure, Emani and the surgical team collect a small sample of skeletal muscle from the patient, and McCully then isolates whole mitochondria from the tissue and prepares them in a syringe. He refined the isolation technique so the time from collecting the muscle sample to injecting mitochondria is only 30 minutes. Lately, the team has been developing a technique they can perform in the operating room, rather than in a lab, which could cut the time to 20 minutes. Emani uses various tests, including echocardiography, to see which areas of the heart tissue move the least, and injects mitochondria straight into those areas.

"It's great to be able to see something you've done and worked on for so many years actually provide a benefit," McCully said.

Dr. Giuseppe Orlando thinks that mitochondrial transplantation could serve as a potential method for fortifying donated organs that are intended for transplant patients.

While McCully is trying to protect infant hearts, other scientists want to do the same for other organs — including those destined for transplant surgeries.

To Orlando, mitochondria represent a potential way to make donated kidneys work better. "In transplant medicine, one of the major issues is making sure that the organs that are procured are well stored and kept viable until implantation," said Orlando, who is also president of the Cell Transplant and Regenerative Medicine Society.

Maintaining an organ's viability means preserving mitochondrial function as much as possible, but the transplantation process is tough on the organelles. "That energy plant is damaged. So it's pretty obvious that you should start thinking about a way to replace the damaged mitochondria," Orlando said.

Donated organs suffer some damage when they're unplugged from the donors' bloodstream, in part because this cuts off mitochondria's crucial oxygen supply. And then, paradoxically, the donor organs also get damaged when they're plugged into the recipient's bloodstream. That's because the fast flow of blood triggers the production of free radicals — unstable molecules that damage tissues.

While healthy organs normally produce some free radicals, reperfusion unleashes a flood. "It's more than the organ can bear and sustain," Orlando explained. This damage contributes to a phenomenon called delayed graft function, in which a transplanted kidney doesn't work right away so the patient ends up needing dialysis in the first week after surgery.

"You want to make sure that the kidney wakes up faster," Orlando said. That's where mitochondria come in.

Orlando was introduced to the idea of mitochondrial transplantation around 2019 through a collaboration with Dr. Benedetta Bussolati, a nephrologist and full professor of laboratory medicine at the University of Turin in Italy. Her lab had been studying mitochondrial transplantation in isolated kidney cells in lab experiments, and they reached out to Orlando about extending that work to lab animals.

In pigs, the researchers ran experiments in which the animals' kidneys were collected and stored in the same way human kidneys commonly would be prior to being transplanted. One set of kidneys received a placebo treatment, while another got an infusion of mitochondria from the donor pigs' muscle tissue. Upon being reperfused, the treated kidneys produced fewer free radicals and accrued less damage than the untreated kidneys did, the team reported in 2023.

They backed up this finding by analyzing RNA, a molecule that reflects which genes are active in cells. Compared with the untreated kidneys, the treated kidneys showed greater activity in genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and lower activity in genes involved in repairing injuries.

Orlando thinks that mitochondrial transplanations could help organs "wake up" faster after being transferred from an organ donor to a recipient.

Some groups are exploring mitochondrial transplantation in other donor organs, like the lungs — specifically, lungs treated with "ex vivo perfusion" (EVP), an emerging approach that helps retain the viability of transplant organs. Rather than placing a donor organ in a cooler of ice, as is generally standard, EVP flushes an organ with nutrient- and oxygen-rich fluid, helping to maintain its function until the transplant surgery. In lab experiments with pig and human lungs, scientists found that introducing fresh mitochondria during EVP further improved the organs' function while reducing inflammation and free radicals.

Across different organ transplants, Orlando sees mitochondria as a potential means to improve patient outcomes and expand the pool of available organs. There are scenarios in which would-be organ donors die unexpectedly of cardiac arrest and their organs are damaged in the process; mitochondrial transplants may help make such organs fit for patients, Orlando has said.

In the near term, Orlando and his colleagues are continuing to study the basic science of mitochondrial transplantation for this clinical purpose; they've also been cleared to run a clinical trial with donor kidneys but need more funds to proceed.

Looking to the more distant future, he and other experts in the field envision a world where transplant organs can be bioengineered and stored in banks, ready and waiting for the patients who need them, Orlando said. If that vision materializes, he suggested, mitochondrial transplants might be useful for preparing banked organs for transplantation "by giving them kind of an energy boost."

If infusions of fresh mitochondria could help the heart, kidney and lungs, what about the brain? That's the question Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues at the University of Washington School of Medicine (UW Medicine) want to answer.

Walker, a clinical professor of neurological surgery, treats patients who have had ischemic strokes, which are caused by blood clots blocking blood flow to the brain. The immediate aim of post-stroke treatment is to clear out the blocked "pipe" and restore circulation to the brain as quickly as possible, she said. But no matter how quickly this is done, some brain cells are damaged. And once the blood clot is removed, the brain may then suffer a reperfusion injury.

Standard treatments can dissolve the clot but don't protect the brain, Walker said. "What about all those cells that are maybe not quite dead — they're on the verge of maybe dying? What can we do to support those guys?" she asked.

The UW Medicine team had heard about McCully's work in Boston and wondered if something similar could be applied in stroke patients. But while heart surgery exposes the tissue in need of new mitochondria, accessing the brain is trickier. "You don't do a craniotomy to give an IV medicine," Walker told Live Science.

But Walker realized that a harmful downstream effect of stroke might provide an opportunity for treatment. Immediately after a stroke, the brain's protective shield — known as the blood-brain barrier — becomes more permeable than usual, allowing more substances to pass from the bloodstream into brain tissue. That might open a door for mitochondrial transplantation.

One method of treating ischemic strokes is to physically remove the clot using a procedure called a thrombectomy, which a surgeon is preparing for in the photo above. Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues tried combining this approach with mitochondrial transplantation.

A 2023 mouse study spearheaded by University of Virginia researchers and co-authored by Walker backed this idea, finding that mitochondria entered the brain after stroke and integrated into brain cells. These mitochondria had been gathered from muscle tissue, as in McCully's studies, and introduced to the brain via an artery. The treatment increased ATP production while reducing cell death caused by the stroke, compared with untreated mice's brains.

This work paved the way to the first trial using mitochondrial transplant in the human brain. The small safety trial included adult patients who'd had ischemic strokes and underwent thrombectomies ‪—‬ surgeries to remove the clots from their blood vessels. Four received mitochondrial transplants during their procedures and 12 did not. Mitochondria were injected near the site of each patient's stroke, into the closest branch of one of the brain's major arteries.

No negative side effects were tied to the transplants, hinting that the procedure is safe in humans. "But the next question is, how do we understand if it helps? And those are harder trials to design," Walker said. That's partly because the transplants are tacked onto the clot-removal procedure, so it's difficult to separate their effects from those of the clot removal itself, she noted.

Future trials will also need to explore exactly where the transplanted mitochondria end up in the human brain, how well they function once inside brain cells, and how the dose and timing of the transplant affect patients' outcomes, the trial runners wrote in their report. For the moment, Walker said her team is focused on exploring the safety aspects of the approach and have no further trials planned at this time.

Beyond heart defects, transplant organs and stroke, researchers are looking to mitochondrial transplantation as a solution for genetic conditions that harm mitochondria directly. Brestoff and colleagues are investigating the therapy's potential for treating Leigh syndrome, a rare neurological condition caused by genetic mutations that disrupt the fuel-producing machinery in mitochondria.

"Those kids have a terrible prognosis," Brestoff said. Most children with the most common form of the syndrome, whose symptoms show up by age 2, die by age 3. There is no cure for the syndrome, and treatments to relieve its symptoms are limited. So if it works, mitochondrial transplantation could fill a big gap.

So far, the approach shows promise in lab mice with a severe form of Leigh syndrome, improving the rodents' function and extending their median lifespan by 19% to 24%, the researchers demonstrated in 2024. They're now studying the approach in cells derived from patients with the disease.

I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter.

Some companies, such as Israel-headquartered Minovia Therapeutics, are already running clinical trials with patients with other types of mitochondrial disease. Minovia is running one with children with Pearson syndrome, in which missing mitochondrial DNA hinders the function of bone marrow, which normally makes blood and immune cells.

While patients with a heart or brain problem may be able to pluck mitochondria from healthy muscles, people with mitochondrial disease don't necessarily have healthy mitochondria to spare. Especially for these patients, getting mitochondria from other people ‪—‬ known as heterologous transplantation ‪—‬ likely makes the most sense. What's more, for transplantation to be used widely for any purpose, there would need to be an "off-the-shelf" mitochondrial product available, Brestoff said.

Such a product could eliminate the step in Boston Children's heart procedure where mitochondria have to be isolated from a patient while they're waiting, open on an operating table. "Getting them from the recipient can sometimes be problematic, because the recipients are sick. All the organs, all the tissue is quite distressed," McCully noted. A standardized and safety-tested mitochondrial product would therefore be a boon for the field.

Brestoff is on the scientific advisory board of LUCA Science, a company developing mitochondria as therapeutic agents, and a consultant for Cellergy Therapeutics, which is making mitochondrial products to combat conditions from muscle degeneration and aging. These companies exemplify the effort to come up with ready-made products that could someday bring the therapy to more patients.

A shift to heterologous transplantation does raise concerns about immune reactions. "You have some variations in the proteins that are present in your mitochondria that I don't have," Brestoff noted. "So it is possible that our immune systems recognize heterologous mitochondria as non-self."

But McCully doesn't expect immune reactions to be a big problem, based on his research in animals. "I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter," he said. Early trial results from Minovia and others suggest heterologous transplantations come with minimal side effects, at least at doses tested so far.

Another roadblock is that the FDA has not approved any organelles as therapies yet, so the standards and regulatory framework for the field are still being established, Brestoff said.

Despite that hurdle, the field has advanced significantly since its start as a niche, theoretical interest and then a highly experimental procedure for the sickest newborns. Scientists are now exploring the treatment as a solution to many common conditions, from rheumatoid arthritis to chronic pain.

Becker compared the state of the field to the early days of organ transplantation.

"It just turned out that it was revolutionary, when all of a sudden you could just give a person a kidney transplant," he said. "I think it's going to be kind of similar with mitochondria."

#6320. Nov. 12, 2014: The Philae lander touches down on a comet

The European Space Agency’s Rosetta mission launched March 2, 2004, on a 4-billion-mile (6.4 billion kilometers) path to Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. The mission consisted of the Rosetta orbiter and the Philae lander, both designed for in-depth study of the comet. The spacecraft arrived at 67P/C-G on Aug. 6, 2014, and began orbiting the body a month later; on Nov. 12, 2014, the Philae lander descended to the comet surface. Both the spacecraft orbiting a comet and the landing on the comet’s surface were firsts in space exploration history.

Unfortunately, there were some complications with the landing: The harpoon system that was designed to hold the lander in place didn’t work, causing Philae to bounce and to float and drift above the surface. When it finally came to rest, it was in a shadowy location now known as Abydos, limiting to the sunlight its solar panels received.

Despite these challenges, Philae was able to operate for three days on battery power, and still sent back photos and data about the composition of the comet’s dust and its analysis of the body’s magnetism. (In short, the comet didn’t have a magnetic field.) Additionally, the orbiter transmitted data about water and oxygen in the tail that led to new understanding of such comets’ makeup.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6319. A twisted pattern inside the club of a mantis shrimp stops the animal from breaking its own arm when it punches

Scientists found that mantis shrimp arms have a corkscrew pattern that filters out dangerous vibrations, shielding their bodies from the massive force of their own punches.

Every time a peacock mantis shrimp strikes a shell with its club, the shell gets hit twice. The club hits first. Then bubbles in the water collapse and release shock waves, and those shock waves also travel through the club.

Lab tests suggest the club has a built-in filter for that second blow. Deep inside the club, twisted layers of fibers block some of the fast vibrations in those shock waves. If so, toughness isn’t the club’s only protection.

Horacio D. Espinosa led the study. He’s a mechanical engineering professor at Northwestern’s McCormick School of Engineering. His partner on the project was Maroun Abi Ghanem of the Institute of Light and Matter.

The team tested clubs cut open in the lab, not live animals. To estimate what the twisted layers do during a real strike, the team used a simplified computer model.

The peacock mantis shrimp lives on the seabed of the Indo-Pacific and measures about 1 to 7 inches (3 to 18 centimeters) long. It’s one of the smashers, the mantis shrimp that hit their prey with a club.

A strike can reach a peak force of roughly 340 pounds (1,500 newtons). That’s more than 1,000 times the animal’s body weight. Such a strike “can break mollusk shells and even crack aquarium glass,” Espinosa said.

A strike is mostly preparation. For about a third of a second, muscles tighten to store energy. Then a latch releases that energy.

The club touches the shell for less than 50 millionths of a second.

The strike also creates bubbles in the water. When those bubbles collapse, they release their energy in tens of billionths of a second, as shock waves.

At its peak, the blow from the bubbles has about half the force of the club’s hit. But its vibrations are much faster: millions per second, and possibly as many as a billion. That rate, vibrations per second, is called frequency.

Bending or squeezing a material very quickly can be as damaging as pushing on it very hard, or more damaging, the authors wrote.

Espinosa said most earlier research focused on how tough the club is and how it resists cracking.

The club’s outer layer is a thin, hard mineral coating. Under that coating, fibers hardened with mineral are arranged in a zigzag pattern called herringbone. That pattern stops cracks or turns them aside.

The third layer lies deeper inside, and it’s the one this study focused on. There, bundles of fibers are stacked in sheets. Each sheet is turned 2 to 6 degrees from the one beneath it, like the steps of a spiral staircase.

After enough sheets, the fibers point the same way they did at the start, and the pattern repeats. Near the striking surface, one repeat of the pattern is about 0.003 inches (80 micrometers) thick.

Deeper in, the repeats get thinner. The thinnest are about 0.0004 inches (10 micrometers), an eighth as thick as the thickest.

The twisted layout was already known to add toughness. A 2015 study proposed that it also filters certain stress waves, the vibrations that travel through a solid after a blow.

Experiments hadn’t yet confirmed that idea, the authors wrote.

The team cut open the mantis shrimps’ clubs and coated each cut surface with a layer of aluminum.

Then the team crossed two laser pulses on the metal. Each pulse lasted less than a billionth of a second. The metal heated up and expanded, which sent waves along the club’s surface. Another laser tracked those waves.

The lasers don’t damage the sample. The team could also aim them at one layer at a time.

In the herringbone layer, every wave the team tried, long or short, moved at the same speed, about 5,300 miles per hour (2,380 meters per second).

The twisted layer was different. Waves there behaved the way they do in an engineered material made of repeating units.

The measurements showed gaps: bands of frequencies where waves are blocked or strongly weakened. The gaps were in the tens of millions of vibrations per second.

Experimental evidence of structures like this in living things is still rare, the authors wrote. They cited one example from moth wings.

In certain moths, the wing scales absorb sound at 20,000 to 160,000 vibrations per second. That helps hide those moths from bats that hunt by echolocation.

The club’s filter works at much higher frequencies, in the millions of vibrations per second. The authors wrote that building a structure this precise would normally take advanced manufacturing at microscopic scales.

To mimic the blow from the bubbles, the team sent a pulse through a computer model of the twisted layer. The pulse was centered at 10 million vibrations per second.

The team tried two kinds of wave. A pressure wave squeezes and stretches material along its path. A shear wave shakes it from side to side.

By the team’s calculation, 100% of the pressure wave’s energy passed through. The shear wave lost energy.

With repeats of one thickness, the modeled layer let 66% of the shear energy through. With repeats that get thinner, like the club’s, it let through 43%. That’s less than half.

Each thickness blocks its own band of frequencies, so a range of thicknesses blocks a wider band.

High-frequency shear waves are particularly harmful to soft tissue, the authors wrote. They cited studies of blows that body armor stopped. In those studies, shear waves were major contributors to tissue and organ injuries.

A strike takes precise nerve control, they wrote. So the animal’s nerve fibers need protecting.

The filter works on the highest frequencies and lets lower ones through. Blocking lower frequencies would take thicker repeats, and the authors linked that limit to the layer’s small size.

Researchers haven’t recorded a mantis shrimp strike at the frequencies where the filter works. Measurements of real strikes stop at 170,000 vibrations per second, and the authors wrote that the sensors set that limit.

The team also didn’t test whether shear waves injure a mantis shrimp. The idea that shear waves would harm the animal’s nerves and soft tissue comes from research on blunt impacts and brain injuries.

And the computer model was flat, with only two dimensions. It left out the water, the curve of the club’s surface, and the club’s other layers.

Future research should include three-dimensional simulations of the club and underwater experiments with more advanced instruments, Espinosa said.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6318. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

#6317. The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak

Friday, November 20The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

Already 60° high in the east by 8 P.M. local time is M33, the Pinwheel Galaxy in Triangulum. This lovely spiral glows at 6th magnitude and is technically visible from a dark site with sharp eyes — just wait until after moonset if you want to give it a try. You’ll find it in far western Triangulum, about 4.3° west-northwest of 3rd-magnitude Alpha (α) Trianguli.

Any telescope will show M33, but larger ones are better because its considerable size — some 70’ across along its longer axis — spreads its light out and makes its surface brightness quite low. Instruments 10 inches or larger will show some detail along the spiral arms, including brighter knots of star formation.

Located some 2.7 million light-years away, M33 is the third-largest galaxy in our Local Group, after Andromeda and our own Milky Way. This cosmic neighbor is a classic spiral with no central bar and a round, bright nucleus wrapped by its dusty arms. Oriented more closely to face-on than Andromeda, M33 is a popular target for visual observers as well as astrophotographers.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M. Sunset: 4:45 P.M. Moonrise: 10:54 A.M. Moonset: 7:55 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 14Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M. Sunset: 4:44 P.M. Moonrise: 11:33 A.M. Moonset: 8:56 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)

Sunday, November 15Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

Sunrise: 6:45 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:05 P.M. Moonset: 9:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (38%)

Monday, November 16It’s a great night to catch Saturn’s largest and brightest moon, Titan, as it skims south of the planet. Two hours after sunset, Saturn is roughly 40° high in the southeast, outshining all the other stars in this region of the sky. It lies to the lower left of the Circlet of Pisces and to the upper left of the bright star Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus.

Zoom in on Saturn with a telescope to first catch sight of its ring system, stretching 43” from end to end and tilted 8° to our line of sight. Currently we are seeing Saturn’s southern side, including the entirety of the planet’s southern hemisphere. The gas giant’s disk now measures 19” across.

Titan is difficult to miss, shining at mid-8th magnitude just south of the ringed planet. Don’t be fooled by a fainter 10th-magnitude field star, which lies just to Titan’s west. The three next-brightest moons, also 10th magnitude, are Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They lie closer to the planet. Tethys sits about 40” west of Saturn’s center shortly before 8 P.M. EST, while Dione is just west of the limb and Rhea just east of the planet. Dione and Rhea are moving westward, and Rhea will skim just north of Saturn’s pole along the way, standing due north of the planet around 10:40 P.M. EST. Tethys is moving east, and will disappear behind the planet’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 2:35 A.M. EST on the 16th (still late on the 15th along the Pacific Coast).

Sunrise: 6:46 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:32 P.M. Moonset: 11:00 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (47%)

Tuesday, November 17First Quarter Moon occurs at 6:48 A.M. EST, floating among the stars of Aquarius.

Early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Check out tomorrow’s entry for more detail.

Sunrise: 6:47 A.M. Sunset: 4:42 P.M. Moonrise: 12:56 P.M. Moonset: — Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)

Wednesday, November 18The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early this morning after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per hour.

Sunrise: 6:49 A.M. Sunset: 4:41 P.M. Moonrise: 1:19 P.M. Moonset: 12:03 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (67%)

Thursday, November 19The solar system is a dynamic place. Let’s return to the predawn sky today to check out the inner planets’ progress relative to the stars of Virgo. An hour before sunrise, both Mercury and Venus are again well above the eastern horizon, with the stars around them still visible before twilight brightens too much.

Compared with earlier in the week, Venus now sits to the upper left of Spica, rather than directly above it. Venus will pass 1.8° due north of Spica later today at 6 P.M. EST. Now moving steadily east, it will track along the ecliptic, slowly headed for Libra. Mercury has already reached the Balance, sitting within its domain and to the far lower left of Kappa (κ) Virginis, as opposed to the pair’s close proximity a few days ago.

Pull out your telescope to see how the planets’ appearances have changed, too. Mercury is now 55% lit and 7” across, while Venus is 18% lit and has shrunk more noticeably, now 47” across.

Sunrise: 6:50 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 1:41 P.M. Moonset: 1:07 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%)

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST. We’ll check out the planet in the predawn sky in next week’s column.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

#6316. A massive buried church in Old Dongola is larger than the White House, but archaeologists have only dug down to a single staircase so far

At Old Dongola in Sudan, a church about 154 feet wide and 187 feet long is still mostly unexcavated, and a monumental staircase is now exposed.

Inside the medieval citadel of Old Dongola, in Sudan, a Sudanese-Polish team has cleared a monumental staircase that leads into a church still almost entirely unexcavated.

In that stairwell, the archaeologists reached the building’s original floor for the first time.

Artur Obłuski of the University of Warsaw now puts the Great Church of Jesus at 154 feet (47 meters) wide and about 187 feet (57 meters) long.

He says that makes it larger than the White House, although the team has examined only a small part of it and the final size is still open.

The expedition first came across the building in 2021. Old Dongola was then the focus of work funded by the European Research Council, and the team was cleaning the wall of an apse, the curved end of a church that holds the altar.

The university’s 2021 report gave the church a width of about 85 feet (26 meters) and the apse a diameter of about 20 feet (6 meters). That apse was already the largest found in Nubia. Murals on its walls showed two rows of monumental figures.

The new figure of 154 feet follows the latest season. Workers also exposed the buttresses that reinforce the apse. Obłuski cautiously estimates the height at 69 feet (21 meters).

The university describes the building as probably the largest church of medieval Nubia. Arabic sources call it the richest.

Good preservation has become the main obstacle. Part of the stairwell wall survives to about 36 feet (11 meters), so the trenches must go unusually deep and need far more resources than a normal dig.

Obłuski said the team wants to settle the size of the church next season. Speaking in the university’s Polish-language statement, he compared the building with the presidential residence in Washington and added a plan for it. The next two quotes are our translation from the Polish.

“This is a building larger than the famous White House in Washington,” he said. “And we plan to dig it out.”

Old Dongola was the capital of Makuria, a Christian kingdom on the Nile. The Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology has worked in the region since 1964, and a 17th-century paper from the site recently helped confirm a long-debated Nubian king.

Until now, specialists treated a different church, outside the citadel, as the cathedral of Dongola. Obłuski said in the new statement that scholars will probably have to reconsider what that building was for.

In the 2021 report, he said the find “will radically change the knowledge” of the city and of the Nubian church. The team compared the layout with Faras, where a cathedral stood at the center of the citadel with a bishop’s domed tomb to its east.

At Old Dongola, a domed building about 25 feet (7.5 meters) across adjoins the apse.

The cathedral identification remains a working conclusion. The 2021 report said the church may have housed an archbishop responsible for about 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) of the Nile, between the 1st and 5th cataracts (rapids).

In the same statement Obłuski compared the church to Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, calling such buildings “trendsetters” (our translation) for planning and engineering. He described the Great Church as a natural candidate for that role in Nubia, and perhaps in that part of Africa.

The dig also produced a surprise. A second, smaller church stood on the upper floor of a structure added to the Great Church, and its walls survive to only about 3 feet (1 meter).

Traces of painting remained on those walls. Fragments of painted plaster from the room now fill six large shelving units.

Obłuski contrasted this with a similar annex on the north side, connected to the Makurian King David in the 13th century, which the team found in 2023 with its paintings still on the walls.

In the debris of the smaller church, excavators recovered small pieces of plaster with Greek writing. Agata Deptuła, the expedition’s epigrapher, identified them as biblical canticles, or odes, which are prayer songs added to the book of Psalms.

One fragment comes from the prayer of Hannah, the mother of the prophet Samuel in the Old Testament. A scribe wrote it in a careful book hand, with letters only about a fifth of an inch (half a centimeter) tall.

Deptuła said Old Dongola had mostly yielded psalm texts until now, which makes the odes new for the site. At Hippos, above the Sea of Galilee, Greek inscriptions fixed the last known renovation of a Byzantine cathedral with two baptism rooms.

The Great Church is also separate from the Sudanese church built around a carving of a possible Kushite ruler at Miseeda.

Flooding in autumn 2024, the worst at Old Dongola since 1988, damaged some of the roofs that shelter the monuments.

Before digging resumed, the team stabilized the site together with the Faculty of Civil Engineering at Warsaw University of Technology.

The expedition also built a solar power installation, paid for by Poland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs through its Polish Aid program. It powers the motors of pumps that bring Nile water to the homes and fields of about 10,000 people.

Obłuski said the team added an installation for eight stations that raise water pressure, so homes on higher ground can be supplied. The conflict in Sudan had left those residents without water.

The work runs with Sudan’s National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums and with local residents, who formed an association to help care for the site. During the last season, the archaeologists also joined local evening meals that break the fast at Ramadan.

The 187-foot length is approximate, and the 69-foot height is an estimate. Only the stairwell has reached floor level, so the plan of the interior remains largely unknown.

The university’s statement is a news report and not a peer-reviewed paper. It gives no construction date for the church and does not name any odes beyond Hannah’s prayer.

For now, the original floor of the Great Church is known only at the bottom of one staircase.

The information was obtained from the University of Warsaw.

#6315. The 7 Best Pellet Stoves to Help Save Money on Heating

If you’re looking for an efficient way to heat your home during the cold winter months, pellet stoves offer several advantages over wood stoves or fireplaces.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The novelty of a wood burning fireplace wears off when you have to trudge outside to grab a bundle of logs. Installing a wood burning stove can be expensive, and once it’s running, it produces ash that needs to be cleaned out. Pellet stoves, however, are an efficient, convenient option for heating a room while appreciating the glow of a live fire.

Powered by compressed hardwood pellets stored in a hopper that can hold over 100 pounds, pellet stoves can provide a fire that burns for dozens of hours without needing to be tended. Those pellets drop into a combustion chamber where they are burned to produce heat. Exhaust is then vented through a flue pipe out a sidewall or your roof.

A pellet stove offers consistent, reliable heat without a lot of fuss. More expensive models will cost several thousand dollars, but often come with programmable digital thermostats and larger hoppers that allow a fire to burn longer without the need for additional pellets being added.

Wood stoves require a bit more effort and knowledge—you’ll have to learn about the different burn rates of wood and clean out ash more regularly. Still, wood burning stoves are typically quieter and may last longer than pellet stoves because they don’t have electronic components.

As for installation, freestanding pellet stoves need an available outlet with an open plug and a vent to the outside, which may require the installer to cut a hole in the wall. If your power goes out often during storms, that means your pellet stove won’t work without a generator or separate power source. Pellet stoves that insert into your fireplace require a chimney liner, a pipe that vents gas outside.

Pellet stoves are designed to warm up everything from your patio to your rec room. Different models can stand on their own, be mounted to the wall, or inserted into a fireplace. Here are the 10 best pellet stoves to buy now that bring the heat.

For a sizable pellet stove that can heat a large area, this model from ComfortBilt is a top choice. The EPA-certified design can provide heat for up to 2,800 square feet thanks to its 50,000 BTU output.

It offers a large window where you can watch the fire burning inside. With a 55-pound hopper, the ash from the fire falls down into a removable pan that only needs to be emptied every 2 weeks. The stove offers five power settings, and on the lowest setting, you can get up to 20 hours of continuous heat.

The PelPro Pellet Stove is an efficient option that gives you plenty of heat for your buck. The EPA-certified stove has a large hopper (the manufacturer says the stove can run for 40 hours before needing to be reloaded) and convenient features like an automatic ignition at a lower price point.

The main compromises are a manually controlled dial thermostat and only a 1-year warranty on parts.

If you like the ability to control your appliances remotely, this pellet stove has built-in Wi-Fi that allows you to adjust its settings, create a heating schedule, and more, all from your smartphone.

The stove has a three-sided bay window that makes it a great focal point for your living space, and it can heat up to 2,500 square feet. It has a large hopper that can hold up to 66 pounds of pellets, providing a long run time between refills, and the unit’s quiet blower won’t disturb your family while it’s running.

One of the downsides of pellet stoves is they require electricity to operate their augers and inner fans, and this means you’re left without heat when the power goes out. However, this pellet stove from US Stove Company is one of the few designed to work without electricity. Instead, it uses a gravity-fed hopper and manual start.

With a tall, narrow form and a pellet feed that zigzags down to the burning chamber, this stove can heat up to 2,000 square feet. You can adjust its temperature by opening and closing the fresh air intakes on the front of the stove, and the 60-pound hopper holds enough fuel to run for up to 30 hours.

If you’re hoping to heat a large area or even your whole house, this pellet stove can warm up to 3,000 square feet when temperatures are mild.

The EPA-certified stove has a unique heat exchanger design and powerful blower that help to produce maximum heat from pellets, and there are five power settings and a programmable thermostat that let you adjust the warmth to your liking.

On the lowest setting, the 51-pound hopper has enough fuel to run for up to 19 hours, and the stove is reasonably priced considering its high heat output.

The Ashley Pellet Space Saver Stove is like a genie in a bottle—lots of power in an itty bitty living space. With a small profile thanks to thoughtful curves and an efficient design, this steel stove can heat up to 2,200 square feet for 32 hours.

Adjust the temperature and heat output via remote control and the side panels pop off for maintenance. A large glass window lets you enjoy a lovely view of the fire.

If you don’t have space for a freestanding pellet stove, this unique model can be mounted to your wall instead. It’s ideal for spaces up to 1,000 square feet and has a direct vent design that doesn’t require the traditional chimney installation.

The unit comes with everything needed for installation, including the mounting bracket, and its 28-pound hopper delivers up to 35 hours of heat between refills on the lowest setting. It has digital controls and a remote control for easy adjustments, and it’s even approved for use in mobile homes.

I’ve worked with pellet grills and wood stoves to get through Midwest winters, so I know the differences and potential benefits of different stoves. To discover popular pellet stoves, I dived into articles on Field & Stream, The Spruce, and Wirecutter. I considered which models did well in tests and cross referenced them with reviews on Amazon. Also, I delved into message boards and talked with pellet stove owners to understand what was frustrating and what was delightful about owning one.

I also weighed the cost and size of each model, as well as the warranty. Finally, I relied on some of the previous research done for this article by writer Camryn Rabideau. Here are the 10 pellet stoves that will warm your heart and your living room.

A pellet stove can be a big investment—multiple thousands of dollars to cover the stove and installation—so it’s important that you find one that fits your room and heats it efficiently.

Pellet stoves come in three main styles: freestanding, wall mounted, and insert. A freestanding stove—which can be larger or more powerful than the other options—evokes a classic cabin feel and sits on the ground or on feet. A wall-mounted stove hangs free of the floor and kicks out heat like the heads of a mini split. Inserts are meant to slot inside your fireplace and could take a non-functioning fireplace and make it a focal point of your room once again.

More Cozy Options to Consider: Best Electric Fireplaces • Best Space Heaters • Best Heated Blankets

Pellet stoves are efficient, producing less creosote (the tarry byproduct of burning wood) and ash than wood stoves. The compact pellets—thanks to their small size and low moisture content—burn hot and quickly. Pellet stoves that receive certification from the United States Environmental Protection Agency typically offer between 70 and 83 percent fuel efficiency. In some cases, certification comes with a tax credit so check before you purchase a given model.

Pellet stoves often have multiple settings. Higher settings release more pellets so the stove can burn hotter, whereas the lowest setting will enable you pellets to last longer, but you might not get as much heat. A stove with a smaller hopper running outdoors may only last 6 hours per full hopper, like the Even Embers Pellet Stove, which is fine if you’re looking to gather in the backyard at night. Larger pellet stoves can burn unattended for more than a day, like the PelPro Pellet Stove which can run for 40 hours.

The larger the hopper, the longer the burn time, and the longer you can go between pellet refills. Most hoppers will need to be refilled once a day. But larger hoppers (60 pounds and up) typically mean bigger stoves, so you’ll have to consider whether or not it will fit your space. Likewise, it can be cumbersome to pour heavier bags—50 pounds at a time—into the hopper.

The heating ability of pellet stoves is measured in British Thermal Units (BTUs) per hour. The higher the BTUs, the easier it will be for a stove to heat a room or multiple rooms. If you’re considering heating multiple rooms or a whole home, a pellet stove rated at 60,000 BTUs can heat approximately 2,000 square feet.

Warranties typically cover parts and repairs for several years. A well-maintained pellet stove should last longer than the warranty—a decade or more if properly maintained; but it’s a comfort to have some financial coverage in the first few years after investing a decent amount of money in a pellet stove.

Empty your ash pan and clean the firebox once or twice a week. If your pellet stove has baffles, clean them every few months. And you’ll need to do a deep clean of the venting probably once a year.

Check your manual for the specific instructions, but cleaning can follow a simple rule—if you see ash build up, clean it out once your stove has cooled.

Pellet stoves heat up quickly—it’s one of their best features. They’ll be raising the temperature of your room often inside of 30 minutes.

Pellets may be more expensive; but they’re convenient. Pellets take up less space and produce less ash than firewood. Wood stoves can be used for cooking (even if it’s just s’mores) and require tending that you’ll either see as a nice part of the ritual or a chore that you’d rather not do.

#6314. Rock shelter full of old charcoal suggests that Neanderthals burned 24 pounds of wood per day and had a cleaning system

Researchers mapped 640 charcoal fragments from a Neanderthal camp and found two distinct zones of burned wood.

From 2019 to 2022, excavators at Abric Romaní in Capellades, Spain, picked 640 charcoal fragments out of one layer of sediment by hand. They logged the position of every piece.

The largest measured about half an inch (13 millimeters). Together the pieces show where Neanderthals burned wood about 60,000 years ago, and where some of the waste may have gone.

Most of the charcoal lay around hearths near the shelter wall. Smaller patches lay to the south, and the study’s authors say those could be cleared hearth waste, though charcoal alone cannot prove it.

The layer is known as Level Ra. IPHES-CERCA, the Catalan institute that works at the site, calls it a Neanderthal camp specialized in deer hunting.

Amador Romaní discovered the shelter in 1909. The current project began in 1983, and more than 200 hearths have been identified. A wooden club with no clear parallel also came from this site.

Sediment built up fast here, at up to 31 inches (80 centimeters) per thousand years in Level Ra. The team did not sieve it, because sieving could have broken the charcoal. The authors note that hand-picking can bias the sample.

Crews took three-dimensional coordinates for each fragment by hand and with a total station, a surveying instrument. The 2022 season aimed to finish the whole surface of Level Ra.

On Aug. 19 of that year, the crew working in Level Rb lifted bone pieces coated in mineral crust. Specialists identified them as part of a Neanderthal skull.

Irene Cazalla, a restoration technician at IPHES-CERCA, then conserved them. The institute said no Neanderthal remains had turned up in more than 40 years of research at the site.

Tomás Fernández-Iriarte of IPHES-CERCA analyzed the charcoal and wrote the first draft, the paper’s author statement says. The work ran on an Olympus BX41 microscope at up to 500 times magnification.

The team checked its identifications against a collection of modern charred wood kept at the institute. A total of 484 fragments, about 76 percent, came from the Pinus sylvestris type. That group covers three mountain pines with very similar wood.

Those pines live today above about 1,970 feet (600 meters). The authors think their range was probably wider during the Ice Age.

Compression wood showed up in 501 fragments. It is a growth trait tied to stress and is common in branches. The authors say the occupants most likely burned branches, but more tree-ring work is needed to separate them from trunks.

A test on 100 fragments gave an alteration score of 0.55, within the range for rotten wood. The authors read this as a sign that the fuel was deadwood in varying states, moderately rotten, though the test covered only that subsample and not every wood type separately.

The paper cites ethnographic reports on small groups of five or six people in temperate climates. Those groups used up to 24 pounds (11 kilograms) of wood per day.

With that much to haul, the authors think the wood did not travel far. Mountain pines drop a lot of dead wood, so the people in the shelter probably took what lay nearby.

Squares R60 and S59 of the excavation grid held something different. The team found a group of Prunus charcoal there, from a genus represented by only 17 fragments in the whole sample.

The authors listed kindling or the extraction of a specific resource as possible reasons. They also raised fruit gathering, but no fruit or seeds have turned up in this level.

The northern sector held 495 fragments and the southern sector 145. The team mapped them with Kernel Density Estimation, a method that turns scattered points into a density surface.

Squares U53, T57, T54 and U56 were the densest, at 68 to 87 fragments per grid unit. They sit inside a larger spread from U51 to U59, beside the wall and on top of the hearths.

Southern patches reached 51 to 68 fragments per grid unit and overlapped less with hearths. The authors wrote that this pattern “could be explained by discrete hearth-cleaning events.”

Excavators have proposed a dump with burned bones in Level M and drop-and-toss areas in Level O. At Hohle Fels Cave in Germany, analyses found dumped residues from hearths, including some tied to Neanderthal occupations.

Other research has compared Neanderthal and Homo sapiens living spaces and explored early Neanderthal ideas of home.

Water flowed out of the rock walls here and carried minerals over the floor. Mineral inclusions marked 47.6 percent of the fragments.

The team first logged small reddish dots on the charcoal as “spores.” An electron microscope at Rovira i Virgili University showed they were iron deposits that formed later.

Fungal threads called hyphae appeared in 15.7 percent of the pieces. The southern sector had proportionally more of them, along with more mineral alteration.

The authors call the southern patches compatible with displacement or maintenance of hearths, but say their position alone “is insufficient to demonstrate such processes.” Weathering and water could also have shaped them.

Charcoal also cannot show if the fires belonged to one stay or several. One group may have cleared its own hearths. A later group may have come back after a gap and reused old fire spots.

Bones, stone tools and a geoarchaeological study of the hearths still have to be mapped across the same floor. The authors say they are working to upload the data, which is available on request for now.

Level Ra is fully excavated, and its 640 pieces of burned wood now exist as points on a grid.

The full study was published in the Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology.
