Archaeologists have discovered thousands of stone artifacts in Saudi Arabia, some of which suggest people were using poison-tipped stone tools to hunt large game 125,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have found what may be the world's oldest poisoned weapons at a 125,000-year-old site on an ancient lakeshore in Saudi Arabia. The stone tools, which were likely used to hunt large animals, had traces of residue from a poisonous tree historically used for its toxins.

"At 125,000 years old, these would be substantially older than the poisoned arrowheads recently identified in South Africa, which date to around 60,000 years ago," study co-author Chris Clarkson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany and Griffith University in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "But we haven't demonstrated exactly how the poison was prepared or whether it was effective. So I'd describe these as potentially the oldest evidence for poisoned hunting weapons, rather than an unequivocally established first."

In the new study, published Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Science, researchers investigated a 125,000-year-old site in southern Saudi Arabia known as 'Uruq Aljelibah, which means "sand dunes of a watering hole," study co-author Frans van Buchem, a geologist at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia, told Live Science.

Today, the area is "hot, extremely dry, with extensive sand dunes," Clarkson said, located as it is within the Empty Quarter — one of the hottest, driest deserts on Earth. But the scientists found the site was once home to a freshwater lake measuring about 130 square miles (340 square kilometers) and up to 95 feet (29 meters) deep. Fossils there suggest it once supported a rich diversity of flora and fauna, including hippopotamuses, buffalo, ostriches, camels, gazelles, oryx, palms, reeds, trees and shrubs, which early modern humans likely exploited for food and other resources.

"The idea of hippopotamuses and enormous buffalo living around a lake in what is now the Empty Quarter really brings home just how dramatically these landscapes, and global climates, have changed," Clarkson said.

Saudi Arabia is a desert today, but it used to be a lush landscape.

The archaeologists discovered more than 5,500 stone artifacts at the site, along with extraordinarily preserved traces of plant materials, such as fibers, resins and wood. Several of these artifacts were stone points that showed impact damage consistent with hunting large animals, and a microscopic analysis revealed traces of animal tissue near the point tips. The distribution of the stone tools closely matched clusters of animal bones, suggesting that the lakeshore was a focal point for hunting and processing game, according to the study.

"At most Paleolithic sites, we're lucky if we get the stone tools and perhaps a few animal bones," Clarkson said. "Here we can actually begin to reconstruct what those tools were doing and what other materials people were combining with them."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers found that people may have hunted animals with poison-tipped tools. Several stone points had chemical residues linked with the arrow poison tree (Acokanthera schimperi), which is known historically for its toxins and is native to eastern and central Africa and southern Arabia. African hunters have coated spear tips and arrowheads with extracts from this plant to paralyze or kill game.

It remains unclear how hunters who poisoned their targets might have avoided poisoning themselves upon eating the game.

"The effects of a poison depend on the substance, the dose and how it enters the body," Clarkson said. "A poison introduced directly into a wound doesn't necessarily behave in the same way when swallowed." Hunters throughout history "are known to sometimes remove the meat around the wound before eating the rest of the animal," he added.

These findings emphasize how researchers have often underestimated the technological complexity of early human populations, because so much of what they made was organic and has simply disappeared," Clarkson said. "These weren't just people knocking stone flakes off cores," Clarkson noted. "They were combining stone with wood, plant fibers, resins and potentially toxic substances to make complex tools and weapons."

To have so much evidence for how people were making and using tools in a site like this "is remarkable," Eleanor Scerri, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany who did not take part in this research, told Live Science in an email. "This goes from both the micro-scale, in finding traces of how people hafted spear tips, for instance, up to the bigger scale of the whole site and the very convincing spatial relationship between hunting-related tools and the bones of animals such as hippos."

Sites in Arabia that possess both stone tools and animal bones are rare, Jeffrey Rose, a Paleolithic archaeologist at the University of Algarve in Portugal who did not participate in this study, told Live Science in an email. "This one has thousands of artifacts on an old lakeshore alongside hippo, buffalo and ostrich, and some of the flakes fit back together, so the tools were made on the spot," he said. "It's valuable new data."

The Arabian Peninsula sits between Africa and the rest of Asia and was a major corridor for humans as they dispersed across the world. Recurring spans of increased rainfall could have made its otherwise hostile landscapes more habitable in the past. However, the hot desert that now covers much of Arabia has made it difficult for scientists to excavate many details about this vital bridge during this critical point in human history.

The researchers did not unearth any human remains. Still, they suspect the site most likely belonged to modern humans (our species, Homo sapiens), as opposed to a different human species.

"We know that H. sapiens had already expanded out of Africa and were present in Southwest Asia during this period," Clarkson said. "The age of the site fits with those early movements."

These findings add to growing evidence that wetter intervals in Arabia created migration corridors between Africa and Asia and supported productive habitats capable of sustaining repeated human occupation.

"What our site shows is that people weren't necessarily just passing through these environments," Clarkson said. "They were exploiting them in quite sophisticated ways, using a range of technologies and resources."

But Rose cautioned that all of the stone artifacts found in this study were collected from the surface. "Not one was excavated from the layers that were dated," he said. "The 125,000-year date belongs to the lake, not to the tools. For the tools, it is only a maximum age." Future research at the site should look for stone artifacts sealed in lake beds. "That's hard in Arabia, where wind has stripped most sites down to surface scatters, but it can be done," Rose said.

Clarkson agrees that further work is needed. "I'd really like to keep going back to this site to find more fossils, both animals as well as hopefully human fossils," Clarkson said. "I'd also really like to push the chemical and functional analyses further, particularly the evidence for toxic plant compounds. It would be fascinating to determine exactly which substances were being used, how they might have been prepared and whether they were deliberately applied to hunting weapons."

Future research focusing on the ancient lake margins may reveal more information. "There must be other places where people were living and carrying out activities, and some may preserve better stratified archaeological deposits," Clarkson said.

But the combination of discoveries at this site is amazing, the researchers said.

"I've spent much of my career studying stone tools, and one of the great frustrations is that we're usually only looking at the small fraction of ancient technology that survives," Clarkson said. "Here we have a chance to see much more of the complete technological system."

Clarkson, C., Price, G.J., Kalifi, A., Losi, G., Matheson, C., Al-Jibreen, F., Alsharekh, A.M., Armitage, S.J., Blilou, I., Boivin, N., Breeze, P.S., Drake, N., Duval, M., Gradwell, S., Groucutt, H.W., Guagnin, M., Guzmán, J., Hapiot, L., Martínez-Pillado, V., … van Buchem, F. (2026). Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore. Science. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aef9342

#6311. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

#6310. Experts who study AI in classrooms ranked what matters most, and it isn’t the technology

Seventy experts from 18 countries rated 15 trends in AI in education, and teaching AI skills to both students and teachers came out at the top of the list.

Most conversations around integrating AI in classrooms focus on flashy new tech, like AI tutors for every student or programs that grade homework overnight.

But according to 70 specialists from 18 different countries, the most critical AI trend for the next three years has nothing to do with buying new software.

Their number one priority is basic AI literacy. Both students and teachers need to be taught what these tools are actually doing and when to question their answers.

Rwitajit Majumdar of Kumamoto University in Japan led the study. Colleagues at Dublin City University, Griffith University, the University of Twente, and universities in Germany and Finland joined him.

It’s an expert survey, not a trial in classrooms, so its answers are the panel’s judgment rather than measured results.

The team used a Delphi process, which is a way of drawing a consensus out of experts in rounds. First, 17 researchers submitted 56 trends in AI and education. The team grouped those into 15 themes, from virtual teaching assistants to automated grading to equal access.

Then 70 people rated each theme from 1 to 10 on three questions. How important will it be for learning and teaching within three years? How much impact will it have? And how hard will it be to get right?

Twenty-six of the raters came from academia and 23 from research. Eight worked in policy, eight were teachers, and five came from industry. Germany and Ireland between them supplied 31 of the 70.

The ratings were then argued over in person. About 130 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners met in Dublin in June 2025 at EDUsummIT, a gathering endorsed by UNESCO.

In small groups, each participant took on the role of a teacher, a developer, a researcher, or a policymaker and argued from that seat.

AI-related competences for learners and educators scored highest on both impact, at 8.57 out of 10, and importance, at 8.64.

The panel rated it moderately hard to achieve, at 7.49. That left it with a positive balance of payoff to difficulty, which the authors read as strong consensus that competence comes first.

Two themes tied for second on impact, at 8.13 each. One was automated assessment and feedback, the AI tutor that marks work and responds to each student. The other was the changing role of the teacher who works alongside such tools.

The two parted ways on difficulty. The experts rated automated feedback a moderate challenge, at 7.13. They rated the teacher’s new role one of the hardest things on the list, at 8.40, which the authors read as high impact and high complexity at once.

Two more themes rounded out the top five. One was whether an AI system can explain itself and be trusted, with an impact score of 7.84. The other was whether every student gets equal access to it, at 7.81.

Both drew challenge scores above 8. The authors read those as barriers in ethics, infrastructure, and policy rather than in the technology itself.

Two cheaper wins also stood out in the panel’s arithmetic. AI-assisted content creation and AI for administrative paperwork both paired high importance with lower difficulty, which the authors flagged as candidates for near-term action.

The themes at the bottom were the most technical ones and were also rated as hard. This made them the least urgent.

Linking AI to classroom devices such as virtual reality headsets scored 5.39 on impact. Software that connects AI to a school’s older data systems scored 5.60, and AI-built maps linking subjects across the curriculum scored 5.90.

Across all 15 themes, the panel’s average importance score was 7.31. That sat slightly above its average impact and challenge scores, but the three didn’t differ in any reliable way.

The experts saw AI in education as roughly as hard as it is promising.

A consensus method can narrow the range of views it reports, the authors wrote. The 70 experts were also a convenience sample rather than a representative one.

Furthermore, no students and no parents took part, though they are the people for whom the systems are built.

The ratings forecast three years ahead. Whether the themes the panel ranked highest turn out to be the ones that matter in real classrooms hasn’t been checked.

The authors called for larger panels in each region, with students and parents included, and for work that goes beyond ranking priorities to testing them.

The full study was published in the journal Computers and Education Open.

#6309. The Best 4K TVs Bring Everything You Watch and Play to Life

4K is the standard, and there are so many great options right now.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Now more than ever, you should hold your TV to a higher standard. More and more streaming content is available in 4K UHD resolution, which has four times as many pixels as standard Full HD (1080p). Video games, including PlayStation 5 and Nintendo Switch 2, support higher refresh rates that only TVs from the past few years support.

4K TVs are the standard, and have been for some time. Technically, 8K TVs are available, but there’s no indication that anyone is making content to take advantage of them anytime soon.

While tech prices are abnormally high in 2026, the tech is still improving rapidly. And since most of us buy a TV every five to 10 years, even last year’s models will offer a huge upgrade and are generally much more reasonably priced. New TVs are out there for everyone, at every price point.

I handpicked 4K TVs based on my testing and included options at various price points from current leading manufacturers: LG, Samsung, Hisense, and TCL. The selection process involved parsing through hardware specs, attending live demo sessions, and consulting with other industry experts.

Unless indicated otherwise, I usually test the 65-inch version of each TV, since it usually offers the best balance of price and capabilities as the primary home entertainment centerpiece in your space. Most sets are also available in smaller, less expensive versions. And many are available in even XXL formats, 75 inches and higher, for households with larger spaces and bigger budgets.

A note on these picks: Even though we’re well into 2026, we still primarily recommend TVs that launched in 2025, even when a newer version is available. From what my colleagues and I have seen so far, I believe that last year’s models represent the best possible value right now. In time, as last year’s models sell out, the value proposition will change. But trust me when I say that these TVs provide the best value and will make your shows, movies, and games look great for years to come.

Now that the price has come down a bit, we’re prepared to recommend this year’s LG C-series TV, the C6 evo, as the best option for most people. Though it isn't dramatically different from its predecessor, this mid-range OLED maintains the line’s legacy as impressively slim, elegant, and capable of delivering a stunning picture. It also runs a feature-packed platform with deep smart home integration.

With millions of individually backlit pixels, the C6’s OLED display is a rock-solid contender for the best in its price range. The panel’s flawless black reproduction delivers perfect contrast and vivid colors, making any content—from a newscast to a blockbuster movie to an AAA video game—look its best.

Speaking of gaming, the C6 is also one of the best TVs on the market for the task. In addition to being a great companion for the latest gaming consoles, the TV can double as a top-tier gaming monitor, thanks to a 165 Hz refresh rate and support for AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync. It can also deliver high-powered cloud-based gameplay via an Nvidia GeForce Now subscription.

As with previous years, the C6 also gets extra credit for its wide size range. Depending on your needs and budget, you can choose a compact 42-inch, a private movie theater-worthy 83-inch model, or one of several additional sizes in between. Keep in mind that larger screen models have brighter Tandem OLED screens.

With a price cut shortly after launch, the TCL QM8L is ready to replace its predecessor, the QM8K, as the top Mini-LED TV. It looks incredibly sleek sans top and side bezels, and the picture looks just as impressive. While OLED technology still broadly produces the richest and sharpest image quality, mini-LED TVs are no slouch, delivering great detail and a brighter screen that improves performance in less-than-stellar lighting conditions.

With thousands of local dimming zones and an upgraded AI-powered processor to control them, the QM8L’s super quantum-dot mini-LED screen delivers a captivating picture with rich colors and deep contrast. The TV’s picture quality comes close to a top-tier OLED TV. Its higher peak brightness and lower cost sufficiently make up for its lack of individually backlit pixels.

If you are looking for a mini-LED 4K TV with SQD color proficiency on a tighter budget, I think this model’s more affordable cousin, the TCL QM7L, is also a very good choice. You lose some peak brightness and local dimming zones, but it still provides amazing performance for its much lower price.

RGB Mini-LED TVs deliver a unique combination of high peak brightness and stellar color accuracy, with the latter made possible by separate red, blue, and green light diodes instead of a single one in their display panels. Of all the TV newcomers to offer this screen technology in 2026, the Hisense UR9 is the one I’d recommend to most buyers. Beyond the exceptional picture quality from its new display panel, the TV also delivers surprisingly powerful sound and a rich set of futureproof connectivity features.

In addition to producing a bright picture with vibrant-yet-accurate colors and deep contrast, the Hisense UR9 surprised me pleasantly by handling direct light reflections surprisingly well. Dubbed “Obsidian” by its maker, the standout glare-reduction feature results in a top-tier viewing experience in bright spaces.

The TV’s screen supports a high 180Hz refresh rate, cutting latency in video games and smoothing blurred movement in live sports. I’m also a big fan of its 4.1.2-channel speaker system tuned by Devialet — a French luxury audio brand — and its two-year warranty.

Consider the Hisense UR8 if you are looking for an RGB Mini-LED TV on a tighter budget. It is a step down in peak brightness and audio performance from the UR9, as its model number suggests, but the lower price makes up for the shortcomings. Unlike its flagship sibling, the UR8 is also available with a 55-inch screen.

TCL’s QM6K is my favorite 4K TV on a budget. Spending less than $600 before additional deals and discounts, gets you a TV with a sleek design, superb picture quality, a feature-packed platform, and an abundant set of connectivity options. With a high-performance game mode and support for variable refresh rate, the TV is also a top-notch gaming console display.

The TCL QM6K delivers superb picture quality and color rendering for a TV at such an agreeable price point. Its quantum-dot mini-LED display panel with hundreds of local dimming zones produces punchy colors and dramatic contrast that defy its price category. I can’t think of a better 4K TV for the money.

On the audio front, the TV is as impressive as it is in terms of picture quality. Its speaker system, tuned by Onkyo, has a built-in subwoofer, allowing it to deliver immersive sound with surprisingly powerful bass.

TCL offers the QM6K in several screen sizes, with the 98-inch model as the largest. The biggest screen size costs a little over $2,000, which is quite a bargain for the full-blown private movie theater experience it provides. The 85-inch version at a tad above $1,000 is also a great value for money.

The Samsung S95H is the 4K TV to get if you want stunning design and picture quality to match. The TV’s metal frame gives it a unique presence, especially when wall-mounted, and makes any rival look generic in comparison. Its super-bright QD-OLED display predictably produces vibrant colors and deep contrast. Plus, a sophisticated onboard processor with access to AI neural networks makes lower-resolution content look sharper than ever.

Most importantly, the Samsung S95H can effortlessly deliver this viewing experience from any angle, even in bright spaces. The TV’s screen has a glare-free finish, which makes it practically impervious to light reflections. This means its picture quality stays superb even when it’s facing a lamp, a window, or another light source. This quality alone makes the TV worth every penny.

In keeping with its price category, the Samsung S95H is also a bona fide gaming powerhouse, capable of delivering exceptional visuals when connected to a gaming console or a high-powered computer. Samsung’s Tizen platform also supports cloud gaming, so all you need is a wireless controller and a monthly subscription to enjoy AAA titles.

We like that the TV’s intuitive remote has a rechargeable battery that you can charge via a light source or a USB-C port, so you never have to swap batteries. Its multi-speaker Dolby Atmos audio system, meanwhile, defies its form factor.

The TCL X11L is the best big-screen TV on the market today, with an elegant design, outstanding picture quality, and immersive sound tuned by Bang & Olufsen. We often think of TCL as the bang for your buck, but this set shows the brand can also deliver something out of this world for folks willing to spend big for the best possible picture.

The secret is the X11L's first-of-its-kind SQD Mini-LED display—that's "Super Quantum Dot"—which blends brightness-enhancing quantum dot technology with Mini-LED dimming zones to boost high-dynamic-range performance.

At a $7,000 launch price, it was hard to imagine not insisting on an OLED TV over the TCL X11L, but things have changed dramatically since then. Now that it starts at $3,000 for a 75-inch version, the high-end TCL offering is a great buy. Its color accuracy and contrast are both top-notch, and the overall picture quality is tremendous. Frankly, I’d take the TV over any OLED on the market today.

TVs that double as home decor pieces by displaying artwork or photos became a thing when Samsung launched The Frame almost a decade ago. Since then, frame-like TVs have grown from a niche category into something with broader appeal and a surprisingly rich selection across the price spectrum. The Hisense S7 CanvasTV is the one I’d recommend to most buyers in 2026, because it strikes a fine balance between elegant design, stellar picture quality, and a rich selection of onboard features, all at a reasonable price and in multiple screen sizes.

Thanks to a quantum-dot display with a matte finish to reduce pesky reflections and an ambient light sensor, the S7 CanvasTV can display beautiful visuals in any scenario, whether it’s live sports or a vacation photo. Still, you should know the device’s picture quality can’t match that of similarly priced conventional Hisense TVs or rival brands with quantum-dot or RGB mini-LED screens. The matte screen, customizable frame, and slim wall mount make the S7 CanvasTV worth considering, since it will look great when not in use.

When it comes to alternatives, the first that comes to mind is Samsung's The Frame Pro. It offers a more polished design and a fancier quantum-dot mini-LED panel with superior glare resistance and artwork display capabilities. The Frame Pro will look much nicer as an art piece, but I’d still take the Hisense S7 CanvasTV for offering Dolby Vision HDR support and a full set of built-in connectivity features. Samsung has these essentials in a separate box for The Frame Pro.

Though they all look like black slabs on the wall, the quality of the images produced by 4K TVs can vary dramatically from model to model. Many also have distinctive features that make them better for specific applications—like a high refresh rate for gaming. And, of course, all that impacts how much they cost. Here are the most important things to keep in mind while shopping:

There is all manner of exotic formulae for determining the exact distance you should sit from a large screen TV—X-times the screen height, X-times the screen’s diagonal size—but there isn’t a right or wrong answer. The best rule of thumb is if the screen fills your frame of vision from where you’re sitting, and you don’t have to turn your head to see one side of the screen or the other, you’re fine. (Note: Sitting too close to a 4K TV won’t ruin your eyes despite what your mother may have told you.)

What size TV you choose, however, may be predetermined by your room geography and/or furnishings, such as the interior of an existing TV cabinet, or dictated by a spouse’s objections to a larger-size set. If you plan to buy a new TV larger than your current set, measure the width, height, and depth of your home’s TV space, and then check the actual width and height of the TV with stand, not the diagonal screen size. A flat panel 65-inch screen 4K TV usually measures less than 60 inches wide, less than 36 inches tall, and about 15 inches deep with the stand.

Building a Home Theater? Check These Guides Next: Best OLED TVs • Best Wireless Surround Sound Systems • Best TV Wall Mounts

Some TVs come with center stands, while many larger models have feet at either end of the set, which may be too widely spaced apart for your TV stand. Check the width of your TV tabletop and the space between the feet of your prospective TV purchase to make sure its feet will fit.

Planning to hang your TV on a wall? All TVs follow a version of the VESA (Video Electronics Standards Association) wall-mounting standard, including variations such as VESA MIS-D, MIS-E, and MIS-F, which mainly address a TV’s rear mounting-hole spacing, supportable weight, and size.

A VESA wall mounting kit can work with virtually any wall-mountable TV, but double-check your TV’s specifications to confirm any VESA variation.

A 4K TV’s display is composed of 3840 x 2160 pixels, but that’s only the screen resolution. A dizzying array of screen technologies creates different levels of stunning 4K images. These technologies include:

A TV screen's image speed is measured by its refresh rate, expressed in hertz (Hz). This equals frames flashed per second; for comparison, movie film is projected at 24 frames per second, while Normal TV broadcasts refresh at 60 Hz, or 60 frames per second.

If you’re a heavy gamer, you want a display that more accurately reflects the eye-blinking speed of the animated action, which means you’ll want a TV with a refresh rate of at least 120 Hz or higher, and a set equipped with VRR (variable refresh rate), which automatically adjusts the refresh rate depending on the content being displayed.

Another screen technology gamers want is low latency, or input lag, which is how quickly the display responds when you push a button on your controller or joystick. Many higher-end TVs include Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), which automatically switches your TV to a faster, more responsive mode measured in milliseconds (ms).

Yes, but you only need to concern yourself with the types your 4K TV includes. Nearly all bigger-screen 4K TVs are equipped with a type of HDR (high-dynamic range) that creates visibly punchier, higher-contrast images when viewing 4K content from Blu-ray or streaming channels.

Different HDR versions include the standard and most common HDR, as well as the more specialized HDR-10, HDR-10+, Dolby Vision, and HLG (Hybrid Log Gamma), designed to deliver HDR benefits to lower non-4K broadcast, cable, and satellite TV fare.

While there are subtle visual benefits associated with each type of HDR, and while some TV makers, 4K Blu-ray producers, and streaming channels opt to deploy some HDR versions but not others, compatibility really isn’t an issue since all include a plain and widely compatible HDR version.

Bottom line: Any set featuring any type of HDR will produce a visibly better 4K picture than a set without HDR.

8K TV makers may not want to hear this, but probably never. 8K TVs offer a display with a resolution of 7,680 x 4,320 pixels, or 33 million pixels, more than four times the 8 million pixels that comprise a 4K TV display.

Prices are coming down to near 4K TV price levels for 8K models. But, for a variety of reasons, there is no existing 8K content—no 8K broadcast or cable, no 8K streaming, no 8K Blu-ray—and there isn’t likely to be for the foreseeable future.

The only benefits of an 8K TV are via upscaling or up-conversion of lower-resolution programming to 8K. But realistically you’ll need at least a 75-inch TV to appreciate the difference between 4K and 8K.

Imagine watching the movie "Jaws" without feeling that "bum-bum, bum-bum" bass in your gut, or not being able to understand character dialogue over a swelling orchestral passage, or subtle sounds that lend a dramatic scene its key ambience.

A 4K TV may produce excellent picture quality, but most do not produce equally excellent sound, which can dull or ruin your viewing experience. There is a fix for this. Instead of relying on a TV’s poor audio, you may want to pair your 4K TV with a soundbar via an ARC (Audio Return Channel) or eARC (enhanced Audio Return Channel) HDMI connection.

An ARC-compatible soundbar connected to a TV via an ARC HDMI jack lets you control your TV’s picture and sound with a single remote, as if the soundbar were your TV’s speaker.

Just make sure to measure the space between your TV tabletop and the bottom of the TV display area so your prospective soundbar won’t block either the screen or the TV’s IR remote control sensor.

#6308. The Sky Today on Friday, November 13: Spot Mirach’s Ghost

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Friday the 13th with something spooky: a ghost in the constellation Andromeda. This evening, point your telescope toward 2nd-magnitude Mirach (Beta [β] Andromedae), already nearly 60° high in the east by 7 P.M. local time. One of the Princess’ brightest stars, Mirach is a cool, reddish M-type giant. It lies some 200 light-years away and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly as our Sun.

But Mirach is not quite our target — we’re looking for its so-called ghost, just 6.8’ northwest of the star. You’ll need a big scope to see it, but look carefully: Can you spot a faint smudge of light, about 4’ across, close to the star? This is the Ghost of Mirach, a far more distant elliptical galaxy glowing at 10th magnitude and cataloged as NGC 404. It lies some 8 million to 10 million light-years away, just beyond the gravitational bounds of our Local Group of galaxies. It’s called a ghost because it appears almost like a ghostly image of the bright star Mirach, which dominates the view.

#6307. Scientists learn why a sensitive part of our DNA is actually a built-in shield against the sun

Under early-Earth ultraviolet light, thymine broke faster than uracil but steered the damage toward lesions that can be undone.

Before Earth had an ozone layer to block the sun, early life was constantly blasted by intense ultraviolet light. Because of this, scientists were puzzled by why DNA evolved using a chemical building block called thymine. It takes significantly more UV damage than similar molecules.

Thymine initially looked like a big evolutionary mistake. But new measurements reveal a clever survival trick.

The specific damage thymine takes from UV light is incredibly easy to undo. Instead of being a weak point, thymine actually takes the hit so the rest of the DNA stays safe.

Peter Rentzepis and two members of his lab at Texas A&M University, Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar, exposed both letters to the same ultraviolet light and tracked what broke.

Thymine fell apart faster overall, but it formed the permanent kind of lesion more slowly than uracil did.

“We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form,” said Khosh Abady, a research assistant in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering.

He added that this suggests early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight by controlling the damage and making it easier to repair, not by avoiding the damage.

RNA and DNA each spell their code with four letters, and three are shared. RNA uses uracil. DNA uses thymine, which is uracil with one small carbon group attached.

Thymine absorbs ultraviolet light most strongly at 265 nanometers, and uracil at 259. A six-nanometer shift matters on a planet with no ozone layer.

Models of the early Sun suggest the light reaching the surface was about 2.5 times more intense at thymine’s peak than at uracil’s. Thymine’s absorption band is also about 9 percent wider.

On paper, life swapped in the letter that catches more of the most damaging light.

The team dissolved each letter in water and froze the solutions at 5°F (-15°C) in quartz cells. Then they shone a narrow ultraviolet LED on them at 265 nanometers.

Freezing pushes the molecules out of the growing ice into crowded pockets, which mimics how letters sit side by side in a strand, where the main lesions form between neighbors.

Over an hour of exposure, the team tracked three things. They measured how much light the molecules absorbed and how much they glowed.

They also recorded each sample’s Raman spectrum, a fingerprint of chemical bonds that shifts as bonds break and form.

Judged by how fast its absorption faded, thymine degraded in ultraviolet light nearly three times as fast as uracil. It also glowed about 4.5 times more brightly.

The team reads the glow as a sign that excited thymine lingers longer before settling down, which leaves more time for reactions.

Ultraviolet light produces two main lesions between neighboring letters. In one, two letters lock together in a small ring. The team classifies this lesion as reversible, since it can come apart again without enzymes.

In the other, the letters bond in a way that rearranges them for good.

Thymine formed the permanent kind at a rate of 1.56 per minute in the team’s fitted curves, against 2.04 for uracil. So thymine took more damage but steered it toward the repairable kind.

The authors wrote that the letters appear to have been selected to keep damage confined and reversible, not to avoid it. Repair enzymes did not yet exist.

“In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule,” Khosh Abady said.

The experiment used single letters packed in ice, not strands of DNA or RNA in water. The authors wrote that the frozen setup does not capture the full chemistry of real genetic molecules.

The 2.5-fold difference in early sunlight is a modeled figure that depends on the atmosphere assumed.

A separate test, published this month, found that life’s letters were not consistently tougher under ultraviolet light than alternatives that life does not use. So the sunscreen idea is one explanation among several.

There is also a later, better-known reason for thymine. Cytosine, another DNA letter, slowly decays into uracil on its own, and a cell that used uracil as a normal letter could not tell that mistake from the real thing.

That defense needs repair enzymes, so the authors place it after the sunlight pressure, as a reinforcement rather than the origin.

The measured signatures of thymine and uracil, before and after damage, have a second use.

The team wrote that the data could help read ultraviolet damage in whole cells, which would show whether a water-treatment lamp has actually inactivated microbes.

Next, the lab plans to look earlier in the story. The open question is what brought the letters together in the first place, and whether some arrived on meteorites rather than forming on Earth.

The full study was published in the journal PNAS.

#6306. New study shows that a home video game using brain stimulation electrodes can help depression, but a fake version worked just as well, confusing scientists

People with depression used a brain stimulation kit at home for six weeks, but a switched-off sham with a decoy game worked just as well.

Strap on a cap wired to a small box, play a video game on a tablet for half an hour, and repeat every weekday for six weeks. Adults with major depression who applied that brain stimulation at home got better.

So did the adults whose cap switched itself off after a few seconds and whose game was a look-alike with the training taken out.

The cap carried a weak electric current through the scalp, a low-cost form of brain stimulation that researchers are testing for home use. The video game was built to exercise attention, memory and self-control.

Together they were no more effective than the fake pair, and the authors wrote that the combination isn’t ready for clinics in its current form.

What the trial did show is that people with depression can run a treatment like this at home, which was the question the trial was built to answer first.

Mor Nahum of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem led the trial, called DiSCoVeR. In an interview with Earth.com, she said the improvement on both sides was the first of two surprises.

“Substantial improvement in control groups is in fact well known in depression research, including in medication trials, but it is still striking to see it so clearly in a carefully matched control condition,” Nahum said.

The 109 people in the final analysis were between 18 and 65 years, and had major depression that had lasted between a month and five years.

They were recruited at Hadassah Medical Center in Jerusalem, LMU Munich and Riga Stradins University. Most were already taking antidepressants on a steady dose, and about four in ten were in talk therapy, which the trial allowed.

Each person had up to five sessions in the clinic to learn the kit, then took it home. Software guided the placement of the electrodes on the scalp before each session. The target was 30 sessions of 30 minutes, on weekdays, over six weeks.

Half the group, chosen at random, got the real current and a game that got harder as players got better. The other half got a sham: a cap that ramped up and then stopped, plus a slower game with the same look and none of the training exercises.

Neither the participants nor the doctors scoring their symptoms knew who had which.

Of the 109, 86 finished at least 20 sessions, which cleared the bar the researchers had set in advance: a majority finishing at least 20. Participants completed nearly 2,500 sessions across the three countries.

Side effects were about as common in both groups. Two people in the active group were hospitalized, one with suicidal thoughts and one with worsening depression, and both cases were judged unlikely to be related to the treatment.

Symptoms were scored on a scale from 0 to 60, and the average at the start was about 25. After six weeks, the active group had dropped 7.3 points and the sham group 8.2. A gap that small could easily be chance, and it was no different a month later.

On one well-being questionnaire, the sham group improved more. People in the active group also reported feeling more pressure during their sessions in the last two weeks, and less confident in their own performance.

Researchers asked participants at week one and week six which group they thought they were in. In the first week, 57 percent of the active group guessed right and 35 percent of the sham group did.

By the end, the two groups guessed about equally well, at 59 and 65 percent respectively. Those who believed they were in the sham group improved less than the others, whichever group they were really in.

Nahum told Earth.com that about a quarter of participants consistently held that belief, and that the gap in their scores appeared early.

She called it an exploratory finding. Nahum said the team cannot yet tell whether low expectations held people back or whether people who were not improving concluded they must be on the sham.

“But it suggests that what patients believe about their treatment may matter a great deal,” she said.

Because the team always paired the real current and the real game, the trial can’t say what either one does alone. Nahum said the two may even have interfered with each other, given the extra pressure the active group reported.

The paper advises a four-way design next time: current alone, game alone, both, and neither.

Other recent trials found the same. Pairing this kind of brain stimulation with psychotherapy or with a digital program added no benefit either. A 2025 review concluded that its effects on depression are small and inconsistent.

Follow-up here stopped at ten weeks, so lasting effects are unknown. And the researchers can’t rule out that playing a game every day had effects of its own, such as relaxation.

Nahum and several co-authors have applied for a patent for the game used in the active arm.

Asked by Earth.com what someone curious about home brain stimulation should take from the trial, Nahum drew a line between the home setup and the shop shelf.

“I would strongly advise against buying devices online and self-treating,” she said. Trial participants were trained in the clinic and monitored remotely, she said, and anyone struggling with depression should first talk to a mental health professional.

What drove the improvement in both groups is the open question. Nahum listed the candidates: the stimulation, the training, expectations, engagement, ongoing care, or simply the structure of returning to a treatment every day.

Next, she wants to measure expectations before treatment starts and test whether they predict who improves. The bigger problem, in her view, is the average itself.

“Depression is very heterogeneous, and an average result can hide people who respond well alongside others who don’t,” she said.

The markers that would sort patients that way, clinical, cognitive or brain-based, are what she plans to look for next.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#6305. The Universe May Be Twice as Old as We Think. A Rebellious Theory Says We Can Prove It.

A model built only on matter we can see still nails the Big Bang’s first elements—and doubles the universe’s estimated age.

We can all agree that the universe is more or less 13.8 billion years old, right? That figure comes largely from the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite, which mapped the cosmic microwave background (the leftover glow of the Big Bang), with results released in 2013 and finalized in 2018. Ground-based observations from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) in Chile later arrived at nearly the same number. Both fit the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). There’s just one problem: That age depends on the existence of dark matter and dark energy, neither of which has ever been directly detected.

What would happen if we tried to figure out the age of the universe with only tangible matter and energy? Physicists Rajendra Gupta and Nikolaos Samaras of the University of Ottawa are asking this exact question. Frustrated by theories built on invisible matter and on an expansion driven by energy no one has detected, Gupta and Samaras developed their own cosmological framework, called covarying coupling constants plus tired light (CCC+TL). In this model, only quantities measured in units of length change together over cosmic time, while dimensionless constants stay fixed. The researchers tested whether CCC+TL could reproduce Big Bang nucleosynthesis, the process that forged the universe’s first light elements in its earliest minutes. It could. The same model puts the age of the universe at 26.7 billion years, nearly twice the standard estimate.

“In this framework, only quantities with explicit length dimensionality covary through a universal scaling function, while dimensionless constants and dimensionless ratios remain invariant,” the researchers wrote in a study recently published in Universe, also adding that their model ensures “[Big Bang nucleosynthesis] predictions are preserved.”

In 1929, astronomer Edwin Hubble (namesake of the Hubble Space Telescope) found that the farther away a galaxy is, the more its light is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum. Most astronomers came to read this redshift as evidence that the universe is expanding. That same year, astronomer Fritz Zwicky proposed a different explanation, known as “tired light”: Light gradually loses energy as it crosses vast distances, so light from more distant galaxies arrives redder simply because it has traveled farther. Most cosmologists set tired light aside decades ago, but Gupta has revived a version of it as part of CCC+TL.

Gupta and Samaras are challenging the prevailing view. In ΛCDM, the hot plasma of the newborn universe expanded and cooled, and ordinary (baryonic) matter then gathered inside vast haloes of dark matter to form galaxies. Dark energy, meanwhile, is thought to be driving the universe’s accelerating expansion. CCC+TL abandons both of those hypotheses. Instead, the new theory modifies the standard equations for gravity and expansion, yet still reproduces the observed expansion of the universe and the amounts of hydrogen, helium, and other light elements formed in its first minutes. It can also reproduce galactic rotation curves, which measure how fast stars and gas orbit at different distances from a galaxy’s center.

Gupta has also argued, in earlier papers, that CCC+TL gets around the objections that sank tired light the first time, including time dilation. In an expanding universe, light from distant supernovae is stretched out in time, so the supernovae seem to brighten and fade more slowly than nearby ones. Simple tired-light models don’t provide an explanation for that phenomenon. Time dilation itself comes from Einstein: Because light always travels at the same speed, observers moving at different speeds experience time differently, and time passes more slowly for someone moving very fast. That’s why astronauts aboard the International Space Station, which circles Earth at about 17,500 mph (28,000 kph), age very slightly more slowly than people on the ground. Gupta says his new theory works better because the tired-light effect runs alongside cosmic expansion, instead of replacing it.

Dark matter and dark energy have been used to explain phenomena that would otherwise make no sense. CCC+TL tries to explain the same phenomena with modified gravitational effects instead. It also changes the cosmic timeline. In a 2023 paper, Gupta used CCC+TL to put the age of the universe at 26.7 billion years. That would give the first galaxies billions of years longer to form, which could explain surprisingly mature galaxies in the early universe and the Methuselah star, which some age estimates make older than the universe itself.

“A central requirement for any alternative cosmology is that it preserves the key empirical successes of standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis,” Samaras and Gupta wrote. They concluded that “the CCC+TL model is consistent with the [Big Bang]-predicted primordial helium and other light-element observations.”

The idea remains well outside the mainstream. Most cosmologists still see ΛCDM, for all its unknowns, as the best fit to a wide range of observations, from the cosmic microwave background to how galaxies are spread across the sky. CCC+TL will have to pass many more tests to win them over.

#6304. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6303. An Apollo astronaut flew tree seeds around the Moon, but no one kept track of where the trees were planted when they returned to Earth

Apollo 14 carried tree seeds around the Moon in 1971, creating Moon Trees across America. Artemis I launched a new generation of seeds in 2022.

In 1971, Apollo 14 command module pilot Stuart Roosa carried tree seeds in his personal kit while he orbited the Moon. The seeds came from five species: loblolly pine, sycamore, sweetgum, redwood and Douglas fir.

Back on Earth, the seeds grew into seedlings that were later planted across the United States. Yet no list was ever kept of where the trees ended up.

Since 1996, a NASA scientist has kept a list of the surviving trees, built from reports sent in by the public. In 2022, a new batch of tree seeds flew around the Moon on Artemis I.

Roosa was born in Durango, Colorado, in 1933. In the early 1950s, he worked for the Forest Service as a smokejumper, a firefighter who parachutes in to fight forest fires.

Ed Cliff, then chief of the Forest Service, knew Roosa from his smokejumping days and contacted him about bringing seeds into space. Stan Krugman of the Forest Service was put in charge of the project and selected the seeds.

Roosa carried “possibly 2,000 or more seeds” in a canister, according to NASA’s history office.

After the return to Earth, the seed bags burst open during decontamination. The seeds were scattered around the chamber and exposed to vacuum, and it was thought they might not survive.

A first attempt to germinate some of the seeds in Houston worked, but the seedlings did not survive long because the facilities there were inadequate.

A year later, the remaining seeds went to Forest Service stations in Gulfport, Mississippi, and Placerville, California, which received the redwoods and Douglas firs. Many of the seeds, and later cuttings, grew into viable seedlings.

Most of the seedlings were given to state forestry organizations in 1975 and 1976, to be planted as part of the nation’s bicentennial celebration. They went to sites reportedly in 40 different states.

A loblolly pine was planted at the White House on January 19, 1977. That tree is no longer alive.

A sycamore was planted at the visitor center of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland on June 9, 1977. It is still growing there.

Others went to the International Forest of Friendship and to Washington Square in Philadelphia, where the tree has since died. A few were planted abroad, including in Brazil and Switzerland.

After more than 40 years, NASA reports, there is “no discernable difference” between Moon trees and trees grown from seeds that stayed on Earth.

The list began after Joan Goble, a third-grade teacher in Indiana, asked NASA for information about the trees in 1996.

Her request led Dr. David R. Williams, now a retired curator at NASA’s National Space Science Data Center, to start a list of Moon trees. Dozens of people have since sent in information about others.

The list sorts the trees into living, status unknown and no longer alive. Survivors include trees at the Indiana Statehouse, the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery and Capitol Park in Sacramento.

Second-generation trees, grown from seeds or cuttings of mature Moon trees, are also growing around the world. Roosa’s daughter, Rosemary Roosa, has promoted planting them.

Artemis I launched on November 16, 2022, and its Orion spacecraft splashed down on December 11. Nearly 2,000 tree seeds flew on board, according to a 2023 NASA announcement.

The seeds traveled about 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) beyond the Moon and about 270,000 miles (435,000 kilometers) from Earth. They came from sycamores, sweetgums, Douglas firs, loblolly pines and giant sequoias.

Kasten Dumroese is a research plant physiologist and national nursery specialist with the Forest Service’s Rocky Mountain Research Station.

“Four of the five species flown on the original Moon Trees mission were onboard again,” Dumroese said.

Before the flight, the Forest Service X-rayed the seeds to check their internal tissue. The scans were repeated after the flight to look for any changes caused by spaceflight.

“We made sure the seeds were filled with good tissue before we sent them up,” said Kayla Herriman, a seed extractory manager with the Forest Service in Bend, Oregon.

NASA’s call for applications, which closed on October 6, 2023, drew more than 1,000 submissions from organizations. NASA scheduled distribution in four planting cycles, from spring 2024 through fall 2025.

The first batch went to almost 50 institutions across the contiguous United States, NASA said when it announced the first recipients in April 2024.

On June 4, 2024, a sweetgum seedling was planted on the U.S. Capitol grounds, with the crew of Artemis II in attendance.

The seedling had left the Forest Service’s Moscow Forest Science Laboratory while dormant and spent three months at the U.S. Botanic Garden before the ceremony.

“I actually feel a little jealous, because that little sweetgum has been to the moon, and it has come back,” said Reid Wiseman, the Artemis II commander.

#6302. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests.

The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development.

However, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss.

"I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein, a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email.

Using information from two U.S. insurance databases, the researchers analyzed 224,870 pregnancies in people ages 12 to 55. More than 218,230 of these patients were treated for respiratory tract infections, and over 6,630 were treated for acne, between conception and the end of the first trimester. About 4,385 of the women filled a prescription for doxycycline during that time frame, while the others received an alternative antibiotic.

Among women with respiratory infections, those prescribed doxycycline had a 40% to 54% higher risk of pregnancy loss, compared with those prescribed amoxicillin, another broad-spectrum antibiotic in a different class. The exact level of risk varied between the two databases.

The researchers also compared the doxycycline users against women prescribed macrolides, the class of antibiotics that includes azithromycin (or "Z-Pak"). Again, the doxycycline users saw a higher risk — 39% and 36% higher, respectively.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Among the patients treated for acne, doxycycline users had a 49% higher risk of pregnancy loss in one database than those given the antibiotic clindamycin. In the second database, though, the difference wasn't statistically significant. Winterstein said that may be because there were fewer patients included in that analysis.

Overall, doxycycline was associated with seven to 11 additional pregnancy losses per 100 pregnancies, compared with the other antibiotic options assessed, the researchers reported.

The researchers examined the risk associated with taking various antibiotics in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

It is not yet clear how the drug might contribute to pregnancy loss. Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that the antibiotic itself caused those losses, which included miscarriages and stillbirths. (Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of pregnancy, whereas stillbirth refers to pregnancy loss after the 20th week.)

Animal studies hint that doxycycline could interfere with early placental development, potentially making it harder for the placenta to support a growing pregnancy, Luke Grzeskowiak, an associate professor and clinical pharmacist at Flinders University in Australia who was not involved in the study, said in an email.

The study authors also noted in their report that the drug may have direct effects on the developing embryo. But these explanations remain hypothetical; the researchers have not established that either mechanism occurs in humans.

"Pregnancy loss affects around one in four pregnancies and can happen for many reasons," Grzeskowiak noted. Although doxycycline exposure may add to that risk, taking the antibiotic does not necessarily mean pregnancy loss will occur. The available data suggests that it is just one risk factor among many.

Because doxycycline may be prescribed before a pregnancy is recognized, doctors should consider the possibility of pregnancy when prescribing this drug to women of reproductive age, particularly those who are sexually active, Grzeskowiak suggested. That does not mean doctors should avoid prescribing the antibiotic to these women, he emphasized; rather, clinicians should consider pregnancy plans and medical history when choosing a treatment.

In some cases, doxycycline may still be the best option for a severe infection, Winterstein told Live Science, and that infection could itself put a pregnancy at risk. But for less-serious infections, safer alternatives may be available, she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6300. Nov. 13, 1971: Mariner 9 orbits Mars

On May 30, 1971, Mariner 9 launched, setting off on its mission to Mars. On Nov. 13, 167 days later, it entered orbit around Mars, making it the first spacecraft to orbit another planet.

With Mariner 8, Mariner 9 was one half of the Mars 71 mission. But when Mariner 8 launched on May 9, it failed to achieve orbit and tumbled out of the sky after five minutes, crashing into the Atlantic Ocean. As a result, Mariner 9 inherited all of 8’s goals in addition to its own, giving it an extensive list of objectives: surface mapping, atmospheric monitoring and analysis, surface data collection, and returning around 3,000 photographs.

When Mariner 9 arrived at Mars, it encountered a global dust storm. Because it had been designed for longevity, the orbiter was able to wait out the storm and begin its mission afterwards. (Soviet spacecraft Mars 2 and Mars 3 did not fare as well.) Over the course of about a year, Mariner 9 returned 7,329 photos and mapped 85% of the martian surface. It also revealed a dynamic and active world – including shield volcanoes, dry river valleys, ice at the martian poles – and gave researchers close-up views of the surfaces of Phobos and Deimos.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.
