#6297. REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127

The smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years. Most of these scopes focus primarily on electronic imaging, though, and while amateur astronomers may marvel at the images, they also still enjoy the simple pleasure of looking directly through a telescope.

That’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach. Rather than replacing direct observing with a screen-based experience, the SP127 combines a traditional 5-inch (127 millimeters) f/15 Maksutov-Cassegrain telescope with a smart guidance and imaging system.

At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount. But looks can be deceiving.

The secret lies in that “finder.” On closer inspection, it is not a finder at all, but a 2.1-inch (53 mm) f/4 ED refractor outfitted with a digital camera. This second optical tube is the heart of the SP127’s electronically assisted system, serving as both guide scope and imager. The guide scope determines the telescope’s position through plate solving, slews to selected targets, maintains tracking, and captures images. Spectrum Optics also includes the same intelligent camera and 53 mm refractor in its separately sold SPi53 Smart Telescope system.

The camera is built around a Sony IMX662 CMOS color sensor with 2.9-micrometer pixels and a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels. It includes 64 gigabytes of onboard storage.

The MirroSky app, available for iOS and Android, is central to the SP127’s operation. It controls target selection, image capture, live stacking, and display, while the guide scope and camera work together to find objects and produce live-stacked images.

Meanwhile, the Maksutov is dedicated primarily to visual observing. The optical tube weighs approximately 6.5 pounds (2.95 kilograms) and measures 14.6 inches (370 mm) long. A Vixen-style dovetail makes it easy to remove the optical tube from the mount. Total weight for the assembled SP127 is about 26 pounds (11.8 kg).

In addition to the guide scope/imager, the SP127 comes with a 25 mm Plössl eyepiece, a 90° 1¼” star diagonal, a screw-on visual back, an adjustable tripod with steel legs 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) in diameter, cables, an AC adapter, and a Bahtinov focusing mask for the guide scope. The camera’s nosepiece is also internally threaded to accept standard 1¼” filters.

In its standard configuration, the included camera photographs through the 53 mm refractor rather than the Maksutov. Although the camera is removable, Spectrum Optics recommends a separate camera for imaging through the Maksutov because its long focal length and narrow field are not well-suited to the included camera’s plate-solving system. That doesn’t mean you have to invest in more equipment, though; I took some very nice shots of the Moon simply by holding my iPhone to the Mak’s 25 mm eyepiece.

The SP127’s hybrid arrangement works well in practice. After the user selects a target in the app, the guide scope directs the mount to the correct location, then tracks the sky. The observer can view the target visually through the Maksutov while the guide scope stacks and displays images via the app. A word of caution, however: Be careful not to shake the instrument when looking through the eyepiece. Even a slight motion will blur the image being photographed.

Like most Maksutov-Cassegrain systems, the SP127 excels at medium and high magnifications. Its 1,900 mm focal length is especially well-suited for observing the Moon, planets, planetary nebulae, and double stars.

Spectrum Optics MirroSky SkyPilot SP127 Primary Optical Tube: 5-inch 127mm Maksutov-Cassegrain Focal Length: 1900mm Length: 14.6 inches (370 mm) Focal Ratio: f/15 Guide Scope Optical Tube: 53mm ED refractor with Sony IMX662 CMOS camera Focal Length: 200mm Focal Ratio: f/4 Assembled Weight: 26 lbs. (11.8 kg) Mount Payload: 9 lbs. (4 kg) Connectivity: built-in Wi-Fi, 2.4 and 5 GHz Camera Storage: 64GB onboard storage Tripod: Full-size adjustable steel-leg tripod Eyepiece: 25mm Plössl Price: $999.99 Contact: Spectrum Optics 2175 S Grand Ave Santa Ana, CA 92705 1-888-879-5143 spectrumoi.com

For this review, I arranged to receive a sample SP127 directly from Spectrum Optics. It arrived securely packed and in perfect condition.

Setup was easy, thanks to the well-illustrated paper manual that came with the scope. After I aligned the guide scope with the Maksutov during the day, as the instructions suggested, the scope was ready to go. I had everything together in under half an hour.

Control is handled entirely through the MirroSky app. To initialize the scope to the sky, the system uses onboard sensors combined with date, time, and location information supplied by the connected smart device. The camera includes dual-band Wi‑Fi capability supporting both 2.4 and 5 gigahertz connections. During use, the app’s interface was straightforward and easy to navigate. Target acquisition was quick and accurate. Chosen objects were always centered in the field of view. The app also provides guided tours and a database containing more than 100,000 stars, solar system members, and deep-sky sights.

Tracking performance was accurate for visual observations and short-exposure imaging. Since the SP127 uses an alt-azimuth mount, field rotation may become evident around the edges with longer exposures.

The SP127 can be powered by eight user-supplied AA batteries in the mount, a suitable external 12-volt power source, or the included AC adapter.

I found that the Maksutov performed very well. Lunar views were well-defined, with crater walls, rilles, and other surface features standing out crisply. I was especially impressed when, in moments of steady seeing, the SP127 detected a few of the craterlets on the floor of Plato. It passed another tough test by resolving Schröter’s Valley, a sinuous rille near craters Aristarchus and Herodotus.

Planetary performance also proved impressive. Multiple cloud bands as well as the Great Red Spot were clearly visible on Jupiter, and shadows cast by Galilean moons could also be seen on the planet’s cloud tops.

Double stars were another strong point, thanks to the long focal length. The Trapezium in the Orion Nebula, for instance, was striking. The included eyepiece did well, but the view really sparkled when I swapped in my own eyepieces with shorter focal lengths.

Throughout it all, I was very impressed with the crispness of the images, showing the high quality of the Maksutov’s optics. Like most catadioptric telescopes, the SP127 focuses by moving the primary mirror. This takes tight manufacturing tolerances to maintain a precise focus without tilting the mirror. I found that alignment stayed spot-on after swapping eyepieces and refocusing the view.

I was equally impressed with the imaging results using the 53 mm guide scope. The app allows you to customize settings, including gain, exposure length, number of frames to capture, and dark frames. After I experimented with the settings, the Orion Nebula appeared in vivid color after only two minutes of exposure, even as it was setting in my light-polluted sky. The Pleiades also recorded beautifully, although not all members squeezed into the guide scope’s approximately 1.6° by 0.9° field. The Horsehead Nebula, the Whirlpool Galaxy, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, and more displayed details exceeding what you might expect from such a small aperture, especially after post-processing using apps like PixInsight, GIMP, and Photoshop.

The SkyPilot 127 is one of the most original entries in today’s smart telescope market. For observers who still enjoy looking through an eyepiece but appreciate the convenience of app-driven targeting and imaging, the SP127 offers something genuinely special. In a small but growing group of smart telescopes that combine traditional eyepiece observing with integrated electronic imaging, the SP127’s hybrid design makes it an appealing bridge between conventional astronomy and the smart telescope revolution.

Contributing Editor Phil Harrington received the Walter Scott Houston Award in 2018 for his lifelong work in astronomy.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space. Science, eaea5324. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aea5324

#6295. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

#6294. Ancient European Trees Just Solved a 3,500-Year-Old Cold Case: When Did Babylon Fall?

It’s a detective story jam-packed with historical ramifications.

Mesopotamia in the second millennium B.C.E. left behind an unusually rich written record. Yet historians still can’t agree on exact dates. Rival chronologies hinge on when Babylon fell, and they disagree about that by more than a century, so it’s hard to line up events across the Near East and eastern Mediterranean.

Babylon may be best known today from sacred texts, from the Hebrew Bible to the Quran. But long before those books were written, the fabled city on the Euphrates was the capital of one of the ancient world’s great powers. It was home to King Hammurabi, whose law code ranks among the oldest written legal systems on record.

On paper, Mesopotamia should be easy to date. Scribes left behind king lists, administrative records, and royal inscriptions that lay out what happened and in what order. The catch is that they counted time by kings’ reigns, not calendar years, so the whole sequence had no fixed link to dates we’d recognize.

Venus should have fixed that. Babylonian scribes watched the sky for omens, believing the planets’ movements foretold harvests, wars, and the fate of the king. During the reign of King Ammisaduqa, they wrote down when Venus appeared and disappeared on the horizon, dating each sighting by year of his reign. Because Ammisaduqa also appears in the king lists, those sightings tie the whole sequence of kings to the sky, and modern astronomers can work out when they could have happened.

The trouble is that Venus repeats itself, so the observations fit several possible points in history. That left four rival timelines (high, middle, low, and ultra-low) that place Babylon’s fall as much as 150 years apart.

The key witness turned out to be wood. Timbers from ancient buildings in Anatolia, in modern-day Turkey, had tree rings that could be lined up in order, but no one could pin that sequence to actual calendar years. Yet those same sites are tied to Mesopotamia through the Old Assyrian trade network, whose merchants left records that line up with Mesopotamian kings. So dating the wood would date the history, too.

Now, researchers believe they’ve done just that. In a study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team wrote that they used “patterns captured in single-year radiocarbon measurements from tree rings to calendar-date Anatolian wood samples from sites with direct archaeological links to Mesopotamia.”

Led by Charlotte Pearson of the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research at the University of Arizona, the team measured carbon-14 in single annual growth rings from the Anatolian timbers. They partnered with ETH Zurich’s Laboratory of Ion Beam Physics to make the measurements.

To anchor the Anatolian wood, the team turned to precisely dated Tyrolean stone pine from Austria and oak from Germany. That pinned the Anatolian tree-ring sequence to the calendar, with each ring now tied to a specific year from 2072 to 744 B.C.E. The payoff reaches beyond Mesopotamia. “These data can now be used for samples from anywhere else in the world,” Kurt Nicolussi of the University of Innsbruck told Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF, in a translated report.

“Tree-ring dates are combined with archaeological and high-resolution ice-core evidence to evaluate the competing chronological frameworks for Mesopotamia between 2000 and 1500 B.C.E.,” the authors wrote.

The verdict: The Old Babylonian Empire fell in 1587 B.C.E. The authors found “strong support” for what they call a middle-low chronology, a timeline that falls between the middle and low models.

“This illustrates how high-precision radiocarbon methods, in combination with other interdisciplinary evidence, can enhance chronological accuracy across many time periods,” the authors wrote.

#6293. How to watch Starship Flight 15

SpaceX is set to launch its 15th test flight of Starship on Friday, Nov. 13. For the first time, the company will try to catch both stages of the rocket — the Super Heavy booster and the upper stage, which SpaceX calls “Ship” — with the arms of its launch tower. If it works, Starship will become the first orbital rocket ever recovered in full.

SpaceX is targeting a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (4:45 p.m. CST) Friday from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas, pending regulatory approval. Starship launch dates often slip, so check the company’s Flight 15 mission page for the latest.

SpaceX’s live webcast begins about 30 minutes before liftoff — around 5:15 p.m. EST if the launch holds at the start of the window. You can stream it on the Flight 15 mission page or on SpaceX’s X account.

If you’re near the Texas-Mexico border, crowds typically gather on South Padre Island, across the bay from the launch site. On the Mexican side, the public beach at Playa Bagdad offers a head-on view of the launch tower.

About six and a half minutes after liftoff, Super Heavy should fly back to Starbase and be plucked from the air by the tower’s “chopstick” arms, a catch SpaceX has made three times before. Ship will continue to orbit and release 26 of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink V3 satellites.

The real test comes the next day. Ship will circle Earth about 14 times at roughly 171 miles (275 kilometers) up before heading home. Until now, Ship’s test flights have ended with a practice landing at sea: it flips upright, and then fires its engines to set down gently on the water. This time, it will run that same maneuver over Starbase and hopefully settle into the tower’s arms instead. SpaceX’s flight timeline puts the catch about 22 and a half hours after launch — around 4:18 p.m. EST on Saturday, Nov. 14, if Starship lifts off on time.

SpaceX says Ship will head for the tower only if flight controllers confirm that every system it needs for reentry, the landing burn, and the final approach is healthy. If not, the company can bring Ship down at preplanned spots in the Pacific, with go/no-go checks built into the flight for splashdowns near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

#6292. No Central Air? No Sweat. These Tested Window Air Conditioners Cool Down Spaces Fast

We got our hands on multiple units and looked for models that are quiet, energy-efficient, and easy to install.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When it’s really hot or humid out, opening a window or turning on a fan only gets you so far, especially when your house feels like it’s holding onto heat long after the sun goes down. If you’ve ever tried to sleep in a hot, airless room, you know how quickly feeling “a little warm” turns into being completely miserable. For homeowners and renters without central air conditioning, the standard solutions are typically ductless air conditioners, freestanding units, or window air conditioners.

Window air conditioning units work by pulling in warm and humid air, cooling and drying it, and sending it back into the room while pushing heat outside. Most units double as fans, and many now include dehumidifier modes, which is something you’ll appreciate on those sticky, midsummer days when the air feels truly soupy. And, unlike central air, a window air conditioner can run on a generator during a blackout. That’s a major plus in extreme climates.

The tricky part is finding a window air conditioner that actually fits your space, is easy to install, and doesn’t drive up your energy bill. We looked at a range of models with various features and specs. Some of these we’ve tested hands-on, and a few are newer standouts with great customer reviews. Continue reading to find the window air conditioners that are worth buying right now.

As someone who lives in an older home without ductwork, I’ve owned quite a few window air conditioners over the years in my never-ending quest to find the perfect unit for my house and family. Beyond this personal experience, I worked with a team of testers here at Popular Mechanics to find units on the market that feature reliable construction, notable energy efficiency, quiet operation, and exceptional functionality.

I also spoke with industry expert Kim Lincoln to make sure our recommendations check every box. She’s a third-generation HVAC expert and sales trainer at Service Experts with 25 years of experience.

For the most recent update, I added three new products. The GE 14,000-BTU Smart Window Air Conditioner is an excellent air conditioner for cooling spA/Ces up to about 700 square feet (like living rooms or some open space floors). Meanwhile, the LG ThinQ Window Air Conditioner includes the best collection of smart features I’ve seen out of a window AC.

The GE Profile ClearView sits on your windowsill, taking up just a few inches of space while preserving most of your view. This type of AC may not work well in older homes with radiators below the windows, but it’s a great option if you have the clearance space.

We love that you can still fully open the window for fresh air, which is a rare win for a window unit. This AC also uses an inverter compressor for efficient, low-noise cooling, which makes it perfect for offices and nurseries. The digital controls are simple and straightforward, and the app makes it easy to adjust settings without needing to walk over to the unit itself. Installation can be a bit of a project due to its shape and length, so plan on having an extra set of hands close by.

Full GE Profile ClearView Window Air Conditioner Review

There’s a reason my family owns several of these air conditioners: it’s a no-frills model that’s inexpensive, reliable, and well-sized for rooms up to 150 square feet (most small- to medium-sized bedrooms). My family was gifted one, and we loved it so much that we purchased more for our kids’ bedrooms because the knobs are easy to use and there are no smart features for them to mess with.

This air conditioner has a simple two-knob control system. The top knob controls the cooling setting, while the bottom knob controls fan speed, and you have the option to run the fan with or without cooling. The appliance’s thermostat cycles the air conditioner on and off to keep the temperature within range based on the temperature you set with the top knob.

The lack of smart tech means it can only be controlled from the knobs. That was a pro for us, but it may be a con for other shoppers. Still, it’s an efficient window unit that won’t hurt your wallet and its washable filter saves you money on having to buy replacements.

Full Frigidaire FFRA051WAE Window Air Conditioner Review

This Windmill AC stands out for combining energy efficiency with reliable performance and quiet operation, all of which make it especially useful in bedrooms up to 350 square feet. Its CEER rating of 15 is one of the strongest in this lineup, and the inverter design helps it maintain temperature without the hard stop-start cycling of many traditional window units.

On lower settings, our testing team found it to run subtly enough for overnight use, and we loved how the display dims automatically for better sleep. The fan alone can handle cooler evenings, while hotter days call for full cooling. The app is intuitive and truly smart, letting you adjust settings remotely and sending helpful alerts when it’s time to clean or replace the filter. Maintenance is a key factor in air conditioner longevity, so that’s a huge plus.

Similar in design to our best overall pick, this Midea window unit uses a true U shape so the window can close deeper into the body of the air conditioner. The end benefit is quieter cooling: Once it’s properly installed, the window acts as a sound barrier between the compressor outside and your room inside. That makes it a strong choice for offices up to 350 square feet, where excess noise can become an unwelcome distraction.

The U shape also means the window does not need to be all the way closed—you can lift the window midway up the body of the unit, and let in air from the outside without uninstalling the entire air conditioner. The biggest issue with this option is that it requires a more skilled hand when installing it, with many customers reporting difficulty doing it themselves.

We’ve been using this beast of an AC to cool the entire first floor of our home with great success for a few summers now. It’s a solid pick for larger rooms up to 700 square feet, per the unit’s specifications, which is about the total square footage of our first-floor foyer, dining room, living room, kitchen, and pantry. Depending on your home’s layout and airflow, it’s hard to guarantee it will successfully and sufficiently cool multiple spaces, but it packs serious power for big rooms, too. That said, it’s noisier than other models, so take that into consideration.

While we didn’t need smart features, it’s nice that it connects to Wi-Fi so you can control settings from your phone (or with the included remote), and the interface is straightforward. The unit is designed with energy efficiency in mind, which helps to keep operating costs reasonable for its size. Installation is fairly standard with the included kit, though the unit is heavy, so you’ll want an extra set of hands. It’s likely you’ll need a support bracket, too.

Overall, this is a dependable option for cooling bigger living spaces without overcomplicating things or having to install a mini-split.

If you need an AC that can bring down the temperature quickly in a medium-sized room, take a look at this model. This smart GE unit impressed our team with speed, cooling a 100-square-foot room from 85 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit in about 15 minutes, and it’s rated for spaces up to 350 square feet. That powerful fan helps move cool air farther into the room, so it’s a good fit if you want quick relief without jumping up to an oversized unit that will drive up energy costs for no reason.

The standout feature here (and the reason for that great performance) is the powerful fan, which kept air moving even when full cooling wasn’t necessary. We love the unit’s eco mode, which cycles the compressor and fan to maintain temperature without overworking the unit. We found the installation to be manageable, but easier with two people. We love that GE includes insulation, though you may need to purchase some additional products to create a perfect seal depending on your window. The main drawback is the app, which was difficult to connect to, despite troubleshooting. Customer service at GE is great, though, and the one-year warranty gives peace of mind.

Read Full GE 8,000 BTU Air Conditioner Review

This LG 6,000 BTU unit is a strong small-space pick that adds genuinely useful smart features without overcomplicating things. It’s designed for rooms up to about 250 square feet, making it a better option for bedrooms and home offices than larger living areas.

It pairs easily with LG’s ThinQ app, so you can adjust temperature, fan speed, and schedules from your phone (or with Alexa or Google Assistant). While it’s easy to find an app-controlled window AC these days, this one stands out from the pack a bit. LG has a deeper smart-home ecosystem than most brands manufacturing window ACs, and this model brings that app control, voice-assistant compatibility, scheduling, energy-saver mode, and filter alerts to rooms up to 250 square feet. Customers find the cooling performance is consistent, and the unit includes practical touches like a filter alert and energy saver mode. It’s not the quietest or most powerful option out there, but it balances size, features, and price well for a smart-enabled window AC.

Air conditioners are rated in British thermal units (BTUs), which indicate how much space they can effectively cool. A unit that’s too small will run constantly and never quite get there, but one that’s too large will cool too quickly without removing enough humidity. This leaves the room feeling clammy and uncomfortable.

That’s why several of our superlatives are organized around room size and use case, rather than just standout features. A 5,000-BTU unit may be a smart pick for a small bedroom, dorm room, or compact home office, while an 8,000-BTU model is better suited to a medium-size room where faster cooling and stronger air movement matter. Larger living rooms, open layouts, or rooms with high ceilings may need 10,000 BTUs or more. As a loose rule of thumb, small bedrooms may need around 5,000 to 8,000 BTUs, while larger living areas can require 10,000 BTUs or more. Lincoln says the most common issue is choosing a unit that is too small.

“A window unit may be able to knock down the temperature right near the unit, but that doesn’t mean it’s doing a good job across the full area,” says Lincoln. “In oversized rooms or open floor plans, I see units run nearly nonstop while still leaving parts of the space warm and damp.” She says that’s when customers note a room feels cool but clammy. “The system may be lowering temperature near the unit, but it isn’t really winning the humidity battle across the space.”

This also explains why a powerful fan, efficient compressor, or smart app only matters if it supports the way you’ll actually use the A/C. A stronger fan is most helpful when it moves cool air across a medium or large room, while an efficient inverter unit is especially useful in bedrooms or offices where the AC may run for long stretches. Smart controls are most valuable when they make daily use easier, whether that means scheduling, remote adjustments, energy tracking, or filter reminders.

Before you buy, measure your window—twice. Window units are designed for specific opening widths and heights, and some, like casement or sliding windows, require specialized models. Even with careful planning, you may strike out at first.

“Not every window unit fits every window well, even when the box says it should,” says Lincoln. “Consumers need to look at more than width. The window style, the sash opening, the weight of the unit, and the need for support all matter.” A window unit should be level side-to-side and pitched slightly outward so condensed water drains out of the house—not into your room.

It’s important to consider the unit’s weight, too. Larger units may require a bracket or homemade support to avoid strain and damage to the window and air conditioner.

CEER stands for Combined Energy Efficiency Ratio, and it tells you how efficiently a unit uses electricity over time, not just when it’s actively cooling. Older ratings like EER measure efficiency only while the compressor is running. CEER goes a step further by also factoring in energy used when the unit is idle, like when it’s on standby or cycling on and off throughout the day.

Efficient units use less electricity to deliver the same cooling power, which matters if you’re running the A/C daily through peak summer. Features like programmable timers, eco modes, and inverter technology can further reduce energy use.

When it comes to energy efficiency, Lincoln says it’s just as much about the rating as it is about how you install the unit—specifically how well-sealed the gaps are.

“The best sealing materials are simple, cheap, and worth the effort,” says Lincoln. Foam weatherstripping, rope caulk, and other similar materials can go a long way. “I’ve seen homeowners blame the A/C when the real issue was a half-inch gap letting hot, wet air pour in all afternoon. Sealing is not just about stopping heat. It’s about stopping humidity. And in summer comfort, that distinction matters.”

If you’re used to old-school window units, you’re familiar with the buzz and crackle as they cool. Thankfully, advancements in technology have resolved that issue a bit. Not all A/Cs are created equal when it comes to sound, though. “Traditional window units tend to be louder because they cycle on and off more abruptly,” shares Lincoln. She says inverter models are often better for bedrooms and offices. An inverter unit works more like a dimmer switch than an on/off switch. Instead of turning the AC off, it slows down once it reaches your desired temperature and maintains it by running at a lower, steady speed. “The difference between a hard compressor kick and a steadier low hum is noticeable when you live with it every night.” We’ve noted this feature on the units we reviewed when applicable.

Check the decibel (dB) rating, too. Units in the low 40s are considered quiet, while anything pushing 60 dB or higher can be disruptive, especially at night.

Modern air conditioners do more than just cool. Remote controls, WiFi connectivity, and app integration let you adjust settings from anywhere. Some units include dehumidifier modes, sleep settings, or directional airflow controls that improve comfort without cranking the temperature.

Lincoln says that the “extras” worth paying for don’t often top the specs list, though. “The features worth paying for aren’t always the flashy ones. A lot of people get distracted by phone apps and forget the basics,” she says of most consumers. “The extra features I’d actually pay attention to are variable-speed operation, a true dry mode if you live in a humid climate, auto-restart after a power outage, and a thermostat or sensor that’s actually useful for where people sit or sleep.”

“Window units can be efficient, but only if the install is right,” says our expert Kim Lincoln. “A poorly sealed window AC is basically paying to cool the air around the leak.”

With the right setup, though, window air conditioners can be surprisingly efficient — especially compared to cooling an entire home with central air. Window units give you the option of cooling only the rooms you need at that time.

The key is choosing the right size and looking for models with strong CEER ratings or Energy Star certification. Features like eco mode, programmable timers, and inverter compressors can further reduce energy use by preventing the unit from constantly running at full power.

BTUs measure cooling power, and getting this right is critical. As a baseline, you’ll need about 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. For example, a 150-square-foot room typically calls for a 5,000–6,000 BTU unit. You should also factor in real-world conditions: increase capacity for sunny rooms, kitchens, or higher ceilings, and scale down slightly for shaded spaces.

“When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close.” Be careful about over-purchasing power, though. That doesn’t mean your room will be cooler. Oversizing can lead to quick cooling without proper dehumidification, while undersizing can leave the unit running constantly.

“This is the least glamorous advice and still one of the most important,” says Lincoln. “Clean filters are still one of the biggest performance factors. For window units, the filter should be checked regularly and cleaned about once a month during heavy cooling season, sometimes more often if the home has pets, dust, smoke, renovation debris, or high traffic.”

Most manufacturer specs recommend cleaning the filter every two to four weeks during periods of heavy use, as well. A clogged filter restricts airflow, which can reduce efficiency and force the unit to work harder. The good news is that most window AC filters are washable—just remove, rinse, let dry, and reinstall. Keeping the filter clean helps maintain strong airflow, improves cooling performance, and can extend the lifespan of the unit. If your AC does not have a washable filter, Lincoln recommends keeping a spare on hand. If your AC does not have smart features or a filter reminder, it’s clutch to add this task to your personal calendar so it is not neglected.

#6291. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 14: Venus and Mercury in Virgo

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M.Sunset: 4:44 P.M.Moonrise: 11:33 A.M.Moonset: 8:56 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time on the 15th, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6289. Which Kindle Should You Buy? We Break Down Each Model

Here's what to know about the newest models and which ones are worth buying.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There's something about reading on a Kindle that makes it easier to get through your reading list. Instead of carrying a stack of books or getting distracted by phone notifications, you can keep thousands of titles in one lightweight e-reader. Whether you're reading on your commute, relaxing by the pool, or finishing one more chapter before bed, a Kindle makes it easy to take your library wherever you go.

And Amazon's latest lineup gives readers even more reasons to make the switch. In October 2026, the company introduced a completely redesigned collection of Kindles, including updated versions of its entry-level Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft. The new devices feature thinner and lighter designs, flush-front displays, and faster performance. Amazon also introduced its first aluminum Kindle, giving its smallest e-reader a more premium feel, along with new colors like Ube, Alpine Sky, and Seaglass Green.

The differences between the models go beyond their designs. The standard Kindle is still an excellent option for readers who want something small and affordable, while the Paperwhite offers a larger display that comes with adjustable warm lighting and waterproof protection. For readers who prefer graphic novels and illustrated books, the Colorsoft brings color to an E Ink display. And if you're interested in taking notes or marking up documents, Amazon's Kindle Scribe lineup offers an entirely different experience.

With so many models to choose from, finding the right Kindle ultimately comes down to how and where you like to read. We've broken down the best Kindles available right now, so read on to find the one that's right for you.

The Kindle Paperwhite continues to hit the sweet spot between features, portability, and price. Amazon's newest version is thinner and lighter than its predecessor, with a redesigned 7-inch display that offers exceptionally sharp text and improved contrast. It's comfortable enough to hold for extended reading sessions while offering more screen space than the standard Kindle.

It also has adjustable warm light, letting you shift the display's tone from white to amber for more comfortable nighttime reading. The waterproof design makes it a great choice for reading by the pool or in the bathtub, while its battery can last up to 12 weeks on a single charge. For most readers, the Paperwhite offers everything they need without the higher price of Amazon's premium models.

Amazon's entry-level Kindle has always been a great option for readers who value portability, and the latest version makes an even stronger case for choosing the smaller model. With a 6-inch display, it's the most pocket-friendly Kindle in the lineup, making it particularly convenient for commuting, traveling, or reading on the go.

Amazon redesigned the device with a thinner body and a flush-front display for a more modern look. Books also open 30 percent faster than on the previous model. The 300 PPI display keeps text sharp, and the battery lasts up to six weeks on a charge. You won't get the Paperwhite's waterproof protection or adjustable warm light, but for readers who simply want an easy way to carry their favorite books, the standard Kindle is an excellent choice.

The standard Kindle gets a premium makeover with Amazon's first aluminum version. It keeps the same compact 6-inch display as the entry-level model but replaces the traditional exterior with a sleek, matte aluminum back made with 80 percent recycled aluminum. The result is a more refined e-reader that still fits easily into a pocket or small bag.

Another advantage is the additional storage. The aluminum Kindle comes with 32GB, double the capacity of the standard version, and doesn't include lock-screen advertisements. It's also offered in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green, making it one of the more visually distinctive Kindles available. If you like the portability of the smallest Kindle but want something that feels a little more premium, this version is worth the upgrade.

The Paperwhite Signature Edition takes everything that makes the standard Paperwhite great and adds a few premium features. Like its more affordable counterpart, it has a sharp 7-inch display, waterproof protection, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. However, it also comes with an aluminum rear housing, 32GB of storage, and an auto-adjusting front light that responds to your surroundings.

The latest version adds double-tap page turning, letting you advance through your book with a simple gesture. It also supports charging through a compatible pogo-pin dock (sold separately) or the USB-C port. None of these features are essential for enjoying a book, but they make the reading experience more convenient. For anyone who spends hours reading every week, the Signature Edition offers a particularly polished experience.

If you frequently read comics, graphic novels, travel guides, or other illustrated books, the Kindle Colorsoft makes a compelling case for upgrading from a traditional black-and-white e-reader. Its 7-inch color E Ink display brings book covers, photographs, and illustrations to life while maintaining the paper-like appearance that makes Kindles comfortable to read.

Amazon redesigned the latest Colorsoft with improved display technology intended to provide richer color, better contrast, and more consistent illumination. It also has adjustable warm lighting and waterproof protection, making it versatile enough for reading at home or while traveling. The battery lasts up to eight weeks, which is less than the Paperwhite but still impressive compared to most tablets. For readers who want to see their books in color without sacrificing the distraction-free Kindle experience, the Colorsoft is an excellent option.

The Colorsoft Signature Edition is Amazon's most feature-packed dedicated reading Kindle. It combines the standard Colorsoft color E Ink display with additional features designed to make everyday reading easier, including an auto-adjusting front light, double-tap page turning, and charging through a compatible dock.

Its aluminum housing gives it a premium look and feel, while the 32GB of storage provides plenty of room for books, audiobooks, comics, and graphic novels. It also comes in Graphite and Fig, the latter offering a more colorful alternative to the traditional black e-reader. Readers who primarily enjoy text-based novels probably don't need to spend extra for these upgrades. But if you frequently read illustrated content and want Amazon's best color-reading features in a compact Kindle, the Signature Edition is a strong choice.

For young readers who gravitate toward graphic novels, comics, and illustrated stories, the Kindle Colorsoft Kids offers a more engaging way to read. Its 7-inch color E Ink display brings illustrations and book covers to life without the distracting apps, videos, and games found on traditional tablets.

The newest version also features an adjustable warm light, waterproof protection, and up to eight weeks of battery life. Parents get access to Amazon's parental controls, while the included one-year Kids+ subscription provides plenty of books to explore. The Colorsoft Kids costs considerably more than the other children's Kindles, but its color display makes it especially appealing for young readers who enjoy books where illustrations are as important as the words.

The newest full-featured Kindle Scribe is much more than a traditional e-reader. With an expansive 11-inch display and an included Premium Pen, it doubles as a digital notebook for jotting down ideas, taking meeting notes, reviewing documents, and annotating books. The redesigned device is thinner and lighter than previous generations, with faster writing and page turns that make the experience feel more natural.

Amazon also introduced productivity features that set the Scribe apart from its smaller e-readers. You can import documents from supported cloud services, organize notebooks, and use AI-powered tools to search and summarize notes. The built-in front light makes it practical for reading and writing in different lighting conditions. While the larger size and higher price won't appeal to everyone, the Scribe is one of Amazon's most versatile devices for readers who also enjoy writing.

Amazon's Kindles come in several screen sizes, and choosing the right one depends largely on how and where you read. The standard Kindle has a compact 6-inch display that's particularly convenient for commuting and traveling. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft models increase the screen size to 7 inches, offering more room for text and illustrations without becoming significantly less portable.

For readers who want to write notes or work with documents, the Kindle Scribe models have much larger 11-inch displays. They're better suited for desk use or studying, though their size makes them less convenient to carry around.

Most Kindles use black-and-white E Ink displays, which are ideal for traditional books and text-based reading. However, the Colorsoft and Scribe Colorsoft offer color displays that can make a noticeable difference when reading comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, or documents with colorful charts.

If you primarily read novels, there's little reason to spend extra for a color display. However, readers who enjoy illustrated content may appreciate the additional versatility.

The standard Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft each offer 16GB of storage, which is more than enough for thousands of traditional e-books. Signature Edition models and the aluminum Kindle increase that capacity to 32GB, while select Scribe models offer up to 64GB.

Battery life is also impressive across the lineup. The newest standard Kindle offers up to six weeks on a single charge, while the Paperwhite can last up to 12 weeks. The Colorsoft models promise up to eight weeks, depending on usage. For the Scribe lineup, battery life depends on whether you're primarily reading or writing with the included stylus; frequent note-taking uses more power.

Amazon's more expensive Kindles offer features that can make reading more convenient, including waterproof protection, adjustable warm lighting, and auto-adjusting brightness. The new Paperwhite Signature Edition and Colorsoft Signature Edition also support double-tap page turning and charging through an optional dock.

For many readers, these upgrades aren't necessary. However, they're worth considering if you frequently read at night, take your Kindle near water, or want a more premium device that you'll use every day.

#6288. The Beachy Bungalow in La Jolla That Let Me Cosplay as a California Surfer

As a travel editor, people are always shocked when I tell them I’ve only been to California once. Especially when I tell them that my one trip was to Napa—a blur of rolling hills and full-bodied Cabernets. There are so many sunny cities I’ve dreamed of visiting in the Golden State, but the world is big, and the flights from NYC are long. This fall, I finally got the push I needed to see more of America's most populous state: One of my dearest friends decided to get married in San Diego. My husband and I booked our plane tickets without blinking an eye, eager to see two fabulous people tie the knot and experience some excellent beaches, sunsets, and burritos along the way.

While deciding where to hunker down during our visit, I couldn’t get La Jolla out of my mind. A vibey little surf town about 14 miles north of downtown San Diego, it seemed like the perfect base—just a short drive from the wedding venue in Rancho Santa Fe, and boasting plenty of iconic restaurants (the Marine Room!) and attractions (the sea lions!). When I found Hamilton I, an adorable bungalow just three blocks from the beach, available for rent through Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy, it sealed the deal. I nabbed it for three nights.

Check Availability at Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy

Tucked into a long, quiet side street off of one of La Jolla’s main roads, I knew Hamilton I would do us just fine from the moment our Uber dropped us off. We had spent the first two days of our trip in downtown San Diego, getting our fill of the city; the energy in this neighborhood was just different. Imagine the shaka sign, but as a feeling. We walked past Hamilton II, the bungalow’s sister property, before reaching our home's front door, where a keypad granted us entrance. The first thing I noticed upon stepping inside was the sun-dappled living room, with its massive TV and walls bursting with beachy-cool art. The next was the basket of snacks in the kitchen left by the hosts—a huge green flag in my book.

Happy to have some space to spread out, my husband and I dropped our suitcases and toured the rest of the home, which has three small bedrooms (two kings, one queen), two bathrooms, a washer and dryer (huge news for us city folk), and a dining nook with a long oval table and eight rattan chairs. We chose to sleep in the largest of the three bedrooms, the only one with an en suite bathroom, and used the other two bedrooms as our closets. As I mentioned, the bedrooms aren’t huge and share walls at the back of the bungalow, so the property is probably best suited to close groups of friends or families with kids.

The biggest draw of the home is the backyard, accessible via a sliding door in the living room. You come to California for the sunshine, and the compact but well-designed outdoor space allows guests plenty of opportunities to soak up every last ray. Depending on the time of day, you can bounce between a smattering of adjustable lounge chairs, a small dipping pool, an outdoor dining table next to a barbecue, and a lounge area with a firepit. Despite backing onto a busy street, the backyard feels like a little oasis, thanks in part to the walls of greenery bordering the space.

Over the course of our three days at Hamilton I, my husband and I hit most of La Jolla’s most popular attractions, either by foot or via a quick Uber ride. We managed to dip our toes in the salty sea, kayak over to La Jolla Cove, wander through nearby Coronado, peruse the shops in La Jolla Village, eat a shocking amount of Mexican food, attend a magazine-worthy wedding, and so much more in so little time, returning to the bungalow to sleep peacefully each night. Every amenity we could have needed had already been thought of by the host, from extra blankets and fans to strong Wi-Fi and water pressure. We also had 24/7 access to a dedicated hospitality manager, who sent a couple of check-in texts throughout our stay to make sure everything was hunky-dory (it was).

Every morning, we’d make coffee in the kitchen or pick it up from a nearby café, passing longboarders and surfboard-toters along the way, then sit out in the backyard to wake ourselves up with the ultimate duo: caffeine and vitamin D. Having an entire home to call our own was such a treat, and cosplaying as a laid-back surfer couple, if only for a few days, was a welcome salve for our New York City–dwelling souls. I mean, who can be mad when you have the beach a few blocks away and laundry in-unit?

By the end of our stay, it was clear to us why our friends decided to get married in San Diego, and why it has become an increasingly popular travel destination as of late: Good vibes go a long way, and this part of California has them in spades. Also, the burritos are as good as people say. I’ll be back for more adventures in the Golden State—and I’ll be looking for a home away from home just like Hamilton I when that time comes.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6287. The 8 Best Cheap Washing Machines for Fresh Laundry on a Budget

If you don’t mind skipping the bells and whistles, these affordable appliances—all priced under $1,000—get the job done.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You can get by without a washing machine, especially if you live near a laundromat, though you can’t beat the luxury of having one in your basement.

Many of today’s high-end washers have price tags in the thousands, but if you’re shopping on a budget, the good news is that you can find cheap washing machines that cost much less and work just as well.

Whether you want a full-size washing machine to handle your family’s oversized loads or a more compact model that can be tucked in a closet, there are a number of highly rated appliances well under $1,000. Some even have high-end features that are generally reserved for more expensive machines, such as a built-in water faucet or sanitization cycle, which helps make laundry day quicker and easier than ever.

For more of the best washing machines available today, check out our top picks for front-loading washers, top-loading washers, and all-in-one washer-dryers.

To offer a selection of cheap washing machines that will work for every home and budget, we looked for the top products in each of the categories outlined above—full-size, portable, and manual—and only included highly rated models that cost less than $1,000. All the products have a rating of three stars or higher, and we prioritized washing machines from well-regarded brands with good customer service and warranties.

For our most recent update, we reviewed current pricing and availability across major retailers, replaced outdated models, and added new picks based on what offers the best features for different situations. We also consulted with Amy Chernoff at AJ Madison to make sure our buying advice reflects how today’s budget washers compare to their pricier counterparts.

A full-size, high-efficiency washing machine for under $700 isn’t easy to find, but this model from Whirlpool checks all the boxes. The top-loading machine has a 3.5-cubic-foot capacity, and it uses a dual-action spiral agitator to deeply clean your clothing.

This popular washing machine comes with a wide selection of cycles and settings to customize each load. It has options for quick washes, delicates, and bulky items, as well as an auto-sensing feature that uses just the right amount of water for each load.

If all you want is a dependable full-size washer for the least money, this Amana is where I’d start. The high-efficiency agitator and wash system dig into everyday dirt and stains, and I like that the stainless steel wash basket won’t chip or rust over the years the way porcelain-tubs can. When you need to fully soak a bulky load like towels or a comforter, the Deep Water Wash option fills the tub to the max instead of leaving you stuck with an auto-sensed water level.

There’s also an automatic fabric softener dispenser that releases at the right point in the cycle, plus a Quick Wash for small, lightly soiled loads. And thanks to the Late Lid Lock, you get extra time to toss in a stray sock or forgotten shirt before the spin cycle kicks in.

The trade-off is no Wi-Fi, no app, and no sanitize cycle. For a no-frills workhorse that just gets laundry clean, though, those are easy features to give up.

This Samsung washing machine packs an impressive number of features, including a quick wash cycle that completes a full load in under 30 minutes. It has an extra-large 5.2-cubic-foot drum that can easily handle king-size comforters and bulky loads, and a built-in faucet at the back of the tub for pretreating stains before starting a cycle.

Unlike most washers in this price range, Samsung includes Wi-Fi connectivity and smart home integration, so you can remotely start, stop, and schedule loads and get end-of-cycle alerts on your phone. It also works with Alexa and Google Assistant.

Other features include a soft-close lid, a manual water-level override for filling the tub higher than the automatic sensor would, and Energy Star certification, which many budget washers lack. The only notable omission is a steam cycle, but that’s a minor trade-off at this price.

At 4.5 cubic feet, this GE model has a drum that’s big enough to wash a comforter or a week’s worth of clothes for a small family. Similar to the Amana, this GE washer uses a dual-action agitator, where the top half moves independently from the bottom to guide clothes through the water while the lower section agitates along the bottom of the basket. That two-piece design circulates clothes more evenly than a single-piece agitator, which tends to push everything in one direction.

Stainless steel lines the tub instead of porcelain-coated plastic, so chipping and rust spots aren’t a concern down the road. You can also manually control the water level up to 26 gallons—something other high-efficiency washers don’t let you do.

A sanitize cycle hits temperatures high enough to kill 99 percent of bacteria, which is useful for towels, bedding, and sweaty gym clothes. There is no app support, so you can’t start a load remotely or get a notification when a cycle finishes. Instead, you’ll have to listen for the buzzer or set your own timer.

The agitator in this Whirlpool can pop out, setting it apart from other machines on this list. You can remove it when you need to fit something bulky, like a comforter or sleeping bag, then snap it back in for everyday loads. The capacity shifts from 4.2 to 4.3 cubic feet with the agitator removed, and bulky items sit flatter without bunching up around a center post.

In addition to its removable agitator, there are twelve wash cycles that give you several options for different loads. A presoak option lets you loosen stains and wash in a single run instead of soaking separately in a sink or bucket. The sanitize cycle uses higher water temperatures to kill bacteria, which is useful for bedding and gym clothes. A soft-close lid keeps it from slamming every time you load clothes.

While other models on this list let you manually override the water level to fully submerge a bulky comforter or sleeping bag, this Whirlpool relies on auto-sensing only, so you’re stuck with whatever the sensor decides is enough.

Samsung’s front-load washer can easily stack with a matching dryer to cut your laundry footprint roughly in half. It has a depth at just over 31 inches with the door closed, so it can tuck into tighter spaces than a standard front-loader. The drum itself is also 4.5 cubic feet with a stainless steel interior, matching the capacity of the full-size top-loaders on this list.

Samsung’s vibration reduction system dampens noise and movement during spin cycles, which matters if the washer sits on an upper floor or shares a wall with a living space. You can pause a cycle and add a forgotten item through the door—something some front-loaders won’t let you do.

Ten wash cycles cover the basics, plus there’s a prewash and a soak option. However, there’s no sanitizing cycle, so you may have a harder time hitting the higher temperature needed to kill bacteria in towels or bedding.

Other washers push hair around and hope it goes down the drain, which can clog pipes over time. This Maytag model features a built-in filter that catches pet hair during the wash cycle, collecting it so you can clean it out later. The Pet Pro option adds extra water and a deep rinse specifically to work with that filter, so hair actually lifts off fabric instead of reattaching during the spin.

The drum is 4.7 cubic feet with a stainless steel basket and agitator. An Extra Power option adds a pre-wash and extra agitation to any cycle, which helps get rid of stains, rather than pretreating by hand. There’s also a built-in water faucet on the machine itself for spot-treating stains before you start a load.

There are 11 wash cycles, plus an option to add more water when auto-sensing isn’t enough. It’s a good option to have when washing heavy blankets or dog beds that need to be fully submerged. Note, though, that there isn’t a delay start feature, so you can’t load it and schedule it to run so it finishes right when you get home from work.

This GE model features app support, allowing you to start, stop, and monitor cycles from your phone. It can also send you notifications when a load finishes and download extra wash cycles that weren’t on the machine when you bought it. It works with Alexa and Google Assistant too, so you can check on a load with just your voice.

The drum is a spacious 5.0 cubic feet with an impeller instead of an agitator, so there’s more room for bulky items. Antimicrobial protection is built into the tub cover, dispenser drawer, and drain hose to help keep mildew and odor from building up between washes. There’s a sanitize cycle too, while the dispenser has separate slots for liquid detergent, detergent pods, fabric softener, and bleach.

There is no steam option and the agitator isn’t as tough on stains, but the GE is a great option if you’re looking for smart features.

When shopping for a cheap washing machine, you’ll need to decide whether you want a full-size, portable, or manual model. Most of the full-size options you’ll find under $1,000 are top-loading washers, and they offer a large capacity as well as more settings and cycles. However, there are a few select front-loading models in this price range, as well.

For those with limited space, portable washing machines have a more compact footprint and can easily be stored in a closet. However, these machines typically require a faucet connection for operation and don’t always wring out your clothes, making them trickier to dry.

Finally, manual washing machines are the most affordable, but they require a bit of elbow grease for operation. You usually have to crank or agitate the machine by hand, but these models don’t require electricity, making them ideal for camping or off-the-grid living.

The capacity of washing machines is generally measured in cubic feet. Most standard-size appliances have a capacity of 3.5 to 5 cubic feet and are suitable for average households. For reference, a washer with a capacity of 4.5 cubic feet can wash a king-size comforter. If you have a small household, you’ll likely be fine with a smaller-capacity washing machine. A compact machine with 2.3 cubic feet can wash about 6 towels.

Cheap washing machines often have fewer wash cycles than more expensive models. In general, you’ll find most affordable washers have between eight and 12 wash cycles, including standard ones like quick or light wash, delicates, and heavy-duty. There are also several temperature settings on most washers, and some allow you to select the water level and soil level as well. These basics are generally sufficient for most loads of laundry, but if you want more advanced settings—such as sanitization or fabric-specific cycles—you may need to spend a little extra.

To help save money on operation costs, you may want to look for a high-efficiency washing machine, frequently abbreviated as HE. These models use 20 to 66 percent less water, saving around 6,000 gallons of water per year for an average family. You may also want to look for an Energy Star-certified appliance, which uses 25 percent less energy than standard models.

Amy Chernoff, VP of Marketing and Appliance Expert at AJ Madison, says that budget washing machines will still get the job done. The differences are in everything else—build quality, noise, fabric care, and how long the machine holds up under heavy use.

The trade-offs at lower price points are less about cleaning power and more about small details. “You are usually giving up fabric care refinement and overall build quality rather than basic cleaning performance,” Chernoff says.

That means simpler drum movement, fewer specialty cycles, and suspension systems that don’t dampen vibration as well. Over the years, a pricier washer tends to be gentler on your clothes, but for most people washing everyday loads, a more affordable model gets the job done.

A cheap washer doesn’t automatically mean higher utility bills. “Many affordable modern models are still quite efficient, especially if they carry an Energy Star certification,” Chernoff says. Some of the machines on this list are Energy Star certified, so they should be just as efficient as more expensive models.

A single person or couple can usually get by with 3.5 to 4.5 cubic feet. Families should look at 4.5 cubic feet or larger, which offers enough room for bedding, towels, and several days of clothes in one load.

“Choosing a slightly larger machine than you think you need can reduce the number of loads per week and make laundry more convenient over time,” Chernoff says. Every washer on this list falls between 4.2 and 5.0 cubic feet, so even the smallest option here handles a full week of laundry for two people without cramming everything in.
