#6278. The 4 Best Nugget Ice Makers to Get Soft, Chewable Ice at Home

We tried out the best versions that sit on your countertop and churn out several pounds of ice per day.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a fan of soft, crunchy, chewable ice, a countertop nugget ice maker can bring that sought-after texture right to your kitchen. Also known as pellet or “Sonic” ice, nugget ice is made of compacted flakes that are soft, airy, and easy to munch on and slow to melt. It’s especially good for soaking up the flavor of whatever you’re drinking, making it a favorite for everything from sodas and cocktails to iced coffee and just plain, old water.

Nugget ice makers have become increasingly popular home appliances, but the machines themselves can be relatively advanced. They require more complex internal components than basic ice makers, and thus tend to cost more—often starting around $400 for a high-quality design. Depending on the appliance, you’ll also find features like large ice baskets, water reservoirs, self-cleaning cycles, and high daily production.

To help you find the right machine for your kitchen and budget, we researched, tested, and reviewed the best nugget ice makers from manufacturers such as GE, Euhomy, and Gevi. Whether you’re entertaining friends or just ready to retire the built-in ice maker on your fridge, these are the models we recommend.

The selection of countertop nugget ice makers available from trusted and reliable brands is limited, so we dug to find and test the best options by considering product specs, capabilities, and prices. During testing, we ran cleaning cycles to get the systems ready to go. We then timed how long it took for each machine to produce one batch of ice, and again for how long it took to fill the ice basket completely.

Throughout our setup and testing, we evaluated each model’s ease of use, reliability, and the quality of the ice they made. We took note of any cool or unique features like app compatibility, storage options, and more.

Our home appliance writer, Nick Hilden, also spoke with Jessica Randhawa, founder and head chef at the Forked Spoon, and Yu Jiang Zhao, mixologist, about what to keep in mind when choosing a nugget ice maker.

This was the nugget ice maker that made our tester throw out their ice trays once and for all. It takes everything we liked about the previous version, GE Profile Opal 2.0, and boosts the ice production speed, upgrades a smattering of components and functions to make it easier to clean and enhance its lifespan, and includes an external water tank and ice scoop to boot.

We’ve found that it churns out ice at a rapid enough pace to keep round after round of cold beverages for a sizable gathering. It has an easy-to-use app that offers smart functions such as scheduling alerts for maintenance. Additionally, its sleek design has a timeless vibe that won’t look dated two years from now.

It’s got a footprint nearly that of two shoeboxes side by side, which is a bit big for a smaller kitchen. It can also get somewhat noisy when it’s actively producing ice—about the volume of a loud refrigerator—though it’s basically silent when it’s just keeping it cool. But if you’re looking for reliable, convenient ice on demand, there’s none better.

Full GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget Ice Maker Review

This little unit packs a surprising amount of ice production power, churning out as much or more than any of the larger models on our list (40 pounds per day). Additionally, its compact size makes it perfect when you have less countertop real estate to spare, or if you want portable ice production for a backyard barbecue or camping in an RV.

Our testing found that it churns out ice fast, with the first batch in under ten minutes. Its operation is as straightforward as they come, and its cleaning is easier than most other machines, with an automatic cleaning mode that requires little effort on your part besides draining out the water that runs through the system.

All told, it’s a great ice maker for anyone who wants a no-fuss model that will look nice in the kitchen without taking up too much space. It also offers similar performance to larger, more expensive models, minus the roomy storage capacity.

Full Euhomy Smart Countertop Nugget Ice Maker Review

The Gevi 2.0 is the kind of ice maker you won’t mind taking up prime countertop real estate, given its polished design. The bin holds almost five pounds of ice (the largest capacity on our list), and the machine has thick insulation on all sides to keep cubes frozen for longer.

One of our favorite features is the door on the ice maker that opens to a 90-degree angle. To achieve this, the Gevi ditches the viewing window that’s present on other models, but this design choice allows you to pull the ice basket forward. This made it very simple to scoop our pellet ice once the container was full.

The instruction manual says that it takes about 15 to 30 minutes for the first cubes to form, but I noticed a couple of pellets had dropped around the 9-minute and 20-second mark. They were fairly wet to start but began forming more compactly over time and were the perfect, crunchy texture. However, it takes a few hours to get a full basket, which is tricky if you need ice immediately.

The water reservoir is kind of awkward to access with the door style, but the Gevi also comes with a hose that hooks up to your tap if you want it to fill automatically.

Ice makers require regular cleaning to ensure both quality ice and a long lifespan for the unit, and we found that the Silonn Nugget Ice Maker makes it easier than the rest. Most notable is its self-cleaning function, which is as effortless as it gets: Push a button to start the clean cycle, and let it do its thing. This is unlike other models that require removing a lot of parts or going through a complex series of steps. We also like that you can just toss its removable water reservoir and ice bin in the dishwasher, with no hoses or bottles to clean.

In terms of operation, it delivers most everything you want from a solid ice maker. It produces a hefty 44 pounds of ice a day, and its 2.6-pound bin holds plenty of ice for several rounds of drinks. It’s straightforward and intuitive to use—all you need to do is fill it with water—and is somewhere in the middle in terms of countertop footprint.

It does produce more noise than other popular models. Most nugget ice makers crank the volume up when actually producing ice, but this one has a noticeable hum even when on standby. For reliable ice with no-hassle cleaning, however, it’s hard to beat.

One of the key benefits to a good nugget ice maker is that it can churn out upward of 30 or even 40 pounds a day, making it ideal for hosting large, thirsty groups. The best models can have the first cubes ready within about 10 minutes, and will have a full bin within an hour or so.

A countertop machine, of course, can’t store three dozen pounds of ice. Most ice bins hold 1 to 3 pounds, which will replenish as depleted. It’s rare to go through a full bin, so unless you expect to host a particularly large number of people, this may not be the most pressing concern.

The vast majority of home nugget ice makers are equipped with a built-in water reservoir. These are great for at-home use as they don’t require installation and are highly portable, making it easy to pack them away for storage.

The larger the tank, the more ice the machine will produce. However, this also means that it will require more counter space. Models with smaller water reservoirs eat up less room, but require you to refill them frequently.

You can plug some models directly into your home plumbing system, which eliminates the need to fill a tank as it will draw water continuously. These, however, may require expert installation depending on your DIY skills, and will usually end up in a cabinet or closet rather than on your countertop.

The bigger the ice maker, the more countertop space it uses, so consider how much room you have in your kitchen. Our top pick, the GE Opal 2.0, is a great ice maker, but it has a pretty big footprint for a kitchen with limited counter real estate. When measuring dimensions, don’t forget about the inch or two of clearance that you’ll need for the fan, which keeps the motor from overheating.

If you have the space for it, Randhawa recommends placing the model in the pantry. This not only keeps your countertops open, but can muffle the operating noise.

“With most nugget ice machines you should expect some sound when operating on standby, but they can get pretty noisy when producing ice,” says Randhawa. “That might not matter in the din and clatter of cocktail hour, but could be more bothersome when things quiet down.”

It’s difficult to determine how loud a particular model will be without actually hearing it as there is no standardized noise rating. Your best bet is to check reviews for what previous buyers or reviewers have to say.

Nugget ice makers use a large metal cylinder with an auger inside that freezes as the machine runs. Water then pours into the cylinder and starts to freeze along the walls, producing a thin sheet of ice that the auger scrapes and pushes through the machine as ice flakes.

The machine then squeezes the flakes to push out excess water and compacts them into small, airy pieces so that what you end up with is a soft, porous nugget of ice that (probably) won’t crack your teeth when you chew it. They’re ideal for beverages because they take on the flavor of the drink, and there’s really nothing quite like that taste and texture.

Unfortunately, nugget ice makers aren’t ready to use right out of the box. Once you’ve gotten your unit, it’s best to let it sit upright on a level surface for at least two hours before plugging it in. This helps the refrigerant settle. The time may vary depending on the model you have, so it’s best to refer to the manual for the specific time.

You should also run the self-cleaning or sanitizing cycle before getting started. A combination of equal parts water and vinegar can get the job done. By doing this, you’re clearing the machine of any lingering residue or grime that could affect the clarity and taste of the ice. After completing a cycle with the solution, you can run another one with just water for a full wash-down.

Nugget ice makers are not a set-it-and-forget-it machine—they require regular cleaning and additional upkeep. One of the main concerns with these appliances is calcium buildup, or limescale, which accumulates if you have hard tap water.

To prevent this, it’s a good rule of thumb to occasionally descale your ice maker. You can make a 1:1 solution of distilled white vinegar and water, put it in the reservoir, and run it through the machine for a few cycles. Another tip is to use filtered water.

Self-cleaning modes should be run at least once a month, but if you’re a frequent party host, every other week couldn’t hurt. If you’re using a nugget ice maker that hooks up to a water line, you would benefit from an inline filter. Vacuuming the fan and blowing out the condenser also prevents clogs from dust and debris that may cause overheating.

Nugget ice makers make anywhere from 24 to 44 pounds of ice in a 24-hour period. They start up relatively quickly (as little as 10 minutes) but may take up to an hour to fully fill the ice bin.

Models with large capacity bins are best for big groups, while smaller ones are good for home bars and entertaining a couple of friends. Some options have ice bins that are insulated to keep ice from melting, while others just have an acrylic bucket in which ice melts faster.

For those that regularly host large gatherings or just don’t want to run out of nugget ice, we suggest running your nugget ice maker the day before and storing nugget ice in the freezer. Alternatively, you could stockpile extra nugget ice just in case you’re burning through more than expected the day of your event.

Most nugget ice machines are countertop units, so special installation isn’t necessary. We’ve specifically recommended models that don’t require you to install them, as the vast majority of owners will want something user-friendly and easy to store when not in use. Typically speaking, ice makers that require installation are heavy-duty, professional-grade units for serving large groups of people.

According to Randhawa, “Most nugget ice machines just use a standard outlet and require space around it to vent per the instructions.” Without proper ventilation space, your unit could overheat and break down.

“[Nugget ice makers] run compressors constantly and consume more power than people think it should for a countertop appliance,” says Zhao. “If energy consumption is a concern to you, look for those with an Energy Star rating, and factor in that it will likely be running a good portion of the day.”

Newer models tend to need about 0.05 to 1 kilowatt-hour per day, depending on your ice use. The more ice you make, the more power you’ll need. That’s roughly the equivalent of an energy-efficient fridge, which increases electric bills by about $10 to $15 a month.

If you always want ice at the ready, then you’ll have to run your nugget ice maker at all times, but it’ll likely shut off once the bin is full. “This is a normal operating procedure,” says Zhao. “Turning it off and on [manually] every day reduces its life and means you are waiting 15 to 20 minutes for your first batch every day.”

However, these machines don’t technically need to run year-round if you’re worried about possibly running up your electric bill. “You can turn them off and put them away when you don’t plan on using them,” says Randhawa. “We put ours away during vacations and over the winter, after the temperature drops, which is generally when we don’t want ice in our drinks.”

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

From Augustus to Nero, see how much you know about ancient Rome's famous leaders with our Roman emperor quiz!

#6276. The 8 Best Space Heaters to Keep the Chill Out of Your Home and Office

We compared different models’ heating levels, timer functions, safety features, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Take the edge off those chilly winter nights without ballooning your energy bill. Space heaters offer immediate warmth for cozy nights in the bedroom and for brisk days in a drafty office. The small radius of heat also makes them ideal for improving the temperature in your immediate surroundings without wasting energy turning up the thermostat and heating the entire house. Some even double as fans during the summer.

The top space heaters run quietly and efficiently, offer multiple heating levels, and come with safety features like automatic shut-off for accidental tipping. We researched and tested the most promising models from brands like Vornado, Lasko, and Dreo. Below, you’ll find our selections for the most efficient, durable, and safest space heaters out there.

We tested space heaters by first evaluating each model based on important factors like safety, setting variety, and size. We paid attention to how well the appliances were able to warm up a space by using them around our homes and offices. We also took note of the number of heat settings each unit had and the temperature range they offered.

To evaluate the unit’s heat capabilities, we took into account its temperature range and wattage, and prioritized heaters that offered a broad range with good control and output of at least 1,200 watts or more. We’ve made a point to include options that operate via remote-controlled desktops and smart picks that come with a companion app as well.

For heaters that we haven’t had the chance to try in person, we heavily vetted specs and assessed each space heater based on the same factors we used during testing.

Lasko calls the CW100 bladeless because it doesn’t technically have a fan, per se. Instead, it uses a multi-vane impeller. That design contributes to the appliance’s quiet operation because it pulls in air through its base and into the tower. It comes with a cleanable air filter, which is accessible via a tool-free hatch at the back of the heater—no tools required.

We appreciate the slick touchpad on the front for adjusting the wattage for the heating element, tower oscillation, and the eight-hour timer. The space heater only has two actual heat settings—high and low—but there is a manual thermostat for controlling temperatures, which helps make up for the lack of power options.

The wide window of airflow and consistent heat distribution helps bring a room up to temp faster than most space heaters on this list, and this unit covers up to 300 square feet. One gripe: The battery hatch cover on the remote is tricky to remove. There is a holster for that remote control, though, making for one tidy package.

Full Lasko Oscillating Bladeless Ceramic Tower Space Heater Review

For a low-cost option, the Vornado MVH Vortex Heater heats a surprisingly large area—up to 256 square feet—with minimal noise. This unit worked well in a bedroom that has exterior walls on five sides, even during cold overnight temperatures. We like how simple, compact, and lightweight this unit is, and the appliance case stays cool to the touch, so you can move it around safely without concern.

The unit’s controls are a miss for us, though. While we liked the simple on/off button and the three-position toggle for heat levels, the thermostat dial is vague. The numbers on this dial range from 1 to 7, which don’t really show how warm each setting is.

As a result, we had to experiment with different settings until we figured out what worked best for us (you’ll likely have to do the same). Despite this drawback, the thermostat feature is helpful for when temperatures dip or get too high, as it manages the unit’s auto shutoff/on feature.

Full Vornado MVH Vortex Space Heater Review

It’s rare to come across a space heater that oscillates both horizontally and vertically, and that’s the feature we liked the most while testing the Dreo Whole Room Heater. It rotates 60 degrees up and down and 90 degrees from side to side for noticeably more coverage. Better yet, you can use both oscillation modes at the same time.

This space heater also has three heat and fan settings, and we appreciated being able to control the fan speed separately, even if we were running on high heat. Temperatures range from 41 to 95 degrees Fahrenheit, so we were able to truly customize the output. We kept our space heater at 73°F a majority of the time, and we never felt overheated or chilly.

The space heater comes with a remote, but there’s also a control panel on the base of the unit. The main thing we don’t like is that the remote was a little confusing to navigate at first. You have to use one button to access the fan speeds, heat levels, and temperatures, so we found ourselves clicking through a few times to get to the setting we wanted.

If your office is generally cold, then a heater small enough to sit on your desk might be the perfect solution for dealing with the frigid temperatures of your building. At only 12 inches tall, the Ellipse ceramic heater from Lasko is truly a compact model— discreet enough to tuck into the corner or underneath a workspace.

The highest settings pump out powerful heat in seconds, but there are medium and low settings if you want toned-down warmth. Temperatures are adjustable through the touch panel on the space heater.

We appreciate that even though this is a smaller design, it comes with its own remote. You can make the space heater oscillate and conveniently set a timer with the press of a couple buttons, and everything is viewable from the LED panel on the front.

The only thing we didn’t particularly like is that the Ellipse turns on at the highest setting automatically, so you’ll have to make adjustments almost immediately to find the ideal temperature and power.

A tech-facing space heater certainly has its benefits. The Lasko Therma-Smart tower heater has WiFi connectivity and pairs with the Aria home app for a virtual remote.

Connecting the heater was fairly easy: simply hold the WiFi button on the space heater for five seconds so it enters “pairing mode,” and then connect the device to the app. You can see wattage use and heat levels, and there’s a temperature dial in the center of the page to adjust to your liking. The Therma-Smart heater also pairs with Google and Alexa if you prefer to use voice commands.

Otherwise, the space heater has similar settings to other Lasko models that we recommend, like touch-sense controls and a digital window for viewing purposes. There are low, medium, and high heat settings, a max heat output of 1,500 watts, and a 12-hour timer function for running most of the day. One thing we noticed is that the oscillating feature seems to move very slowly, so you still might get hit with targeted heat if you’re sitting directly in front of the heater before it starts the rotation again.

The Lasko 751320 Ceramic Tower Heater is a reliable, mid-range option for homes and offices. Tester and Popular Mechanics editor Tom Price loves this model for its versatility. “The tower design and mid-sized build mean you can comfortably place it on a coffee table in the living room without it taking over the space. At the same time, it isn’t so small that I don’t feel the heat in larger spaces.”

The space heater has programmable controls that will turn the unit off and on after a certain period of time (or once the room has reached the desired temperature). It’s also equipped with an oscillating mode and comes with a multi-functioning remote control, too.

Although the gate on the front of the heater is designed to be cool to the touch, one aspect to keep in mind is that this unit does not come with an auto shutoff feature in case it gets tipped over.

A cold bathroom early in the morning feels like punishment, but a space heater on the floor near a bathtub or shower isn’t exactly a safe alternative. This fixed, wall-mounted unit from Dreo is a more reliable alternative. It’s IP24 waterproof-rated, so it’s protected against splashes from every direction, and has the same kind of ALCI plug you typically find on hair tools.

The bathroom heater accommodates spaces up to 200 square feet. With smart functionality, the companion app allows you to schedule timers, adjust temperatures, and change heat levels remotely.

Though this model has a child lock and a cool-touch exterior, we recommend mounting it out of reach of littles because the exhaust vent gets pretty warm.

If noise is one of your biggest concerns while shopping for a space heater, then an oil-filled radiator heater might be the right option. The Pelonis heater doesn’t use an internal fan, and offers the quietest noise operation on our list, maxing out right around five decibels.

It offers just about the same features as the ceramic heaters we recommend, with three different heating modes, tip-over security, and overheat protection. The heater has 360-degree warmth circulation, so you’re covered from every angle.

The radiator sits on four casters so it easily moves from room to room. It has a carrying handle, but it’s relatively small compared to the overall size of the unit and may overheat, so we recommend moving to your desired space before turning it on.

Simple, affordable, and versatile, these use electrical resistance to warm your space. A ceramic block or element is electrically conductive and heats up, and that heat is transferred to the air with an internal fan. The majority of the heaters on our list fall into this category.

Ideal use: These are great for general household use, shared offices, or wherever quiet heat is needed. Their simplicity makes them quite rugged; they have fewer parts to wear out or break.

This style of space heater emits infrared radiation rays that heat objects and individuals rather than the air, and it’s one of the more straightforward designs. They provide warmth almost instantly and aren’t loud while running, but they do have limited range.

Ideal use: Spot heating or small areas that need to be warmed up in a short amount of time.

These appliances burn propane or kerosene to warm an infrared emitter that projects the energy to heat your space. They’re considered convection heaters because they transfer thermal energy through a fluid, either by gas or oil.

They elevate the temperature of the air in certain spaces and are most suitable for delivering warmth in an area where you might walk around, like the surroundings of your desk or workshop.

Ideal use: Construction sites, garages, or work areas are the best places to use these heaters, since you want to place one at a comfortable distance and keep the work area unobstructed. Gas or liquid-fuel heaters direct the heat wherever you’re working.

Most residential space heaters use about 1,500 watts of power. If you’re using one of these devices as a primary heat source, it’s recommended to choose a model that offers 10 watts of heat output per square foot of space. 150 square feet is the common standard for coverage. You may consider investing in more than one unit if you’re trying to warm a larger space, or finding a design that has the right power combined with a fan or oscillating mode to disperse heat more evenly.

If you have pets or young children, then choosing a space heater with safety features is especially important for avoiding accidental burns and fires. The majority of the heaters on our list come with an automatic shut-off feature if it tips over. A good portion of our recommended heaters also include a timer to prevent the device from running for the entire day if you forget to shut it off.

During our testing and research journey, we learned some other valuable safety tips along the way such as the “three feet rule” (keeping the space heater at a distance from anything flammable) and not using these appliances in moist areas. But most importantly, you should never plug a space heater into an extension cord, power cord, or power strip. They’re not equipped for the electrical load that these devices require, and can be a potential fire hazard.

The short answer is it depends. Whether it’s “a lot” depends mainly on how long you run the heater and your local electricity rate. In the U.S., residential electricity prices typically range from $0.12 to $0.20 per kWh, with the average being around $0.17 per kWh as of December 2025.

Because most space heaters operate at 1,500 watts, they can cost between $0.18 and $0.30 per hour at average electricity rates. To find a more accurate estimate, divide the heater’s wattage by 1,000 to convert to kilowatts, then multiply that number by the number of hours the heater is running, and multiply that result by your electricity rate per kilowatt-hour (kWh).

These appliances aren’t intended to replace your home’s central heating system, so it’s better to use them supplementally if you don’t want to pay more on your electric bill.

You should turn them off when sleeping or left unattended. Common overnight hazards like a unit tipping over, bedding sitting too close to the heater, or an outlet overheating pose significant risks that you might not notice until you wake up. While most space heaters have preventative safety features like automatic shutoff or built-in thermostats, and may even be rated for continuous use, it’s best to resist the temptation of 24-hour warmth for safer operation.

#6275. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6274. Singapore Airlines Unveils the ‘Largest Double Bed in the Sky’ As Part of a $1.6 Billion Redesign

Getting a good night's sleep on a long-haul flight isn't easy, even when you're lucky enough to be flying first class. But Singapore Airlines—consistently voted as one of the best airlines in the world by CNT readers—is taking things to a whole new level, unveiling what it claims will be “the largest double bed in commercial aviation” as part of a major revamp of its long-haul cabins.

The airline announced the $1.6 billion redesign on Friday, November 6, with the first aircraft expected to enter service in the second half of 2027.

Singapore Airlines's new first class cabin

And the luxury doesn't stop there. The new suites will feature Italian Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, personal wardrobes, dedicated dining spaces, and 32-inch 4K entertainment screens. Passengers can also expect proper bedding, including cotton sheets, duvets, a choice of pillows, and mattress toppers from German bedding specialist Paradies.

The new business class seats also come with adjoining seats, offering the option to sleep alongside a traveling companion.

But what about those of us traveling farther back? Premium economy will benefit from additional personal space, adjustable leg rests, dedicated storage, and larger entertainment screens. Meanwhile, economy passengers can look forward to redesigned seats with more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The new economy class will feature more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The upgrades will be introduced gradually across Singapore Airlines's new Boeing 777-9 aircraft and 41 retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft, including its ultra-long-range fleet. The latter will also receive first class cabins for the first time.

There's no confirmed date yet for when passengers will be able to try the new double beds, but one thing is certain: cuddling up at 35,000 feet has just become a little more appealing.

This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6273. Airport Luggage Tag Scam: How to Protect Your Checked Bags in 2026

Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.

Then the officer points to the luggage tag and says, “Then why is your name on it?”

That is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026. It is called baggage tag switching, and it is exactly what it sounds like: the luggage tag from an innocent passenger’s checked suitcase is allegedly removed and placed onto another bag.

Baggage tag switching scams happen when the luggage tag from a traveler’s checked bag is allegedly removed and placed on another suitcase. To protect yourself, take a video of your suitcase before check-in, photograph the bag on the scale, take a close-up photo of the baggage tag, keep your baggage receipt, place a tracker inside your suitcase, and report any damaged, missing, delayed, or retagged bag before leaving the airport.

According to a W5 investigation, innocent passengers flying from Canada have been detained after their real luggage tags were allegedly moved onto suitcases containing illegal drugs. The investigation focused on flights from Canada and alleged cases connected to Toronto Pearson, but the larger lesson applies to travelers everywhere: once your checked bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting the system to protect your luggage, your tag, and your name.

We have traveled to more than 130 countries on all seven continents, and checked bags have always been part of travel. But the old habit of simply handing over your suitcase and hoping for the best needs an update.

In 2026, protecting your checked luggage is not just about stopping theft. It is about protecting the paper trail that connects you to your bag.

This is part of a bigger shift in how travelers need to think about airport safety, baggage scams, and common airport security mistakes before they fly.

Editor’s note: This article is based on our video about baggage tag switching, which has reached more than 86,000 views on our travel YouTube channel.

Before you check a bag, take two minutes to create proof that the bag is yours.

It also helps to run through a full pre-travel checklist before you leave for the airport so you are not rushing through check-in.

This may sound like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes at check-in. And those two minutes could matter if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

We covered this luggage tag scam in detail in the video below, including the simple two-minute routine we now recommend before checking a bag.

Baggage tag switching is when the tag printed for your checked luggage is removed from your actual suitcase and attached to another bag.

When you check luggage, the airline prints a baggage tag that usually includes your name, flight, destination, routing information, barcode, and bag number. That tag is the airport system’s way of connecting that suitcase to you.

The problem is that once your bag goes behind the counter, you cannot see what happens next.

In the alleged scheme reported by W5, corrupt baggage or ramp workers could remove a legitimate tag from a passenger’s suitcase and attach it to another suitcase heading to the same destination. If that second bag is intercepted, the paperwork points back to the innocent passenger.

That is what makes this scam so dangerous. You may have done everything right: checked your own suitcase, kept your boarding pass, and boarded your flight. But behind the scenes, one strip of paper may now connect your name to a bag you have never seen.

Most airport workers are honest. Let’s be clear about that. The vast majority are doing hard jobs under pressure, moving thousands of bags through complex systems every day. But a baggage system only needs a few bad actors to create a very serious problem.

This story has received attention because of Canadian cases, but this is not only a Canada problem.

The bigger issue is that every major airport has the same basic weak point: you hand over your suitcase, it enters a restricted area, and from that point on, you are relying on the system to protect the tag, the bag, and the records connected to your name.

That is true in Toronto. It is true in New York, London, Paris, Dubai, Bangkok, Mexico City, Sydney, and anywhere else checked luggage moves behind the scenes.

International travel also adds another layer of risk. If your name gets tied to a suspicious bag in another country, you may be dealing with a different legal system, different customs procedures, and possibly a language barrier.

The Government of Canada warns travelers that drug offences abroad can have serious consequences and that you should never carry anything across a border for someone else. The Canada Border Services Agency also specifically reminds travelers that trafficking cannabis or other drugs across the border is a criminal offence and warns people to beware of anyone asking them to carry something.

That is why documenting your own luggage matters. You are not being paranoid. You are creating a simple evidence trail.

Before your suitcase disappears behind the counter, take a clear video of it.

Do a full 360-degree view. Show the front, back, sides, wheels, handles, color, brand, straps, stickers, scratches, dents, or anything that makes your bag identifiable.

Yes, you may feel ridiculous filming your suitcase at the airport. Do it anyway. People film lattes. You can film the thing that might keep you out of a holding room.

This video creates a time-stamped record of what your suitcase looked like before it left your hands. If someone later claims a different bag is yours, you have proof of what your actual luggage looked like at check-in.

When your bag is placed on the airline scale, take a quick photo or video showing the weight.

This matters because weight is part of the paper trail. If your suitcase weighed 19 kilograms at check-in and another suitcase connected to your name weighs 32 kilograms, that difference may matter.

You are not trying to become a detective. You are simply creating a record that says this was your bag, this was the weight, this was the condition, and this was the tag attached to it.

That is the kind of simple documentation that can help if your bag is delayed, damaged, retagged, or questioned later.

Once the airline attaches the baggage tag to your suitcase, take a close-up photo or video of it before the bag goes onto the conveyor belt.

Make sure you can clearly see the barcode, destination airport, flight number, routing, and bag number. Also check that the airline has looped and attached the tag properly.

You are not being difficult. You are checking the one strip of paper connecting you to your luggage. That little tag is doing a lot of legal heavy lifting.

Air Canada’s own baggage information explains that self-service kiosks can print baggage tags, receipts, and boarding passes, and that travelers then attach the tags and proceed to bag drop. That means passengers are often handling or reviewing this paperwork themselves before the bag disappears into the system.

Never throw away the little baggage receipt sticker you receive at check-in.

Keep it somewhere safe. Don’t stuff it in a random pocket, lose it before boarding, or assume the airline app is enough. Put it with your passport or travel documents until your suitcase is back in your hands.

That receipt usually contains your bag number. If something goes wrong, that number becomes part of the evidence trail. That number can help airline staff or investigators compare what you checked, what arrived, and whether someone intercepted or retagged another bag.

This is one of the easiest travel habits to fix, and it costs nothing.

Before you close your checked bag, take one clear photo of the inside.

You do not need to photograph every sock like you are filing a museum inventory. Just take one clear photo of the contents: clothes, shoes, toiletries, chargers, jackets, and the usual chaos of travel.

This helps show what you actually packed. If a suitcase connected to your name contains items you have never seen, you have a record of what was inside your real bag before check-in.

This is especially useful on international trips, where proving what you packed may become more complicated once you are outside your home country.

It is also a good reminder to double-check what not to pack in checked luggage before you leave for the airport.

A luggage tracker will not stop someone from tampering with a baggage tag, but it can help show where your real suitcase went.

We use Apple AirTags, but there are also Tile trackers, Samsung SmartTags, and other luggage tracking options.

The important thing is this: put the tracker inside your suitcase. Do not hang it outside where it can easily be removed.

If authorities are asking about a suitcase connected to your name and your tracker shows your actual suitcase is somewhere else, that becomes another part of your evidence trail.

Trackers are also helpful if your bag arrives late, gets separated from its original tag, or ends up in the wrong baggage area. They are not perfect, but they give travelers one more layer of information when airline systems fail.

We use AirTags in our checked bags, but Samsung SmartTags and Tile trackers are also good options depending on your phone. The key is to keep the tracker inside the suitcase where it cannot easily be removed.

We also recommend pairing a luggage tracker with a few simple anti-theft travel accessories especially on longer international trips.

A plain black suitcase is basically the airport version of camouflage.

Make your luggage easier to identify with a bright strap, ribbon, sticker, or distinctive luggage tag. You want to be able to spot your bag quickly and prove what makes it different from hundreds of others.

But do not put too much personal information on the outside. Your name and phone number are enough.

You do not need your home address waving around the baggage hall like an invitation that says, “Please rob us while we’re in Italy.”

Keep luggage identifiable, but not overly revealing.

This rule has always mattered, but it matters even more now.

Never carry a package, gift, suitcase, envelope, or item for someone else. That means no favors for strangers, no “harmless” packages, and no quick airport errands for someone you barely know.

If you did not pack it, you do not carry it.

The CBSA specifically warns travelers to beware of people who ask them to carry anything and notes that consequences for drug trafficking can be serious in Canada and abroad.

That is the cleanest rule in travel: your bag, your responsibility.

If your checked bag arrives without the original tag, with a damaged tag, with a rush tag, or through a different baggage process than expected, do not just shrug and leave the airport.

Do not rely on a quick conversation at the counter. Conversations disappear the second you walk away. Written reports create a record.

This matters if your bag was mishandled, delayed, retagged, or separated from its original tag.

When your suitcase comes out at baggage claim, do not grab it on autopilot and leave.

Check that it is actually yours. Look at the tag, compare the bag number against your receipt, check your tracker, inspect the condition, and make sure the contents have not obviously been disturbed.

We have seen people accidentally walk away with someone else’s luggage. It happens more easily than people think, especially after long-haul flights when everyone is tired and half the carousel is filled with identical black suitcases.

Before you leave the airport or customs area, take one minute to confirm everything looks right.

Not necessarily. We have traveled for decades, and carry-on only is not always realistic. Sometimes you need to check a bag, especially on longer trips, family trips, cruises, cold-weather destinations, camera-heavy travel, or extended international travel.

For a smoother trip overall, our easy air travel tips can help before you even reach baggage claim.

For longer flights, our long-haul flight tips can also help make the journey easier before you even get to baggage claim.

The point is not to scare people out of checking luggage. The point is to update your habits.

The old way of checking luggage was simple: check the bag, keep the receipt somewhere, and hope for the best.

It sounds like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes — and those two minutes could make a huge difference if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

If authorities ever question you about a suitcase that you do not recognize, stay calm.

Do not guess, don’t joke and do not become argumentative.

Ask for legal assistance and show the documentation you collected: your suitcase video, scale photo, baggage tag photo, receipt, tracker information, and photos of what you packed.

This article is not legal advice, but from a traveler’s perspective, the goal is simple: create proof before there is a problem.

If your name is ever attached to a bag you did not pack, your documentation may help show what your real suitcase looked like, what it weighed, what was inside it, and where it went.

Before every checked bag disappears behind the counter, take two minutes to create a simple record of your suitcase.

That’s it. Two minutes. No drama. No paranoia. Just smart travel.

Most airport workers are honest, and most checked bags arrive without a problem. But airport systems are massive, complicated, and not completely invisible-proof. Once your bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting a chain of people, machines, tags, scans, and systems to keep your suitcase connected to your name.

So before your next flight, take two minutes to protect yourself. Film your bag. Photograph your tag. Keep your receipt. Use a tracker. And never carry anything for anyone else.

The goal is not to travel scared. The goal is to travel smarter.

Because when travelers get smarter, scams get riskier for the people trying to pull them off.

#6272. You Were More Conscious as a Child Than You Are Now, Neuroscientist Claims

What if growing up makes you more knowledgeable but less aware of reality?

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When you were a child, did you ever wonder what happened to the sea at the horizon? Perhaps you imagined it stretching forever. Or perhaps, like me, you believed that where the blue ended, the water simply fell off the edge of the world, spilling over in some enormous, invisible waterfall. It made perfect sense at the time, and there was quite a lot of magic involved, too. Then came geography lessons, maps, explanations, terminology, and the gradual realization that the world did not end where your vision did—that it was, in fact, far vaster than anything the eye could take in. So why has it become so difficult to recapture the purity and intensity of that experience as an adult?

Could there be a chance, however counterintuitive it sounds, that you were actually more conscious back then?

It sounds counterintuitive, but Alysson Muotri, PhD, a professor of pediatrics and cellular and molecular medicine at the University of California, San Diego, has given this poetic—almost philosophical—idea scientific legs. To do so, he used one of the most futuristic tools that currently exists for investigating the human brain: brain organoids, tiny clusters of living neural tissue grown from stem cells in a laboratory. He wondered whether these tiny lumps of living human brain tissue could illuminate that elusive inner experience. What he found was that as we grow and learn about the world, this process might really be changing how we perceive reality.

But before you can explore consciousness in a lab, you need to build the organoids. The process begins with ordinary human cells, often collected from the skin. Scientists reprogram them into induced pluripotent stem cells, which regain the ability to develop into almost any cell type in the body. Researchers use chemical signals to turn these cells into neurons and other brain cells. The cells multiply, gathering into tiny clumps of tissue. Inside them, neurons begin making contact, and electrical signals pass between them. However, calling these organoids “brains in a dish” is rather generous, though tempting; they lack much of the anatomy of a developed human brain. Still, organoids allow scientists to watch human neural tissue take shape in ways that would be impossible to witness inside a living person’s skull.

Muotri’s team discovered in 2019 that maturing organoids produced electrical rhythms resembling certain features of brain activity recorded in premature infants. Here was human neural tissue, deprived of the sights and sounds accompanying a child’s development, nevertheless organizing itself into patterns observed in living brains. Four years later, researchers at Indiana University Bloomington incorporated brain organoids into an experimental computing system that used their electrical responses to help recognize spoken sounds and predict mathematical patterns. By 2025, other scientists had reported that repeated electrical stimulation could alter how individual neurons in organoids responded, with some changes lingering for hours after the stimulation came to a halt—evidence of cellular mechanisms associated with learning and memory.

Muotri, meanwhile, had begun wondering whether the electrical activity of his brain organoids could offer any clues to that elusive inner experience we call consciousness. Of course, even if we assume that consciousness arises entirely from the brain, there is something peculiar about trying to measure it. It’s not as though you can insert a thermometer into someone’s head and pinpoint the experience of being alive and aware—or the feeling of experiencing the world as a child.

Muotri decided to investigate by borrowing an approach from consciousness research called the perturbational complexity index (PCI). In humans, the method involves delivering a brief magnetic pulse to the brain and recording the resulting electrical activity through electrodes placed on the scalp. Earlier researchers have analyzed the responses and calculated a score that has helped distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep and general anesthesia; a higher score indicates greater conscious awareness. While PCI cannot measure consciousness directly, it offers clues about the brain’s capacity to sustain it.

In preliminary findings, Muotri measured the organoids’ electrical activity before exposing them to repeated stimulation, using an approach similar to PCI. To say that he found a startling degree of complexity in the way their neurons communicate with one another—with scores that exceeded those typically recorded in awake human brains—is an understatement. Because the organoid and human measurements use different methods, however, the scores cannot be compared directly. Still, he wasn’t expecting the organoids to have this PCI level, he says. “It’s very new, and I’m still thinking about what it means.”

Muotri also found something shocking about how the organoids behaved as they were stimulated repeatedly with light. Gradually, the cells began reacting differently to the stimulation, and some of those changes lingered after the light was switched off. “So there is some kind of a memory embedded in those networks,” he says. But even more astounding was that, as the organoids adapted to the stimulation, their complexity score actually fell, similar to the way human brains with lower PCI scores were less aware.

He thinks the reason is that a brain organoid increases its bias as it learns, just as we become more biased as we learn more over the years. By bias, Muotri means that experience makes certain neural responses, particularly those reinforced through repeated exposure, more likely than others. Learning, apparently, does more than give us knowledge. It may also condition us to overlook parts of the world we once experienced more freely.

“It’s almost like when you are born…as soon as your brain is naive and fresh, you’re more conscious than when you are an adult,” Muotri continues. By adulthood, however, experience has cramped your brain’s style. “Because you already experienced so many things, you’re already [so] attached to the physical environment, that you become less conscious than you were [as] a baby.”

The suggestion is extraordinary, especially coming from experiments involving tissue that has never seen a sunset, heard a lullaby, obeyed a teacher, or encountered anything resembling a childhood whatsoever.

Yet there is a recognizable human parallel. Developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik has compared adult attention to a spotlight, concentrated on what matters for an immediate goal, and children’s attention to a lantern, illuminating more of their surroundings. A toddler entering an unfamiliar room might become absorbed by a patch of sunlight that an adult barely notices. The adult knows more about the room, but familiarity helps determine what deserves attention. Noticing more of the world doesn’t necessarily mean being more conscious of it.

However, a baby’s brain, already shaped by months of development in the womb, is hardly comparable to an organoid that has never experienced the world outside a laboratory. That’s why Kenneth Kosik, MD, a neuroscience professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, is skeptical. In a 2024 paper published in the journal Patterns, titled Why Brain Organoids Are Not Conscious Yet, he argued that organoids lack much of the organization and communication between brain regions that may be necessary for consciousness. And electrical activity, however complicated, is not enough to prove an inner life. Neurons firing independently can produce unpredictable signals that are difficult to reduce to a simpler description, even when there is no evidence that anything is being experienced. “So we still have a little bit of a jump there, yeah, to say that compressibility is related to consciousness,” Kosik says.

Muotri himself is cautious about what the numbers mean and says they are still preliminary data. Nor does he claim that his organoids actually experience anything. “I should not say they are conscious outright,” he says.

For now, Muotri’s experiments cannot definitively tell us whether we were more conscious as children than we are as adults, but they do open a window onto something just as intriguing: what happens to our experience of the world if learning itself changes how our brains encounter our environment? After all, the day I discovered that the sea did not plunge into an abyss, I gained precious knowledge that generations before me had strived to acquire. But have I ever again experienced the sea quite as fully as I did when I was a child, believing it could spill over the world’s edge? That is a whole different question, and we don’t have the answer yet.

Stav Dimitropoulos is a Gold and Community Anthem Award–winning journalist, and writes about consciousness, science, and culture for Popular Mechanics, Nature, and the BBC. Her work often explores mind-stretching angles where science meets philosophy. Her debut nonfiction book, Slow, Lazy, Gluttons (Greystone Books, 2026) asks: What if the traits society shames — laziness, darkness, nostalgia, and more — are actually survival superpowers?
