#6271. 14 Best Steakhouses in New York City for Old-School Chops, Wagyu, and the Perfect Martini

No single steakhouse can beat out all the others in NYC. Each has its strengths, and some are certainly better than others. There are the classics—Keens and Gallaghers in Midtown, Delmonico's in the Financial District, Peter Luger over in Williamsburg—that have been here for a hundred years or more, and for good reason. They are dimly-lit, tavern-like, with walls clad in wood. The menus do not change. The new and newish guard variously emulate and do their own thing. Increasingly, we are seeing steakhouses taking the basic assignment—red meat and sides in a formal dining room—and running with it in various cultural directions. Below, we've rounded up our favorites across this board. What's most important is their shared ability to make its diner feel important, a feat that goes beyond (but does require) the ability to gorge on good steak.

Read our complete New York City guide here, which includes:

Seagram Building, 99 E 52nd St, Midtown Manhattan

I am forming the opinion that a steakhouse's cardinal function is to make its diners feel important. No place has succeeded so impeccably in this mission as The Grill, where I was whisked from a downstairs lobby into the glamorous dining room as though a visiting board member come to town to be courted and impressed. I went for lunch, so the metal chain curtains that undulate (yes, they are ever-moving) over the massive windows shimmered in the daylight. Everyone except for me, it seemed, as there on very important business. I was the only male diner that I could see not in a jacket. The menu is very spendy (you cannot get a cocktail for less than $26) and therefore especially reserved for special occasions. Peppered filet mignon and martini, I'd say, are the way to go, but if it's lunch and the prime rib roast beef sandwich is being served, it's a worthy detour. —C.H.

The best thing that happened to me at 4 Charles Prime Rib was that I made a new friend. Steak and martinis and burgers, they're all fabulous—make no mistake. But sometimes it’s the life that comes at you in pursuit of those delicious menu items that leaves you feeling the most full. Too corny? Allow me to elaborate.

4 Charles is one of the toughest tables in town. Like Torrisi, it’s practically a private members' club where the only people who can land a reservation are those who’ve eaten there before. Hopeful walk-ins start lining up over an hour before opening at 4 p.m., and I got there at 2:45 p.m. to find myself second in line. I sat on the West Village townhouse stoop and enjoyed the day, enjoyed the sight of the staff puttering around setting up, glared at the people with reservations who we in line agreed were “line cutters.” When the host began seating people around 3:45 p.m., she told me that I was the first single walk-in and would therefore enjoy the one table by the door that they reserve for such parties. The man behind me, who arrived nary five minutes after I did, was told he would therefore have to wait until I was done. “Can’t I just sit with him?” he asked in earnest bewilderment. “Sure!” I responded.

And so together we unhinged our jaws and ate the 10-ounce double wagyu smash burger with thick slabs of bacon, his with an egg, and together we poured the beef jus over the pink center of the titular 4 Charles Cut and expressed our unexpected delight with the horseradish cream accoutrement. Together we drank martinis—I, a perfect vesper; he, an espresso; and then a chocolate each. If you’re going to try to go, I recommend you do so in this way. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Peter Luger isn't just the Brooklyn steakhouse. It just might be the New York City steakhouse, especially if history carries any weight with you, dear reader. This fine establishment has sat at the same address in the Williamsburg Bridge's shadow since 1887, and the interiors carry about as many frills as your average public house—dark wood, plaster walls, and so on. The menu is just as unadorned, with the most popular menu items being the dry-aged steak for two, steak for three, or steak for four. You can also, rest assured, get a single steak, lamb chops, salmon, or filet of sole. The Luger's sizzling bacon is not to be missed, nor are the sliced tomatoes and onions with Luger's Own sauce (pro tip: they go quite well together.) If you're there before 3:45 p.m., you'd also be wise to order the over-½-lb Luger burger, which is so simple and bloody with optional American cheese that your eyes will roll back in your head. —C.H.

This summer, the Montecito and Malibu staple Lucky's Steakhouse came to roost on a bustling street in New York’s Soho—and has been a fun addition to the city’s oft-stodgy steakhouse landscape ever since. Importantly, it’s a cool counterpoint—with its intimate size, Jazz Age-y murals, sexy date-night vibe, and a menu that accommodates non-steak eaters (i.e. me, a pescatarian). I know what you’re thinking: Why is a non-meat eater reviewing Lucky’s? Well, precisely for the fact that steakhouses can be wincingly non-inclusive, despite often being the restaurant of choice on special occasions. And Lucky’s feels different, not least because of its ambience. On a recent night, we started with the oysters, the peaky-toe crab cocktail, house chips, and Jimmy’s Greek salad (named after a family member of the owner). I then got the salmon, initially a perverse choice—because it usually plays poor country cousin at most steakhouses—but it was excellent. And we really dug into the sides—onion rings, market vegetables, and creamed corn. Both times I ate there, my companions ordered the 10-oz Gene’s Filet and I heard murmurs of firm approval. Whatever your dietary preference, don’t miss Lucky’s martini service, for which multiple servers will shake (or stir) your drinks table-side and in unison—because a little theatre hurts no one.

Head 10 blocks south of New York’s Koreatown (see an itinerary of the neighborhood here), and you'll find Cote, a Korean steakhouse and one of the city’s best and buzziest restaurants. There’s no shortage of a la carte options, but the prix-fixe Butcher’s Feast is where diners should start. For $74 a person, you're treated to seasonal ban-chan, savory egg soufflé, two stews (including spicy kimchi stew), and the house selection of beef, including USDA Prime and Wagyu, cooked on the table with smokeless grills. The restaurant’s award-winning wine list features an impressive Champagne selection, and all by-the-glass pours come from Magnums, the large-format bottles that sommeliers say keeps wines younger and fresher. There's also a second location at 550 Madison that's a bit grander, should that suit you. —D.F.

Gallaghers is the best steakhouse to eat at before a Broadway show. Wood paneled walls covered in framed old photographs (one of singer Perry Comon had to be labeled “this is not Jeffrey Epstein” due to those two men’s shared resemblance) offset the inhumane Midtown environment just beyond the front door. This is a place that’s as good for steak (and it really is good for steak) as it is for all of the accoutrements one expects of a good steakhouse—beyond the bovine, highlights include the old fashioned, the creamed spinach, the house-smoked bacon, and the beautifully browned veal chop parmigiana. Putting it all over the edge is the people watching—real live businesspeople drowning their sorrows at the bar alongside the theatergoers, and haughty waiters doing buttoned-up to the max. —C.H.

The only difficult choice to make when entering Keens is where to look first. Is it up, at the 90,000 pipes lining the ceiling? To the glass cases, where the most famous churchwardens—15-inch pipes—smoked by the likes of Babe Ruth and General MacArthur are stored? In the bar, are you mesmerized by the Miss Keen painting (a nude, lounging on her bear rug) right away, or are you too distracted by the New-York-ad-men-in-the-'50s vibe? This steakhouse, open since 1883, delivers something new to look at every time you go. Keens was originally called a chop house, in recognition of its famous mutton chop, and although that is good and musty and intense, most people are ordering steak. There’s the porterhouse for two or three, the chateaubriand, and the filet mignon—which is actually fabulous here. You want the béarnaise or au poivre sauce on the side, and the creamed spinach, which is less a vegetable than it is dessert. There's also the matter of the burger, which can be ordered up to the dining room from the more casual bar menu. —Alex Van Buren

1271 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown Manhattan

From the moment you walk into Cuerno, there's a sense of importance—the crowd, in suits and slicked back hair, is well-dressed; the dining room is always bustling and full, necks turning to see who else has walked in; and tableside preparations are happening left and right. This is Northern Mexican meat at its finest, in a space that feels true to that spirit—big leather booths, a colorful tile mural of a skeleton riding a bull—and with a menu that won't let you down. There are expected starters, like fresh guac and queso fundido, but also a chicarrón de pulpo bursting with flavor, and a charcoal-roasted cauliflower complemented by truffle and habanero. The main event, of course, are the steaks, like the decadent Taco Taquero with perfect skirt steak, and fire-roasted bone marrow scooped onto each tortilla tableside, or the Norteño-style arrachera served with chiltepin butter and avocado salsa.

Portions are generous, so come in a group of four people minimum to actually try different sections of the menu. And though most steakhouses focus on wine (and the wine list is good here), I like the chance to pair smoky mezcal and tequila cocktails with the heavier food. —Megan Spurrell

355 Metropolitan Ave, Williamsburg, Brooklyn

Not just in Williamsburg, not just in New York City, but truly one of the coziest, best-value steakhouses I’ve ever been to, St. Anselm manages a rare balance: laid-back yet elevated, intimate without trying too hard, and consistently delicious. The space feels like a hidden tavern—dark wood, low light, and just enough buzz and energy to make it feel like a special night out. The Butcher’s Steak is the standout—charred to perfection, tender and juicy inside, and ideal for sharing (for two) alongside fingerling potatoes and long green beans. Go for a group lunch or, better yet, settle in after dark when the candles are lit and the place feels like a warm, secret pocket of the city. Ask your server—or better yet, belly up to the bar—and you’ll get a wine recommendation that pairs not just with the food, but with your mood. —Jessica Chapel

513 E 6th Street, East Village, Manhattan

Buenos Aires earns major points for nostalgia: The tiny dining room is adorned in hanging soccer jerseys, televisions showing live games and commentary, and scarfs and pendants for teams like the Boca Juniors. There are couples on dates, families with kids, and even, in my case, a dude who came in alone and ordered his regular with his headphones in. (Ask about celebrities and they'll bring out an iPad with photos of grinning staff beside countless Latin America soccer players, American actors, and even Matt Damon who apparently hosted two birthday parties here in the early 2000s.) All to say, this isn't the place to bring the corporate account or close the deal, but it is the place to roll up your sleeves and tuck into a massive skirt steak, expertly cooked, and served no-frills—just a great piece of meat on a plate. Do save room for the empanadas (carne cortada a cuchillo, of course); on my next visit, I'm planning to order the sweetbreads as well. —M.S.

Glam, glam, glam with a capital G. Golden Steer's New York iteration—the original is in Vegas, and little of that location's trademark opulence has been sacrificed in adapting the brand for New York. We're not in Midtown either, but in the West Village, and this is a fitting addition to that neighborhood as it increasingly wears its wealth on its sleeve. Entering this crimson bunker is a cinematic experience—long hallways flanked by side quests like the capacious but moody bar. What to get? Sink into your plush booth and go full Sin City: the bloody bull oyster shooter (where a rich beef broth-spiked shot of bloody mary chases the slime), the big ole baked potato, and a Caesar dotingly mixed tableside. Any cut of meat will do. —C.H.

56 Beaver St, Financial District, Manhattan

The definitive downtown steakhouse is also New York City's oldest. Its home since 1837 is 56 Beaver Street, a dramatic triangular lot at the intersection of Beaver, William, and South William in the Financial District. When I visited on a mid-May evening, the exterior was bedecked in American regalia—they were to film an episode of The Gilded Age there the next day (the new season is currently airing on HBO) depicting the ticker tape parade welcoming the Statue of Liberty to the city. All of this history would be moot were the steakhouse inside not very good, which it is from top to bottom—superlative, doting service in the mural-clad dining room, stiff drinks, perfect cuts of meat. As with every steakhouse, there are a couple of signature items beyond steak that you should consider. Here, it's wedge salad and buttery Lobster Newberg, said to have been invented there. Don't miss either, but steak is still the thing, namely the titular flagship cut—a glistening 18-ounce ribeye that stands alone on the plate, needing no accoutrements. —Charlie Hobbs

Dinner and a show in New York City’s midtown sounds fabulous, but in practice usually means settling for a meal that delivers more on convenience than cuisine or atmosphere. Carvesteak, a newish steakhouse on the west side of 48th street, stepped up to all these qualities after I saw The Rocky Horror Show earlier this year. Designed by David Rockwell and the Rockwell Group, it’s moody, mirrored interiors are filled with little nods to the Broadway history it shoulders—including a dramatic velvet curtain that the bartender at the martini bar told me was once part of the set for Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Phantom of the Opera (even if untrue, it certainly looked the part). Speaking of the martini bar, it’s not to be missed: a pocket-sized station to post yourself up at before or after dinner. Food-wise, this is a classic steakhouse menu, but with a little bit of flashiness thanks to the restaurant’s Las Vegas origins (it debuted at Resorts World Las Vegas in 2021): think, prime cuts and aged rib eyes with all the sides and sauces you would expect, but also the option to order a potato and caviar “popsicle.” There’s a pre-theater menu, too, but for the full experience I suggest coming hungry and catching the last call before 10 p.m. —Lale Arikoglu

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6270. GLP-1s Extend Life Span, New Research Suggests. Could They Be Key to Human Longevity?

This may mean the drug also has benefits outside of diabetes management.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Roughly 11 percent of American adults are on a GLP-1 for weight loss, according to a 2026 Gallup survey; so chances are, you likely know someone who is using one for diabetes management, obesity treatment, or heart health—but the benefits might not stop there. Now, semaglutide, the popular GLP-1 medication found in Ozempic and Wegovy, is drawing serious attention from longevity experts.

A recent study published in Nature found that semaglutide administered to female mice late in life significantly extended their life span. The results pose a legitimate question: Could GLP-1 drugs lengthen human lives as well?

To understand whether GLP-1s have anti-aging benefits, researchers put mice that were 20 months old—or roughly 60 human years—on a semaglutide regimen for the rest of their lives. There was also a control group of female mice the same age that received saline injections instead of the semaglutide. The team targeted older, non-obese, non-diabetic female mice to minimize the effects of male aggression and injury, consistent with previous long-term aging research, according to study author Danica Chen, PhD, professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at the University of California, Berkeley.The results? The median life span of the mice that received the GLP-1 drug increased from 742 days to 834 days, roughly a 12 percent extension. The researchers also saw reduced inflammation and preserved cognitive and muscle function in the GLP-1 group.

But there’s a rub here: This study was done in mice, which are a far cry from human adults, meaning we don’t yet know the effects of GLP-1s on people—at least not yet. However, there has been research that suggests lower-calorie diets lead to longer life spans in humans. “The general cause of aging is accumulation of cellular damage,” Chen says. She explains that calorie restriction can reduce cell damage and improve the function of tissues (a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific task), both of which contribute to a longer life span.

Michael Corley, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, thinks the Nature study is “important and exciting” because it looks beyond the established metabolic benefits of GLP-1 drugs and tests whether they can influence the biological aging process. (Biological age denotes how well the body is functioning on cellular and molecular levels, while chronological age refers to the number of years a person has been alive.)

“The finding that semaglutide extended life span by approximately 12 percent in older female mice, while improving several measures of physical and cognitive function, adds important evidence to the emerging field of GLP-1 therapies as potential gerotherapeutics,” or treatments that target the root of aging, Corley says. In fact, Corley was involved in a separate study, published earlier this year in Nature Communications, that found that 32 weeks of semaglutide treatment improved multiple epigenetic aging clocks, including measures of biological age and the pace of aging.

Findings presented at the 2026 Aging Research and Drug Discovery Meeting have also strengthened this emerging picture, Corley explains. Novo Nordisk, a Danish pharmaceutical company with locations around the world, reported that semaglutide improved measures of biological aging across multiple organ systems, including the heart and kidneys.

Likewise, Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical company headquartered in Indiana, presented findings that tirzepatide—another GLP-1 medication, which is found in prescriptions like Mounjaro and Zepbound—positively influenced several epigenetic aging clocks, including organ-specific markers that measure the biological age of the heart, kidney, liver, and immune system.

“Together, these independent observations suggest that GLP-1-based therapies may affect biological aging through multiple molecular pathways,” Corley says. “The new mouse study is particularly interesting because it extends these molecular observations to actual life span, while also demonstrating improvements in several hallmarks of aging.”

So, could GLP-1 drugs actually extend the life span of humans? Corley thinks the more compelling opportunity isn’t necessarily extending life span, but extending health span—or the number of years people live in good health, free from chronic disease and disability.

“Human life span has biological constraints, and it is unlikely that GLP-1 drugs alone will dramatically extend the maximum limits of human longevity,” he says. “However, by reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, and other age-related conditions, these medications could help more people remain healthy and independent for longer, potentially increasing average life span without fundamentally changing the upper limits of human longevity.”

However, improvements in biological aging don’t necessarily translate into longer lives, Corley cautions.

“The critical next step is determining whether these molecular changes predict meaningful improvements in physical function, cognition, and resilience,” Corley says. “I think the greatest potential of GLP-1 therapies is not to push humans beyond the limits of longevity, but to help more people reach older ages while maintaining their health, function, and independence.”

To find out whether or not GLP-1 drugs can eventually be used as a legitimate longevity tactic in humans, Chen says clinical trials in humans are an important next step. For now, GLP-1s remain a titan of diabetes and weight management—but their role in human longevity remains to be seen.

#6269. 25 Best Travel Apps for 2026: The Apps We Actually Use

We reviewed every recommendation and added new apps for AI trip planning, eSIMs, flight tracking, budgeting, and travel safety.

After travelling to more than 130 countries, we have used travel apps for everything from finding a last-minute room and navigating a city offline to translating menus, tracking flights and staying connected without paying ridiculous roaming charges. Some apps have earned a permanent place on our phones. Others have become outdated, overpriced or unnecessary.

For this 2026 guide, we cut through the clutter and chose the travel apps that solve real problems before and during a trip. You do not need to download every app on this list. Choose the ones that match your destination, travel style and the problems you are most likely to face.

The best travel apps for 2026 are Google Maps for navigation, Google Translate for language help, WhatsApp for communication, TripIt for organizing reservations, Google Flights for comparing airfare, Booking.com for hotels, Airalo or another destination-appropriate eSIM for mobile data, Uber for rides and AllTrails for hiking. Most travellers need only one or two apps from each category.

The Best Travel Apps for 2026 at a Glance

Our picks are based on usefulness, ease of use, geographic coverage and whether the app solves a genuine travel problem. We have also included alternatives where the best choice depends on your destination.

Before getting into specialized apps, these are the five we would start with. They cover navigation, translation, communication, flight updates and trip organization.

Google Maps is still the app we use most often while travelling. It handles driving, walking and public-transit directions, lets us save hotels and restaurants, and shows opening hours, recent reviews and nearby services.

Before leaving reliable Wi-Fi, download the map for your destination. Offline maps are especially useful when you land without mobile data or drive through an area with poor reception. Keep in mind that live traffic, some transit information and certain search features may not work offline.

What we like: It combines navigation, trip planning and local research in one place.

What to know: Directions, opening hours and business listings are not always accurate. Double-check important information directly with the business.

Our verdict: Download it before almost any trip.

Google Translate has helped us order food, read signs and have simple conversations in places where we did not speak the language. You can type a phrase, speak into the phone or point the camera at text for an instant translation.

Download the languages you expect to use before your trip. That gives you a useful backup when you do not have data, although online translations can be more complete.

What we like: The camera function is incredibly useful for menus, ticket machines and signs.

What to know: Translations can be awkward or wrong, especially with slang, regional phrases and complicated instructions.

Our verdict: It is one of the most useful free international travel apps.

WhatsApp is the default communication tool in many parts of the world. Hotels, tour companies, drivers and local contacts often use it instead of standard text messages.

It supports individual and group chats, voice calls, video calls, photos, documents and live-location sharing over an internet connection. That makes it useful for keeping a travel group together or confirming a pickup without paying international texting charges.

What we like: It is widely used and keeps trip communication in one place.

What to know: It needs mobile data or Wi-Fi. Check the phone number carefully before sharing personal information or sending money.

Our verdict: Install it before leaving home and verify your number while you can still receive regular text messages.

This may not be the most exciting recommendation, but it is one of the most practical. Download your airline’s official app before departure and sign in to your booking.

Airline apps can provide mobile check-in, boarding passes, gate notifications, delay information and rebooking options. During a disruption, the app may update before airport screens or email notifications do.

What we like: It gives you a direct line to the airline’s current information about your flight.

What to know: Push notifications are useful, but do not rely on them alone. Keep checking the departure board and listen for airport announcements.

Our verdict: Download it for every flight, even if you delete it after the trip.

TripIt turns confirmation emails into one organized itinerary. Forward your flight, hotel, rental-car and activity confirmations, and the app puts the details in chronological order.

This is particularly useful on complicated trips with several flights, hotel changes or train journeys. Instead of searching through your inbox at a check-in desk, you can pull up the reservation in one place.

What we like: It reduces the chaos of juggling confirmation emails.

What to know: Review imported details because automatic parsing is not infallible. Real-time alerts are generally part of the paid plan.

Our verdict: Best for multi-stop trips, business travel and anyone who likes everything organized.

AI can be helpful for brainstorming routes, comparing neighbourhoods, creating packing lists and turning scattered ideas into a first-draft itinerary. It should not be treated as the final authority on visa rules, border requirements, prices, opening hours, transit schedules or safety alerts. Verify anything that could cost you money or prevent you from entering a country.

ChatGPT is most useful when you give it real constraints: your travel dates, budget, interests, pace, mobility needs and where you are staying. It can then help turn those details into a practical first draft rather than a generic list of attractions.

We also use AI to compare neighbourhoods, create checklists and identify questions we still need to research. The trick is to treat the result as a planning assistant, not a booking engine or government authority.

What we like: It is flexible and can quickly reorganize a complicated trip.

What to know: AI can produce outdated or invented information. Always confirm bookings, travel rules, prices and operating hours through official sources.

Our verdict: Excellent for planning and editing; unreliable as the sole source of truth.

Wanderlog combines itinerary planning, maps, reservations, notes and collaboration. It is useful for road trips and group travel because several people can add places and adjust the plan.

The visual map helps reveal when an itinerary makes no geographic sense. That sounds obvious, but it is remarkably easy to plan breakfast on one side of a city, lunch on the other and dinner back where you started.

What we like: The shared planning and map view make group trips easier.

What to know: A detailed itinerary can become cluttered. Keep some flexibility rather than scheduling every hour.

Our verdict: A strong choice for collaborative planning and road trips.

Finding a cheap flight is only part of the job. These apps help us compare dates, monitor prices and track disruptions once the trip begins.

Google Flights is not a conventional downloadable app, but it remains one of the fastest ways to compare airfare. The calendar and price graph make it easy to see whether leaving a day earlier or using a nearby airport could reduce the fare.

Set a price alert when you are not ready to book. Google Flights sends updates when fares change, but you will usually complete the purchase with the airline or another booking provider.

What we like: It is fast, flexible and excellent for comparing dates.

What to know: It does not show every airline or every possible fare. Compare the final price, baggage allowance and change rules before booking.

Our verdict: Our first stop for airfare research. Before pressing confirm, read our guide to airline booking traps that can make a cheap flight cost more

Skyscanner is useful when you know you want to travel but have not settled on a destination. Its flexible search tools can surface options by month, country or broad destination.

It also compares hotels and rental cars, although we mainly use it for flight discovery. Once you find a fare, pay close attention to whether the booking is through the airline or an online travel agency.

What we like: Flexible searches are ideal for travellers who can follow the deal.

What to know: The cheapest result is not automatically the best one. Customer service and change policies vary by booking provider.

Our verdict: Best for inspiration and flexible travel dates.

Available on: iOS and supported Apple devices

Flighty turns a flight number into a detailed timeline with schedule changes, aircraft information and disruption updates. Frequent flyers appreciate how quickly it presents complicated flight information.

It is most useful on travel days, especially when weather or airport congestion starts knocking schedules sideways. The free version is enough for occasional travellers, while frequent flyers may value the paid alerts.

What we like: It presents flight changes clearly and can reduce airport uncertainty.

What to know: Some of its best features require a subscription, and platform availability may not suit every traveller.

Our verdict: A specialist app worth considering if you fly often.

Finding the right place to stay is about more than price. We look at location, recent reviews, cancellation policies, hidden fees, and whether the property actually suits the way we travel. These accommodation apps make it easier to compare hotels, apartments, hostels, and vacation rentals without bouncing between a dozen websites.

Booking.com remains one of the easiest places to compare a wide range of accommodation, from simple guesthouses to luxury hotels. The filters are especially useful when we need parking, a specific neighbourhood, breakfast, air conditioning or a refundable rate.

Read recent reviews rather than relying only on the overall score. We pay particular attention to comments about noise, cleanliness, construction and whether the room matches the photos.

What we like: Huge inventory and practical search filters.

What to know: Cancellation and payment rules vary by property. Confirm whether taxes and resort fees are included before booking.

Our verdict: Our top general-purpose hotel app.

Airbnb is most useful when we want a kitchen, laundry, a living area or enough bedrooms for a group. It can also provide options in neighbourhoods with few conventional hotels.

Compare the total price rather than the nightly rate. Cleaning charges, service fees and local taxes can change the value quickly. Read the house rules and cancellation policy before paying, and check whether the host has a substantial history of recent reviews.

What we like: It can provide more space and practical amenities than a hotel.

What to know: Quality is inconsistent, and fees can make a seemingly cheap stay expensive.

Our verdict: Best for longer stays and groups, not automatically the cheapest option.

Best for: Hostels, dorms, private rooms and social accommodation

Price: Free to search; booking deposit or fees may apply

Hostelworld makes it easy to compare hostels by location, room type, atmosphere and recent guest reviews. It is particularly useful for solo travellers who care about communal spaces and meeting other people.

Do not assume every hostel is a party hostel—or that every quiet-looking property will actually be quiet. Read recent reviews for comments about security, lockers, bathrooms, noise and the surrounding area.

What we like: It provides hostel-specific details that general hotel sites often miss.

What to know: A low bed price can rise after taxes, linen fees or deposits. Check whether lockers require your own padlock.

Our verdict: The most useful specialist app for hostel travellers.

There is no single eSIM provider that is cheapest or fastest in every country. Compare the local network, amount of high-speed data, hotspot rules, validity period and whether the plan is data-only before buying.

Airalo makes it straightforward to buy and install an eSIM before a trip. You choose the destination, select a data package and follow the installation instructions on a compatible phone.

We like that it removes the need to find a physical SIM card immediately after landing. Regional plans can also be convenient on multi-country trips, although a country-specific plan may offer better value.

What we like: Easy setup and broad destination coverage.

What to know: Most plans are data-only, and the local network or speed can vary. Check phone compatibility before purchasing.

Our verdict: A convenient starting point for travellers new to eSIMs.

Ubigi is worth comparing with Airalo because eSIM value changes by country. In some destinations, one provider may offer a better local carrier, more data or a longer validity period.

Install the app and eSIM before departure whenever possible. Take screenshots of the setup instructions in case your connection disappears halfway through activation.

What we like: It gives travellers another established option instead of assuming one provider always wins.

What to know: Coverage and value depend on the specific plan. Read the plan details rather than buying based only on the headline price.

Our verdict: Compare it destination by destination.

Getting around an unfamiliar city can be one of the most confusing parts of travel. These apps help us compare public transit, plan longer connections, and arrange rides when trains or buses are not practical.

Citymapper can be easier to understand than a standard map when a city has several transit systems layered on top of one another. It compares routes, shows transfers and often gives useful instructions about which station exit to use.

We find it particularly useful in large cities where choosing the wrong train direction or exit can add a surprising amount of time.

What we like: Clear transit directions and route comparisons.

What to know: Coverage is limited to supported cities, and live information depends on local transit data.

Our verdict: Excellent in cities where it is available.

Rome2Rio is useful during the early planning stage when you know where you want to go but not how to get there. Enter two places and it outlines possible combinations of flights, trains, buses, ferries and driving routes.

We use it as a starting point rather than the final booking authority. Once we understand the route, we verify schedules and buy tickets directly from the transport operator whenever practical.

What we like: It makes complicated overland connections easier to visualize.

What to know: Estimated times and prices can change. Confirm every important connection with the operator.

Our verdict: One of the best tools for answering, ‘How do we actually get there?’

Uber can remove the uncertainty of explaining a destination, handling cash and negotiating a fare in an unfamiliar city. The app shows the route, vehicle and driver details before the ride begins.

Availability and regulations vary widely. In some destinations, another local app is more common, and airports may require pickup from a designated ride-hailing area.

What we like: Upfront trip details and cashless payment are convenient.

What to know: Surge pricing can be expensive. Always confirm the licence plate and driver before getting into a vehicle.

Our verdict: Useful where it operates, but check the dominant local alternative.

Managing money abroad can get complicated quickly. Exchange rates, foreign transaction fees, ATM charges, and shared expenses all add up, especially on longer trips or when travelling with other people. These apps help us understand what things really cost, manage different currencies, and keep track of who paid for what without turning dinner into an accounting meeting.

Wise lets eligible customers hold and exchange several currencies and spend with a linked card. It can be useful for frequent travellers, remote workers and anyone receiving money in more than one currency.

Always compare the total conversion cost with your regular bank or credit card. The best option depends on your country, card benefits and the type of transaction.

What we like: Transparent conversion information and multi-currency tools.

What to know: Availability, card features and fees vary by country. It is a financial service, so protect the account with strong security.

Our verdict: A useful tool for frequent international travellers.

XE is the app we open when a price full of unfamiliar zeros makes our brains quietly leave the room. It converts currencies quickly and helps you understand what a meal, taxi or hotel actually costs in your home currency.

Remember that the rate shown in a converter is not necessarily the rate your bank, ATM or exchange desk will give you after fees.

What to know: It shows a reference rate, not a guaranteed retail exchange rate.

Our verdict: Keep it on your phone for quick price checks.

Splitwise prevents the end-of-trip ritual where everyone stares at a pile of receipts and suddenly forgets who paid for the rental car. Add shared expenses as you go, assign who owes what and let the app calculate the running balance.

It is particularly helpful for groups using different payment methods or taking turns covering major expenses.

What we like: It reduces awkward money conversations and messy arithmetic.

What to know: It records debts but does not automatically settle every balance. Agree on currencies and exchange rates at the beginning of the trip.

Booking tours and activities in advance can save time, especially when popular attractions have timed entry or limited availability. We use these apps to compare tours, skip-the-line tickets, day trips, and local experiences, but we always check the operator, recent reviews, cancellation policy, and exactly what is included before booking.

GetYourGuide is useful when timed-entry tickets sell out or when a guided visit adds real context. It covers major attractions, walking tours, food tours, day trips and airport transfers in many popular destinations.

Read the cancellation policy and identify the actual tour operator before booking. A marketplace can list several versions of what looks like the same experience.

What we like: Strong inventory in major tourism destinations.

What to know: Quality depends on the local operator, not only the booking platform.

Our verdict: A good place to compare organized experiences.

Viator has a broad inventory of tours and activities around the world. We use it to see what is available, compare departure times and identify experiences that may be difficult to organize independently.

As with any marketplace, read the newest reviews and check exactly what is included. A low starting price may refer to a basic option without transport, admission or the advertised upgrade.

What we like: It covers an enormous range of destinations and activities.

What to know: Listings from different operators can look very similar. Check inclusions, pickup details and cancellation terms.

Our verdict: Best for comparing a wide range of tours.

Finding the right trail or campsite takes more than choosing the prettiest photo. We look at distance, difficulty, recent trail conditions, offline map access, weather, and whether the route matches our experience level. These hiking, camping, and outdoor apps help us plan more confidently, but they should always be used alongside proper preparation and local safety information.

AllTrails is an easy starting point for finding hikes by location, distance, difficulty and user rating. Recent reviews can reveal muddy sections, closures, parking problems and trail conditions that a static guidebook cannot.

Download the route before leaving reception and carry a backup. A phone app is useful, but it does not replace proper preparation, weather awareness or a dedicated navigation tool in remote terrain.

What we like: It makes trail discovery accessible and provides recent user feedback.

What to know: Crowdsourced routes can be inaccurate. Do not rely on a single phone app for serious backcountry navigation.

Our verdict: Best for day hikes and casual outdoor planning.

Gaia GPS is aimed at travellers who need more detail than a simple trail list. It supports topographic maps, route planning and map layers useful for hiking, camping and remote travel.

Learn how to use it before heading into the backcountry. Download the required maps, carry power and tell someone your route. Technology is helpful right up until the battery dies.

What we like: Detailed mapping and route-planning tools.

What to know: It has a learning curve, and important map features may require a subscription.

Our verdict: Better suited to experienced outdoor travellers than casual city walkers.

The following apps can be excellent, but they are more specialized or depend heavily on your destination:

Hidden-city ticketing involves booking a connecting itinerary and intentionally leaving at the connection instead of taking the final flight. It can violate airline conditions, makes checked baggage impractical and can cause the rest of an itinerary to be cancelled. We would not build a trip around it.

Price forecasts can be useful signals, but airfare and hotel prices remain unpredictable. Treat predictions as estimates, not promises. Book when the price, schedule and cancellation terms work for your trip.

Use apps to organize information, not to replace official immigration sources. Entry requirements can depend on nationality, residency, passport type, trip purpose and even transit airports.

Google Maps can provide offline driving navigation for downloaded areas, and Google Translate supports downloaded language packs. Outdoor apps such as AllTrails and Gaia GPS can offer offline maps depending on the plan. Save boarding passes, hotel addresses and reservation numbers before leaving Wi-Fi.

AI can build a useful first draft, but it should not be allowed to quietly invent your holiday. Use it to organize ideas, compare possible routes and identify questions. Then verify flights, hotels, opening hours, ticket rules, visa requirements and safety information through official or first-party sources.

An eSIM can be useful when your regular carrier charges high roaming fees. Compare the local network, data allowance, hotspot rules and validity period before purchasing.

Google Maps and Google Translate support downloaded offline content. Some hiking apps provide offline maps through paid plans. Download everything before leaving reliable Wi-Fi.

The best travel app is not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that solves a problem at the moment you need it. For us, Google Maps, Google Translate, WhatsApp, an airline app and an itinerary organizer cover the basics. From there, we add an eSIM, flight tracker, budgeting app or hiking map depending on the trip.

Download your essentials before leaving home, test that you can sign in and save critical information offline. Then put the phone away once in a while. The app is supposed to help you experience the trip—not become the trip.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6267. The Best Stocking Stuffer for Jet-Setters Is This Viral Handbag Accessory

If there’s one thing I love almost as much as planning a trip, it’s having a cute lineup of travel gear to help me get there. The perfect carry-on, a reliable travel tote, a passport holder that doesn’t look like everyone else’s—and, as of late, a bag charm (or three). The accessory du jour has officially made its way from our handbags to our airport ensembles, and I can’t think of a more delightful stocking stuffer for the traveler in your life.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is showing off Coach's signature cherry bag charm

Bag charms have a longer fashion history than their current moment suggests: Jane Birkin famously adorned her namesake Hermès with personal keepsakes. Hermès then introduced its Rodeo charm in 2005, and Fendi sent its furry Monster charms down the runway in 2013. After a runway revival at Miu Miu and Balenciaga shows in 2024, the look made its way back to stylish travelers everywhere.

It makes sense, really: We put so much thought into what we pack and what we carry, so why not have a little fun with the bags that get us there? A bag charm is an easy way to give a well-loved weekender a fresh look, or make that familiar canvas tote feel a bit more like your own. There are colorful beads, mini leather accessories, nostalgic trinkets, whimsy characters, and even designs with a practical purpose. Some bag charms are simply there to look good; others offer a clever place to tuck away small essentials. And when your suitcase is circling the baggage carousel among a sea of lookalikes, a fun, personal detail is hardly a bad thing.

Beyond the styling, I like to think of bag charms as a new kind of travel keepsake. We’re always bringing pieces of our trips home: a street market find, a knickknack from a beach town, some wonderfully impractical souvenir that means everything to us and very little to anyone else. Rather than tucking them away on a shelf, clip these charms onto a tote or suitcase, and they’ll join you for the next adventure. The same goes for a charm gifted by a friend or one that reminds you of home. Nothing says, “think of me on the road,” quite like this.

Bag charms add a pop of color to a neutral bag or suitcase

And there’s no shortage of ways to make the look your own. Layer a few bag charms together, mixing colors, textures, and shapes, or keep things more understated with a single leather accent or jewelry-like detail. Think of it as accessorizing your luggage with the same consideration you give the rest of your travel outfit. Whether you’re shopping for the friend who’s always planning a weekend away, the family member with an enviable vintage luggage collection, or the frequent flier who appreciates thoughtful detail, there’s something in the mix for just about every kind of traveler.

Bag charms are small, they’re personal, they’re wonderfully extra, and truthfully, a whole lot more exciting to unwrap than another pair of compression socks. (Sorry, compression socks). Ahead, I’ve rounded up the best bag charms to gift this season, from playful fashion finds and colorful conversation starters to travel-friendly designs that do a little more than just look pretty.

A little cherry on top, quite literally. Made from glittery resin and metal, this bright red pick brings a playful pop of color to a tote, backpack, or set of keys. It’s a particularly good choice for the friend whose wardrobe could always use one more fun thing.

For the person who prefers their accessories a little more understated—but still appreciates a good detail—this bad boy pairs deep green beads with gold-tone hardware and a lobster clasp, offering their favorite bag a subtle hit of color and texture.

For the New Yorker in your life, here's some Big Apple nostalgia to take on the road. Kate Spade pays homage to its hometown with this mini MetroCard-inspired design—and for those who remember the ol’ swipe of a subway card, it's a fun yet tasteful piece of the city to carry along.

I’m adding this gold boot gem to my cart. For a little Western flair—minus the need to break in a new pair of boots—the iconic brand Tecovas has turned its Loretta boot into a mini accessory crafted from solid brass with an antique finish. It comes with both a key ring and a D-ring, so it can go wherever its owner does—whether that’s a road trip, a dude ranch weekend, or simply the daily commute.

Talk about chic! Sézane’s Juliette keychain has a caramel-color resin exterior with delicate white lace detailing, but the real treat is inside: a pocket mirror that opens with a pivoting mechanism. It’s ideal for a quick lipstick check before stepping off the train or heading out to dinner.

For the friend who has approximately 1,000 photos of their dog on their phone—and would happily add one more to the rotation. This little Jack Russell is embroidered onto supple full-grain leather, with a debossed Lauren Ralph Lauren logo on the back. A rather handsome stand-in for a four-legged travel buddy.

A handbag for your handbag? I’m listening. This mini zippered pouch is styled like a classic carryall, with leather construction and gold-tone hardware, and clips onto a larger bag to keep small essentials close. It’s available in red, cobalt blue, and silver, and can be personalized with a foil-debossed monogram—making it an especially sweet gift for a loved one.

A little luck for the road never hurts! This Madewell design brings together a wishbone, stone, and moon motif in a red-and-gold-toned cluster, and is finished with a dog-clip closure. It’s a playful pick for the friend who loves a meaningful trinket—or could use a little good fortune on their next big adventure.

For the friend who's always planning their next trip, this miniature version of Away’s signature hard-shell carry-on is made from the same durable polycarbonate shell and opens into two little compartments for small essentials like a spare key or folded cash. It clips onto a bag or backpack, and the Coast Blue shade is a nice nod to the real thing.

Meet the mini-me of one of our editors' favorite travel bags. Calpak's best-selling Luka duffel—this compact zip pouch comes in a pearlescent finish and clips onto a larger bag with a carabiner-ready loop. Better yet, it actually earns its keep: There’s room for keys, earbuds, cash, or whatever small essentials you’d rather not fish around for at the bottom of your tote.

A flower that doesn’t need watering—or a vase. Inspired by the marigolds of Diwali, this three-dimensional design is made from layered Italian leather petals and comes in yellow or orange. The leather leaf can also be monogrammed, making it a thoughtful gift with a personal touch. It’s a lovely way to bring a little color to someone’s everyday bag.

#6266. Anker’s New Power Station Is the Most Efficient I’ve Tested, Capable of Running My Fridge for 2 Days

My capacity test showed the Solix S5000 is nearly 97 percent efficient.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

How long a power station lasts has the most impact on your experience when using one, whether you’re experiencing a blackout or enjoying a weekend off the grid. This year, Anker has upped its game with the S-series stations. Advanced algorithms have improved how its inverters deliver power and extend battery life. Not long ago, I reviewed this technology in the small but powerful S2000 and was impressed. Now, I’ve put the newer and larger S5000 power station through its paces, and it didn’t disappoint.

For context, I also compared the S5000 to Anker's other large power station, the F3800 Plus (now only available as a bundle with other home power accessories), which has been on our list of the best portable power stations. Each model offers both 120- and 240-volt output, but the S5000 has a much larger battery capacity of 5,024 watt-hours (compared with 3,840 watt-hours with the F3800 Plus), and the S5000 is much smaller in size. While it offers less total power output (4,500 watts versus 6,000 watts for the F3800 Plus), I think the S5000 represents an overall improvement for those looking to buy a home backup station that’s more powerful than a typical portable power station.

This is what I cared about the most because better inverter efficiency is the primary feature Anker touts with the S5000. To evaluate its efficiency, I ran two tests. The first was to turn on the AC output and let it run overnight with nothing plugged into it, making sure to deactivate any auto-off features. I did this because, even when idling, most power station batteries lose some stored energy. But after 18 hours, the S5000’s battery capacity was still at 100 percent—that’s impressive. To make a comparison for context, I ran the F3800 alongside it for the same amount of time, and its battery capacity dipped to 81 percent.

For the second test, I plugged a watt meter into the station and plugged a space heater into the meter. I then ran the heater at full power, drawing around 1,500 watts, until it drained the battery fully. Using a resistive load like this (a device that turns energy to heat) can drain a battery pretty quickly, but this also gives you a good read on a power station's performance. It lasted just over three hours, and my meter measured just under 4,900 watt-hours. Compared with its official spec of 5,024 watt-hours of capacity, I determined that this station is around 97 percent efficient. Many stations hover around 89 percent on average, so this was a big win for the S5000.

The technology behind this ability enables the inverter to throttle itself up and down to meet the demands of the devices plugged into it. This is especially significant for lower-powered devices and cyclical appliances with fluctuating power needs, like refrigerators, because the inverter maintains its efficiency, regardless of what’s plugged into it. That means longer run times across the board. This station could easily power my full-size refrigerator for more than 48 hours.

The size of this station in relation to the battery capacity is its second most striking feature. It’s two-thirds smaller than the F3800 but offers 1,184 more watt-hours. At 99 pounds, I wouldn’t call it light, but with two wheels and a telescoping handle, it’s easy enough to roll around, and it’s not too hard to lift in and out of a vehicle. It would be easy to transport this to and from a second home or a job site.

There are a few other enhancements, as well. The 30-amp, 240-volt connection (great for powering an electric dryer or other 240-volt appliance) has its own on/off button, so it won’t create any unwanted drain when all you need is 120-volt AC power. It also accepts both low- and high-powered DC input, which means you get up to 3,000 watts of solar power if you have enough panels to achieve that.

There’s also a port connection for adding up to five expansion batteries, potentially increasing the total battery capacity to as much as 30,000 watt-hours. That same port can be used to connect to Anker’s Solix 5000 Smart Tri-Fuel Generator for direct DC recharging, which is three times faster than standard AC charging. I had this very generator on hand and was able to test this out. I observed around 4,000 watts of input while the generator was running on gasoline. In an emergency where the power has gone out for several days, you could use this method to fully recharge the S5000 in less than two hours.

The only downside is the maximum total output of 4,500 watts. While that’s perfectly fine for very basic home backup and RV use, it’s not going to power a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, let alone a full bank of circuits on a manual transfer switch, no matter how many expansion batteries are attached (they only add capacity, not output). True whole-home backup would require a larger station.

Sometimes, newer power station models are just more of the same, with only minor tweaks to power output, capacity, or outlet configuration. But the Anker S5000’s inverter efficiency technology is a notable upgrade that delivers on its promise of longer runtime than comparable models with the same capacity.

It’s not a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that) and doesn’t have as much output power as the F3800, but it can bring substantial power during an emergency to several appliances or a couple of critical circuits, and it’s much more portable. And if you’re an RV owner looking for a compact yet powerful station, this should definitely be on your list for consideration.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6265. 13 Travel Slippers That Are Comfier Than the Ones From Your Favorite Hotel

After a full day of sightseeing—or an even longer one spent in and out of airports—few things feel better than kicking off your shoes and sliding on a cozy pair of slippers. The complimentary slippers at a luxury hotel are always tempting to take home, but if we're honest, they rarely last beyond a few wears. Fortunately, plenty of more durable—and more comfortable—options exist, from plush, shearling slides and classic wool slip-ons to lightweight travel slippers that barely take up any room in your suitcase. Some have cushioned footbeds and rubber soles sturdy enough for a quick trip outside; others feature soft, suede soles better suited to padding around the house.

Whether you want a warm, fluffy pair by your bed or a foldable option for your next long-haul flight, there’s a slipper for everyone on this list. Read on for the very best pairs to pick up this season from Bombas, Cozy Earth, Ugg, and more.

⁠These lightweight, fuzzy slippers feature a soft, wool-like polyester upper, a breathable lining, and a memory foam footbed for a cushy feel underfoot. The nonslip soles are sturdy enough for quick trips outside to grab the mail or take out the trash, but they're best suited for indoor wear. Even better, they're machine washable, so you can easily keep them in pristine condition all season long. Available in five colors and backed by more than 10,000 Amazon reviews, they're an affordable option for wearing around the house or packing for a weekend away.

It's easy to see why this under-$25 Amazon find has racked up more than 23,000 five-star ratings. Not only are these slippers ridiculously soft (and just the right amount of over-the-top), but they're also pretty practical, thanks to the thick memory foam insole that retains its shape even after daily wear.

While your winter wardrobe likely contains a cashmere sweater or two, don’t sleep on these cashmere slides from Garnet Hill. Thanks to the slip-on slides’ sumptuous cashmere construction and breathable, thermal-insulating fibers, they’ll keep your feet warm and toasty—but not sweaty—all winter long. The padded footbed provides an extra layer of pillowy-soft comfort.

After a long day on your feet, you'll be glad to have these Quince slippers waiting by your bed. They have a soft suede leather upper and thick Australian shearling lining that feels plush against bare feet. And unlike some fuzzy slippers that leave your feet sweaty, the shearling material naturally wicks away moisture and regulates temperature, so you can wear them year-round.

The soft, moisture-wicking sheepskin wool lining of this classic shoe has made it an all-time favorite from the nostalgic Australian brand. The Scuff comes with a thin rubber sole that has just the right amount of support and stability for being on your feet in the kitchen or just puttering around the house on the weekend. Colors include the popular chestnut (shown above), dark gray, and black.

This luxury slide keeps your feet dry and cool, thanks to its moisture-wicking and temperature-regulating design. They're fluffy and warm, and so easy to slip on when you first wake up in the morning. Plus, they feature a slip-resistant sole, making them one of the sturdiest picks on the list.

One of the little luxuries of a hotel stay is slipping into the plush robes and slippers hanging in the closet. Now you can capture that vacation-level comfort at home with The Ritz-Carlton Frette slippers. Crafted from ultra-soft microfiber, they feel cozy and spa-like, while the nonslip soles make them practical for everyday wear around the house. The embroidered hotel logo adds a touch of opulence, and when they need a refresh, simply toss them in the wash.

These striped slippers from Parachute look like something you'd find at a cool boutique hotel. Made in Turkey from thick, absorbent cotton terry, they're soft underfoot and comfortable to slip on after a shower or while lounging at home. The stripes add a little more personality than your typical spa slippers, and the rubber soles grip slippery floors effortlessly. They're durable enough for everyday wear, too, though you may want to size up for a roomier fit.

Made with ultra-soft sheep fur and a plush shearling lining, these chic slippers provide plenty of warmth on chilly fall and winter mornings. As warm as they are, they're also naturally odor-resistant and breathable, so you don't have to worry about your feet getting too hot. They offer a grippy, durable outsole, so while they're best suited for lounging indoors, they can also be worn outside if necessary; you'll feel a little more secure wearing them out on the Airbnb's deck or down to the hotel lobby than in other pairs. They come recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, who regularly turns to them for extra warmth on cold weekend mornings at home.

Bombas has quite a few solid slippers from which to choose—including the Gripper Slipper that really blurs the line between sock and shoe. But the Sunday Slipper, with its super-soft faux fur and slip-on, slip-off capability, sits at the top of the heap when it comes to versatility. If you're stumped on what to gift someone for the holidays, the best-selling style is foolproof.

Birkenstock manufactures footwear of fabulous durability and quality, from the popular sandals and clogs that you can wear here, there, and everywhere to the more indoor-friendly Zermatt shearling slipper. Despite being supremely soft, the latex sole offers a boost of support, which is why they make such a great house shoe. They come in men's and women’s sizes, and you can pick between wide or narrow fits for optimal comfort.

The Ugg Tasman slipper might be the most recognizable slipper on this list, and it's popular for good reason: The closed-back design makes it a more practical alternative to the brand's classic Scuff slipper; the plush sheepskin lining and durable suede upper ensure coziness and durability; and the Fair Isle–inspired Tasman braid around the trim adds a hint of character.

L.L.Bean fans rave about these clog-like slippers for their arch support, heel cushioning, and playful patterns, featuring designs ranging from turtles to moose to ombré forest trees. They have a fleece lining and rubber anti-slip sole, and are roomy enough to wear your thickest socks underneath in colder months, making them our top pick for cold feet.

What are the best brands for travel slippers?

Bombas and EverFoams design lightweight slippers that are conveniently packable, while Ugg and Quince offer cozy shearling options that take up a bit more suitcase space. If you love the slippers you usually find at luxury hotels, The Ritz-Carlton also sells its signature Frette spa slippers online, so you can bring five-star comfort right to your home.

Slippers can be a welcome change from sneakers or boots on a long-haul flight, especially if you’re hoping to get some sleep. Choose a lightweight, packable pair with nonslip soles, but switch back to shoes when walking around the cabin or using the bathroom.

What should you look for in the best indoor slippers?

When shopping for indoor slippers, fit and material matter most: Wool and shearling provide warmth without trapping too much heat, while memory foam adds cushioning. Look for a soft, flexible sole with enough grip to keep you from slipping on hardwood or tile floors.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.
