If you typically fly with American Airlines and its partner airlines, earning elite status in the AAdvantage program can unlock many perks, from complimentary upgrades to priority boarding.

In 2022, American AAdvantage revamped the method for earning elite status to a system based on Loyalty Points.

Nowadays, members earn Loyalty Points through eligible flights, credit card spending and purchases with participating partners.

Here’s what you need to know about American Airlines elite status, including how to earn it and what benefits it brings.

American Airlines elite status gives perks to AAdvantage members who interact with the program and its partners. The program lets you earn Loyalty Points toward elite status through many activities unrelated to travel, including shopping, dining and spending on cobranded American Airlines credit cards.

You can earn each American Airlines elite status tier by accumulating a set amount of Loyalty Points during the elite-qualification year that runs for 12 months from March 1 through the end of February. Once you reach the threshold, your status takes effect immediately and remains valid through March 31 of the following full year.

Note: Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles are not the same thing (but more on that below).

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning American AAdvantage elite status

You’ll find four published tiers of American Airlines elite status that you can earn by accumulating Loyalty Points during the 12 months starting each March 1:

In addition to these tiers, there’s also the exclusive, invite-only Concierge Key status. However, American AAdvantage doesn’t publish any specific requirements for this status.

You’ll also earn Loyalty Point Rewards as you reach specific Loyalty Point thresholds, including some that fall between elite status tiers. You’ll earn your first Loyalty Point Rewards choice after earning 15,000 Loyalty Points within the 12-month qualification period beginning March 1.

Related: Your guide to American Airlines Million Miler status

To qualify for American Airlines elite status, you must earn the required number of Loyalty Points during each 12-month qualification period following March 1. As discussed, you’ll need to earn 40,000 Loyalty Points for Gold status, 75,000 for Platinum, 125,000 for Platinum Pro and 200,000 for Executive Platinum each qualification period.

We have a full guide to earning Loyalty Points. But, in short, you'll earn two types of American Airlines miles: base and bonus. And while both base and bonus miles are redeemable, generally only base miles earn Loyalty Points. The exception is the elite status bonus on flights, which also counts (more on that below). So, each time you earn a base mile with AAdvantage, you'll also earn a Loyalty Point.

You can earn American AAdvantage base miles through many different activities. Here’s a noncomprehensive list of some ways you can earn base miles (and hence Loyalty Points):

There are many other ways to earn American Airlines miles. However, check whether you’re earning base or bonus miles before you get too excited about how many Loyalty Points you’ll earn. Bask Bank mileage accounts are one example of an activity earning only bonus miles — hence, no Loyalty Points. Basic Economy fares on American don't earn Loyalty Points either.

Note: American and Hyatt ended their enhanced loyalty partnership in 2026, so World of Hyatt status is no longer offered as a Loyalty Point Reward. You can still earn 500 AAdvantage miles per eligible Hyatt stay by giving your AAdvantage number at check-in.

Related: Be careful: 9 times you won’t earn American Airlines Loyalty Points, even if you earn miles

American Airlines elite status comes with some valuable benefits. Here’s a look at some of the most noteworthy benefits, including how they differ by status tier.

American Airlines elite members receive complimentary upgrades on eligible flights to select destinations within North America, the Caribbean and Central America, subject to availability. Depending on the aircraft, these upgrades can move members from Main Cabin to premium economy, from Premium Economy to business or domestic first class, or directly from Main Cabin to business or domestic first class (on aircraft without a Premium Economy cabin).

These upgrades are automatically requested and are available on paid tickets and award tickets. Members can also receive a complimentary upgrade for one companion traveling on the same flight. However, Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026, aren't eligible for complimentary upgrades.

American will start processing these upgrades at different times depending on your American Airlines elite status tier. Executive Platinum members may have their upgrades confirmed as early as 100 hours before departure, Platinum Pro members as early as 72 hours, Platinum members as early as 48 hours and Gold members as early as 24 hours.

American Airlines prioritizes upgrades — including complimentary upgrades, mileage award upgrades and systemwide upgrades — in the following order:

Members with American Airlines elite status — and up to eight passengers traveling with you on the same reservation — can select Preferred seats without any extra fees during booking or anytime after booking (based on availability). Preferred seats have standard legroom but are located in more desirable locations throughout the economy cabin. This benefit does not apply to Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026.

Main Cabin Extra seats, which offer additional legroom, are also complimentary for AAdvantage elite members and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation (based on availability). Executive Platinum, Platinum Pro and Platinum members can select these seats at booking, while Gold members must wait until within 24 hours of departure. Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026, are not eligible for complimentary Main Cabin Extra seats.

American Airlines elite members get a mileage bonus as follows when flying on eligible flights:

The status bonus is added to the base miles earned on eligible flights, and unlike most bonus miles, it counts toward Loyalty Points as well. For example, on flights marketed by American, a member without status earns 5 miles and Loyalty Points per dollar, while an Executive Platinum member earns 11. That makes it easier for higher-tier members to requalify through flying.

AAdvantage elite members enjoy priority access at check-in, security and boarding on eligible American Airlines flights. Specifically, Executive Platinum members board in Group 1, Platinum Pro in Group 2, Platinum in Group 3 and Gold in Group 4. Boarding with any of these groups might mean there’s still space in the overhead bin for your carry-on suitcase.

AAdvantage status members also get priority when standing by for a different American Airlines flight on the same day of travel (and can standby for a later flight the same day) on eligible flights within the U.S. and between the U.S., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Executive Platinum and Platinum Pro members — and up to eight companions traveling with them on the same reservation — can enjoy complimentary same-day confirmed flight changes on American when flying to or from the U.S., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

AAdvantage elite members also enjoy complimentary checked bags when flying American Airlines: Gold members get their first checked bag free, Platinum members get their first two checked bags free, and Platinum Pro and Executive Platinum members get their first three checked bags free. Best of all, this checked baggage allowance is also offered to guests traveling with the status member on the same reservation.

American Airlines elite status offers a variety of other perks, including the following:

Finally, American Airlines offers additional rewards at specific Loyalty Point milestones. Though these rewards are separate from AAdvantage elite status, you’ll inherently unlock them as you accumulate Loyalty Points toward the program's elite status tiers.

Here’s a look at the Loyalty Point Rewards you could choose as you progress toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required for Executive Platinum status:

Related: Why (and how) I'm earning AAdvantage Platinum Pro elite status and not going for AAdvantage Executive Platinum

Having a cobranded American Airlines credit card is extremely helpful if you want to earn American Airlines elite status. Although the sign-up and category bonuses provide bonus miles — which won’t give you Loyalty Points — you’ll earn 1 Loyalty Point per dollar spent with all U.S.-issued AAdvantage credit cards. This means you can boost your Loyalty Point balance as you use your card for purchases and even qualify for American elite status from credit card spending alone.

If you value Admirals Club access, the (see rates and fees) is an excellent choice. Meanwhile, existing cardholders who had the AAdvantage® Aviator® World Elite Silver Mastercard® and were transitioned to the (see rates and fees) can still earn up to 15,000 additional Loyalty Points by meeting specific spending thresholds during the qualification year ending Feb. 28, 2027. Unfortunately, this benefit is not available to new Globe card applicants.

The information for the Aviator Silver card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

American Airlines elite status is worth it for some travelers. I've held Platinum Pro or Executive Platinum status since 2016 because I value the domestic upgrades, waived checked bag fees, Priority check-in lines and Oneworld Emerald status these tiers provide.

But, after reconsidering what I value in American Airlines elite status, I've only strived to qualify for Platinum Pro in recent years. In short, I decided the incremental value of Executive Platinum over Platinum Pro didn’t justify the extra costs I’d incur to earn the higher status.

It’s important to consider how much you’ll use your AAdvantage perks and the cost of earning American Airlines status. If you’ll organically earn American Airlines status through flights, then it’s likely worth earning. But if you’ll have to earn a significant number of Loyalty Points through other means, such as using the AAdvantage eShopping portal or spending on an AAdvantage credit card, there’s an opportunity cost to doing so.

Finally, if you’ll only use your American Airlines elite status perks occasionally or only need a specific perk, consider whether you can get what you seek through booking premium-cabin fares or applying for a credit card that offers that particular benefit.

Related: Which credit card should you use for American Airlines flights?

American Airlines offers four elite status tiers you can earn by accumulating Loyalty Points: Gold, Platinum, Platinum Pro and Executive Platinum. These tiers offer perks including Preferred seats, complimentary space-available upgrades on eligible American Airlines flights, and Oneworld perks on select partner airlines.

If you frequently fly with American Airlines, British Airways or Iberia on expensive paid fares or spend a significant amount on American Airlines credit cards or when shopping through the AAdvantage eShopping portal, you’ll likely find it easy and worthwhile to earn American Airlines elite status. Otherwise, it's smart to consider whether the value you'll get from American Airlines status is worth the cost you'll incur to earn it.

#6193. US Flights Have Been Grounded Nationwide

The United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, with all outbound flights from the US being directed to halt ground operations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated in a press conference that there was “no indication as of yet” that anything “nefarious” caused the ground stop, and suggested that it was due to a broad was a telecommunications outage.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA said in a statement on X. “Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement that the ground stop was due to a "communication issue" and that “FAA technicians are investigating.”

The halt on take offs and landing is in place for both domestic and international flights operating within the US. United Airlines, one of the four largest airlines in the nation, said that the order did not apply to in-transit aircraft: “United Airlines is responding to a nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. United flights that are already airborne will continue. New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place,” United Airlines said in a press release. “United will work with our customers to get them to their destinations once this issue is resolved.”

The last time a nationwide ground stop occurred in the US was in January 2023 following a computer outage in the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) pilot notification system (NOTAM).

CNBC reported that the widespread server outages affecting telecommunications over the past 24 hours were to blame, citing internal information from Alaska Airlines.

According to Cirium, an aviation analytics company, there are 26,284 flights scheduled to depart on November 13 from the US. As of 5:50 p.m., 600 flights have been diverted so far, with 496 of those 600 flights (82.7%) returning to their origin airport and the other 104 diverting to a different airport. At this time 481 have been canceled or no fly nationally, representing 1.83%. This will grow today,” a company spokesperson said. “After 4 p.m. Eastern time today, there were still some 11,000 flight scheduled to depart from US airports today.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. #6192. The Angry German On My British Airways Flight

I’ve written about the seat recline debate on many occasions, but finally experienced a real-life incident on a British Airways flight.

My position has been consistent over the years. Whether you recline your seat is your prerogative, not the prerogative of the person behind you. Even though a reclined seats often results in an uncomfortable position for the person behind you, that is the reason their seat reclines as well.

There are two exceptions. First, one should always recline their seat gradually. A sudden recline may result in a broken laptop. Second, seats should rarely be reclined during meal service (there are exceptions).

I was seated far in the back of the aircraft in 38H. Of course, my seat was up for the meal service. Of course, I reclined my seat gradually. But that wasn’t good enough for the passenger seated behind me.

He was a portly German gentleman, probably in his late 60s. He began cursing as I reclined my seat, then hitting it. I turned around and glared at him and he said nothing.

I turned back around and he began muttering to himself in German, cursing me out (assuming I was an Englishman and calling me some choice expletives). Zoning him out, I leaned back to go to sleep.

About 20 minute later he began shaking my seat. I got up and turned around. He made motions for me to put my seat up.

I proceed to lecture him, without expletives, in German that it was my right to recline my seat and that I had no choice when the person in front of me also reclined.

He was shocked that I spoke German and quickly shut up. I did not hear from him again during the flight.

When we landed, I offered him my hand and noted that economy class is difficult for everyone. He nodded and shook my hand back, noting that due to our late arrival he had missed his connection to Dusseldorf.

Tight seat pitch leads to air rage, but it is a reality of flying in economy class. I’m glad my own incident did not spiral out of control.

With those weapons in my onboard hand luggage I believe I will be able to endure my trip. And would you believe I even dieted for this trip. So I guess I am even more prepared than some.

It’s one thing to have seats that don’t recline for short flights, say up to 3 hours – but quite another for flights longer than that, and especially for an overnight, long haul intercontinental flight.

The real problem is the continued insistance by airline managers who fly in premium cabins that NEVER, EVER have to worry about the indiginities and discomfort they intentionally create to better line their own pockets, yet whom seem to think its perfectly OK to create teensy-weensy seats packed into 31” pitch, no legroom rows that they never have to subject their precious, royal bums squeezing into.

Fact is, aircraft used for long-haul flights should be subjected to a minimum row pitch of 32”-33” and 18” wide seats.

Using high density confirgurations that were originally designed for short hops on domestic routes in Japan is one thing.

Subjecting adults to those types of seats and row pitches for flights lasting 3-16 hours is immoral and unconscionable – especially when the fat cats in the C-suite and greedy shareholders never, ever deign to sit in the awful seats that seek to profit so handsomely off of others from,

I’d love to see how long these shameful 31” row pitch seats remained at BA, United, American, Delta et al if the likes of Alex Cruz, Oscar Munoz, Doug Parker, Glen Hauenstein & all of those Wall Street “Analysts” actually had to sit in these despicable seats for their flights all the time as most flyers do.

If these seats are not good enough for the folks in the C-Suite, then they shouldn’t be sold at all.

A few of the products you can save big on are socks (take up to 10% off when you buy three or more full-priced pairs), cycle accessories (take up to 15% off bike accessories, clothing, and shoes when you purchase any full-price Co-op Cycles bike that same day), REI Co-op brand camping gear (save 10% on bundles of full price tents, sleeping bags, and sleeping pads, as well as 10% on backpacking food and snacks when you meet the minimum purchase requirement of 8 and 10 respectively), and finally 15% off full-price paddles when you purchase a kayak, canoe, or stand-up paddleboard.

For more ways to save with REI, head straight to their discount page for the most up-to-date information on active REI coupons.

One of the easiest ways to score a discount is by signing up for REI’s email newsletter. Upon sign-up, you’ll score 15% off one full-priced item, which you can redeem on anything eligible on the site, from backpacks to hiking boots. After signing up, you’ll receive a unique coupon code sent directly to your email; keep in mind you have to use it within 30 days of receipt, or you’ll forfeit your discount. A newsletter subscription means more than just a one-time discount—once you sign up, you’ll be one of the first people to receive updates on all the latest gear arrivals, any upcoming sales, and exclusive coupons in the future, all delivered directly to your inbox.

For the greatest bang for your buck, head to REI’s deals section, which features all of last season’s gear for up to 77% off. Looking for a rain jacket or parka to protect you from the elements? Score savings of up to $200. In need of some hiking boots for your next excursion? They’ve got you covered with up to 70% off your desired footwear, including savings on favorites like 19% off men’s Bondi 9 Road-Running shoes and 50% off Merrell men’s Moab 2 Decon SE hiking shoes. You can also expect savings on backpacks (up to 30% off top brands like Osprey, The North Face, Patagonia, and more), as well as socks (10% off bundle deals when you buy three or more full-priced socks).

Thinking of starting another hobby? There’s never been a better time to exercise your free will (and just plain exercise) by scooping up a new bike or tent to start your next outdoor adventure. Customers can expect savings of up to 30% off bikes and a whopping 50% off camping gear on REI’s deals page. Score big on electric and mountain bikes, like 20% off the Co-op Cycles CTY 1.1 bike, so you’ll be able to traverse any terrain in style.

For those interested in dipping their toe into the camping lifestyle, expect savings on plenty of the gear you’ll need to get started, including tents, sleeping bags, and camping essentials, like a whopping 50% off the REI Co-op Campwell 6 tent. Head out on your next big trip through Yellowstone National Park or Glacier in style, and without the worry that you’ll be underprepared once you arrive. From camping chairs to keep you comfortable around the firepit to video cameras that always capture that perfect shot for your Instagram (or your memories), there are plenty of ways to save on all your necessities—and a few extras just in case.

No longer do you need to head to a store in person and battle it out for the last jacket on the rack: REI’s online outlet has tons of great gear to save on, all shoppable from the comfort of your own home. From shoes and socks to helmets, boots, and bags, expect huge savings on something for everyone. One of my favorites includes 27% off Smartwool Active Fleece Wind pants. There’s also plenty of other deals on travel gear worth calling out, like 30% off the CamelBak All Around travel tumbler and 41% off the Osprey Arcane small crossbody bag. On REI’s outlet page, shop top brands like Arc’teryx, Hoka, Keen, Osprey, Patagonia, Salomon, and Columbia, all in one spot.

For something a bit more consistent, sign up for an REI lifetime membership to score an estimated 10% off every year on all eligible purchases. Memberships are a one-time payment of $30, and last the rest of your life, so you’ll be able to score benefits for years to come. To get your rewards, simply shop as you usually would, and earn back an estimated 10% Co-op Member Reward annually on eligible full-price co-op purchases. Your reward will automatically be uploaded to your account in the following month.

Members get more benefits, like free standard shipping on every order (5–7 business days)—a convenience that non-members can only reap the reward of when they hit the $60 minimum spend. Members also save 20% off on bike and snow shop services, have extended return windows of up to a year rather than the usual 90 days, get free ski and board wax and a flat tire tube with repair, and up to 33% off gear rentals. All of these benefits more than make up for the $30 fee.

As an added bonus, those who sign up by November 12, 2026, will also receive a $30 gift card, which they can use on whatever they please for 30 days after they sign up. To be eligible to receive this gift card, all you have to do is make a $50 purchase at REI and buy your membership in the same order. This means your $30 one-time membership fee is basically free once you take advantage of the gift card.

Give your gear and clothing a second life when you trade in gently used products to REI’s Re/Supply platform—and receive a gift card for eligible items. Simply fill out the trade-in form to get an estimate on your product’s eligibility and credit value. Then drop your products off at your nearest REI store. Once your trade-in is complete and your product has been evaluated, you’ll receive an email with an REI e-gift card that you’ll be able to use to purchase more of your favorite gear.

Your used products will head to REI’s Re/Supply shop. Not only is this a great way to keep textiles and other items out of landfills, but you’ll get money back to spend on something else. These gently used secondhand products are shoppable as well, and at great discounts, so if you’re open to taking home a pre-loved item rather than springing for a new piece, expect to find some excellent savings. The brand is closing its online version of the shop, but customers can still purchase gently used items in its brick-and-mortar stores.

One final way to keep to your budget and still get some great deals is by signing up for the REI credit card. Customers who open an REI Co-op Mastercard get a total of 15% in REI rewards (5% card rewards on all REI purchases and 10% Co-op member rewards). Cardholders also earn 1.5% in rewards on all other purchases when not shopping at REI. As a bonus, there is no annual fee, and the rewards no longer expire.

REI credit cards are only available to members, so you’ll have to complete the one-time sign-up and $30 membership fee, but once you do so, you’ll be able to sign in online and validate your Co-op membership to join and start racking up rewards. All rewards are ready to be redeemed online and in stores at REI as soon as they pop up in your account. As a bonus, customers can expect a $100 REI gift card after their very first purchase outside of REI, but use it quickly, as the gift card expires 60 days after your account is opened.

JetBlue’s newest premium seats are ready for takeoff.

The airline just unveiled its new domestic first-class product called “BlueFirst.” It’s set to debut on flights next month, but TPG got a sneak peek at the seats ahead of the launch.

The new first-class seats will take up the first few rows on most of JetBlue’s planes, going forward.

Eventually, JetBlue flyers will see first-class on all of the carrier’s aircraft — except for jets that already have its lie-flat Mint cabin.

And with complimentary upgrades on the horizon for JetBlue’s Mosaic elite members, the addition of BlueFirst should offer TrueBlue loyalists some enticing new status perks in the near future.

Read more: JetBlue announces first-class upgrades, new elite benefits for 2027

JetBlue plans to offer three — or four — rows of BlueFirst, depending on the plane.

Like most domestic first-class products in the U.S., the seats are arranged in a 2-by-2 configuration.

JetBlue outfitted its BlueFirst seats with a handful of thoughtful touches, such as “flex foam” cushioning from mattress and bedding company Tuft and Needle.

The headrest also sports a special BlueFirst logo.

Beyond that, expect a host of seating upgrades from JetBlue’s core cabin. These seats have cocktail trays, extra storage and a large tray table with a personal device holder.

The 13-inch seatback screens are the first in JetBlue’s fleet to offer Bluetooth connectivity, which means passengers will be able to connect their wireless headphones, such as Apple AirPods.

The screens also offer a unique twist on ordering drinks inflight. “Mixologist Mode” allows BlueFirst flyers to customize their cocktail order with a base and mixers.

JetBlue is also rolling out a new “soft product” around the BlueFirst seats, including a new line of inflight food, drinks and amenities.

While the carrier won’t offer hot meals (no ovens!) on its domestic aircraft, there’s an array of creatively assembled bento box meals. Options range from sesame beef noodles with crispy wontons and Szechuan dip to tortellini pasta salad and a pastrami sandwich (and more).

JetBlue has a strong track record for its on-board food. And while the lack of ovens probably means its BlueFirst food won’t stack up to what you’d get on a long-haul Mint flight, the spread the airline showed off this week looks impressive — even if it will be served chilled.

BlueFirst service will also include a new array of wines curated by New York-based Parcelle Wine — plus a fresh lineup of amenities, glassware, and coasters designed by a local artist.

JetBlue’s new first-class product will debut on Dec. 8, on its service from Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL).

The airline has dozens of routes already slated for the new seats, which will continue to roll out across its fleet as JetBlue retrofits its planes.

Among the biggest winners in its first-class launch: JetBlue frequent flyers with elite status.

All TrueBlue Mosaic members will be eligible for complimentary, space-available upgrades.

Plus, customers who carry JetBlue’s top-end premium credit card will also be able to join the upgrade queue.

High-level Mosaics will also be eligible to use their confirmable upgrade certificates on BlueFirst (However, you can also still use those to upgrade to Mint, which will remain the airline’s top seat).

You can read all about JetBlue’s new upgrade policy and updated Mosaic benefits in our latest story about the TrueBlue program.

The launch of BlueFirst marks a new chapter for JetBlue’s on-board product.

The carrier began flying at the turn of the century with all-economy cabins.

It first waded into the premium space in 2014, when it launched Mint. Now, it's time to add domestic first-class to the mix — a cabin executives described Wednesday as “very JetBlue.”

‘Cheap chic’: How JetBlue’s first 25 years of flying helped reshape US aviation

It comes as U.S. travelers are about to see a wave of new first-class seats hit the market — from JetBlue to budget airlines Frontier and Allegiant.

There are some drawbacks to JetBlue’s new seats at the front of the plane.

To make room for the new recliner seats, the carrier’s long-celebrated economy legroom will shrink on some planes.

There’s also no divider between first-class and coach — and, as we noted, the meals won’t be hot.

But BlueFirst will certainly raise the bar on JetBlue's top-level service on domestic flights, and serve as a worthy complement to its popular Mint product.

Also, the chance for complimentary upgrades will be a key new perk for Mosaic elites.

And for an airline hoping to give customers more reasons to prioritize its TrueBlue loyalty program, the new seats could prove a meaningful addition for years to come.

#6189. Inside 'Grand Theft Auto VI'—and the Real-Life Florida Locations That Inspired It

Set to be released on November 19, 2026, Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of media ever created. Pre-sale estimates suggest the game has made a staggering $476 million in revenue already.

Dreamt up by Scottish developers Rockstar Games, the GTA series has been big business for some time now. The previous instalment, Grand Theft Auto V has reportedly made a whopping $11 billion since its release in 2013. Not bad for a game in which you essentially steal cars and shoot guns.

If you haven’t played the games, you should know that they take place in a sort of shadow version of the US, with each game taking place in a new city inspired by a real-world counterpart. For me, they’ve been a fascinating companion to my travels in America. When I’m in New York, walking among towering skyscrapers, I can’t help but be reminded of Liberty City, the location of 2001’s dark and atmospheric Grand Theft Auto III. On holiday in Los Angeles, driving along the Pacific Coast Highway, the long, ocean-view roads of GTA V’s Los Santos were front of mind.

It works both ways. Red Dead Redemption 2, an open-world cowboy game released by Rockstar between GTAs V and VI, is perhaps the most immersive video game to date. In it, you can wander everywhere from dry, open deserts to lush forests where you can kick back with your horse, camp, and look for rare herbs and flowers. For me, it’s inspired trips to the deserts of the American Southwest and served as an interesting entry point into learning about US history. Now when I’m abroad, I’m thinking of these games, but also learning more about the real-world events and cultures that inspired them. It’s a full-circle moment that only enriches my travels.

These gaming vacations, or ‘gami-vacations’, are becoming increasingly popular. Fans are traveling to Tokyo to visit real-life locations from the Yakuza series and role-playing classic Persona 5, to Paris to see locations featured in the Assassin’s Creed series, to the Pacific Northwest to soak up the vibes of zombie classic Day Gone, and to Iceland to walk dramatic black sand beaches like those in the Hellblade series.

“Santa Monica, the Sunset Strip, and Griffith Observatory from GTA V,” one Reddit user replied to a post asking about video game locations fans wanted to visit in real life. “Old town Tallinn feels like a very fairytale environment to me. If you went in winter, it would feel like a set from Assassin's Creed,” suggests another Redditor.

Far from being confined to their rooms, crouched over consoles, gamers are increasingly inspired to get out into the world. It’s a beautiful tradition, and one that GTA 6 looks set to continue. Set in the fictional state of Leonida, GTA 6 is set to be the franchise’s largest map to date. With six key locations, there promises to be something for every type of traveller. Here’s what you need to know, along with the real-world inspirations for each game location.

“We’re a long way from the ‘80s, but Vice City is still the sun and fun capital of America,” reads Rockstar’s official guide to GTA VI’s base of operations, Vice City.

As fans are aware, the new game returns to the setting of the 2002 release, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. Set in the 1980s, that game borrowed pretty heavily from the story of Brian De Palma’s brace of crime films Scarface and Carlito’s Way, giving players the ability to control one Tommy Vercetti as he rises from the streets to build a narcotics empire. As expected, disco, perms, neon signs and flared trousers were the order of the day.

Updated for 2026, GTA VI’s Vice City is a modern cityscape full of high-rises, trendy rooftop bars, nightclubs. and more. It sounds pretty idyllic, but this being GTA, there’s a shadier side, too. “When the sun fades and the neon glows, everyone has something to gain—and more to lose,” the official longline reads.

The recent Netflix preview of the upcoming game gave us a bit more insight into the locale, including shots of BASE jumping from city bridges, a jewelry store robbery and subsequent high-speed escape, and a shootout through a drug den in a down-on-its-luck neighbourhood. In other words, as the main large city in the game, it looks like there’s plenty to keep Vice City residents occupied—on both sides of the law.

Inspiration: While Rockstar doesn’t explicitly explain that ‘game location X equals real world location Y’, it’s pretty obvious that Vice City is based on South Florida’s party capital, Miami. Despite the criminal element of Vice City, the real-world city has been keen to play on the connection. A New York Times story suggests the city is keen to embrace its fictional twin due to a drastic drop in real-world crime recently. Which is, of course, great news for tourists. For the full GTA experience, you can enjoy Miami’s beaches, bars, and car culture, alongside iconic EDM nightspots like Club Space and E11EVEN Miami.

In Leonida Keys, the dress code is casual and the bars are loaded. “Life in this tropical archipelago isn’t flashy, but it’s easy,” runs the official description. In game, the Keys look like an ideal place to hit pristine tropical waters for a dive, jet ski, or scuba trip. Naturally, there seems to be a strong party boat presence too, with a Spring Break vibe. While we’re sure some absolute in-game carnage will take place there, at present, it actually looks like quite a nice place to unwind and escape the more criminal elements of the game’s plot.

Inspiration: The obvious IRL comp here is Key West, nestled at the very southern tip of Florida. In fact, here you can see the southernmost point in the continental US, just 90 miles from Cuba as the crow flies. As well as a plethora of luxury hotels, casual bars, and seafood spots, you can kick back on white beaches, or enjoy a glass-bottomed boat tour.

For a break from all of this, you can visit the Hemingway Home, where Ernest Hemingway finished books including A Farewell to Arms and To Have and Have Not—that is, when he wasn’t out big-game fishing. The house is home to the first-ever swimming pool built in the Keys, as well as descendants of Hemingway’s famous six-toed cats.

Fans don’t know much about GTA 6’s Grassrivers yet, although the official synopsis does suggest some intrigue: “You never know what lies beneath the surface of this primordial expanse. The gators may be the most famous attraction, but there are far deadlier predators and weirder discoveries among the mangroves.” So far, all we’ve seen is an airboat tour and a birdwatching tower, suggesting a heavy emphasis on encounters with the natural world. Watch this space.

Inspiration: Clearly inspired by the Florida Everglades, Grassrivers will surely have a feel and flavor all of its own. The real Everglades has a rich cultural history. Yes, there are airboat tours catered to tourists during which you can spot ‘gators and learn all about the invasive pythons that are terrorising the ecosystem. And yes, you will be able to try deep-fried gator afterwards. But the real treasure is traditional foods like thick and chewy fry bread, swamp cabbage, or sofkee, a thin porridge made from corn.

And, at the Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum near Fort Lauderdale in the north of the Everglades, you can learn about the Seminole nation, a group made up of Native Americans moving south to escape the British, mixed with escaped formerly enslaved peoples from the area’s plantations.

If GTA 6 were represented on an old-timey naval map, Port Gellhorn a “failed resort on the edge of the map" might be marked “here be monsters.”

We know very little about the area yet, except for the fact that it’s rooted in poverty, with locals pushed to extremes to make ends meet. According to Rockstar, “Cheap motels, shut-down attractions and empty strip malls won’t bring the tourists back, but there’s a new economy in this once-popular vacation spot. It’s fuelled by malt liquor, painkillers and truck-stop energy drinks. Jump on a dirt bike and hold onto your wallet.” In other words, it sounds like a great place for a video game, less so for a holiday.

Inspiration: Again, Rockstar hasn’t been open about which area of Florida Port Gellhorn is based on, but fans and Florida locals think it takes inspiration from Panama City and the surrounding areas in the Florida Panhandle. Off the beaten track of most holidays, Panama City nevertheless has a strong reputation for seafood and water sports. Given its deepwater port, there’s also a strong maritime history. St Andrews State Park might be your best bet for snorkelling, swimming, kayaking and a calm and safe designated tidal pool.

Ambrosia sounds, possibly, like the least appealing locale in GTA 6. It’s reportedly a factory town, overseen by vicious biker gangs. “In the heart of Leonida, American industry and old-school values still reign supreme – whatever the cost. The Allied Crystal sugar refinery provides the jobs, while the local biker gang provides almost everything else,” runs Rockstar’s official primer on the place. The Netflix preview didn’t help. We saw a shootout in a dilapidated house, backyard wrestling, and possibly some mud-wrestling too. Mark this one as the biggest unknown of the game.

Inspiration: Florida locals think Ambrosia is based on Clewiston, Florida and the surrounding agricultural area around Lake Okeechobee. The main crop here is sugar, with Clewiston known as "America's Sweetest Town.” The irony in the in-game depiction is pretty obvious here, but the IRL location is well worth a visit if you’re a fan of fishing, with the local largemouth bass on Lake Okeechobee a particularly sought-after prize.

Mount Kalaga National Park looks like a truly beautiful in-game location, teeming with wildlife and activities from bicycle riding to kayaking. What’s not to love? Well, this bucolic utopia may actually prove to be too good to be true. In the Netflix preview, a televised advert for the ‘Prairie Sandwich’ seemed to take place in the park, suggesting that rather than enjoying the park’s animals in their natural habitat, your main goal might actually be to shoot them. If so, hunting will be an interesting addition to the game, and one that worked well in Red Dead Redemption 2. Of course, players will probably be able to opt out of the bloodshed and just enjoy a nice stroll among the trees instead. Here’s hoping.

Inspiration: While there’s no one-for-one comp for Mount Kalaga National Park, the Southern US States in particular are well known for their stunning national parks. Fans think this one takes inspiration from North Carolina’s Table Rock Mountain, Georgia’s Providence Canyon State Park, and the Suwannee River, which runs through Georgia and Florida. Whatever the real inspiration, if you are visiting Florida, it’s a reminder to get off the beaten path and out of the cities into lovingly preserved wild areas.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. #6188. Alaska Adds Service to Four New U.S. Cities

Alaska Airlines will bring four new destinations into its domestic network next summer.

The carrier announced Thursday that it will serve Charlotte, North Carolina, Jacksonville, Florida, Norfolk, Virginia, and Des Moines, Iowa, from Seattle. Three of the four cities – Jacksonville, Norfolk, and Des Moines – have never had nonstop flights to Seattle.

Currently, only American Airlines connects Charlotte and Seattle.

The Des Moines service will also mark Alaska’s debut in Iowa.

All four connections will operate daily, year-round. Flights to Charlotte and Norfolk will begin June 10, 2027, with Jacksonville and Des Moines launching later that month, on June 24.

Alaska will also offer seasonal service from Seattle to Guadalajara, Mexico, from March 18, 2027, to Aug. 9. Flights will operate three times weekly, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

#6187. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM ET on November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is structured as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status, and purchased points will post within 72 hours of an eligible purchase (though usually much faster than that).

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses, and that’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 200,000 points, pre-bonus.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

#6186. United Clears Halfway Mark on Starlink Rollout

Starlink satellite internet service is now available on more than half of United Airlines’ daily flights, the carrier announced Thursday.

The airline said it accelerated Starlink installations ahead of the Thanksgiving travel period. It expects to fly an average of 500,000 people per day between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1.

Customers can use United’s Starlink Wi-Fi tracker to check whether their upcoming flight is equipped with the service up to three days before their departure.

United selected Starlink as its onboard wireless internet provider in 2024. It first installed the technology on its regional jets and is now working on its long-haul widebody fleet.

Starlink Wi-Fi is free for MileagePlus members.

United expects to have Starlink on nearly 64% of daily flights by the end of the year. Installations should be complete by the end of 2027, officials said.

#6185. A TikToker Went Viral for Kayaking 500 Miles of Congolese River—and Started an Even Bigger Conversation

Last month the Welsh adventurer and self-described extreme athlete Ash Dykes was paddling along the placid waters of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River flowing through Cameroon, Central African Republic, and Republic of the Congo, when something stirred underneath his vessel, kicking up bubbles. Dykes, with the local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire and cameraman Will Perez, had just pushed off on a kayaking trip through the Congo Basin, the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike. The team knew they might encounter lowland gorillas, or perhaps forest elephants, as they made their way nearly 500 miles down the river. Perez then brought up another possible cause for the sudden ripples: a hippo. If the travelers had happened upon a hippopotamus, as many locals had warned them about, they were in immediate peril.

In October, adventurer Ash Dykes, local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire, and cameraman Will Perez embarked on a 500-mile kayaking trip in Republic of the Congo.

When Dykes posted the minute-and-a-half-long video of this “encounter” in the Sangha—cause still unknown—the post racked up over 8 million views on TikTok. The thousands-deep comments section, full of viewers hooked as to what might happen next, burst with theories: Some swore that Mami Wata, a water spirit said to frequent the riverbanks, had caused the sudden movement. One user mused that the three men were in “a real game of Hungry Hungry Hippos,” while others zoomed in on Perez’s visibly tense expression. Another user quipped: “I quit my job to focus on this expedition.”

Though intended as a joke, the latter reaction succinctly illustrates the attention this trip has garnered on social media. For weeks millions of viewers were glued to the team’s frequent TikTok dispatches—which they later fleshed out into a longer YouTube series of deep dives. The videos documented the logistical hurdles in reaching the Sangha; their trudging amid the heat and threat of parasites and disease; their day spent with the Ba’Aka people, a seminomadic Indigenous tribe in Dzanga-Sangha Protected Area, where they foraged for wild coconut and joined a traditional hunt; and extended stretches of the three bobbing through calm waters. Those following online celebrated alongside the men when they spotted forest elephants, and their pulses quickened when they outran a swarm of bees chasing their kayaks. When the team went abruptly silent for a prolonged stretch, following a power bank failure, viewers worried that something catastrophic had happened.

The Congo Basin is the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike.

The Sangha expedition—or “mission,” as Dykes has dubbed it—was the first leg in an ambitious undertaking called Project 6. The venture involves the Welshman—who’s made a career of adventure travel and breaking world records (such as becoming the first person to walk the length of the 4,000-mile-long Yangtze River, which took him nearly a year)—traverse “extreme” parts of the globe by performing intensive feats of athleticism. He will soon cross Kyrgyzstan on horseback in subzero temperatures for the second installment of the project; he is revealing ensuing stops one by one.

“I'm fascinated with corners of the world that I am unfamiliar with and learning from the people there that call it home,” Dykes says. “Then [it’s] mixed in with the challenge of: Can I do what is deemed impossible, or can I do what people have tried to do before but failed to complete?”

Aside from accomplishing the athletic challenge of constantly paddling down the Sangha every day for weeks, Dykes says he aimed to showcase the beauty of the Congo Basin, and its inhabitants, in a responsible way—stressing to viewers that “you can go to places like this as long as you put the right preparation in,” he says.

Video on TikTok and Youtube showed the trio of Tuyumvire, Perez, and Dykes on their river adventure.

Dykes is quick to credit those who made the Congo Basin excursion possible—especially Tuyumvire, who works in conservation advocacy and ecotourism through his Kigali-based company, Kumbukumbu Tours. Born in a forest village near Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of Congo, he fled the region following the civil war and lived in a refugee camp for over a decade before founding his tour company in 2015; he says those experiences shaped his belief that responsible tourism can be a means of helping make a local impact, particularly for young people. Tuyumvire agreed to join Dykes’s excursion because he saw an opportunity to tell meaningful stories about the Congo Basin for a larger audience.

“Because we have been surviving these out-of-context stories or even more exaggerated stories,” says Tuyumvire. “I myself feel the responsibility to always say yes to someone who has the microphone, and I tell the right context.”

Ahead of the excursion Tuyumvire worked with Dykes to pick the specific location for the journey and scouted out the upper headwaters of the Sangha. Tuyumvire offered context and commentary in videos throughout the trip, speaking about the critical endangerment of forest elephants, the deforestation threatening the Congo Basin, and noting that women were on the front lines of hunting when they met the Ba’Aka people.

Yet straddling the line between education and entertainment for a predominantly TikTok viewership resulted in unexpected tensions. Internet connectivity posed a challenge due to the forest canopy; still, Dykes insisted the journey be “as live as possible” online. “I can’t be claiming that this is a lifetime expedition and then we use either recycled content or we go dark,” he says.

Forest elephants are among the wildlife that inhabits the Congo Basin through which the team traveled.

While a plurality of viewers seemed genuinely fascinated by the three-week-long trip, even during less-exciting moments, Dykes noticed that some expressed a morbid glee for destructive content. Dykes says that some online commenters even started to bet money on how the trio might die in the Congo Basin, perhaps at the hands of a hippopotamus or a crocodile. “I think people are lost or confused as to what is a video game and what is a movie, and then what is reality,” he says. “So it's almost like this disconnect where people just wanted to be entertained: ‘If I'm going to the Congo, I want to see you escaping wildlife, wrestling.’” Tuyumvire saw the conflicting responses from viewers as “another kind of challenge for me to…create a story that will continuously be fed to the audience, but that will not also be overcrowded by too much exaggeration.”

Others have criticized Dykes, drawing parallels between him and other foreigners entering so-called forbidding places and, intentionally or not, reinforcing outdated tropes. Guy Dieudonne Moukandi N'Kaya, a lecturer and researcher at Marien Ngouabi University in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, says that Dykes’s trip through the Sangha felt honest in that it showed the “tense coexistence” between humans and wildlife in the region. Yet the way Dykes framed the expedition gave N’Kaya pause: Leading up to the trip, Dykes noted in a TikTok teaser that he would be “dropping into the heart of darkness,” a phrase culled from Joseph Conrad’s controversial, turn-of-the-20th-century novella about a Belgian trading company siphoning resources from the Congo River. N’Kaya says that descriptors such as “heart of darkness” and “unexplored,” which Dykes has also used in some of his posts, erase the presence of those who have long lived within the region: “The Sangha is not empty,” N’Kaya writes over email. “For centuries it has been traversed by people in dug-out canoes—fisherfolk, traders, and families.”

The water of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River, is tranquil—but the threat of disease-carrying bugs, dangerous wildlife, and the physical challenge of traveling 500 miles on human power made this one of Dykes' six missions.

While Dykes emphasizes that he wanted to raise awareness of the Congo Basin, which is under dire threat of deforestation, some viewers have questioned whether the adventure has truly benefited the region—or whether it’s more of a boon to his Project 6 venture. The Congo Basin has long grappled with interlacing issues including extreme poverty, corruption, and illegal mineral mining, which Tuyumvire says stem from the legacy of colonialism and slavery. “People are poor in the sense that they are ready to sell anything they are able to, to be able to just survive,” Tuyumvire says. “People seeing a white person in this region, it brings memories of the past: ‘This guy’s coming for timber. This guy’s coming for minerals.’ Things that really don't give them any kind of hope to develop the area. And that itself, the mindset, is a threat to the forest.”

After returning from the trip in late October, Tuyumvire has been resting and resuming his routine following the physical demands of kayaking. He’d never kayaked at length before a few weeks ago; he says his real motivation was to “share the stories and to try to transform the adventure into something impactful.” The widespread interest in the videos hasn't translated to bookings of his tours, but that was never the goal: “The audience we had is not an audience of travelers, to be honest,” he says. He has been reflecting on how, in hindsight, he wishes he had created a stronger call to action so that TikTok viewers’ curiosity could have a direct impact on the region. (Alongside his tours Tuyumvire helps run the Congo Rainforest Fund, a local NGO that works with local communities to understand threats to the forest and create solutions, such as shoring up educational efforts and job opportunities.)

But he believes that broadcasting the journey did help viewers further understand a place that they may not have been familiar with. “[The] Congo Basin has been represented as a difficult place to access, a difficult, complex place to understand,” Tuyumvire says. “So people were saying, ‘Finally, someone is going to give us the real information’…we want to see them in the reality."

If you carry the (see rates and fees) in your wallet, chances are you appreciate its premium travel perks and valuable rewards.

But even a card with a $795 annual fee can't cover every spending category or travel need. That's where a second credit card can come in handy.

I carry the Sapphire Reserve myself, but it's not the only card I reach for. Whether you're looking to maximize everyday spending, enhance your airline experience, or pick up hotel-specific perks, the right pairing can help you get more out of your wallet.

Here are seven cards worth considering alongside the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Here's a quick look at seven options, including how much you'll pay in combined annual fees.

The Capital One Venture Rewards is a solid option for Sapphire Reserve cardholders looking to earn more on everyday purchases.

Why the pairing works: One area where the Sapphire Reserve falls short is everyday spending that doesn't qualify for a bonus category. Those purchases generally earn just 1 Ultimate Rewards point per dollar spent, while the Venture Rewards earns at least 2 Capital One miles per dollar spent on all purchases, regardless of category.

For example, you could use your Sapphire Reserve for purchases that earn bonus points, then reach for your Venture Rewards when shopping for clothing, furniture or other purchases that wouldn't earn elevated rewards with the Reserve.

For a $95 annual fee, the Venture Rewards also gives you access to Capital One's 15-plus transfer partners, opening up additional redemption opportunities beyond Chase Ultimate Rewards.

Key drawbacks: While the Venture Rewards has a relatively modest annual fee, it still brings your combined annual fees to $890.

You'll also be managing two separate rewards currencies, since Chase Ultimate Rewards points and Capital One miles can't be combined directly. While this opens up more redemption opportunities across different rewards programs, just make sure you're comfortable managing two rewards currencies before committing to both cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the Venture Rewards.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

If you regularly fly United, pairing your Sapphire Reserve with the or can help you enjoy additional airline-specific perks.

Why the pairing works: The Sapphire Reserve offers valuable travel benefits and flexible Ultimate Rewards points that you can transfer to United MileagePlus at a 1:1 ratio. However, it doesn't offer some of the perks that come with carrying a United credit card, like free checked bags and priority boarding.

Both United cards can help fill that gap, but they cater to slightly different types of travelers.

With a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 annually, the United Explorer offers:

Meanwhile, the $350-per-year United Quest offers additional benefits for more frequent United flyers, including:

The Explorer may be enough if you only fly United a few times a year, while the Quest makes more sense for travelers who can take advantage of its additional benefits.

I personally carry both the Sapphire Reserve and United Quest, and I appreciate being able to earn flexible Ultimate Rewards points while still enjoying United-specific benefits when I fly.

Key drawbacks: Both cards add another annual fee to your wallet (the Explorer after the first year), so you'll want to make sure you fly United often enough to take advantage of their benefits. There's also some overlap in travel protections and rewards earning, particularly on United purchases.

And while you can transfer Ultimate Rewards points to United MileagePlus, you can't transfer United miles back to Chase, so it's worth considering which rewards currency you'd rather earn on each purchase.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Explorer and our full review of the United Quest.

The and  are two great options for Sapphire Reserve cardholders looking to earn more Ultimate Rewards points without paying another annual fee.

Why the pairing works: Both Freedom cards offer opportunities to earn more rewards on purchases that might otherwise earn just 1 point per dollar with the Sapphire Reserve.

The Freedom Unlimited earns 1.5% cash back on purchases outside its bonus categories, making it a solid choice for everyday spending. Meanwhile, the Freedom Flex earns 5% cash back on up to $1,500 in combined purchases in rotating bonus categories each quarter you activate (then 1%).

Although both Freedom cards are marketed as cash-back cards, they technically earn Ultimate Rewards points, with each point worth 1 cent when redeemed for cash back.

For example, $1,000 in nonbonus spending would earn 1,500 points with the Freedom Unlimited, compared with 1,000 points on the Reserve.

The biggest advantage of either pairing is that you can combine the rewards earned with your Freedom card and Sapphire Reserve, allowing you to redeem them as transferable Ultimate Rewards points.

You could even take things a step further by carrying all three cards, creating a version of the Chase Trifecta. This strategy allows you to maximize rewards across different spending categories without adding another annual fee.

Key drawbacks: The Freedom Unlimited's 1.5% earning rate isn't the highest available for everyday spending, while the Freedom Flex requires you to track and activate quarterly bonus categories to maximize its rewards.

Both cards also have some overlapping bonus categories with the Reserve, so you'll want to pay attention to which card earns the most on each purchase.

Ultimately, I'd lean toward the Freedom Unlimited if you prefer a simple, consistent earning strategy, or the Freedom Flex if you're willing to put in a little extra effort to maximize rotating categories.

The is worth considering if you want to earn bonus rewards on business expenses.

While the travel category overlaps with the Sapphire Reserve, the other categories can be useful for business owners who regularly spend on advertising, shipping or telecommunications.

For example, $10,000 in eligible advertising purchases would earn 30,000 points with the Ink Business Preferred, compared with 10,000 points at the Reserve's standard earning rate.

You can also combine eligible Ultimate Rewards points earned with both cards, helping you build up your balance faster for future travel redemptions.

Key drawbacks: The Ink Business Preferred adds another $95 in annual fees, and you'll need to qualify for a business credit card to apply.

Because of the overlap in travel earning, this pairing makes the most sense if you have enough spending in the Ink Business Preferred's business-specific bonus categories to justify the additional cost.

To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred.

If you frequently stay at Hyatt properties, the can help you unlock hotel-specific benefits that your Sapphire Reserve doesn't offer.

And if you don't regularly stay at Hyatt properties, you may have a harder time getting enough value from the card's benefits to justify its $95 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the World of Hyatt Card.

There's no single best card to pair with the . The right choice depends on where you spend the most and what you want from your next credit card.

Personally, I'd start by looking at where my Sapphire Reserve falls short, whether that's earning rewards on everyday purchases or offering airline-specific benefits that could make my travels easier.

After all, the goal isn't necessarily to have more credit cards. It's to make sure the cards you do carry work well together.

Before adding another card to your wallet, consider how it fits into your overall credit card strategy.

If you're applying for a Chase card, keep the issuer's unofficial 5/24 rule in mind, as well as any welcome bonus eligibility restrictions. You'll also want to weigh the combined annual fees against the additional rewards and benefits you're getting.

Finally, think about whether you'd prefer to pool more Ultimate Rewards points with another Chase card or diversify into a separate rewards currency, such as Capital One miles.

The offers plenty of value on its own, but pairing it with the right card can help you earn more rewards and enjoy benefits you might otherwise miss.

Before adding another card to your wallet, consider where your Reserve falls short, your spending habits and whether the additional rewards and perks justify any extra annual fee.

#6183. Etihad Slashes Flights, Pulls Airbus A380 Off Two Routes (Including Toronto)

Etihad Airways has just filed a major schedule update for early 2027, impacting a couple of dozen routes. In isolation, you might not think much of this, as the first several weeks of the year have weaker demand in many markets. However, in light of what’s going on in Etihad’s commercial division, I can’t help but be curious if there’s a bit more to this, and wonder how things will evolve.

AeroRoutes reports on how Abu Dhabi-based Etihad has filed a schedule change for the first quarter of 2027, with most of the changes taking place for flights as of January 11, 2027. For the most part, the reductions are for around a couple of months, through March 2027. There are two ways to look at this:

The frequency reductions we’re seeing are pretty significant. Just to look at service to North America:

Specific to the A380, it seems that Etihad is taking the jet off the Toronto and Singapore (SIN) routes over that period, and it doesn’t seem like the super jumbo will be flying any other routes in place of that, at least based on current schedule filings. During that period, Etihad will only be flying the A380 to four destinations — Bangkok (BKK), London (LHR), Paris (CDG), and Tokyo Narita (NRT).

It’s a fascinating time for Etihad. Obviously Gulf carriers are having a rather difficult time with everything going on in the region at the moment, and it comes at a unique time for Etihad, as the carrier has been going through a massive expansion.

Now, I’ve been a bit skeptical about the claimed economics of this expansion, but Etihad management has insisted everything couldn’t be better… until Etihad Chief Commercial Officer Arik De recently “departed” the airline.

The can of worms that this departure opened is truly unlike anything I’ve seen at any airline before… and I’ve been following this industry for a long time. Seriously, check out the 520+ comments on my post about his departure, because employees have a lot to say. It’s so salacious that it has gotten OMAAT blocked in the UAE.

The point is, if even a quarter of the things are to be believed — and I’ve had some very interesting conversations with some formerly very high up people at the airline — then the carrier’s entire commercial strategy has been a bit questionable, to put it politely, and more about serving a certain someone’s LinkedIn profile ego, rather than actually developing a commercial strategy.

So with him no longer there, I’m curious to see how this all evolves. Let me emphasize that this is of course in no way a knock on all the hardworking employees at Etihad who have had to endure this “leadership” for too long. It seems like they now have quite the web to untangle, especially given the toxic people who are reportedly still there.

Etihad Airways has just filed a pretty big schedule change for early 2027, whereby a couple of dozen routes are seeing significant capacity reductions. Most notably, the Airbus A380 is being taken off of both the Toronto and Singapore routes.

In isolation, you might not think much of this, as demand is often a little lighter earlier in the year. But what I find interesting is that this follows a period of very rapid expansion, along with the carrier’s head of commercial strategy getting the boot.

Based on what I’ve heard from a countless number of current and former Etihad management employees, the strategy of the past couple of years hasn’t been as sound as a certain someone has tried to make it appear. We’ll see how this all unravels.

What do you make of this Etihad schedule change, and how do you see things playing out?

#6182. American Adds New Routes, Drops Others in Reshuffle at LAX

American Airlines will add new connections and cut others as it works to optimize its network at Los Angeles.

The carrier confirmed Friday that it will launch year-round service from LAX to Reno, Nevada, and seasonal service to Bozeman, Montana, and Grand Junction, Colorado.

LA-Reno will operate three times weekly, starting May 27, 2027, using Embraer E175 aircraft.

The routes to Bozeman and Grand Junction will operate from May 27 to Aug. 9, with Bozeman service using an E175 and Grand Junction flights using a Bombardier CRJ700.

An American official said Grand Junction is a “seasonal market addition” while service to Aspen/Pitkin County, Colorado, is temporarily suspended due to construction work there.

American will also add frequencies on some existing routes out of LAX next summer:

The carrier also confirmed that it will drop service from Los Angeles to Cleveland and Des Moines, Iowa, on February 11.
