#6181. What’s My Lebensphilosophie? I Went to the Austrian Alps to Find Out

When I was told the general rule of thumb at Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort nestled in Austria’s Großarl Valley, was that it’s weird if you’re not naked, I listened.

In Austria, being naked isn’t just a physical state. It’s an emotional state, too. Austrians strip themselves down, both figuratively and literally, to achieve a mindset they call “Lebensgefühl,” a deep mind-body awareness and lifestyle that is difficult to define, let alone translate.

Großarl Valley, also known as the “Valley of Alpine Pastures" in the Salzburger Land region of Austria.

Originally a German concept, the idea stems from “Lebensphilosophie,” a 19th-century intellectual movement popularized by big name thinkers like Friedrich Nietzsche, Georg Simmel, and Wilhelm Dilthey. Translating to “philosophy of life,” the framework is centered around the idea that life can only be understood from within oneself, as opposed to through applying external dogmas like logic and science. Life, according to this framework, is a joyful, vibrant, and embodied experience—a philosophy now widely integrated and cherished by Germany’s neighbor, Austria.

Language, of course, falls short when attempting to describe what Lebensgefühl means in practice; this complete awareness of being is a physicality, an emotion, a lifestyle, and a philosophy all rolled into one. It can’t be described, only felt (ah!). It’s the pleasure of simply existing. Leben (life), Gefühl (feeling). It’s an experience I wanted to understand firsthand. So when I found myself in Munich, less than a two-hour train ride from Hotel Nesslerhof, with a lifelong friend oblivious to my schemes, I decided it was time to get to the bottom of it.

The root of Lebensgefühl is being entirely present in a moment: a conscious effort to slow down, gauge your own energy in the here and now, and choose the way you want to live your life accordingly. While the Austrian National Tourist Board uses the concept of Lebensgefühl as a marketing language, the feeling itself is real–and you can cultivate it anywhere. Admittedly, though—hand of accountability raised—it’s a whole lot easier when you’re surrounded by the postcard-perfect Austrian Alps.

Reaching this state of awareness requires an analog attention span and total presence. This is exactly what is demanded of you at Hotel Nesslerhof, which has dubbed itself the “natural happiness hotel.” The sprawling, sun-warmed property is an emerald-colored garden punctured by buttery blonde oak 1643 Austrian longhouse architecture. Here, the world is calm. Quiet.

I arrive burned out, my attention scattered across screens and obligations. Stepping into a place fully immersed in nature with nothing expected of me, is jarring. It's been a while since I've consumed life this way. We’re conditioned to scroll, desire, save, project, and imagine, rather than to simply be—even to just be for a little bit.

Finding the answer started with carving out time and space, and letting go of everything I thought presence was supposed to look like. Next thing, I was naked in Austria with 40 strangers wondering the same thing.

Natural swimming pond for post-sauna plunges in the Zwanzigsechzehn sauna area for guests aged 16 and older.

The hotel’s dedicated wellness area features five co-ed clothing-optional saunas (plus an additional private sauna in select suites), a salt steam bath, infrared loungers, and expansive natural swimming pools. To practice, or fully embody, Lebensgefühl successfully, you must be aware of your environment. At Nesslerhof, the alpine nature allows your body to break away from any externally imposed schedules and return back to your natural circadian rhythm, where an omniscient digital third person doesn't determine your flow; you do.

A Swiss pine sauna in the Zwanzigsechzehn sauna area for guests aged 16 and older.

As a lifelong advocate for a good time, I mustered some gumption to join one of the daily themed sauna “infusions.” During these sessions, a sauna master leads thematic experiences using natural, regional botanicals like thyme, sage, Swiss stone pine, and eucalyptus. It’s held in the adults-only sauna event room, a space large enough to accommodate nearly 50 people.

I walk in—towel on—and it occurs to me I’m the one making it weird here. There’s a lot I can swallow in life, but one thing I certainly will not do is be the person making things weird in a room. So, I lose the towel, join the crowd, and, in a state of mild panic, take a seat on the floor. Now, retrospectively speaking, I couldn’t grasp how all my choices in life had led me to this single, very conscious state of nudity in front of 40 Austrian strangers. There I was—sitting on the floor, completely floored. Which actually made things weirder, because I was later told you aren’t supposed to sit on the floor.

Enter the sauna master. Also nude. A sauna master is like a spiritual guide to a proper schvitz, and the infusions at Nesslerhof are next level material. At pivotal moments, I’m watching him execute rainbow ice acrobatics, teasing large, colorful chunks of ice around the room in a giant spoon before launching them onto the glowing-hot stones. Steam is sizzling everywhere as thick aromatics sweep across the room.

Hotel Nesslerhof's outdoor saltwater pool (with indoor access) surrounded by the Großarl Valley.

And it’s hot. To make matters worse for myself—still on the floor—we’re given a natural body scrub to apply. So, whatever, sure: I start scrubbing amidst the rainbow ice, dense botanical air, and naked strangers unabashedly sprawled across the room in their entirety. I begin to gain consciousness of the palpable sense of self-assurance emanating from everyone as they laughed and chatted heart-to-heart. They were all having…fun. Slowly, decidedly, I reach a state of compos mentis: the only thing mortifying about this experience is my belief that this is a mortifying experience. This is not an intimidating reality. In fact, it’s pretty funny—and wildly inclusive, despite the fact that no one here speaks English but me. For the first time since arriving here, I feel entirely in the moment, free from any pressure to make it something else. I’m there, existing. I watch as my friend walks by the glass door and we lock eyes—him sending a distress call, and me, now a part of the sauna hijinks, completely in on the bit. Yeah, we’re all naked. So what?

Over the next three days, I continue this conversation with myself about the humility of physical form, alternating between stone pine saunas and crystal-clear mountain ponds. One amber afternoon, as I float between lily pads dotted by flowers and busy dragonflies, I stare at the burgeoning purple-pink Austrian Alps blanketing me, and I remember what it’s like to feel small again. Perception, both of ourselves and from others, has never really been that serious, has it? This is the body that’s given me life, the body that makes everything I do possible. Suddenly, I’m aware of every inch, from my fingertips to my toes. And I’m aware of my awareness. Lebensgefühl, for sure.

Mid-mind-body connection, a group of Austrian regulars hand-signals for me to come over for a beer. “For the electrolytes” is their roundabout scientific mojo after two to three courses of saunas and plunges. I catch what feels like an illegal glimpse of myself in the reflection of a sauna door and laugh. Gratitude emerges.

Hotel Nesslerhof's 800 m² natural swimming pond surrounded by a sunbathing lawn.

Gratitude for your body means food is more than just fuel, it’s an offering. The art of a meal has been a ritualistic practice since we were homo erectus: slowing down to practicing eating as an experience, not a function. And an eating environment can communicate a lot: savor this, stay with me, I’m here.

At Nesslerhof, eating was a slow and meditative practice, always beginning with a dedicated space: a seat at their table that was mine for my entire visit, an altar of sorts. Libations aplenty. In Austria, the Vorspeisensuppe—the traditional first-course soup—is served before almost every meal as a ceremonial anchor of hospitality and warmth. It’s often a non-negotiable, and acts as a symbolic moment to ground yourself before eating, or, as I’m practicing as an honorary Austrian here, to ground myself in a state of Lebensgefühl. For breakfast, lunch, dinner, and even the occasional snack, the soup is served first, and my brain instantly locks into being entirely in the moment. How could I not—I’m sipping on fresh ginger, carrot, and seasonal herb soups pulled directly from the mountains of Großarl—the lush valley an hour outside of Salzburg where the property sits.

Daily breakfast spread by the “Gästeflüsterer” team, including a wide selection of regional specialties.

Austrian Zwiebelrostbraten (pan-seared beef roast with crispy fried onions) served with seasonal Alpine accompaniments from the Großarl Valley.

When you are sick, what do you feed yourself to get better? How do people care for you using food? A lot of roads lead back to soup. It’s nourishing, easy for a strained body to digest, and a slow, intentional practice. It’s an antidote to hurriedness, a gateway to culinary Lebensgefühl.

Outside of the soup, a daily breakfast and lunch menu of fresh regional dishes, served on a strict schedule in the main parlor, makes indecision obsolete. In the evening, a five-course dinner at Atelier N, the hotel’s dedicated dining space, feels like stepping into an Austrian grandmother’s kitchen and hitting all the classics: Perftillbauer lamb, roast venison, fried veal Butterschnitzel, and pan-fried fish fillets. Everything is local, organic, and rooted in a genuine "nose-to-tail" principle—completely free of pretentious trends. And everyone here is known by their first name. The baker, Toni, brings fresh bread and pastries every morning. Elisabeth crafts the butter, curd cheese, yogurt, and whey—a real lactose lady. Anni and Sepp Inhög’s bees live on the sunniest side of the valley, which means their honey is something else entirely. Fresh local salmon trout, rainbow trout, brook trout, Arctic char, and local game are sourced directly from the nearby Hohe Tauern National Park. It’s a literal "alp-to-table" dining experience.

Kreuzkogel mountain in the Großarl Valley, accessed by the Kieserlbahn cable car.

The writer stopping for wild blueberries on a hike in the Austrian Alps.

Hotel Nesslerhof's hospitality was the last dance to Lebensgefühl. Longing for an escape–more often than not–coincides with a longing to feel in touch with yourself again. A weltanschauung, or worldview, can easily become skewed by the monotony of everyday life, which is why it takes displacement to course-correct. Human connection—which in this case took the form of the warm hospitality of Nesslerhof's staff—can serve as the intermediary. An agent [what do you that can create safe third spaces, and abstractly direct you to where your values lie.

On a hike just outside Nesslerhof’s front door in Hohe Tauern National Park, I meet one of Hotel Nesslerhof’s owners, Tina Neudegger. She built the property from the ground up with her husband, Hermann, and their three daughters. That’s over 40 years of family tradition and expertise coursing through this space. Tina is a consumingly luminous person, a natural caregiver. What she fosters at the property extends beyond hospitality–it’s a sense of security. It’s a maternal, comforting awareness that I am entirely taken care of, that my environment is safe, and that I don’t need to be on the defense. At Nesslerhof, I receive the same attention she gives her daughters and her husband, who treat the hotel like their home because, well, it is their home.

Employing my primate purpose, step by step with Tina as I teeter along an intimidating alpine cliffside, and attempting to eat a handful of fresh berries I covertly hoarded from a wily bush because I couldn't stop myself, I tune into her flow. We talk about how life can be a comedy of errors, and how we as humans cling to a gravitas that seems funny from a higher perspective. “Life’s simple. You can do anything once, right? So do it,” is Tina’s cheeky motto, something that makes all the seriousness in the world abruptly fade. I’m arrested by the smell of cows and am drawn back to the present. Weirdly, I like it.

The writer above Großarl Valley with Austrian libation.

The August 2026 total solar eclipse dips behind the Austrian Alps.

Later, Tina drives me up the mountain to watch the solar eclipse from Wolke7, her family’s ski lodge, which is normally reached by the Kieserlbahn cable car adjacent to the hotel. We’re on a 40-minute, long, winding road up the Austrian Alps that feels alarmingly close to vertical. I’m bearing intense witness to the fact that there’s no guardrail, but I'm at ease knowing I can free my gaze because of Tina's confidence. We continue on a path that’s already there, a path that's always been there, a path that will always be there. Something about that feels nice. At the summit, I meet the family she’s created in Großarl: her eclectic collection of friends who uphold this alpine town's legacy. They look at her with complete adoration as they pass me homemade Kaiserschmarrn and a Radler. We watch the eclipse slowly fade behind the Austrian Alps—the totality of it lasting just over two minutes.

But as I stand there, witnessing the world in its most sublime form, surrounded by Tina’s friends, who are vivid, complex, and completely magnanimous, the awe I feel expands from my chest, and those two minutes feel endless. I dub Tina the Mayor of Großarl, and as I overlook her valley, 6,500 meters above sea level, I see the whole picture again. At its deepest level, Lebensgefühl–your Lebensphilosophie–is painfully simple. What made you feel alive today? Build the environment for it. Pause and marvel. Continue forward.

#6180. Cathay Pacific Orders 41 Airbus A330-900neos, As New Regional Workhorse

In August 2024, Cathay Pacific placed an order for 30 Airbus A330neos. There’s now an update, as the airline has just bumped this order by 11 more planes, meaning that there are now a total of 41 of these aircraft on order. Let’s take a look at all the details, and discuss what this means for fleet modernization at the Hong Kong based oneworld carrier.

Cathay Pacific now has a firm order for 41 Airbus A330-900neo aircraft, which are expected to be delivered between 2028 and 2035.

This follows an evaluation of the carrier’s mid-size wide body fleet renewal program, and it will enable Cathay Pacific to modernize its earlier generation A330-300 fleet, and expand its operations on high capacity regional routes. However, the airline is leaving plans for this plane open, and also emphasizes how the jet offers the flexibility to serve longer range destinations.

For those not familiar, the A330neo is the updated version of the A330, featuring improved range and fuel efficiency. The A330-900neo is the larger of the two new variants (with the other being the A330-800neo). The plane has a range of 7,200 nautical miles, plus a capacity for 287 passengers in a standard three cabin configuration.

I think it’s safe to assume that at least most of these A330neos will be equipped with the new Aria Studio business class product, which is expected to be retrofitted on select existing A330s in the coming months. This will finally see the carrier introduce a dedicated regional product with flat beds, which is exciting, though it’s not quite to the level of the long haul Aria Suite business class.

Here’s how Cathay Pacific CEO Ronald Lam described how the A330neo fits into the carrier’s fleet, back when the first 30 frames were ordered:

“The A330 is an aircraft type that has been serving Cathay Pacific well for nearly 30 years. These new aircraft will principally serve our regional destinations in Asia, while also providing the flexibility to serve longer-haul destinations as required. The improved fuel efficiency of these A330neos, together with their high standards of comfort, will enable us to further elevate the experience we provide for our customers while also contributing towards our goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.”

Cathay Pacific refreshing its short and medium haul fleet with the Airbus A330-900neo makes perfect sense, and is just about the safest, most expected aircraft order that Cathay Pacific could place. For context on Cathay Pacific’s fleet, the airline has:

Now Cathay Pacific’s fleet renewal plans are becoming a bit clearer, as the airline has:

So a decade down the road, you can expect that Cathay Pacific will primarily be flying A321neos, A330-900neos, A350s (-900s and -1000s), and 777-9s. That seems like a pretty logical fleet development plan to me.

Cathay Pacific now has an order for 41 Airbus A330-900neos, which the airline will primarily use to modernize and grow its regional fleet. The carrier already flies A330-300s, some of which are nearly 25 years old, so it’s logical that the airline would slowly be looking to replace these jets.

Cathay Pacific now has a pretty impressive (but not overly ambitious) order book, with A321neos, A330-900neos, and 777-9s, used for fleet renewal.

What do you make of Cathay Pacific’s Airbus A330-900neo order?

JSX is bringing its popular semi-private flights to Beantown.

The boutique air carrier plans to begin flying from Boston this winter, JSX said this week. The company's service will be based out of the nearby Laurence G. Hanscom Field (BED) in the town of Bedford, Massachusetts.

The Boston service will launch with a route to New York City on Feb. 8, followed by flights to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF) in Florida beginning on Feb. 11.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and new mountain routes after strong passenger response

JSX will operate four daily flights between Boston and New York from Monday through Friday, with two flights on Saturday and three on Sunday. The Miami service will run once per day five times a week: Monday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

Notably, JSX did not specify which New York airport would host the Boston flights. A spokesperson did not immediately answer TPG’s request for further details. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Because of those restrictions, anyone looking to fly to or from New York has to sign up for the free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. Passengers can also earn United MileagePlus miles under a partnership between the two companies.

The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on both routes, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Fares start at $199 one-way between Boston and New York, with one-way flights between Boston and Miami starting at $599.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s new loyalty program

“Greater Boston represents an exciting new chapter for JSX, marking our first entry into Massachusetts and an important milestone in the continued expansion of our East Coast network,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a statement.

“As one of the nation's leading centers for business, innovation, and higher education, Greater Boston is a natural fit for our unique approach to flying,” he added.

JSX operates as a “hop-on charter” service, which essentially operates private charter flights that anyone can buy a seat on. It means that JSX flights operate more like private flights than commercial, using posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals and allowing passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

The public charter service — which does not bill itself as an “airline,” due to different regulations between charter carriers and public airlines — operates out of 29 airports across the U.S. and Mexico. Although private jet passengers typically bypass TSA screening, JSX implemented a more thorough in-house screening process in 2025 to address security concerns.

Still, the process is remarkably quicker than going through the public terminal, making JSX an appealing option for those looking to skip the hassle of a regular flight.

JSX's flights from Boston are already on sale, with service scheduled to start in February.

With the entry to New England, JSX adds its 29th city, and brings its own entry to the competitive business of moving premium travelers between Boston and New York.

#6178. Livery of the Week: Etihad Partners with McLaren

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

While traditional marketing theories advise airlines to avoid sponsoring events such as motor racing because of perceived associations with “danger” and “uncertainty” — concepts that could reflect negatively on air transport operators — the past couple of decades have seen several airlines establish partnerships with Formula One teams and events.

Today, some carriers are title sponsors of their home Grands Prix. Gulf Air, for example, has been the title sponsor of the Bahrain Grand Prix since its inception in 2004. Singapore Airlines, which has held the same role at the Singapore Grand Prix since 2014, has extended its commitment through 2028.

Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways has been the title sponsor of the UAE Grand Prix since the race’s debut in 2009. This year, it also entered into a partnership with McLaren Racing, bringing together “two organizations with a shared commitment to innovation, ambition, and delivering exceptional experiences for fans and customers around the world”.

To mark the partnership, Etihad has painted one of its Boeing 787-10 aircraft in a special livery, taking McLaren Racing’s distinctive color to the skies.

The livery features McLaren’s signature papaya orange across most of the fuselage — the same color used on its racing cars and team uniforms. The “Etihad” and “McLaren” names appear side by side above the cabin windows, while the McLaren logo is displayed toward the rear of the aircraft against a black background. The tail fin retains Etihad’s signature mosaic pattern, with its colors adjusted to complement the fuselage’s black-and-orange scheme.

Papaya has taken flight 🧡✈️Keep your eyes on the skies and let us know if you spot us 👀#McLarenF1 | #BeyondBorders | @etihad pic.twitter.com/NCHxsdAMTi

The aircraft chosen to showcase the special livery is a Boeing 787-10, registered A6-BMI. It was delivered to Etihad directly from the manufacturer on Oct. 14, 2020.

The aircraft features one of Etihad’s older cabin designs, introduced in 2018. It has 327 seats in a two-class configuration: 32 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout and 295 economy class seats in a 3-3-3 layout. The first 10 rows of the economy cabin are designated “Economy Space,” offering a seat pitch of 35 inches rather than the standard 31 inches.

Not your usual livery 👀 ✈️ See the making of our special edition @etihad x McLaren Racing livery 🧡 #McLarenF1 #BeyondBorders pic.twitter.com/I2SaS0hyR7

#6177. Delta Platinum Amex Card Review: Big Benefits & Strong Welcome Offer

The Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card is the second most premium personal credit card in the Delta SkyMiles and Amex co-brand card portfolio.

If you fly Delta several times a year and want perks like a companion certificate and the ability to spend toward elite status qualification, the Delta Platinum Amex is worth a look, and can easily be worth more than the fee. This post is my in-depth Delta Platinum Card review, so let’s get into all the details.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card

Before we get too deep into my Delta Platinum Amex review, let me give a quick overview of the card’s main features and fees:

I also put together my top pros and cons for the Delta Platinum SkyMiles Card:

Let’s cover the welcome bonus, eligibility details, and fees, of the Delta Platinum Card. After all, these are major factors that people consider when applying for cards.

The Delta Platinum Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 90,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $3,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $990. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

The welcome offer on the Delta Platinum Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal version of the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the less premium cards first, and then work your way up. That way you’re potentially eligible for the welcome offers on each of the cards. Meanwhile if you start with the most premium card, you wouldn’t be eligible for the offers on the less premium cards.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Platinum Delta Amex has a $350 annual fee (Rates & Fees). You can add additional users to the card at no extra cost (Rates & Fees). As mentioned above, this is the second highest annual fee personal card in the Delta and Amex portfolio.

If you are going to put spending on the Delta Platinum Amex, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use the card abroad without paying high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. How does the Delta Platinum Card do on that front? Well, among airline cards, I’d say it’s pretty competitive, so let’s cover those details.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers the following miles earning opportunities for spending:

Since I value Delta miles at 1.1 cents, I think this card offers a 3.3% return on its 3x miles categories (purchases made directly with Delta and directly with hotels), a 2.2% return on its 2x miles categories (restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets), and a 1.1% return on non-bonus spending.

The card has solid bonus categories for a co-branded airline card, but purely in terms of rewards for spending, I think there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, hotel purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Platinum Amex can help you earn status:

For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:

If you’re serious about earning elite status with credit card spending, you’ll want to consider the more premium Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more) instead, since it earns MQDs twice as fast — you earn $1 MQD per $10 of eligible purchases, rather than $1 MQD per $20 of eligible purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on airlines like LATAM and WestJet, which aren’t part of SkyTeam.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Platinum Delta Credit Card has a nice welcome offer. In general, I’d say it could be worth putting spending on the card if you’re trying to earn Medallion elite status with Delta SkyMiles. For most people, the reason you’ll want to keep this card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which for many people will more than offset the annual fee. Let’s go over some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of your Delta Platinum Card, you can receive a Delta Main roundtrip companion certificate. You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. This is a great deal that can be worth significantly more than the annual fee in and of itself.

If redeeming the certificate there are some things to be aware of:

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you can receive up to $150 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you can receive $150 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $150, if you wanted to. If used right, there’s real value here.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers. This is super easy to unlock, though admittedly the increments as such are quite small.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases with U.S. Resy restaurants.

Just for having the Platinum Delta Card you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up.

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a single trip could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Platinum Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you’ll need to ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation (though there’s no need to actually pay for the flight with the card).

This benefit is valid for a total of up to nine people traveling on the same reservation with the primary cardmember.

If you have the Delta Platinum Card, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

The Platinum Delta Amex offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years for the application fee for TSA PreCheck or Global Entry. This can save you time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible. (Enrollment required)

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible Delta Amex card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta (the discount doesn’t apply to taxes and fees). Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. (Enrollment required)

The Delta Platinum Card gets you complimentary Hertz Five Star status. Enrollment is required, and you receive the following benefits with the rental car company:

The Delta Platinum Amex comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Platinum Credit Card isn’t necessarily the best card for the casual Delta flyer, and it’s also not a card I’d recommend putting much spending on, unless you value the MQDs that you can earn with the card. Even if you value MQDs, you’re better off with the more premium card, since you can earn them twice as fast.

However, this card has solid perks, ranging from a companion certificate, to free checked bags, to priority boarding, to savings on award flights, to access to exclusive award redemption opportunities, to valuable statement credits, and more.

Bigger picture, is the Delta Platinum Card worth it, though? There are a few things to consider.

If the Delta Platinum Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. The main earning difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on transit, at U.S. shipping providers, and on single eligible purchases of $5,000 or more (on up to $100,000 of combined eligible purchases per year), while the personal card offers 2x miles at restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets (both cards offer 3x miles on Delta purchases and hotel purchases).

The business version of the card also offers an annual Delta Stays credit of up to $200, rather than one of up to $150, so it’s arguably more lucrative.

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) is a good card for occasional Delta flyers who want basic airline perks. It has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees) and a smaller list of perks, including:

The Delta Gold Card offers the same discounts you get with the Delta Platinum Card, as well as the rideshare credit, but in this case it only kicks in after your first renewal. The Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn MQDs toward status, so that’s another potential downside to keep in mind.

For the very frequent Delta flyer, there’s the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more), which has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). What differentiates this card?

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. These points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50K per calendar year, and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25K per calendar year, and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at amextravel.com

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The information and associated card details on this page for the American Express Green Card have been collected independently by OMAAT and have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The information and associated card details on this page for the American Express Green Card have been collected independently by OMAAT and have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers solid perks for those who fly Delta frequently, especially Medallion members. For many, the annual companion certificate will more than justify the annual fee in and of itself, without even accounting for all of the other perks. Some will also get value from the 2,500 MQDs that are offered annually just for having the card.

The annual fee on this card is potentially quite easy to justify, thanks to all the credits you can earn with rideshares, Resy, and even Delta Stays.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Platinum Amex Card, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (Rates & Fees), and Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (Rates & Fees).

#6176. The US Navy Retired A 10,000-Lb Cargo Workhorse For A Tiltrotor That Carries 4,000 Lbs Fewer

On the surface level, it seems like the US Navy committed a strategic folly when it decided to replace the venerable Grumman C-2A Greyhound carrier-onboard delivery plane with a Bell Boeing tiltrotor. The newer and totally different rotary-wing aircraft has 40% less total payload than the 1960s vintage fixed-wing tail-hook plane it succeeded.

However, there is a crucial caveat that made all the difference when America's Navy decided to trade in for a new cargo plane. Unlike the Greyhound, the Osprey can carry the engine of the Lockheed Martin F-35C Lightning II. This is a vital mission in supporting the new USN Carrier Air Wing, which is now deploying the world's first carrier-capable stealth fighters in combat missions.

Fitting the colossal jet engine into the Greyhound would have required a ground-up redesign of the plane's fuselage, which would have been a massive investment in a nearly obsolete platform. Although the Navy did lose some raw payload capacity, it gained a massive amount of mission flexibility and the benefit of operational commonality with the US Marines.

The USMC has a very large number of V-22 Ospreys, which are deployed daily aboard US Navy vessels. That makes maintenance and logistics much simpler, but also taps into a skill pool of technicians and aircrew that has been refined for two decades to make the Navy's transition smooth.

Beyond the Marine Corps connection, the Osprey fundamentally changed how a Carrier Strike Group handles logistics, moving the Navy away from rigid, predictable Operations. The C-2 Greyhound was bound to the aircraft carrier's Flight Deck and airfields on the shore for every mission. If a C-2 Greyhound needed to pick up supplies near a conflict zone, it required a long, secure, paved military runway ashore.

The CMV-22B eliminates the middleperson. It can fly parts, mail, or personnel from a shore base directly to a destroyer, cruiser, or amphibious assault ship. It can also land on dirt fields, beaches, open drop zones, or small helicopter pads ashore to retrieve critical supplies or evacuate wounded personnel.

Additionally, the Osprey has a refueling probe that allows it to perform air-to-air refueling and extend its mission radius, which the Greyhound was never upgraded to receive. Another game-changing advantage is night operations. The Navy considered the aging C-2 Greyhound too risky for routine night landings on carriers. The CMV-22B, equipped with modern night-vision systems and avionics, can land vertically on a carrier's pitch-black deck at midnight, giving the fleet a true round-the-clock supply chain.

Superior night ops capability significantly improves the operational flexibility of not only Air Wing but also the entire Carrier Strike Group. More than that, the new ability is a force enhancement to the entire coalition as the US Armed Forces pivot to the Pacific with a focus on joint domain operations in a distributed battle space.

Likewise, the ability to resupply forces on remote islands without an airstrip is crucial in the Indo-Pacific. And the ability to perform aerial refueling will make the aircraft not only more practical but also enhance the safety of flight operating over vast expanses of open ocean.

Refocusing on the core capability that spurred the decision to make the transition to the COD mission, the capability to receive replacement engines for the Air Wing aircraft is crucial in a conflict. The Navy does not usually ship the entire, fully assembled engine at once. Instead, they transport the core F135 Power Module. This is the heaviest and most critical component of the engine.

It is, in fact, so heavy that the Osprey cannot perform a pure vertical lift but must execute a short rolling takeoff to get airborne. The C-2’s cabin is too narrow and awkwardly shaped to clear the engine's widest components. The Osprey's cargo bay can physically encompass these dimensions, but it leaves absolutely zero margin for error.

The engine module is mounted to a low-profile, heavy-duty wheeled metal frame that is compatible with a custom-designed skin rail system. The cargo crew pushes the module up the rear ramp, and it locks directly with the cargo floor's locking points to ensure the massive 3,750-lb (1,701 kg) powerplant cannot move during flight. While the engine technically fits, the tight clearance forces the Navy to accept unique operational compromises.

Because the module takes up nearly every cubic inch of the cargo bay, loading and unloading are a slow, meticulous process. Additionally, the F135 engine inside its standard shipping container will not fit inside the Osprey. Consequently, the engine must be flown 'naked,' or loosely wrapped. Ultimately, although it may not be the perfect transport option, it is the best available for the US Navy to sustain its fifth-generation Air Wing in the 21st century.

The legacy behind the latest and greatest Army helo.

The absolute cornerstone of the fifth-generation air wing is the F-35C Lightning II, which has just one powerplant. If an F-35C suffers an engine failure out at sea, that multi-million-dollar stealth fighter is completely useless until a replacement arrives. This is especially critical as the aircraft is a single-engine airframe.

While the F135 is the most powerful fighter jet engine ever made, the fact that the F-35C only has one is a major departure from the recent portfolio of carrier-capable aircraft flown by the USN and USMC. The F-35C is vastly more maintenance-intensive than the Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet.

The Legacy 4.5-generation Strike Fighter will be the support platform that continues to be the workhorse of the Air Wing, while the Joint Strike Fighter takes over the highest-risk missions like penetrating integrated enemy air defenses. To achieve supersonic speeds without a twin-engine layout, the F135 engine operates under extreme temperatures and pressures.

It generates massive electrical power to feed the jet's advanced radar, jamming systems, and electronic warfare sensors. In fact, the entire F-35 fleet of all variants around the world has suffered a critical readiness issue, and the latest upgrade package under Technology Refresh Three, Block Four, has been significantly delayed.

Despite the US Navy pumping nearly 1 billion dollars into a Lockheed Martin contract for advanced electronic warfare equipment, it doesn't solve the problem that these aircraft are more delicate, and working on them on the ship is far more burdensome as well.

The dynamic duo of America's carrier air wings.

The F-35C is built to strike targets deep inside enemy territory while the aircraft carrier stays positioned safely outside the range of land-based anti-ship missiles. This means the carrier operates much farther out to sea than it did in previous decades. The Osprey will liberate the logistical chain of the carrier strike group from airfields ashore and also improve the efficiency of operations to smaller vessels in the CSG.

This is thanks to the fact that the CMV-22B can perform vertical resupply to smaller vessels as well. The Navy variant of the Osprey features massive fuel bladders bulged into the sides of the fuselage. It can fly over 1,150 nautical miles (2,130 km) on a single internal tank of fuel.

Unlike the old Greyhound, the Osprey features an aerial refueling probe. It can take fuel directly from F/A-18 'Buddy tankers' or the upcoming Boeing MQ-25 Stingray drones, which will take over air-to-air refueling for the Air Wing. Aerial refueling gives the Osprey virtually unlimited range, allowing it to fetch an urgent F-35C engine core from a distant shore base and sprint back to a fast-moving strike group without stopping.

Even more importantly, with the entire US Armed Forces concentrating their strategic disposition in the Pacific, the Osprey supports Joint Forces as a whole because it is engineered for the theater, and it can carry the engine of the most important fighter jet for virtually every operator in the region.

Out with old, in with the new for the USMC, but what's the catch?

The Indo-Pacific is an F-35 theater. The Air Force flies the F-35A from mainland bases, the Marines fly the short-takeoff/vertical-landing F-35B from amphibious ships and austere islands, and the Navy flies the carrier-borne F-35C. Crucially, all three variants of the F-35 use the same foundational Pratt & Whitney F135 engine core.

Because the Navy’s CMV-22B can haul this engine, it doesn't just service aircraft carriers. A Navy Osprey can fly an engine from a remote Air Force base in Guam, land on an amphibious assault ship, or drop it off at a rugged island outpost. In the vast Pacific, the Navy doesn’t have to build its own dedicated maintenance hubs on every island.

The military knows that in a conflict, large, centralized bases like Kadena Air Base in Japan will be targeted by enemy ballistic missiles. To survive, the branches have developed decentralized strategies. Under modern Pacific strategy, a 100,000-ton Nimitz- or Ford-class aircraft carrier does not just exist to launch its own planes. It acts as a massive, floating logistical mothership for the entire joint force.

In a shooting war, if a Marine or Air Force F-35 engine fails on a forward island outpost, the Navy's CMV-22B can lift a spare engine directly off the supercarrier's deck or from any depot in the first or second island chain operated by the US or its regional allies. It can then fly it directly to that carrier, 'Big Deck' assault ship, or tiny island airstrip.

Then the Osprey can land right in the dirt next to the stranded jet. It allows all of the US Armed Forces, Japanese, Australian, South Korean, Singaporean, and other regional military allies to pool their resources dynamically, thanks to the universal platform of the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter.

#6175. Korean Air Adds Newark Flights From Incheon, Joining United & Air Premia

Korean Air has just quietly added a new long haul route, as the airline will be adding service to Newark, New Jersey. What’s interesting is just how competitive this market has become, but it’s logical in the context of what’s going on at the airline (thanks to S_LEE for flagging this).

As of May 22, 2027, Korean Air plans to launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Newark. The flight will operate with the following schedule:

KE97 Seoul Incheon to Newark departing 10:00PM arriving 11:00PMKE98 Newark to Seoul Incheon departing 1:00AM arriving 5:15AM (+1 day)

The 6,896-mile flight is blocked at 14hr to the United States, and 15hr15min to South Korea. Korean Air will use a Boeing 777-300ER for the route, featuring 277 seats, including eight first class seats, 42 business class seats, and 227 economy seats.

This technically marks a service resumption, as Korean Air last served Newark through September 2001, but then suspended flights after the 9/11 terror attacks, and never resumed the flights. This new service will complement Korean Air’s existing service to New York Kennedy (JFK), which typically operates twice daily.

On top of that, Korean Air’s destinations in the United States include Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Chicago (ORD), Dallas (DFW), Honolulu (HNL), Las Vegas (LAS), Los Angeles (LAX), San Francisco (SFO), Seattle (SEA), and Washington Dulles (IAD).

Interestingly, Korean Air faces quite a bit of competition in the market between Incheon and Newark. Going back several years, it’s a route that no airline served.

However, that has changed in recent times. In May 2023, South Korean budget carrier Air Premia launched service in the market using a Boeing 787. Then in September 2026, United Airlines launched flights in the market, also using a Boeing 787. Korean Air’s timing is very similar to Air Premia’s in both directions, which isn’t too surprising.

Some people might be surprised to see Korean Air adding flights to Newark in addition to existing service to Kennedy (with no plans to reduce that service), but this actually seems pretty straightforward to me.

Keep in mind that Korean Air and Asiana have merged, and in the coming weeks, the two airlines will even take on the same brand. Historically these carriers were huge competitors, so of course in some markets they’ll be reducing capacity. In other words, the combined Korean Air won’t have quite as many frequencies to places like Los Angeles, New York, and San Francisco, as the two airlines did separately.

That of course opens up the opportunity to serve more new markets, and clearly Newark was identified as one of those opportunities. Also keep in mind that Korean Air operates as part of a transpacific joint venture with Delta, so the airlines can coordinate fares and schedules, and it’s all about the combined depth and breadth of service.

If you’re looking at this from a Manhattan centric perspective, you might be surprised that the airline is bothering to serve both airports. However, service to Newark goes way beyond that, and the idea is that this flight is useful for serving parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania, etc. Admittedly those flyers likely aren’t loyal to SkyTeam, but from a Korea point of sale perspective (especially with the number of people studying in the region), it makes sense.

As of May 2027, Korean Air will be launching daily flights from Seoul Incheon to Newark, complementing existing service to Kennedy. This means we’ll see three daily flights between Incheon and Newark on three different airlines… that’s quite the step up from the zero daily flights we saw several years back!

With Korean Air’s takeover of Asiana complete, it’s logical that the South Korean mega carrier would be looking at adding some new markets, given the increased connectivity and scale of the operation.

What do you make of Korean Air launching Newark flights?

#6174. JetBlue’s New First Class Is Missing A Cabin Divider… But Why?!?

In the coming weeks, JetBlue will be introducing a domestic first class product for the first time, which will be known as BlueFirst. This is an exciting and long overdue development, and I trust it will help JetBlue’s revenue performance, especially given how efficiently planes are being reconfigured (by reducing legroom in economy).

The first aircraft has now been retrofitted with the new cabins, and it appears that JetBlue had a media day today for this showing off both the new hard and soft product. We already largely knew what to expect, but what stands out to me is the one thing that’s missing, which I really can’t make sense of.

I don’t want to bury the lede here, so let me get right to it — on planes with BlueFirst, JetBlue won’t have any sort of a cabin divider between first class and the rest of the cabin. It’s not just that there isn’t a curtain, but there’s not even a divider hanging from the overhead bins.

JetBlue unveiled its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country’s carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.Read more: https://t.co/5o3k2Ru5R9 pic.twitter.com/1BTcLVOr7s

I guess this also explains the very creative angles of the renderings that have been released up until now, which clearly try to avoid highlighting this reality.

I really can’t make sense of this decision. I know we no longer live in an era where there are real, full bulkheads between cabins, since that’s not efficient. But just installing a small, flimsy divider, along with a curtain, costs very little, doesn’t weigh a lot, etc.

To be clear, this isn’t about “oh, I don’t want to be seen by anyone.” Instead, it’s about managing traffic to and from the forward lavatory. At US airlines, the most common policy is that on domestic flights, you can use any lavatory onboard the aircraft, even in a different cabin. There are some exceptions, including for JetBlue Mint, but that’s also easier to enforce thanks to how the A321 is configured, with a lavatory behind Mint, in front of economy.

I’m not sure if JetBlue intends to reserve the forward lavatory for BlueFirst passengers, but either way, you can expect there will be a steady stream of passengers lining up to use the forward lavatory. So it’s not even about potentially not having a dedicated lavatory, but instead it’s about just constantly having people standing in the aisle right by your seat. This will also make the life of the first class flight attendant more difficult.

Take Aer Lingus AerSpace, for example, which is Aer Lingus’ premium product on short haul flights in Europe. It’s simply the first row of seats with blocked middles, and no divider between that and the rest of the plane. The problem is that if you’re seated in the aisle in AerSpace, you basically just have someone’s butt in your face the entire flight. You’re almost better off not booking the product, just to avoid that.

Anyway, I can’t really make sense of this decision, so I’d be fascinated to know what the logic was. There’s not another US airline with first class that has no separation between first class and economy. Spirit’s “Big Front Seat” didn’t have any divider, but that also wasn’t first class — it was just an, ummm, big front seat.

Similarly, Breeze Airways’ “Nicest” product also doesn’t have a divider, but it’s also not a separate cabin.

CNBC’s Phil Le Beau was onboard JetBlue’s first BlueFirst A320 with CEO Joanna Geraghty. I like Le Beau, but this interview is also the perfect example of why I just don’t really value interviewing airline executives in a traditional sense.

Le Beau asked Geraghty a good question — “did you wait too long to add a first class?” If we are being honest, there’s only one correct answer, which is OF COURSE. Like, unarguably, JetBlue was at least years late, if not a decade late, to introducing first class. That’s not even Geraghty’s fault, it’s that previous CEO Robin Hayes was perhaps one of the least focused CEOs the US airline industry has ever seen.

Geraghty’s answer, though, was “I don’t think we’ve waited too long, we’ve had Mint for a very long time, it just takes time with some of these products to roll them out.” I get it — nobody wants to be, like “we screwed up and waited too long, but I mainly blame the guy before me.”

Seriously, though, if she really doesn’t think JetBlue waited too long to commit to introducing first class, then I’d question how observant the executive team has been of the industry. I mean, Frontier announced it would introduce first class before JetBlue, which should tell you all you need to know. Oh, and Frontier will even have divider, even if it doesn’t have recline, food, or drinks!

Also, the below screen grab from the interview gave me a chuckle…

JetBlue’s BlueFirst class is entering service soon, which is exciting. I’m a huge fan of JetBlue, and I think historically they’ve done a great job with both their hard and soft product, and have great attention to detail. So I’m just a bit puzzled as to how they came to the conclusion that there was no need to introduce a cabin divider between first class and economy.

JetBlue will be the first airline in the US with first class to not have any sort of a cabin divider, and I can’t make sense of that.

What do you make of JetBlue’s odd cabin divider decision?

While it would be a dream to get to every new hotel within days of opening to be among the first to experience special properties around the world, the reality is, that’s not always possible. When it is, though, you can bet we jump on the opportunity. Especially when it’s a flagship new points hotel.

That’s how I ended up staying at the gorgeous new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur within a week of its opening on Oct. 30, 2026. To be clear, I understood that not all the hotel’s restaurants would be open, nor would its spa, so this is not a full review, rather a first glimpse at what’s sure to be a favorite Hilton points redemption option soon.

Although it’s the Malaysian capital’s newest hotel, the Waldorf Astoria actually occupies the site of the storied former Hotel Istana in the heart of city’s Golden Triangle district — so called because it is the capital’s main financial and shopping district, with luxury megamalls galore — which means it’s centrally located, but tucked onto a quiet stretch of Jalan Raja Chulan.

Because of that, the hotel feels secluded and quiet, but plugged into the rest of the city, and easily accessible to most of the activities international visitors are likely to seek out while in town.

The hotel feels like a destination unto itself, too, though, thanks to its palatial suites (no mere rooms here) and an impressive slate of bars and restaurants, including outposts from celebrity chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten and Bangkok-based Garima Arora. The hotel will also be home to Malaysia’s first and only La Prairie spa, and the outdoor pool is the perfect place to while away a tropical afternoon.

Here’s what else you should plan to do during your stay at the new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur.

During my stay, only a fraction of the accommodations were ready for guests, but the hotel should be at full strength soon. There are no rooms here, just suites, which start at an impressive 80 square meters (861 square feet).

Deboss Collective is behind the decor, and sought inspiration from traditional Malay construction and crafts, incorporating lots of natural stone and timber, woven textiles and wooden furnishings that feel like contemporary urban updates to what you might find in a traditional rumah kampung, or village house.

To wit, there are huge windows overlooking the hotel grounds and the city skyline, letting in plenty of natural light. The carpet patterns and hardwood are meant to evoke traditional Malaysian marquetry while colorful accent walls call to mind vibrant Peranakan shophouses you can still find in parts of the city.

My suite’s footprint was enormous, with a huge, welcoming living area that included a 65-inch flatscreen television, a breakfast table which could double as a workdesk thanks to a panel of plugs, a rounded sofa and armchair and a low-slung wooden chair that blended colonial and midcentury influences.

In the separate bedroom, a king-size bed was dressed with crisp white sheets embroidered with a “WA,” just in case you forgot where you were. To either side were walls with a terete theme hearkening to the bamboo stalks that grow in gardens around the city. Another 55-inch flatscreen hung on the wall in there.

The bathroom was mostly white marble, including geometric floor tiling, but the countertops were a handsome darker hue. Anchoring the entire space was an elliptical standalone tub with a scalloped shell, while a water closet and separate walk-in shower stood close by. To lend a sense of place, the bath products are from Jo Malone’s Jo Loves line and scented with citrusy-fresh pomelo, which is a staple in Malaysian cuisine.

Considering this was a standard category room, it felt positively palatial, with a huge amount of real estate that provided a variety of distinct spaces to enjoy within the suite at different times.

The Waldorf Astoria isn’t the biggest hotel in town, but it fields an outsize roster of restaurants that should be a draw for guests and Kuala Lumpur locals alike.

You can’t call your hotel a Waldorf Astoria if it doesn’t have a version of Peacock Alley, the famous lobby lounge from the New York City original. The one here sits smack dab at the hotel entrance and has soaring ceilings, sculptural marble columns, dramatic overhead chandeliers and a variety of seating vignettes that feel homey yet upscale.

The all-day menu offers items like chicken skewers with lemongrass and coriander ($10.50), a Waldorf salad ($14.50), a smash burger ($22) and Malaysian nasi goreng ($17) among other options.

Named after the previous hotel to occupy this spot, Istana is the hotel’s all-day dining restaurant and is adjacent to the lobby. Breakfast includes an extensive buffet and both Western and Asian dishes. For lunch and dinner, you’ll find specialties like spiced Borneo chicken wings with a honey glaze ($10.50), chargrilled red snapper with wild ginger chili sambal ($23.75) and fresh fiddlehead ferns from the Cameron Highlands sauteed in coconut milk with tongue-torching bird’s eye chili ($8.75).

If you’re up for it, the durian dessert with coconut cream and a palm sugar compote and served with toasted buttery buns is a rich way to end the evening ($12).

This is Vongerichten’s farm-to-table concept, so you’ll find a menu focused on seasonal fruits and vegetables. The signature eggplant dip is smoky and smooth with tangy coconut yogurt and tomato chutney served with fluffy pita ($9.75). There are also tartines like a king crab crostini with tart lemon aioli and dill ($16.50), various pizzas and pastas, and an array of plant-based dishes including pistachio-crusted broccoli with hazelnut vinaigrette ($14.50).

At the entrance to ABC Kitchens KL, there is a bright, casual area with a cocktail bar and small plates.

Jean-Georges Vongerichten has a longstanding relationship with the Waldorf Astoria brand, so it should be no surprise that the signature restaurant here is a French-Malaysian fine-dining fusion restaurant courtesy of the chef. It is only open for dinner Tuesday-Saturday. I did not have the opportunity to dine here, but the menu features an entire caviar section, starters like diver scallops with caramelized cauliflower and caper-raisin emulsion ($29.50) and spice-charred duck breast with roasted cabbage and chili-lime broth ($39.50).

It was not yet open during my stay, but Yaari will be the hotel’s sophisticated Indian restaurant and will only be open for dinner from Wednesday-Sunday. The chef is Garima Arora, whose Bangkok restaurant, Gaa, holds two Michelin stars.

Located on the fourth floor, Coda feels like a swanky hideaway for those in the know. Glossy dark stone surfaces and emerald-green velvet chairs and banquettes give the space a swanky vibe, as does the menu of libations inspired by various vinyl albums, one of which will likely be spinning on the record player during your visit.

Even the classics get a Malaysian twist, like an old fashioned crafted with jerky-like beef bak kwa-washed Michter’s bourbon, cardamom, clove and cascara distillate and mandarin-infused jaggery for a sweet finish ($20.50).

Here are some of the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur’s other amenities:

Nightly rates at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur start at around $520 or 100,000 Hilton Honors points.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is part of  American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts, so if you have or , you can make a booking through amextravel.com and receive perks like availability-based upgrades, up to a $100 credit to use on-property during your stay for things like drinks or meals, complimentary daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout.

Both cards now offer a biannual $300 (up to $600 per calendar year) statement credit on prepaid stays at Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts, so you could save $300 on a reservation at the hotel if you are able to take advantage of one of these cards’ credits. Just note that this benefit is changing in 2027 and will require cardholders to book two nights or more to take advantage of the credit.

Related: Our favorite American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts around the world

All public areas at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur are wheelchair-accessible thanks to elevators (with wheelchair-height buttons), ramps and wide pathways. The hotel has accessible rooms in the King Urban Deluxe category. These accommodations feature audio and visual alarms, an automatic door closer, and wheelchair-height door viewer.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is an exciting new points option in the Malaysian capital, and one with plenty of award availability. While 100,000 points is a lot to pay, considering the sheer size of the suites here and the relatively high (for Kuala Lumpur) price point, it might be well worth it. Once the hotel’s restaurants and spa are all open and operational, this should become one of the city’s most popular luxury hotels.

#6172. What Pilots Actually Do Hour-By-Hour On An 18-Hour Flight To New York JFK

SQ23/SQ24, Singapore Airlines' Airbus A350-900ULR flights between Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) and New York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), are a technological and logistical marvel. They cover an average of 9,537 miles (15,348 km), requiring the aircraft to remain in the sky for 18 to 19 hours. The world's longest flight also requires the personnel crewing it to remain sharp throughout.

Unsurprisingly, such a long flight time well exceeds the legal limits for a two-person flight crew. The flight crew is bolstered to four members, allowing each crew member to use the crew bunk for a four-hour-long and a 2.5-hour-long rest period. These crew members aren't just sticking the A350-900ULR on autopilot and relaxing. It is essential that they are well rested because they have essential duties to carry out while the aircraft is in flight.

In response to the rapidly approaching launch of Project Sunrise, Qantas' Airbus A350-1000ULR flights from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) to Sydney (SYD), Pilot Nick from Lessons from the Flight Deck gave his reflections on what it's like to fly for such extended periods. He said that:

"The metabolic cost is the constant vigilance. You’re monitoring six fuel tanks, four engine indicators, weather radar, traffic radar, ATC frequencies in three regions, oceanic crossing procedures, alternate airport availability over the next 1,500 miles, and the dozen subtle ways the airplane talks to you."

The table below is an impression of what pilots will do hour-by-hour on the Singapore to New York flight based on each crew member having a four-hour and a 2.5-hour rest allowance. This is an estimation based on an 18.5-hour flight time. It is clear that ultra-long-haul crew do far more than put the autopilot on and watch the world go by. They also do all of these duties in an environment where the air is thinner, and they are steadily dehydrated.

Departure from Singapore. This is a high-workload period, with potential assistance from the reserve crew. It is standard ultra-long-haul procedure to have all four crew members in the cockpit for takeoff and landing.

Initial cruising period with regular route, fuel, and weather checks, along with communication with air traffic control. The reserve crew may rest during this period.

Reserve crew returns from rest and takes over for the middle cruise. They'll receive a briefing from the primary crew on anything that they need to be made aware of. The primary captain and first officer may take a rest period.

The first crew returns, allowing the reserve crew to go for their long rest. This is a period of deep cruise, where remote Pacific airspace is crossed.

The reserve crew returns from rest, allowing the primary flight crew to go for their long period of rest. The reserve crew begins to prepare for arrival, with frequent air traffic control communications as they approach and enter US airspace.

The primary crew returns and receives a handover. The approach to New York begins. This is another high-workload period, with the crew having to navigate New York's exceptionally busy airspace before landing and taxiing to the gate.

One of the main activities that a pilot will be doing aboard Singapore Airlines' flight from Singapore to New York is resting, with each getting almost seven hours away from the flight deck. According to Executive Traveller, A350s come with two upstairs rest areas for pilots and cabin crew members.

The forward rest area, located above the foremost passenger cabin, is for pilots, while the rear rest area is for cabin crew. You can usually tell where these rest areas are because of the lack of central overhead luggage bins. The pilot rest area has two beds, while the cabin crew's space has six bunks. Pilots and crew stay safe in these rest areas because each is concealed behind a steadfast security door with a combination lock.

Singapore Airlines' flights from Singapore to New York don't just need pilots who are talented and well-rested. It also requires a plane, which is an undeniable engineering marvel. While the standard A350-900 can fly 8,500 nautical miles (15,742 km), the A350-900ULR, built bespoke for Singapore Airlines, can fly 9,700 nautical miles (17,964 km), with a maximum flight time of 20 hours.

The table below shows specifications for the A350-900ULR according to data from Aircraft Investigation. It shows a high maximum takeoff weight and fuel capacity and a substantially lower passenger capacity than is standard.

2 x Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-84 producing 84,190 lbf (374.5 kN)

The A350-900ULR will soon no longer be the longest-flying operational A350 variant. That is because of Qantas' Project Sunrise flights from SYD to LHR, which will make use of the upcoming A350-1000ULR. It will be able to fly commercially for up to 22 hours, with test flights exceeding this duration. That will require a reduced seating capacity of just 238 passengers to facilitate a new 4,400-gallon (20,000-liter) rear-center fuel tank.

The Project Sunrise philosophy for a better mechanical range is much like the A350-900ULR: more fuel and a higher maximum takeoff weight to sustain it. Airbus engineers have also been hard at work to show that the fuel system can operate safely, particularly in scenarios where large quantities of fuel have to be suddenly diverted.

This aircraft also makes use of the advantages that come as standard with all A350s, such as the 25% fuel efficiency improvement compared with jets of the previous generation. The Rolls-Royce Trent XWB, which exclusively powers this aircraft family, is also known for being among the world's most efficient widebody engines. The jet achieves all of this while having a 50% lower noise footprint than the A330.

As with Singapore Airlines' ultra-long-haul A350 flights, Project Sunrise trips will be crewed by four pilots, with long and short rest periods built into the schedule. All four pilots will usually make their way to the flight deck during the busiest periods, such as takeoff and landing. These systems have been standardized by ultra-long-haul carriers such as Singapore Airlines, Qantas, Emirates, and Cathay Pacific over the past 20 years.

Project Sunrise flights will cross between nine and eleven time zones, depending on the exact time of year that they will be flying. Qantas' circadian rhythm research will help pilots to recover more quickly from jet lag. Meal times, lighting, and rest cycles will need to be carefully choreographed with this need in mind.

Anticipation is growing for Project Sunrise, which is set to launch in 2027.

It isn't just the flight from Singapore to New York that is long enough for pilots to need plenty of rest. After all, Singapore Airlines also has plenty of other long routes that originate at Singapore Changi Airport (SIN). Away from New York, the North American destinations are Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), San Francisco International Airport (SFO), and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) on the West Coast.

Singapore Airlines also flies its A350-900ULRs to five European airports. These are Manchester Airport (MAN), London Heathrow Airport (LHR), London Gatwick Airport (LGW), Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport (MAD), and Josep Tarradellas Barcelona-El Prat Airport (BCN). The final destination is Cape Town International (CPT).

The shortest of these routes is the 14-hour-and-ten-minute flight to Cape Town, which is operated via Johannesburg (JNB). This route is operated daily. The most frequent route is to San Francisco, which operates twice daily. The flights to LGW are less regular but peak at twice daily. Finally, the longest routes are to the two New York airports, both of which have a block time exceeding 19 hours.

The A350-900ULR deviates from Singapore Airlines' standard A350 layout of 253 seats across three classes. This features 42 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, 24 premium economy seats in a 2-4-2 layout, and 187 economy seats in a 3-3-3 configuration.

Singapore Airlines' A350-900ULR configuration has space for just 161 passengers, with 67 business class seats and room for 94 premium economy passengers. Meanwhile, there is no economy cabin, and the jets will soon be reconfigured with an even more exclusive 132-seat layout.
