#6171. United Airlines Bans “AI Agents,” Claims It’s To “Protect Customers”

United Airlines has just banned travelers from using “AI Agents” to book or service tickets (thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this). That’s an interesting stance for United, easily the country’s most tech savvy airline, to take. So what’s actually going on here?

United Airlines has today updated its contract of carriage, which are the terms that passengers have to agree to when they book a ticket. In the section about prohibited practices at the airline, the carrier added the following:

The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.

The “AI Agents” term is defined by United as follows:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual. AI Agents include but are not limited to: (i) AI assistants built into social media, messaging, search or other consumer platforms; (ii) AI-enabled browsers and standalone AI agents; and (iii) any third-party AI assistant that accesses United through a tool, application or connection provided by a travel agency or other intermediary.

United even put out a press release about this change, claiming that it’s making the change to “protect” customers. Here’s part of the explanation:

Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles. Plus, these automated AI actions have the potential to violate FAA and DOT regulations – as an example, flight check-in requires human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.

United claims it’s taking steps to restrict this kind of access, both directly within its digital platforms, and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third party personal AI agents or assistants.

It goes without saying that use of AI is becoming exponentially more popular in recent times, and is a force to be reckoned with. It’s anyone’s guess just how far it goes, in terms of how much the average person uses it in their everyday life.

There are certainly aspects of AI that are incredibly annoying, whether you look at it as an individual or a business. Admittedly I’m biased, but I’m so tired of feeling like half of what I’m reading online (whether on social media or websites) is written by a computer and not a human. It even extends to things like TripAdvisor reviews.

It’s also frustrating how many people write 30 paragraph emails nowadays, which are clearly 90% AI. I don’t really understand how that makes anyone’s life better. As far as I’m concerned, just give me the bullet points you fed your AI buddy, and we’ll all be better off for it. Anyway, rant over, back to United…

I suspect United’s real motive here is that it doesn’t want AI automatically being able to track and reprice flights (and then issue vouchers for passengers), or being able to too closely compare overall value on different airlines. For that matter, it probably just doesn’t want a third party getting that much data on the airline, not to mention that all of this can take a considerable toll on servers, if this scales.

But here’s what I find most interesting — the way this rule is written strikes me as being incredibly broad, no? Not to repeat the quote again, but this is the part I’m referencing, in particular:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual.

Any software that automatically “discovers” or searches for any product or service offered by United would include all award search tools (along with all kinds of other businesses), no? Is that actually the intent here, or does United just plan to selectively enforce rules? We did see Air Canada engage in a battle over this a few years back, so is United planning something similar?

United Airlines has today updated its rules to ban “AI Agents,” and the airline even put out a press release about it. The company claims it’s making this change to protect customers and their accounts, as AI bots could have unintended consequences.

Many people are understandably skeptical of that explanation, as I imagine the airline also wants to ban these kinds of things to help people reprice tickets, get better fares, etc. For that matter, based on how broadly the definition is written, it seems that even things like award search engines would be banned.

On one hand, it's easy to look at United's motive here. They don't want to lose revenue, and AI / MCP capabilities can easily get around some of the scraping restrictions that they've built over the last decade. But a level deeper, we're also seeing the same thing in finance. And retail. Heck, AI is even eating Google's core business. There's probably a good degree of fear from every industry that something big is coming and rather than learn to adapt, take risks and aim to thrive, they do what America does best: ban it and tell you it's for security.

The future is here. I had 1 of my AI agents (Insight) monitoring hotel reservations. It found cheaper rates on the same dates for 2 existing reservations & asked if I would like it to book the new reservation & cancel the old. I agreed. A hotel in London is > $200 cheaper. One in Perth $10 cheaper (ha ha). But since there was little time cost to me to let it rebook the Perth reservation, I said go ahead. But I gave permission first & reviewed the new reservations & cancellations afterward.

Personally, I am glad they imposed this ban. Whatever their reason is I don't care. As a iT security guy, allowing an agent to interface with booking opens up soooooo many security breach potentials and nearly impossible to explain it to a exec or govt official in a way they would understand. To the point the regulators would just dismiss what they don't understand as fear mongering. Companies just cannot randomly deloy AI features. To date none of them including big tech are treating ai security with any seriousness. The only security right now is good enough for optics and counting on the public not understanding how this stuff works. All the scamming attempts we get now will be magnify by 1000x and the speed of the scale will increase dramatically. Binance getting hacked and losing $6B should be a big big warning given that they have much more security than an airline. I am tell you unequivocally airline data security is laughable. United airline for example, their IT don't even know what 2 FA actually is. Their website have some lame security and they call it 2FA not even realizing what they implemented actually made their security worse. These ceos think AI is magic. They're going to get a very hard lesson on AI and AI security. The one blessing I have is that because I churn credit cards so often I'm not concern about cc data breaches or stolen card #. But everything else, we're in for some pain.

I think this is likely a combination of pricing data protection (there are sites today that have a lot of access but there are limits to how it can be leveraged individually, whereas you could have your own agent do data scrapes specific to flights you want to book), and getting ahead of the potential for thousands of individual agents scraping airline websites and either causing stability issues or running up their hosting costs. They also want to protect their own ability to create their own agents that have unique access to their data (and potentially charging for that). Amazon has done the same thing - and went as far as to limit the descriptions and details they provide in order emails now so Google can't scrape the data from Gmail accounts.

It's pretty clear that when an AI agent books a ticket for the user, United is not liable for mistake. What's more interesting, though, is if there's a third party service like cheapflights.ai or something that the user can pay to book them a good flight. If the website screws up, is the user or cheapflights.ai liable? More abstractly, in an agentic SaaS scenario, does the agent owner or the agent operator bear liability?

#6170. Richard Avedon, Fashion Guru, Does Old Age

A moving, incisive photography exhibition in Toronto and Montreal explores the way of all flesh.

Left: Richard Avedon, Gloria Swanson, actor, New York, September 4, 1980, gelatin silver print. Right: Richard Avedon, The Duke and Duchess of Windsor, Waldorf Astoria, suite 28A, New York, April 16, 1957, gelatin silver print.

© The Richard Avedon Foundation, courtesy of the Museum of Modern Art, New York, Committee on Photography Fund

Old faces — some seem to crease and crumble as we watch — were a specialty for Richard Avedon (1923–2004), the photographer famous for his fashion work for Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, Revlon, and Elle, magazines not known for plugging geezers. I didn’t know this, so I learned something new in my first minutes in Richard Avedon Immortal: Portraits of Aging, 1951–2004, finishing its tour next month, when it goes to The Image Center in Toronto and the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts. Avedon was a pioneer in presenting cool, stark, tough beauty — he gave us a nude Nastassja Kinski with a boa constrictor licking her earlobe, Brooke Shields in jeans, and lots of movie stars and potentates at their peaks. But old age? Shades of decadence are one thing, but decrepitude?

The Image Center is Canada’s premiere photography museum and part of Toronto Metropolitan University. The exhibition there is similar to Montreal’s edition and displays 100 Avedon portraits. Avedon died more than 20 years ago, and the show spans 50 years, so the subjects are from another era. That said, old age is timeless as well as time-limited. On view are superstars such as Gloria Swanson, Ronald Reagan, the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, and the Dalai Lama. Then there are the period pieces like Dorothy Parker, Oscar Levant, Ezra Pound, and Coco Chanel.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

#6169. Singapore Airlines Reconsiders New Business Class Seat Design After Backlash

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled all-new cabins, with the most exciting developments being a new first class and new business class. The new cabins look great (nothing revolutionary, but a huge improvement), with one exception — the new business class seat colors. Not only do they look cheap, but they just seem completely mismatched to the rest of the cabin.

While the airline vehemently defended the color choices for several days, it seems that they’re at least now reconsidering it, though it remains to be seen if it’s too late to make a change…

On Wednesday, November 11, 2026, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong had a town hall with employees, as reported by The Business Times. During this, he was asked about the negative feedback the airline has received about the new business class seat design.

In response to this, he reportedly said “we’ll look at it, we’ll see what’s feasible.” So that signals some willingness to make changes, though admittedly with how far out seats are ordered, that’s not necessarily so straightforward, so I wouldn’t count on anything happening. He did, however, emphasize that customers will come to like the seats after experiencing its comforts for themselves.

At the town hall, Singapore Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin said this was a good learning point for the airline, but indicated that he hopes customers will mind the colors less after experiencing the seats. He also reportedly said “I suppose, you know, it’s the 80-20 rule, you can’t please them all.”

At the time of launch, Singapore Airlines VP of Product Experience, Ong Wah Li, explained the new design was in response to customer feedback, and described it as “modern, fresh, yet elegant and refined, that’s suited to business travel.”

BMW Designworks was behind the design of the cabin, and CEO Julia de Bono defended the color choices at the launch event, describing them as “more refreshing and more progressive.” As she viewed it, “what I see when I look at it, it’s definitely like a nice suit, with the white and the metal really popping out, you know, it’s more like a suit with a sneaker, so a bit more modern and fresh.”

To state the obvious, the trim and finishes on a new business class seat are hardly the most pressing issues facing the world. However, Singapore Airlines prides itself in being perhaps the most detail oriented airline in the world, because management has an obsessive attention to even the smallest things.

So I can’t help but be a bit confused by all of this:

It also just feels to me like the mandate for the design of this product was off, as shared by the CEO of BMW Designworks. Premium travel demand is through the roof, and a lot of people in premium cabins aren’t traveling for business. For that matter, these cabins will be operating the world’s longest flights, so this isn’t a case of a business traveler hopping on a plane in a suit, and going straight to a meeting (at least that doesn’t make up a meaningful percentage of the traffic here).

Is “suit with a sneaker” really the vibe you want to go for with a new business class product that’s on an airline that’s known for its incredible warmth? It’s almost like the airline views warmth and modernity as being at odds with one another, which I don’t at all agree with.

For example, reader Sam asked AI to take the new seat, but preserve the old color concept, and below is what it spit out.

That looks so much more on brand for Singapore Airlines than what the airline actually arrived at.

I would’ve loved to be a fly on the wall when this design was finalized. Was everyone immediately onboard with this, and thought it looked great? Or was there some skepticism, but someone said “trust me, people will love this, this is what a modern cabin looks like?”

I just don’t understand how you can commit to investing in a project that costs billions of dollars, reportedly get feedback from hundreds of customers, and still end up so far off the pulse of public sentiment.

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled its new cabins, which is an exciting development. Everything looked pretty great, except the new business class seat finishes, which seem terribly mismatched to the brand. The airline claimed it wanted something modern and progressive, but I’m not sure “suit with sneakers” is really the aesthetic that the public wanted (or that the chosen finishes actually reflect that).

Singapore Airlines leadership claims it’s now looking into possibly updating finishes, but I wouldn’t count on anything coming of that, given how far along this is.

What do you make of this Singapore Airlines business class design fiasco? And I’m still waiting for someone to please tell me that they love the design, and think it’s great!

#6168. Why Boeing 787 Cockpits Use Electronic Checklists Instead Of Paper

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

The Boeing 787 Dreamliner's flight deck is designed around digital information. Large displays bring together flight data, navigation information, aircraft system indications, and alerts, giving pilots access to information that once appeared across numerous separate instruments and documents. The aircraft’s electronic checklist system follows the same philosophy. Instead of relying solely on printed pages, pilots can access normal and non-normal checklists through the flight deck displays.

This is more than a change in presentation. An electronic checklist can connect checklist procedures with aircraft alerts and, where the system supports it, use aircraft signals to confirm that certain actions have been completed. That can help pilots keep track of a procedure, avoid overlooking steps after an interruption, and manage abnormal situations more systematically. Paper checklists still have an important role, however. Understanding why Boeing adopted electronic checklists means looking at how they work, what they improve, and where their limitations remain.

The 787’s electronic checklist system is integrated into the aircraft’s flight deck information environment. It provides access to normal checklists, which cover routine phases of flight, and non-normal checklists, which address situations requiring a specific response. Rather than searching through a paper manual, pilots can select the relevant procedure on a display and work through its instructions in sequence.

The relationship between the checklist system and the aircraft alerting system is particularly important during non-normal operations. When the aircraft detects a condition that generates an applicable alert, the flight crew can access the associated checklist through the flight deck controls. On the 787, selecting the checklist function can bring up the relevant procedure on a multifunction display. If several alerts have associated checklists, the system can present them for the crew to select. This gives pilots a more direct route from an aircraft indication to the procedure intended to address it.

Electronic checklists can also provide information about whether individual actions have been completed. Some items are designed as closed-loop steps, meaning the system receives a signal from the aircraft that can confirm the required configuration or action. Other items are open-loop steps, which require the pilot to verify completion manually. The distinction matters because an electronic checklist does not automatically know whether every action has been performed simply because a pilot has selected or acknowledged an item.

A closer look at some of the most cutting-edge aircraft in 2026.

Paper checklists are straightforward, familiar, and independent of an aircraft's display systems. They have served flight crews for decades, but they also create practical challenges in a modern cockpit. A pilot must locate the correct page, maintain their place while reading, and ensure that the checklist continues from the correct point after an interruption. During a busy phase of flight, even a small loss of place can require the crew to retrace steps and confirm which actions have already been completed.

An electronic checklist addresses several of these difficulties by keeping the procedure within the flight deck display environment. The crew can access the required checklist without handling a separate document, while the system can provide visual indications of progress. Where aircraft data supports automatic confirmation, the display can also distinguish between an action that has been verified by the system and one that still requires a pilot's confirmation. This reduces some of the administrative work involved in tracking a checklist, although it does not remove the need for careful monitoring.

The move toward electronic checklists also reflects the wider development of flight deck automation. As aircraft systems became more integrated, manufacturers had opportunities to connect operating procedures with alerts and aircraft configuration information. Boeing's work on electronic checklists predates the 787. The company's development of the technology began decades earlier, with its system evolving through the 1990s and becoming part of the Boeing 777 flight deck. The 787 builds on that broader move toward integrated flight deck information rather than representing the beginning of electronic checklist technology.

One of the most important features of an electronic checklist is the difference between closed-loop and open-loop items. Although both appear within the same procedure, they do not work in the same way. A closed-loop item can receive confirmation from an aircraft system or sensor, while an open-loop item depends on the flight crew to perform and verify the action. Understanding this distinction helps explain why an electronic checklist is more than a digital version of a printed page.

For a closed-loop item, the checklist system can use information from the aircraft to determine whether the required condition has been achieved. For example, if a checklist step requires a particular switch or system configuration, an appropriate aircraft signal may allow the system to recognize that the condition has been met. The checklist indication can then change to show completion. The exact indications and available feedback depend on the aircraft system and the individual checklist item.

Can receive confirmation from aircraft data or a system signal

Can update when the required condition is detected

Pilot still monitors the action and system response

Only works where suitable aircraft feedback is available

An open-loop item works differently. The system cannot independently confirm that the required action has been carried out, so the pilot must complete the task and verify it. This is important for actions that depend on human observation, judgment, or confirmation rather than a signal available to the checklist computer. Electronic presentation does not turn every checklist instruction into an automatically verified action. The crew remains responsible for ensuring that each step has been completed correctly.

The aircraft offers exceptional long-haul capabilities.

Electronic checklists are particularly useful when an aircraft generates a non-normal alert. In these circumstances, pilots may need to identify the condition, locate the applicable procedure, assess the aircraft's status, and carry out a series of actions. The checklist system helps connect the alert with the relevant procedure, reducing the need to search manually through a collection of printed pages while managing other flight deck tasks.

On the Boeing 787, the electronic checklist system works alongside the aircraft's alerting functions. When an alert has an associated checklist, pilots can use the checklist control to access the procedure on a multifunction display. If more than one alert requires a checklist, the crew can be presented with the available procedures and select the one they need. The system therefore helps organize procedural information, but it does not make operational decisions on behalf of the pilots.

The display also helps crews monitor progress through a procedure. This is particularly relevant when a checklist is interrupted or when several tasks must be managed at the same time. A clear indication of checklist status can help pilots establish which items have been completed and which remain outstanding. Nevertheless, the crew must continue to monitor the aircraft, communicate effectively, and apply the procedure in the context of the situation. The checklist is a tool for supporting those responsibilities, not a substitute for them.

Electronic checklists offer clear advantages, but they also depend on the availability and correct operation of the aircraft's electronic systems. A display failure, checklist system fault, or loss of relevant system feedback can affect how the crew accesses or completes a procedure. For that reason, paper checklists and approved alternative procedures remain important parts of the wider operational framework. The presence of an electronic checklist does not mean printed procedures are unnecessary.

The Boeing 787's minimum equipment procedures recognize that the electronic checklist system can be unavailable under specified conditions. If the system is inoperative, the applicable maintenance and operational provisions require it to be deactivated and suitable checklist procedures to be used. There are also provisions for situations in which closed-loop indications are unavailable. In those circumstances, crews may need to use the prescribed line-item override procedures to complete the checklist. These provisions demonstrate that the aircraft has procedures for dealing with checklist system limitations rather than assuming the electronic system will always be available.

Available independently of the checklist display

Require the crew to locate the relevant procedure

Can confirm supported aircraft configurations

Depend on functioning electronic equipment

Provide an alternative when approved procedures require their use

Paper procedures also provide another way to access information. They do not rely on the checklist display itself, and they can serve as a practical backup when the approved procedures call for their use. However, paper is not automatically safer or more reliable in every situation. A printed checklist can be misplaced, difficult to manage during a busy phase of flight, or harder to track after an interruption. The key point is that electronic and paper procedures have different strengths, and the aircraft's approved operating documentation determines which method to use in a given circumstance.

Explore the striking Airbus A320 vs. Boeing 737 cockpit differences, from sidesticks to noise, and learn how pilots see these iconic flight decks.

The biggest advantage of an electronic checklist is not simply that it removes paper from the cockpit. Its value comes from how it organizes information and, where the aircraft supports it, connects procedures with aircraft system data. A pilot can access an applicable checklist through the flight deck interface, follow its sequence, and receive confirmation for certain actions. That integration can make checklist management more consistent and help reduce errors associated with losing place or overlooking a step after an interruption.

However, electronic systems introduce their own considerations. Pilots must understand how the checklist interface works, recognize the difference between automatically confirmed and manually verified items, and avoid treating a completed indication as proof that the entire aircraft is in the correct condition. A system can only confirm what its sensors and programmed logic are designed to monitor. It cannot replace the crew's responsibility to assess the aircraft, recognize unexpected conditions and apply sound judgment.

The Boeing 787's electronic checklist system therefore represents an evolution in how flight crews manage procedures, rather than an attempt to remove human involvement. It brings checklists closer to the aircraft information they depend on, provides a structured way to monitor progress and supports access to non-normal procedures when alerts occur. Paper procedures remain part of the operational backup framework, while pilots retain responsibility for every action and verification. The technology has changed how the checklist is presented, but the essential purpose remains the same: ensuring that critical actions are completed, checked, and understood before the flight moves on.

Business-class fliers on United Airlines will soon be able to relax in a fancy new Polaris Lounge at Denver International Airport (DEN).

Design work is underway on the new, exclusive lounge at DEN, Aaron McMillan, the managing director of hospitality programs at United, told TPG on Monday.

“We’re going to build a mezzanine on top of [the existing] mezzanine and expand the floor plate a little bit,” he said referring to a location at DEN near the end of Concourse A between gates A18 and A20. “We’ll have a two-story Polaris lounge there.”

United aims to open the new DEN Polaris Lounge by late 2028 or early 2029, added McMillan.

The news comes amid a club building spree by the airline. United opened a massive Washington, D.C.-inspired United Club in the new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Tuesday. The space is second in size only to the new club at Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) that opened in October.

United is also building a new club at San Francisco International Airport (SFO) that is scheduled to open by the end of the year, and is in talks for new clubs at Southwest Florida International Airport (RSW) in Fort Myers and Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

The Polaris Lounge is United’s premium airport space accessible only to fliers booked in same-day, long-haul business class or in business or first class on several partner airlines, including All Nippon Airways (ANA) and Lufthansa.

The spaces compete with American Airlines’ Flagship Lounges and Delta Air Lines’ Delta One Lounges.

United has six Polaris Lounges: Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), IAH, Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), SFO and IAD.

DEN is United’s only mainland U.S. hub without a Polaris Lounge.

When United opened its first Polaris space at ORD in 2016, lounges were only planned at its main international gateways and not DEN. The Colorado hub boasted only one long-haul nonstop at the time: Tokyo’s Narita Airport (NRT), schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

Today, United flies five intercontinental routes from DEN: Frankfurt Airport (FRA), London’s Heathrow Airport (LHR), Munich Airport (MUC), Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO) and NRT. It will add its sixth route, to Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), next summer.

“Aside from the local departures we’ve grown out of Denver, there’s also a fairly significant number of local customers that are connecting over like Chicago, and Houston, and San Francisco that are traveling Polaris that can take advantage of the product,” said McMillan.

And while McMillan was mum on the look and feel of the new Polaris Lounge at DEN, he was confident in one thing: it will not have an outdoor patio.

All travelers at DEN have access to the public outdoor patios at the ends of concourses A, B and C.

#6166. FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop

Flights were grounded across the U.S. Friday afternoon over suspected air traffic control communications issues.

The FAA issued a highly unusual mass ground stop shortly after 3 p.m.

“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped,” the agency said in an advisory. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis.”

In a separate statement, the FAA said a communications issue affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers is to blame. Agency technicians are now investigating the issue.

According to ABC News, this is only the second time since the 9/11 attacks that departures across the country have been stopped. Flights currently in the air are believed to still be in contact with ATC.

National media outlets showed footage of commercial airplanes queued up but not moving at numerous major airports, including Los Angeles, Boston, Reagan National, New York-LaGuardia, Houston Bush, Dallas/Fort Worth, and Raleigh–Durham.

The ground stop will almost certainly cause a cascade of cancellations and delays lasting into the weekend.

The first Cabinet-level official to comment in person on the incident was Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who spoke to reporters outside the White House. Mullin said there is no indication that the outage is a cyberattack, or connected to the recent Microsoft outage.

The situation is close to “unprecedented,” the secretary added, but there is no threat to public safety or reason to panic. Mullin said it is still too early to say when the problem will be resolved.

It was not immediately clear if the outage is connected to ongoing upgrades on ATC systems and infrastructure. The FAA has been moving rapidly to replace outdated equipment, such as old radios and floppy disks, and install more automated technology. The agency is also ripping out old copper wiring and replacing it with fiber optic cables.

We’re currently seeing a massive elevated welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, making it an ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

The Amex Business Platinum Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $20,000 within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Upon completing minimum spending, bonus points will officially post after 8-12 weeks, though in practice, typically post much faster than that.

#6164. Elizabeth Warren’s Plan to Abolish Credit Cards

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.) host a roundtable on housing affordability and accessibility on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., January 7, 2026.

Elizabeth Warren, never short on annoyances, thinks that interest on consumer credit cards is too high.

The average rate currently hovers around 21 percent. Her solution: Pass a law to cap interest rates at 10 percent. She says she has a bill ready to go, and like-minded lawmakers have signaled their support for controlling rates.

Like any other price ceiling, an interest cap would create a shortage of the product it attempts to make more affordable. With only a tiny fraction of credit cards now offering interest at 10 percent or less, capping rates at that level would force lenders to dramatically restrict accounts — requiring borrowers to put up collateral or limiting access to people with exceptionally good credit — or eliminate them outright.

To progressives, interest on credit cards is nothing but usury — the exploitation of poor borrowers who can’t afford to pay their bills on time. Warren’s sales pitch implies that, under her bill, people would enjoy the same credit just at a lower cost. In reality, almost everyone would see their current credit cards disappear.

Regrettably, Warren may also find allies for her proposal among Republicans. She claims she is open to working with President Trump, who called in 2024 for a temporary cap on credit card interest of “around 10 percent.” Senator Josh Hawley (R., Mo.), a right-wing progressive of sorts, recently joined hands with Bernie Sanders to translate that thoughtless musing into legislation.

Interest rates are not some arbitrary number. They are the price for lenders to provide liquidity on the promise, but never the certainty, that it will be repaid. To issue loans through a credit card, banks must first obtain the money by borrowing it themselves, either from depositors or other financial institutions. Interest must be paid on that debt and passed through to cardholders.

It’s true that rates on credit cards, as well as other consumer loans, are typically much higher than those for mortgages and businesses. That is because personal credit is one of the riskiest kinds to extend. Unlike secured loans, repayment depends wholly on borrowers’ creditworthiness. That often fails to hold up: 13 percent of credit-card balances are seriously past due, and approximately 5 percent of debt is never repaid. Higher interest rates exist to compensate for these losses.

Rates also vary based on individual creditworthiness. Borrowers with poor credit history, or people just starting to build their history after leaving childhood or moving to the country, have the most to lose from interest caps. They must accept costlier rates to obtain any credit whatsoever, and if lenders can’t adjust for their added risk, they will simply be cut off. Those in need of funds will instead have to turn to pawnshops or illegal loan sharks.

The credit card industry could always use more competition to keep interest rates at their fair market level. Ironically, the Dodd-Frank Act that Elizabeth Warren championed likely reduced the availability of consumer credit by increasing lenders’ regulatory burden. She also despises credit reporting agencies for tracking borrowers’ repayment histories, even though they replaced a far more discretionary and intrusive system in which bankers evaluated applicants’ personal reputations. For someone so appalled by alleged discrimination in finance, Warren should love objective credit reports.

By and large, Americans like their credit cards and wish to keep them. In trying to rescue consumers from their own financial decisions, Warren would deprive them of their plastic and consign them to infinitely more treacherous alternatives.

#6163. Update: FAA Lifts Ground Stop

After a roughly five-hour freeze on virtually all commercial aircraft departures, the FAA has lifted its nationwide emergency ground stop.

The FAA canceled the ground stop around 8:20 p.m., and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed it at a press conference at the White House Friday night. He said it will take some time for flights to restart but emphasized that the air space is safe.

According to Duffy, FAA personnel began to see inconsistencies in air traffic data around 3:30 p.m. Friday, and, out of an abundance of caution, the decision was made to ground flights not already in the air. He said old analog ATC communications switches were overwhelmed and “went down,” causing the inconsistency.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the failure was triggered by an attempted technology update, which caused the system to reboot and crash.

There is no evidence of a cyberattack or terrorism, Mullin emphasized, and passengers were never in any danger.

Duffy said travelers should contact their airline for information about potential cancellations and delays. He said his department is in contact with the major carriers and will work with them to restore normal operations.

A small number of mostly international flights were cleared for takeoff at airports such as New York-JFK, Washington Dulles, Reagan National, and Detroit Friday afternoon during the ground stop, but most remained grounded until the FAA reversed its order.

#6162. American Airlines Pilot Arrested At Heathrow For Being Unfit To Fly And Having Cocaine

Every so often we’ll hear stories of pilots being arrested for showing up at the airport intoxicated. Well, here’s an even wilder story, about an American Airlines pilot who not only showed up at the airport unfit to fly, but also had cocaine on him.

View from the Wing flags a story about how on November 1, 2026, a 64-year-old pilot was arrested at London Heathrow Airport (LHR):

So this is sort of wild — not only was he under the influence of something (drugs or alcohol), but then he also had cocaine in his possession. That’s just next level irresponsibility.

It’s not clear how exactly all of this was discovered, in terms of the sequence of events. Was there just a random check, or was he acting erratically, authorities were alerted, and that’s when this all came to light? If so, it sounds like the first clue was how he was acting (which made him unfit to fly), and then presumably he was searched, which is when the cocaine may have been discovered.

This is just so beyond irresponsible. If he was already unfit to fly during boarding and had cocaine in his possession, was he going to consume that during the flight, or just take it home with him?

Keep in mind that in the United States, commercial pilots have to retire by their 65th birthday. So this guy was just weeks or months from retirement… what a sad way to end a career, as you can bet he won’t be flying again. One wonders if he was just trying to party a little before retirement, if this had been going on for some time, or what.

While the authorities haven’t identified the airline that this pilot works for (other than to say he works for a US airline), it’s not too hard to figure out. Based on his name (which I won’t post here, because he’s in enough trouble as is), it’s clear he’s an American Airlines pilot.

American had two flight cancelations out of Heathrow that day — one for flight AA85 to Chicago (ORD), and one for flight AA91 to Miami (MIA). It’s not clear which of those he was scheduled to fly on.

Under UK261 regulations, any passenger who ended up arriving at their final destination four or more hours late would be entitled to £520 ($690) in cash compensation. That’s on top of covering any reasonable expenses incurred. Admittedly some people may have been rebooked on other flights once this flight was axed, but at least a large percentage of passengers would presumably be eligible for this.

An American Airlines pilot who was close to retirement decided to end his career in a rather unfortunate way, as he was arrested at Heathrow for being unfit to fly, while also having cocaine in his possession. The lack of decent judgment shown here is beyond irresponsible, and I hope he gets the help he needs so he doesn’t ever endanger others in this way again. The good news for him is that he was within months of retirement anyway, so at least his “career” impact is pretty minimal.

What do you make of this American pilot being arrested?

#6161. Airlines Warn Ground Stop Chaos Is Far From Over With Planes & Crews Stuck In Wrong Cities

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Travel chaos may continue to linger across the US tonight and into tomorrow, after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the rare nationwide ground stop across airports nationwide. This comes as thousands of airline crew and aircraft remain displaced.

On Friday, a ground stop forced all aircraft to be grounded for more than four hours due to a telecommunications and tech outage stemming from overloaded routers and data inconsistencies. With the Department of Homeland Security explaining that this came from the patching of a new system into the existing framework that led to the older system to become overwhelmed.

Passengers are encouraged to be patient and reconfirm the status of their flights before heading to the airport. President and Chief Executive Officer of Airlines for America, Chris Sununu, spoke with NewsNation and reiterated that while the agency moved quickly to issue the nationwide ground stop for safety concerns until affected systems were restored, this has displaced thousands of airline crew members and many aircraft nationwide.

It is expected that the side effects of the ground stop could be felt by passengers for days, as airlines work around the clock to deal with affected aircraft, crew and passengers. According to CNN, it is suggested that more than 7,500 flights within, into, or out of the US were canceled today following the ground stop.

In addition to canceled flights, more than 10,000 flights experienced delays. The knock-on effect is already hampering Saturday's flight plans, with more than 1,500 flights already being canceled.

The ground stop has sent ripples out across the globe, with many flights destined for the US delayed. While airspace was reopened at 8:15 PM on Friday, flight departures would only resume gradually, and it will take time for airlines to be able to fully restore operations. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted, 'it's going to be slow'.

Highlighted from this event is the ongoing strain of the US air traffic control system, which is plagued with aging technology, equipment and communication problems. This pressure is amplified by the severe shortage of several thousand air traffic controllers. However, in the face of today's travel chaos, some air traffic controllers have already expressed that they 'don't buy' Duffy's explanation for what happened, with Anna Giaritelli telling CNN that a main reason is:

“These types of switches they’re doing that the FAA is doing, they don’t happen during the day. They don’t happen during busy times like a Friday afternoon. They’re doing these midweek, in the middle of the night when there is no air traffic going on.”

Trouble first was identified at 3:36 PM, when air traffic control centres across the country noted instability in radar and communication systems. This quickly escalated with switches and routers that carry critical data becoming overloaded. As a result, inconsistent information from these systems prompted the FAA to issue the rare ground stop for flights nationwide.

The agency cited communication problems for the halt.

A ground stop is exactly what it sounds like, restricting flight operations on the ground. This meant that aircraft already in the air were permitted to continue to their intended destinations without major disruption. Thousands of aircraft were able to land safely during the ground stop; however, no jets were permitted to depart.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stressed that the FAA updates to the aging systems were the reason behind the ground stop, and the halt in flight operations was not due to a threat to the US, and had no links to the Thursday Microsoft outage. The Transportation Secretary has also warned that there could be more disruption in the future unless systems are updated.

As airlines resume flight operations, displaced crew, passengers and aircraft will slowly return to normal; however, this is expected to take several days until services are back to normal. It is not expected to impact the upcoming Thanksgiving travel rush in late November.

As soon as you apply for a credit card, your application is processed by a computer. You’ll typically receive one of three responses: immediate approval, some form of “pending” status or denial.

Receiving instant approval doesn’t guarantee that you can begin using your card immediately. If you receive instant approval, you may be able to view your card number right away; otherwise, you’ll usually need to wait until your physical card arrives in the mail before you can begin using it.

It can take five to 10 business days to get a new credit card after approval. However, that timeframe varies by card and issuer. For instance, American Express offers overnight shipping for its top-tier cards. Some issuers offer expedited shipping on request, but there’s no guarantee. You may need to pay when requesting expedited shipping from some banks (including Barclays).

Getting approved for a new credit card is exciting, but waiting a week or more for it to arrive in the mail isn't. Fortunately, some issuers let you start using your new card immediately after approval, either by providing an instant card number or by allowing you to add your card to a digital wallet.

That instant access can give you a head start on meeting the welcome bonus spending requirement, since the clock starts ticking as soon as your account is approved — not when your physical card arrives. It can also come in handy if you need to make a purchase right away, whether you're booking travel or taking advantage of a 0% introductory APR offer. For cobranded store credit cards, you may also receive a discount on your purchases, starting as soon as you use the card.

Here's a look at which major credit card issuers offer instant card numbers, digital wallet access or both.

Some issuers provide an instant card number, while others, like Chase, instead let eligible cardholders add their new card to a digital wallet immediately after approval. Both options let you start using your card before the physical version arrives.

While there are too many cards to list that offer instant card numbers or access, here are six of our top picks.

American Express provides your new account number immediately after your online application is approved, provided your identity can be verified.

The instant card number will be the same as the physical card you’ll get in the mail, but the four-digit card identification number on the front of the card will be different. Because of that, you may want to wait to set up recurring payments.

Note that instant card numbers for some cobranded cards may only be used with the cobranded company (like Delta, Hilton or Marriott).

In addition to instant numbers for new cardmembers, Amex gives existing cardmembers access to their card information when ordering replacement cards.

Most Amex personal and business cards offer instant card numbers; notable exclusions include the Amazon Business Card and the Amazon Business Prime Card.

Capital One Mobile app users may be able to use instant card numbers immediately after they’re approved, before their physical card arrives in the mail.

This differs from Capital One's virtual card numbers, which are designed to help protect your purchases rather than provide immediate access to a newly approved account.

#6159. Buy Etihad Guest Miles With 60% Bonus (2.0 Cents Each): Worth It?

Etihad Guest has just launched its latest promotion on buying miles, which is being marketed as the biggest offer of the year. With this, members can buy Etihad miles with a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire them for as little as two cents each.

Is that offer worth it? Let’s cover all the details, but I’ll say right away that I think this offer has fairly limited appeal, and you should only take advantage of this with a specific use in mind.

Link: Buy Etihad Guest miles with a bonus

Between 12:01AM GST on November 12 and 11:59PM GST on November 22, 2026, Etihad Guest is offering a bonus on purchased miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger bonus the more miles you buy, as follows:

Note that purchased Etihad Guest miles post within 72 hours of completing the purchase (typically faster than that), and that purchased miles don’t count toward Etihad Guest elite status.

Etihad Guest ordinarily charges 3.2 cents per purchased mile, and there are no further taxes and fees. That’s before any bonuses or discount. With the 60% bonus, if you maxed out this promotion you’d receive a total of 320,000 Etihad Guest miles at a cost of $6,400, which is a rate of two cents per Etihad Guest mile.

Etihad Guest limits members to purchasing 200,000 miles per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. The exception is Etihad Guest Platinum members, who can purchase up to 300,000 miles per year, before any bonuses.

The current Etihad Guest buy miles promotion is described as the biggest offer of the year. To compare this to other offers we’ve seen so far this year, we’ve seen bonuses of 25-50% (2.56 cents to 2.13 cents per mile), as well as discounts of up to 35% (2.08 cents per mile).

As you can see, Etihad Guest’s current offer gives you the best cost per mile so far this year. However, Etihad isn’t exactly aggressive with selling miles, so it’s hard to get too excited about any of these amounts.

Etihad Guest mileage purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

There are lots of ways to redeem Etihad Guest miles. While the airline doesn’t belong to one of the major alliances, there are many ways to redeem the miles on both Etihad and on partner airlines.

Below you can find the award chart for travel exclusively on Etihad. The pricing is based on the one-way distance of travel. Note that these redemption rates are specifically for situations where there’s GuestSeat availability, which is Etihad’s capacity controlled, saver award space.

If you see higher award pricing than what’s listed below, that generally means there’s not saver award space, and redemptions won’t be a very good deal. Furthermore, in some situations you’ll find higher saver level award costs, including for travel in the carrier’s A380 first class.

Etihad Guest has a separate award chart for travel on partner airlines, which is also distance based, and you can find that below. This is based on the one-way distance, and you can’t mix airline partners on a single award.

The main reason to consider collecting Etihad Guest miles is because the program has access to a lot more Etihad award space than partner programs do. Partner programs, like American AAdvantage and Air France-KLM Flying Blue, typically only have access to a subset of premium cabin Etihad availability. Furthermore, if you want to fly in Etihad’s The Residence, your ticket needs to be issued by Etihad, so an Etihad Guest award redemption would qualify.

There are two major catches when it comes to Etihad Guest, in addition to not really having slam dunk redemption values:

I’d really only recommend buying Etihad Guest miles with a very specific use in mind, if you know what you’re doing.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Etihad Guest miles to be worth 1.1 cents each. I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get more value from Etihad Guest miles than that.

Etihad Guest miles don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Note that you can only reset the expiration of your miles by crediting a flight to the program every 18 months, so other activity wouldn’t help in that regard.

Keep in mind that there are many ways to earn Etihad Guest miles, so outright buying miles isn’t the only option. Etihad Guest also partners with select transferable points currencies. In the United States, you can move points to Etihad Guest at a 1:1 ratio from Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so that gives you quite a bit of flexibility.

Admittedly not everyone has access to credit cards in the United States, and some people may also prefer to just buy miles if they can acquire them at a reasonable cost.

Etihad Guest is selling miles with up to a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy miles for as little as two cents each. This could be worth it if you have a specific use in mind, but Etihad Guest just seems rather unserious with its buy miles promotions, since the program isn’t that lucrative, in terms of redemption rates, and the policies for changing and canceling awards is also incredibly frustrating.

So for a vast majority of people, I’d recommend giving this offer a pass, unless you’ve done the math, and it checks out.

#6158. World Of Hyatt Brand Explorer: Free Night Awards For Staying At New Brands

There are several ways to earn World of Hyatt free night award awards. In this post, I’d like to talk about one of the often overlooked ways to earn Hyatt free nights, which is with World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion.

This offers World of Hyatt members the opportunity to earn free night awards for exploring Hyatt’s portfolio. Given the huge brand inflation that Hyatt has seen in recent years, this can potentially offer up to seven free night awards, and counting.

With World of Hyatt’s Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a Category 1-4 free night certificate for every five unique Hyatt brands you stay at. When it comes to earning Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

If you want to see how many Hyatt brands you’ve stayed at, you can do so either through the World of Hyatt website or mobile app. Just go to the “Brand Explorer” section, and there will be a display showing how many unique brands you’ve stayed at (including which ones), and also how many free night certificates you’ve earned.

When it comes to redeeming Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

Of course you’ll maximize value with Brand Explorer by redeeming your free night award at an eligible Hyatt property when the cash rate would be as high as possible. World of Hyatt Category 4 properties can cost as much as 25,000 points per night, and in some situations, could retail for over $300 per night. So if you can find a hotel anywhere in that range, it’s a great way to maximize value.

Hyatt currently has 38 brands, which are as follows:

So as you can see, you’d need to stay at 35 brands to earn seven free night awards. If/when Hyatt adds two more brands, it’ll be possible to earn eight free night awards.

The World of Hyatt Brand Explorer offer is a fun way for the program to engage members and try to get them to try more brands. At least in one case it impacted where I chose to stay, because I do love checking this dashboard every so often, both to see the progress that I’m making, and be reminded of all the brands I’ve stayed at.

Even though I’ve had top tier status with World of Hyatt for over a decade and have now earned lifetime Globalist status, I haven’t even stayed at half of Hyatt’s current brand portfolio. As a matter of fact, I’ve only stayed at 13 of the 38 brands, so that’s just over one-third of properties.

Looking at the Hyatt brands I haven’t stayed at, most of them are all-inclusives, as that’s an area where Hyatt is growing significantly. However, in general this has limited appeal to me, based on the type of travel that I do. I’m sure I’ll knock out a few more brands in the coming years — maybe I’ll get to 15 brands, though I doubt I’ll make it to 20 brands in the foreseeable future.

With World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a free Category 1-4 free night awards for every five Hyatt brands you stay at. This is a way to earn up to seven free nights over time, based on Hyatt’s current portfolio of 38 brands. As Hyatt’s portfolio continues to grow, the opportunities to earn free nights continues to increase.

However, staying at Hyatt’s all-inclusive properties requires some effort, given that they’re not typically places you just drop into for a night.

Given how easy Hyatt makes it to track this, I’m curious — how many Hyatt brands have you stayed at? Which OMAAT reader has the record for the most brands?

#6157. Here's What Passengers Actually Get For The Extra Fare Of Premium Economy & Why It's Increasingly Popular

Premium economy has become an increasingly popular option for passengers on long-haul flights, offering significantly more comfort than economy class without the considerably higher fares associated with business class. In recent years, the cabin has become an important part of the long-haul products of carriers such as Delta Air Lines, Lufthansa, Emirates, and British Airways. Airlines are also continuing to increase the number of seats on their aircraft, often at the expense of regular economy capacity.

According to Going's 2026 State of Travel report, premium economy was the fastest-growing cabin choice among surveyed travelers, increasing from 16% to 20% in just one year. This growing popularity comes as airlines invest heavily in premium products, while passengers become more willing to pay extra for comfort. However, with premium economy fares generally costing 30% to 100% more than regular economy, what do passengers actually get for the extra money?

The most noticeable difference between premium economy and regular economy class is the amount of personal space available to passengers. On most long-haul aircraft, economy class seats have a pitch of approximately 30 to 32 inches (76 to 81 cm), compared to around 38 to 40 inches (97 to 102 cm) in premium economy. Seat pitch is the distance between the same point on two consecutive rows of seats, meaning passengers generally get around seven to nine additional inches of space between seats.

Premium economy seats are also considerably wider than those found in economy class. While regular economy seats typically measure between 17 and 18 inches (43 to 46 cm), premium economy seats are often between 18.5 and 19.5 inches (47 to 50 cm) wide. Most airlines also provide additional recline, generally between six and eight inches (15 to 20 cm), and many seats feature adjustable headrests, calf rests, and footrests. These differences become particularly noticeable on overnight flights, where passengers may spend eight to 12 hours in the same seat.

However, the actual differences depend on the airline and aircraft type. Lufthansa's new Allegris premium economy product, for example, offers 39 inches (99 cm) of seat pitch and features a fixed-shell design that lets passengers recline without disturbing the person behind them. Other carriers, including Emirates and Cathay Pacific, offer premium economy seats with up to 40 inches of pitch, while certain airlines provide even more space.

It seems to be one of the use of space aboard aircraft for maximizing revenue.

Besides the extra space, most airlines include other benefits for passengers traveling in premium economy. On long-haul flights, this often includes upgraded meal services, a wider selection of drinks, and better-quality amenities than those provided in regular economy. Depending on the airline, passengers may receive a welcome drink before departure, meals served on proper tableware, noise-canceling headphones, and an amenity kit. Many airlines have also installed larger inflight entertainment screens and additional power outlets in their premium economy seats.

The differences also extend to the airport experience, as many airlines provide priority check-in and boarding. Moreover, premium economy fares often include a larger checked baggage allowance than economy tickets. However, these benefits can vary considerably depending on the airline and fare type, and lounge access is generally not included. For example, some airlines offer lower-priced premium economy fares with reduced baggage allowances, so passengers should not assume every premium economy ticket includes the same benefits.

It is also important to distinguish premium economy from extra-legroom economy products, such as United Airlines' Economy Plus. While these seats generally provide more legroom, passengers still receive the same basic seat and onboard service as regular economy travelers. Dedicated premium economy cabins, such as United Premium Plus or Delta Premium Select, offer wider seats and a different onboard product. However, unlike modern business class suites, these seats do not convert into fully flat beds.

It seems to be one of the use of space aboard aircraft for maximizing revenue.

Premium economy is generally considerably more expensive than a regular economy class ticket, with passengers often paying between 30% and 100% more for the additional comfort and services. However, the actual difference depends heavily on the airline, route, and time of booking. While the upgrade can sometimes be relatively affordable, particularly on longer flights, premium economy fares can also approach those of discounted business class tickets.

To put these differences into perspective, Simple Flying previously compared British Airways' premium economy and business class fares on three of the airline's busiest transatlantic routes from London Heathrow Airport (LHR). The analysis, conducted on May 25, 2026, examined one-way fares to New York, Boston, and Los Angeles for travel during July 2026 and February 2027.

London - John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK)

London - Boston Logan International Airport (BOS)

London - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX)

During the peak summer travel period, premium economy fares averaged €3,181 ($3,516) across the three routes, compared with €9,587 ($10,596) for business class. This represented a saving of approximately €6,400 ($7,080), or nearly 67%, for passengers choosing World Traveller Plus instead of Club World. Nevertheless, even premium economy tickets were far from inexpensive, with one-way fares exceeding €3,500 ($3,868) on the route to Los Angeles.

John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK)

London - Boston Logan International Airport (BOS)

London - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX)

For travel in February 2027, the average premium economy fare was significantly lower at €1,337 ($1,478), compared with €2,085 ($2,304) for business class. However, the difference between the two cabins also narrowed substantially, with passengers saving an average of €748 ($827).

Importantly, the February flights were examined approximately nine months before departure, while the July flights were only one to two months away. Consequently, the large differences between summer and winter fares cannot be attributed to seasonality alone, as booking lead times and available fare classes also influence prices, but they still provide a rough indication.

USD equivalents have been converted using the European Central Bank's reference exchange rate of €1 = $1.1052 on November 13, 2026. The original fares were collected on May 25, 2026, and do not represent current ticket prices.

The differences go far beyond price, with business class passengers enjoying more space, better service, and lounge access.

According to Going's 2026 State of Travel and Flight Deals report, premium economy was the fastest-growing cabin choice among the travelers surveyed, increasing from 16% to 20% over the previous year. Furthermore, 59% of respondents indicated that they intended to spend more on premium cabin seating during 2026, making it one of the most popular travel upgrades. The same report found that 71% of travelers planned to spend more on accommodation, suggesting that many passengers are increasingly willing to spend more on the quality of their trips rather than simply taking additional vacations.

Part of the increasing demand for premium economy also comes from business travelers, particularly as companies are looking for ways to control their travel expenses. While business class remains an important product for corporate travel, some employers are reconsidering whether employees need fully lie-flat seats on every long-haul journey.

At the same time, affluent leisure travelers have become an increasingly important customer group for premium cabins after the pandemic. Unlike corporate travelers, these passengers generally pay for their own tickets and may be willing to spend additional money on comfort, particularly when traveling for longer vacations or special occasions. This has also blurred the traditional distinction between premium cabins designed primarily for corporate passengers and economy cabins serving leisure travelers.

These seats are often exceptionally comfortable.

While passengers benefit from additional comfort, premium economy has also become an important revenue-generating product for airlines. This is partly because premium economy seats occupy considerably less space than business class seats, while still allowing airlines to charge significantly more than regular economy fares.

The broader shift toward premium travel has also become increasingly visible in airline financial results. During the second quarter of 2026, Delta Air Lines reported $6.92 billion in premium passenger revenue, compared to $6.85 billion in Main Cabin revenue. This marked the first time the airline's premium ticket revenue exceeded its Main Cabin revenue, although the figures include all premium products rather than premium economy alone. In the third quarter, Delta generated another $6.82 billion in premium revenue, up 18% from the previous year, while premium seating capacity increased by 6%.

With passenger demand for premium economy continuing to grow, airlines are allocating an increasing proportion of their long-haul aircraft cabins to premium economy. Airlines such as American Airlines, Emirates, and Alaska Airlines are all continuing to invest heavily in their premium economy cabins. Cathay Pacific, for example, increased its premium economy capacity on updated Boeing 777-300ER aircraft from 34 to 48 seats, representing an increase of approximately 41%. Air France also doubled the size of its premium economy cabin from 24 to 48 seats on certain retrofitted 777-300ERs. These changes demonstrate how airlines are adjusting existing aircraft configurations rather than relying exclusively on new aircraft deliveries to expand their premium offerings.

Call it the ultimate Nile River cruise experience.

River cruise giant Viking has unveiled an epic new itinerary that sails the entire 600-mile stretch of the waterway between Cairo in the north and Aswan in the south.

Dubbed the Grand Nile Journey, Viking's 19-day trip revives a longer Nile cruise route that dates back to the late 1800s, when paddle steamers carried travelers from Cairo on the 465-mile journey south to Luxor, home to some of ancient Egypt's most famous temples and burial grounds.

From there, the vessels would continue to Aswan, another 130 miles to the south, with stops at ancient temples along the way.

Nowadays, most Nile River sailings skip the first 465 miles of this historic route, with ships only traveling along the 130-mile stretch of the Nile between Luxor and Aswan. Passengers reach the ships by flying from Cairo to Luxor, typically after a few days exploring Cairo.

Related: The ultimate guide to Nile river cruises and cruisetours

Only a handful of vessels currently operate a longer itinerary of the sort that Viking has announced — and none at the luxury level for which Viking is known on the river.

Kicking off in 2028 but available to book now, Viking's new Grand Nile Journeys will begin with a three-night stay at a luxury hotel in Cairo (the line often puts guests in the elegant Fairmont Nile City, along the banks of the river). Then, passengers board the line's one-of-a-kind, all-suite vessel Viking Ra for the 14-night journey south to Aswan.

The voyages will include stops at ancient sites along the 450-mile stretch from Cairo to Luxor that most Nile River travelers never see, including the 4,600-year-old Meidum Pyramid near Beni Suef and the striking cliffside Noble Tombs of Beni Hasan.

Other rare stops will include a visit to Tell el-Amarna, the once-lost royal desert capital founded by the Pharaoh Akhenaten, and the Abydos Temple, famous for drawings of ancient pilgrims to the sacred Festival of Osiris.

After a week traveling south along this lesser-visited stretch of the Nile, the Viking Ra will arrive in Luxor for another week of travel southward along the more popular parts of the river.

An extended stop in Luxor will bring visits to the temples of Luxor and Karnak, the royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings and the Temple of Seti I at Abydos.

Additional stops include the Temple of Horus in Edfu and the Temple of Philae near Aswan, among other sites in this area.

Related: The 5 best destinations you can visit on a Viking ship

By following this long route from Cairo to Aswan, the new Grand Nile Journeys will echo the long Nile sailing that Agatha Christie made famous in her 1937 novel "Death on the Nile." She wrote the book after taking one of the long journeys in 1933 on the Thomas Cook & Son luxury paddle steamer S.S. Sudan.

The first few days of each of the new Grand Nile Journeys in Cairo will include visits to the Great Pyramids of Giza, the Great Sphinx and the Grand Egyptian Museum.

At the end of the trip, passengers will also spend a final night at a hotel in Cairo before departing.

Passengers can extend their trips with optional pre- and postcruise land tours that include an extra two-night stay in Cairo and a four-night, fully guided excursion to nearby Jordan for visits to the Dead Sea, Petra and Amman.

While dating back to the late 1800s, when Thomas Cook & Son introduced "rapid steamers" that sailed the Nile from Cairo to Aswan, such longer Nile itineraries continued to be common until 1994, when the Egyptian government officially closed the 465-mile stretch of the river between Cairo and Luxor to overnight passenger ships due to security worries. Low water levels and shifting sandbars in the river also played a role.

After nearly 20 years of closure, the Egyptian government reopened the Cairo-to-Luxor stretch of the river to cruise vessels in 2012, following extensive river dredging, irrigation upgrades and major security overhauls. But long sailings from Cairo to Aswan have been slow to rebound.

Among the handful of other companies offering such trips is Movenpick Hotels & Resorts, which markets 14-night sailings from Cairo to Aswan on the 52-cabin MS Darakum.

#6155. The Fight Over Obamacare’s Phantom Enrollees

The Trump administration is right to take on the problem of improper enrollment.

Administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Dr. Mehmet Oz speaks during a press conference on anti-fraud initiatives at the White House campus in Washington, D.C., September 22, 2026.

More than a dozen Democratic senators are criticizing the Trump administration’s efforts to address the problem of phantom enrollments in Obamacare. In a letter to insurers, the senators accuse the companies of “colluding” with the administration to terminate coverage for more than 760,000 enrollees. Their criticism gets insurers’ financial incentives backward and overlooks the extensive safeguards the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) employed before terminating these highly suspicious enrollments.

Insurers have little incentive to drop phantom enrollees. For years, insurers have been the biggest beneficiaries of the expanded Obamacare subsidies — reaping tens of billions of dollars in higher subsidies. By making millions of plans free to consumers, Democrats created powerful incentives for improper and phantom enrollment. Given these incentives, the administration was right to scrutinize suspicious enrollments.
