#6154. Air Algerie Business Class Review: An Odd Avion Express Airbus A320 Wet Lease

For the next portion of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A320 business class on the one-hour flight from Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, Air Algerie doesn’t actually operate A320s, so this flight was operated by Lithuanian and Maltese charter operator Avion Express (which Air Algerie is really bad at disclosing during the booking process).

I mean, what can one really say about this flight, especially after coming off of Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, which was possibly the worst long haul business class I’ve ever flown? Truth be told, for a short haul flight this wasn’t terrible, but it also wasn’t good. It was just… whatever. As an aviation geek, I always do love a wet lease adventure!

As I explained in the last installment, I booked an attractive one-way business class cash fare on Air Algerie, even though it didn’t start or end where I actually wanted to go. 😉 I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

So in the last installment I reviewed Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and then this installment is my review of the connecting flight.

I’ve already reviewed the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers, which gives strong furniture store vibes and is nothing remarkable, but is still much better than Air Algerie’s onboard experience.

My flight to Tunis was scheduled to depart at 7:10AM, and my boarding pass indicated that boarding would start at 5:40AM. Yes, 90 minutes before departure… for an Airbus A320. Not surprisingly, that was completely inaccurate. I get that airlines don’t want people to miss flights, but I do find it frustrating when airlines don’t actually tell you when you should realistically be at the gate.

Anyway, my flight was departing from gate nine, roughly a five-minute walk from the lounge. Algiers Airport is fairly pleasant — it feels sterile and there’s not much to it, but compared to some other airports in the region, it isn’t half bad. But of course let me remind everyone that nothing holds a candle to Cairo Airport (CAI), easily one of the world’s finest facilities. 😉

I showed up at the departure gate plenty early, but even by 6:10AM (30 minutes after the alleged boarding start time), there wasn’t actually anyone at the gate.

The crew showed up at around 6:20AM, and boarding actually started at 6:35AM. The boarding process was rather strange on a variety of levels.

For one, before boarding started, the gate agent and security staff walked onto the jet bridge and then lit a cigarette and smoked. Nice… real professional.

Second, when boarding did start, it was just a free for all, with no priority give to business class passengers.

Third, there were three separate passport and boarding pass checks on the jet bridge by airport police. So first the gate agent checked documents, then upon entering the jet bridge a security officer checked both, then 100 feet later another security officer did the same, and then at the door of the plane, another security officer checked. After all that hard work protecting us, they definitely deserve a cigarette!

At the forward door to the plane I was greeted by the crew, and then headed toward my seat. I was flying on an 18-year-old Avion Express Airbus A320 with the registration code 9H-AMJ. While Avion Express is a Lithuanian company, this plane was registered in Malta.

This A320 has seen quite some things, as it started its career in 2008 at Wizz Air Ukraine, then in 2015 it moved to the main Wizz Air fleet when the Ukrainian subsidiary shut down, and then in 2021 it was taken over by Avion Express. Since then, it has flown on a wet lease basis with carriers like Eurowings, British Airways, Viva, and more.

For those not familiar with the concept of wet leasing, this is when an airline leases out its plane to another airline, including the crews. So while it’s sold just like any other Air Algerie flight, and the catering is like any Air Algerie flight, the crew and planes are from Avion Express.

This Avion Express A320 had a total of 180 seats, spread across 30 rows in a 3-3 configuration. Unfortunately unlike most of Air Algerie’s own planes, this one didn’t have a dedicated business class cabin with different seats. Instead, the first three rows were designated as business class, and they just had economy seats with blocked middles. That means business class had the capacity for 12 passengers.

I assigned myself seat 3F, the window seat on the right side in the third (last) row. This was a pretty old school cabin, which is a double edged sword. On the plus side, this meant seats were well padded, which you don’t typically find nowadays, given the emphasis on slimline seats.

Legroom was okay when you consider these are really economy seats, so it could’ve been worse.

The seat had a standard tray table, which folded down from the seat in front.

Given how old school the cabin was, it definitely wasn’t in very good condition, though. I mean, just look at the liner inside the window, and how that was coming apart.

Also, given the age of the cabin, it was clear that nothing had really been updated — there were no power ports, there was no Wi-Fi, and there was no streaming entertainment. That’s of course not a huge issue for such a short flight, but I’m just trying to help people manage expectations here.

The overhead console was typical for an A320, and had individual air nozzles and reading lights.

The cabin stayed really empty — there were only two other commercial passengers, and then one pilot who seemed to be commuting to Tunisia, for whatever reason.

Boarding was really efficient, and wrapped up by 6:55AM, as the flight wasn’t very full. That was still 15 minutes before the scheduled departure time. Before departure, the crew came around with juice or water as pre-departure drinks. I opted for a water, and was also given a packaged refreshing towel.

Ironically enough, on this flight the safety demonstration was exclusively performed in English (compared to my previous Air Algerie flight, where it was in French and Arabic, but not in English).

At 7AM the main cabin door closed, and at 7:05AM we began our pushback (sorry for the quality of the pictures, as the windows were super dirty)…

On the taxi out, we saw another Avion Express A320, which looked identical to ours (we also had an all-white A320).

There were quite a few Air Algerie planes parked on the ramp, as very few seemed to actually be at gates. I’m not sure if Air Algerie’s aircraft utilization is just terrible, or what.

By 7:25AM we made it out to runway 23, and were immediately cleared for takeoff.

Our climb out was smooth, and I loved the views on departure… I wish I could’ve actually visited Algiers, but the visa situation is complicated (and after my review, I’m not sure they’d be happy to have me anyway). 😉

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. At that point the crew closed the curtain between the cabin and galley, and got started with the service.

On this morning flight, breakfast was served. There was no choice, but I was served a hot dish with scrambled eggs, veggies, and some sort of meat. There was also a yogurt, a croissant, and a pastry, and additional bread rolls were offered (though I passed).

It sure seems like Air Algerie instructs Avion Express flight attendants to not deviate from their service protocol, which is to say that everything must simply be thrown on the tray, with zero effort put into presentation. 😉

So I couldn’t help but reorganize the tray a little bit, to make it look a little more presentable.

Drinks were also offered. I asked for a coffee, and it was a rather disgusting powdered coffee that I didn’t at all enjoy.

Before the descent, I checked out the lavatory, located at the front of the cabin. It was very basic and worn, though at least it wasn’t dirty.

Since this was a wet lease, the flight attendants onboard worked for Avion Express. I couldn’t actually figure out what country they were from (and they weren’t really friendly enough that I felt like being conversational). But anyway, they went through the motions, and weren’t rude, and they spoke a little bit of English (more than the Air Algerie crew on my previous flight).

There was also one Air Algerie flight attendant onboard, I guess to “oversee” the service, as is common with wet leases like this. In this case, he just plopped down in a business class seat and relaxed for most of the flight.

Around 30 minutes after takeoff, at roughly the halfway of the flight, the captain made an announcement, informing us we were at an altitude of 10,700 meters (35,000 feet), and that we’d be descending in around five minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent as planned, and the seatbelt sign was turned on 10 minutes after that.

The views on approach were gorgeous. Tunis is of course a coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views are tough to beat. I fondly remember my visit to Tunisia around a decade ago.

On our approach, we ended up flying out over the Mediterranean, and then circling back to land toward the south.

We ended up touching down on runway 19 at 8:25AM.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:30AM next to an Etihad A321LR (probably the nicest plane that serves the airport).

From there I cleared transit security, and had an extended layover, before connecting to Marseille (MRS) in Tunisair economy (due to a downgrade from business class).

My Air Algerie flight operated by an Avion Express A320 was perfectly whatever. For an hour-long flight, I thought the meal was quite good. However, the Avion Express A320 wasn’t terribly inspiring in terms of its modernness, seating, amenities, or service. So yeah, I don’t really have strong feelings on this one, other than appreciating that the flight was at least on schedule.

What do you make of Air Algerie business class, operated by an Avion Express A320?

I had a similar experience flying them from Algiers to Constantine. Biz class is just a coach seat (window or aisle) with the middle seat blocked off. Fairly mediocre experience but still miles ahead of Royal Air HardasaRoc, I mean, Maroc. Now that was a craptacular experience.

The tray arrangement does seem to confirm my suspicion they are round-trip catering their TATL flights…!

#6153. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?

Korean Air is adding a second New York-area gateway.

The SkyTeam Alliance carrier will land at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) with flights from Seoul’s Incheon Airport (ICN) in May 2027, Korean Air said on Thursday. The new route to east of the Hudson River complements its long-standing twice-daily service to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Korean Air will offer daily flights to EWR from May 22. It will fly a Boeing 777-300ER on the route.

The airline did not say what 777 configuration it will fly to EWR. It flies planes with several layouts, including an older configuration with eight first class suites.

United Airlines launched its first-ever nonstop from EWR to ICN in September. The Star Alliance carrier flies a Boeing 787-9 on the route.

Korean Air’s new EWR flight comes at a time of change for the airline as it wraps up a merger with fellow Korean carrier Asiana. Korean will complete the customer-facing integration of Asiana on Dec. 17, a combination that will significantly increase its market share at ICN.

While the merger does not add any new U.S. destinations to Korean Air’s map, it does increase its presence at JFK to up to four daily flights including Asiana, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

First look: Inside Korean Air’s stunning new flagship lounge at LAX

Future schedules show Korean Air continuing to serve JFK with four daily flights through June 2027.

The new EWR flight will complement Korean Air’s JFK services and create a new connection with joint venture partner Delta Air Lines. The carriers have expanded their transpacific options in recent years with new routes, including Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) to ICN on Delta.

The partnership allows Delta and Korean Air to coordinate commercial matters, including fares and schedules, between the U.S. and South Korea.

Korean Air highlighted the expanded flight options and New Jersey’s pharmaceutical, biotechnology, financial, and logistics industrial clusters for its new EWR route.

EWR is Korean Air’s first new U.S. destinations since it added Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) in 2019.

#6151. The US Quietly Raided Switzerland's F-35 Account To Pay For Patriot Missiles — Here's What Happened Next

The crunch on America's strategic missile stockpile put Switzerland in a tough position in 2025 when the United States informed Swiss leaders that it would be pausing Raytheon Patriot missile deliveries. Washington declared that the supply chain diversion was necessary to prioritize shipments to Ukraine and replenish the domestic arsenal.

The Swiss government halted payments under its foreign military sales contract that funds the Patriot program; however, the US simply withdrew the outstanding balance from cash earmarked for Swiss fighters. Instead of creating a leverage point in negotiations to resume Patriot deliveries, the Swiss aircraft supply chain was now in jeopardy.

Switzerland is in the process of transitioning its fleet from the Boeing F/A-18 Hornet to the Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II. Switzerland had paid up front in 2021 to secure its position on the production line, but amid the missile dispute, the US now demanded additional payments. American officials not only demanded that the Swiss repay the funds withdrawn for Patriot missiles.

Rather, they also increased the total based on rising production costs, inflation, and supply chain pressures. The US now claims that the contract's original fixed price could not be enforced and is demanding an additional $760 million to $1.5 billion. Instead of paying higher fees, Switzerland cut its order book by 20%, dropping from 36 Joint Strike Fighters to 30.

Under the terms and conditions of the FMS agreements between the US and Switzerland, Washington had the authority to take funding from any pool of Swiss defense program funds. Because the contract allows the US to shift resources if one project runs short on cash, Washington legally bypassed the freeze. It redirected well over 100 million Swiss francs, or $126 million.

Since these events, Swiss lawmakers have openly debated the reliability of Washington as a security partner and considered European alternatives for future defense needs. The Swiss government was bound by a strict, voter-approved budget ceiling, and doubts were beginning to arise concerning the quality of the F-35 as well as the level of control that the US held over the jets after delivery.

The combined friction of the FMS fund redirection, delivery delays, and soaring jet costs has strained US-Swiss defense relations. Urs Loher, head of the Swiss Armaments Agency Armasuisse, described the situation as "very unsatisfactory," according to Blue News. Loher was quoted by Swiss Info as saying that "the risk was too great for us. We'll take whatever we can get."

To avoid risking the delivery of the F-35s or spare parts for their existing F/A-18 fleet, the Swiss Defense Ministry had to quietly transfer tens of millions in advance to plug the resulting budget hole. The financial strain of the FMS pricing dispute forced the Swiss government to fundamentally restructure its Air2030 modernization plans. Adding to Swiss frustration, a US Government Accountability Office report confirmed that the early Swiss aircraft will be delivered in a truncated Block 4 software configuration.

The F-35 program and US-Swiss defense relations have significantly deteriorated, evolving from a strict procurement disagreement into an ongoing diplomatic crisis. Over the first half of 2026, the dispute reached a critical tipping point, resulting in official order reductions, massive advanced Swiss outlays, and public threats from Bern to terminate parts of its defense contracts.

In April, Swiss Defense Minister Martin Pfister announced that Switzerland is actively negotiating a potential termination of the entire Patriot missile contract. Despite the political gridlock, the physical program has forged ahead out of sheer contractual necessity. The first Swiss F-35A entered main assembly at Lockheed Martin’s Marietta, Georgia, plant.

Full Block 4 modernization will not be ready until 2031 at the earliest, creating a massive capability gap as older Swiss fleets age. The initial batch of aircraft will be deployed to Ebbing Air National Guard Base in Arkansas for pilot training, with physical arrivals in Switzerland delayed until 2028. Despite cutting aircraft, the programmatic costs continue to swell. In June 2026, the Swiss Council of States approved an additional credit of $505 million.

Swiss pilots will begin training on the first eight aircraft at Ebbing starting in mid-2027. Following the delivery of the first platform, the remaining airframes are slated to undergo final assembly and checkout at the European production line in Cameri, Italy. Because the timelines have become so volatile, the Swiss government has had to scramble to extend the life of its aging fleet of Hornets.

Warsaw's search for the next air superiority platform.

Switzerland's F/A-18 Hornet Service Life Extension Program has become an expensive, high-stakes anchor for air defense following changes to the F-35 procurement. To free up emergency cash internally and protect the baseline F-35 purchase, Switzerland had to scale back the depth of its Hornet upgrades.

While 30 planes were initially included in the full scope of retrofits, 15 will receive more limited upgrades to save costs. The structural refurbishments were completed across all 30 aircraft. Still, with ongoing uncertainty over the F-35 delivery dates, Switzerland will also study the extreme measure of stretching the F/A-18 fleet beyond 2030 and past the 6,000-hour structural safety limit.

They are also expecting to continue flying the decades-old Northrop F-5 Tigers until the end of 2030. The Swiss Air Force flies high-G, tight-turning air-policing missions through narrow alpine valleys, making structural work non-negotiable.

The issue is that only 15 of the 30 Swiss Hornets received the intended radar updates, modern flight-management software, and secure communications overhauls. This created a split fleet. Half of the Swiss Hornets possess airframes certified to fly structurally into the 2030s but carry outdated radar and electronic warfare systems, leaving them highly vulnerable if deployed in modern battle space.

The chronic issues keeping the fleet of stealth fighters grounded.

The Swiss Federal Council officially stated that any future purchases to bring the fleet back up to its originally required 36 aircraft will be evaluated independently of aircraft type. Instead of buying more JSFs, Switzerland is considering a mixed fleet by pairing the 30 F-35s with 4.5-generation European-made aircraft. Drones could provide a low-cost means of filling the capability gap alongside F-35s.

In terms of crewed platforms, the top contenders are the Eurofighter, Rafale, and Gripen. Airbus previously offered Switzerland a robust industrial package to accompany an order for the Eurofighter Typhoon. The Typhoon excels at high-altitude, high-speed interception, which fits the Swiss alpine air-policing mandate perfectly. Pairing it with the F-35 would reduce Swiss reliance on a single US supply chain.

Dassault's Rafale was a top contender in the original evaluation that led to the F-35 selection as successor to the Hornet. Because Switzerland shares a border and close diplomatic ties with France, choosing the Rafale for a second batch would simplify training and logistics.

Dassault makes both a land-based and carrier-capable variant, and the Rafale F4 is built as the ultimate omnirole fighter jet capable of exceptional air-to-air and air-to-ground performance. Though Saab pulled out of the original flight tests because the Gripen E wasn't fully operational at the time, it remains the ultimate 'budget-friendly' 4.5-generation option.

Its operating cost per flight hour is a fraction of the F-35's, making it an ideal candidate for basic peacetime air policing. The Royal Canadian Air Force has also been considering the Gripen E as an alternative, while Canada is still struggling to decide whether it will fulfill its original order for 88 F-35s due to diplomatic disputes between Ottawa and Washington, as Bern experienced.

Fifth-generation fighters still struggling to live up to the hype.

The ultimate alternative would be to follow suit with some other European Air Forces that have decided to skip fifth-generation fighter technology altogether and go straight to sixth-generation stealth jets. Although the trilateral Future Combat Air System program fell through between Germany, France, and Spain, there is an alternative.

The Global Combat Air Program is progressing in partnership with the United Kingdom, Italy, and Japan. Germany is considering joining the FCAS, relegated to a combat cloud and advanced drone development program. The aircraft is expected to be on par with the Next Generation Air Dominance aircraft, or the Boeing F-47.

Canada and even India are also considering joining the GCAP program at various levels of investment. The primary roadblock to Switzerland joining the multinational program is likely the price point. The GCAP, also known as the BAE Tempest, could be as expensive as $300 million if it were to cost a similar amount to its American equivalent.

The price of an F-35A is around $90 million for the US Air Force, but that doesn't include the add-on cost for support that FMS customers pay, which can increase the flyaway cost by as much as 50%. That would still be half or less of a GCAP, assuming it is priced comparably to the F-47. That may not be realistic for Bern.

However, if they are only planning to procure a half dozen jets on a case-by-case basis, then the value of a small 'exquisite' sub-fleet with European support would significantly elevate Swiss air power. Still, the capabilities of a collaborative combat aircraft, also known as a loyal wingman drone, are likely a better fit if the Swiss Air Force chooses an advanced platform rather than a 4.5-Gen fighter jet.

#6150. Wild: Stolen Delta Bag Tracked From JFK To DC Bus Stop, Thief Nabbed By Police

It’s not totally uncommon to see bags stolen (or perhaps in some cases accidentally taken) from baggage claim belts at airports. In the past that was basically a lost cause, but thanks to things like AirTags, they can often be tracked.

Here’s an absolutely wild version of such a story, where someone in the miles & points community had their bag stolen, and then someone else tracked it down… hundreds of miles away, and with the help of police!

JT Genter is Editor-in-Chief of AwardWallet and a member of the miles & points community who travels full time. On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, he took to social media to share that his checked bag had been stolen off the Delta baggage claim belt at New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) Terminal 4.

He filed a Delta missing bag claim and police report, and pointed out how “so many irreplaceable memories” were lost in the bag, including all his clothing, medicines, all his toiletries, etc. And he claimed that Delta agents didn’t seem like they gave a you-know-what.

God. So many irreplaceable memories lost in that bag. All of my clothing. Medicines. All my toiletries. Literally so many of my worldly possessions stolen right off Delta's baggage claim belt.And @Delta agents couldn't give less of a shit. Acted like it must happen all the time

That’s obviously incredibly frustrating, though this is a story that had a happy ending less than 24 hours later. JT did have a tracker in his bag, so could keep an eye on the movements of the bag, but he just didn’t say so initially. Apparently the person had pretty quickly taken Amtrak down to DC.

But this is where the story gets truly wild. Jamie Larounis, an Upgraded Points contributor and another member of the miles & points community, coordinated with JT to help. Let me just share Jamie’s version of events:

This might be a story for the history books. Man steals backpack in NY. He takes Amtrak train to DC. I decided to play detective and found the thief with the backpack sitting at a bus station. He boards a bus, but luckily I caught the bus number. I found 2 extremely helpful cops to assist and they found the thief a few blocks away and they nabbed him. They asked me to get in the cop car to ID the thief, and we headed to the police station to retrieve the items.

Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today, but with a little perseverance we got this thief locked up!!! Huzzah!

And by "we", I mean @TheForwardCabin! Jamie used the Tile tracking location to get a visual on our bag and found DC police who were ready to protect and serve.What an incredible end to this story!https://t.co/LvFthwBMqt

When asked what was missing from the bag after it was recovered, JT shared that the guy ditched some clothing, supplies, and custom medical equipment, plus “irreplaceable memories.”

When you consider the volume of bags that are checked, obviously a fair number get lost, stolen, etc. In theory, stealing a bag from a baggage claim belt is really easy — you just take it and leave. However:

Publicly, we of course don’t know anything about this thief. Are we to assume that he wasn’t actually flying, and was just there to steal a bag? And of all the bags he could steal, why did that black backpack catch his eye? And was he planning to travel to DC anyway, and if so, was that the plan all along, or was that just the “escape” plan with the stolen goods?

I recognize that people stealing bags off of baggage claim belts probably aren’t the most sophisticated criminals, but in this day and age, you’d think that checking every pocket of the bag for a tracker would be a best practice, given how common they are.

A traveler had their backpack stolen off of a baggage claim belt at JFK after a Delta flight. Fortunately he had a tracker, which showed that the bag was taken down to DC on Amtrak. After posting about this online, someone else coordinated and played detective, and found someone with the bag at a bus station in DC, and with the help of police, it was recovered.

It’s nice when a story like this has a positive ending, and it’s also a good reminder to put some sort of a tracking device in your bag, for situations where your bag gets lost or stolen.

What do you make of this checked bag recovery mission?

Agree with the comment about checking bags on the way out of the airport like in many other parts of the world. In addition, I would add that part of this story may be because he is in the points and miles community.

I think we are missing the point here. The value is that the Apple Trackers really do work great. I track items shipped from Hawaii to Los Angeles and see that they are in the freight receiving area at LAX before anyone with the airlines knows that they have been delivered early. A family member had their purse stolen from them in Venice right on the street when they were pushing a baby carriage with two little ones in it when a late model car stopped and a guy jumped out and grabbed her purse and drove away. A nearby delivery person helped her track the car speeding down Lincoln Blvd and called the police that stopped and arrested him. Purse returned within hours and they guy actually went to jail. I am currently tracking a backpack in Hawaii at a know location where it belongs from Los Angeles 6 months after I left it there by mistake. We find our lost keys, lost phone and purses all the time in our home as they seem to end up in different places all the time.

Why don't airlines/airports in the US have passengers luggage tags checked when they leave baggage claim, like some parts of the world? I'm talking about the baggage tags that you get when you check your bag in. Many foreign airlines' check-in agents stick them to your boarding pass, and in some parts of the world, those tags are compared with the bags you take off the carousel before you can leave the baggage claim area. Is it just about not wanting to spend extra on labor for this task?

If you an are able bodied person, there is 0.0 reasons why your bag should beat you to the baggage belt. Get off the plane and make it your mission to get to that belt. Once there, position yourself where the bags drop or come up.

#6149. An Intellectual History of California’s Proposition 40

How a French academic research project and an elite public university nearly took down the Golden State’s venture capital economy with a wealth tax

People attend a rally in support of Proposition 40 and in opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 ahead of the midterm elections in Los Angeles, Calif., October 5, 2026.

On November 3, California voters narrowly rejected Proposition 40, a 5 percent tax on the net worth of the state’s billionaires. That outcome was not assured. In September, the measure led 52 percent to 46 percent in the Public Policy Institute of California’s survey of likely voters. Had it passed, the state that received 62 percent of all U.S. venture capital dollars in 2025 would have begun taxing founders on the paper value of companies, potentially driving them elsewhere.

The union that sponsored Proposition 40, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, supplied the signatures and most of the campaign money. The idea came from an intellectual movement that began with the French economist Thomas Piketty, found an institutional home at the University of California, Berkeley, and received financing from the foundation of a Boston insurance executive.

People attend a rally in support of Proposition 40 and in opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 ahead of the midterm elections in Los Angeles, Calif., October 5, 2026.

Marc Joffe is a fellow at the California Policy Center.

#6148. Chase Sapphire Reserve Business Bonus: 200K Points Welcome Offer

The Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ is Chase’s premium business card. While the card has a steep annual fee, it also has strong perks, and for many people, will prove to be more than worthwhile.

We’re currently seeing a highest-ever Sapphire Reserve Business bonus, which matches the best bonus we’ve seen on this card. I’d like to recap the details of the offer, including talking about eligibility, and why the card could be worth it. While this is a limited time welcome offer, the end date hasn’t been published.

Link: Learn more about the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business currently has a limited time highest-ever welcome offer of 200,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards after spending $30,000 within the first six months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus on this card is worth $3,400, which is incredible, among the best welcome offers out there. Admittedly the spending requirement is big (you need to average $5,000 per month in spending over six months), but so is the bonus.

For context on the Sapphire Reserve Business bonus history, when the card launched in 2025, we saw the same offer that’s currently available, for 200,000 points. Then in early 2026 we saw an offer for 150,000 points, before the offer for 200,000 points returned. Initially the offer for 200,000 points was supposed to end in September 2026, but it was extended, though we don’t know the official end date.

When it comes to applying for the Chase Sapphire Reserve Business, eligibility is unrelated to that of any other Chase Sapphire or Chase Ink card. That means if you’re eligible for business credit cards, you should be eligible for the welcome offer on this card, making this offer pretty widely available.

Keep in mind the general rules of applying for Chase cards, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (though select business cards don’t count toward that total).

If you’re trying to understand general Chase business card restrictions, the Chase Ink cards probably give you the best sense of what you can expect in terms of eligibility. You don’t need a corporation to apply for the Sapphire Reserve Business, as a sole proprietorship would qualify as well. So even a side gig (like freelancing or having a rental property) would potentially qualify you for the card.

There’s not a specific credit score you need to get approved for the Sapphire Reserve Business, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that goes into deciding on approvals.

The $795 annual fee Chase Sapphire Reserve Business is a pretty compelling business card. As is the case with many premium cards, the idea is that the annual fee can be justified based on a combination of the rewards structure, benefits, and airport lounge access, among other things.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business bonus currently offers up to 200,000 Ultimate Rewards points, which is in line with the highest ever publicly available welcome offers that we’ve seen on the card.

While the Sapphire Reserve Business has a steep annual fee, it also offers strong perks, so I’m sure many people will have no issues justifying this annual fee. Either way, if you’re eligible for the card and can complete the spending requirement, this welcome offer is incredibly tempting, and a great reason to apply for the card.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

The  is one of the most recognizable premium travel rewards cards on the market, offering everything from airport lounge access and hotel elite status to a long list of travel and lifestyle statement credits.

But with an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), it's also a significant investment.

The Amex Platinum offers plenty of opportunities to offset that cost, especially if you travel frequently and can take advantage of its statement credits. However, many of its benefits come with restrictions, and getting the full value requires some effort.

So, who can actually get enough value from the Amex Platinum to justify its annual fee? Let's take a closer look at who should — and shouldn't — consider adding this card to their wallet.

For frequent travelers, airport lounge access is one of the biggest reasons to consider the .

The card offers access to one of the most extensive airport lounge networks available through a credit card, making it especially valuable if you spend a lot of time in airports.

Cardmembers can access American Express Centurion Lounges, receive a Priority Pass Select membership (enrollment required) and visit Delta Sky Clubs when flying on eligible same-day Delta flights. Delta Sky Club access is limited to 10 visits per year unless you spend $75,000 on eligible purchases in a calendar year to unlock unlimited visits. Access is subject to eligibility requirements.

Amex also operates Centurion Lounges at more than 20 airports, so the benefit can be particularly valuable if you live near or frequently connect through an airport with one.

If you travel frequently and would otherwise pay for lounge access, the Platinum could help you save money while making your time at the airport more comfortable. And when combined with the card's other travel benefits and statement credits, lounge access can help make the $895 annual fee easier to justify.

While the is best known for its premium travel benefits, it also offers a growing list of lifestyle statement credits that can help offset its $895 annual fee.

For example, cardmembers can receive up to $400 in Resy statement credits each calendar year (distributed as up to $100 per quarter) at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants* and up to $300 in Lululemon statement credits* (up to $75 quarterly) at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online.

The card also offers up to $300 annually in digital entertainment statement credits* (up to $25 monthly) for eligible subscriptions, along with up to $120 annually toward an Uber One membership to fully cover an auto-renewing $96 annual or $9.99 monthly membership*.

If you're already spending money on dining, shopping and entertainment in these categories, the credits can provide meaningful value without requiring you to change your spending habits.

However, many of these benefits are divided into monthly or quarterly credits, so you'll need to keep track of when to use them. The Platinum is a particularly good fit for someone who doesn't mind managing these benefits and can consistently take advantage of them year-round.

Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum

The Amex Platinum can also be a valuable addition to your wallet if you regularly stay at Hilton, Marriott or luxury hotels.

Cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status, which can provide benefits such as bonus points on stays and potential room upgrades. You'll also receive Leaders Club Sterling status with The Leading Hotels of the World, a collection of independent luxury hotels. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Beyond elite status, one of the Platinum's most valuable hotel-related perks is its up to $600 annual lodging statement credit (up to $300 semiannually).

Cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits every six months on eligible prepaid bookings through American Express Travel®, including stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection properties, as well as select Airbnb Luxe stays.

The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe require a minimum two-night stay, and beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging credit.

Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings also come with valuable benefits, including daily breakfast for two, guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, room upgrades when available and a property credit valued at $100.

If you regularly book these types of stays, the lodging credit and additional perks can go a long way toward offsetting the card's annual fee. Just be sure to compare prices with booking directly, since rates through Amex Travel aren't always the lowest.

Related: How to maximize the Amex Platinum hotel statement credit

Chase's unofficial 5/24 rule generally makes applicants ineligible for many Chase cards if they've opened five or more personal credit cards across issuers within the past 24 months.

Travelers who are still eligible for Chase cards may want to prioritize products such as the (see rates and fees) or (see rates and fees) before exceeding that threshold.

If you've already built a collection of Chase rewards cards, the Amex Platinum could be worth considering as your next premium travel card.

The card also earns Membership Rewards points, giving you access to a separate collection of airline and hotel transfer partners that can complement an existing Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy.

Many people just starting in the points world underestimate the stringency of Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you're just getting started with travel rewards and remain under Chase's 5/24 threshold, you may want to think carefully before applying for the Amex Platinum.

Opening the card could count toward your 5/24 total and potentially limit your eligibility for Chase cards in the future. That could mean missing out on valuable welcome offers or benefits from cards you planned to open later.

However, once you get over 5/24, it may be hard to get back under, and there’s a massive opportunity cost in doing so. Having a plan and sticking to it will serve you well in the long term.

Of course, that doesn't mean everyone under 5/24 should avoid the Platinum. If its benefits are a particularly good fit for your travel habits, it may still make sense.

The provides 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or with American Express Travel (on up to $500,000 of spending each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

A card like the or (see rates and fees) may be a better fit because their broader travel earning categories can include eligible third-party airfare bookings.

The offers a long list of statement credits, but that doesn't necessarily mean every cardholder will get enough value from them to justify the $895 annual fee.

Following the card's 2025 refresh, several of its benefits are geared toward specific lifestyle purchases, including dining at Resy restaurants, shopping at Lululemon and purchasing an Oura Ring. (Cardmembers receive up to a $200 Oura Ring statement credit each calendar year. This statement credit applies to ring purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. Enrollment is required.)

Many of these credits also come with restrictions. For example, the Resy and Lululemon credits are distributed quarterly, meaning you'll need to use them throughout the year rather than all at once.

If you don't already spend money with these merchants, or you don't want to keep track of multiple credits and enrollment requirements, the Platinum may not be the best fit.

Before applying, carefully consider just how much these credits are worth to you; if they provide little to no value, another Amex card might be a better fit.

Related: 4 different flavors of Amex Platinum — which one is right for you?

Business owners with substantial expenses may find that is a better fit than the personal Platinum.

Although both cards carry an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), their earning rates and statement credits differ in ways that could make one more valuable than the other.

For example, the Business Platinum earns 2 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases in select business categories and on purchases of $5,000 or more, on up to $2 million in combined eligible purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar.

The Business Platinum also provides up to $1,150 in statement credits per calendar year for U.S. Dell purchases: up to $150 each calendar year and an additional $1,000 statement credit after spending $5,000 on Dell purchases with the same card each calendar year (enrollment required).

You can also access the Pay with Points redemption option on the Business Platinum card, which gets you a 35% bonus for eligible flights with your selected airline using your Amex points (up to 1 million points back per calendar year). This is notably not available on the personal Amex Platinum.

These business-focused benefits may be more useful for someone with significant company expenses, while the personal Platinum may be a better fit for travelers who can maximize its lifestyle credits.

New cardmembers can find out their offer and may be eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that bonus could be worth up to $3,500, which is nearly four times the card's $895 annual fee.

While this is the card's standard welcome offer, now could still be a good time to apply if you're eligible for an offer you're happy with and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making unnecessary purchases.

Just make sure you'll also get enough value from the card's ongoing benefits to justify its annual fee beyond the first year.

Related: The best time to apply for Amex cards based on offer history

The offers an impressive lineup of premium travel benefits and statement credits, but its $895 annual fee means it won't make sense for everyone.

For frequent travelers who value airport lounge access and luxury hotel perks, and can consistently use the card's lifestyle credits, there's plenty of potential to get more value than the annual fee.

On the other hand, travelers who prefer straightforward rewards or don't regularly use the card's benefits may find better value with a lower-annual-fee option.

Ultimately, the Platinum is worth considering if its benefits fit your existing spending and travel habits — not because of the total advertised value of its credits.

#6146. Watch: 3 Rock Bands Play Mid-Air Concert On Southwest Jet That Narrowly Beat FAA Ground Stop

Passengers on a Southwest Airlines flight from Los Angeles to Orlando on Friday got an unexpected in-flight concert from three of the biggest rock bands of the early 2000s. Hoobastank, Simple Plan and The Used each took turns performing in the aisle, with videos shared by passengers later spreading across social media.

The flight departed from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) just moments before the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) announced a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, bringing all US departures to a halt for more than four hours. According to some onboard, the Southwest flight was among the last to take off before the order took effect.

Videos from the flight show the cabin lights dimmed as passengers sang along, raised their arms and filmed the performances on their phones. According to the Daily Voice, Hoobastank frontman Doug Robb performed the band's 2004 hit "The Reason," while Simple Plan followed with "Perfect" and "I'm Just a Kid," and The Used played "The Taste of Ink."

All three bands are scheduled to appear at this weekend's Vans Warped Tour event in Orlando, of which Southwest is an event sponsor. Hoobastank later shared several passenger videos to its Instagram Stories, including one from singer LØLØ, who captioned her clip, "Every plane was grounded today, but the emo gods made sure this one flew."

It is not clear whether the performances had been planned or were spontaneous. Southwest is listed as the Preferred Airline Partner of Vans Warped Tour. The festival's website says the airline is bringing "the first-ever Vans Warped Tour experience at 35,000 feet" through its Live at 35 program, which features pop-up performances on flights.

Simple Flying contacted Southwest for comment about this flight, but a representative could not be reached before publication.

Southwest launched its Live at 35 program in 2011, bringing musicians onboard to perform for passengers. The program held its 100th concert in October 2024, when Liz Rose performed on a flight from Nashville to Miami. The flight was carrying Taylor Swift fans to the Eras Tour.

In June, the carrier marked 15 years of the initiative with a performance by the Plain White T's, one of the program's earliest acts. The airline said at the time that it planned to hold more of these onboard events in the coming months, and several have since taken place.

Other notable performances include Bowling For Soup performing on a flight to Las Vegas in July, while reggae artist Julian Marley recently performed on a sold-out flight from Orlando to Montego Bay. The onboard performances are typically brief, with a Southwest spokesperson previously stating that each lasts about 10 minutes.

Stranded crews and grounded jets paint chaotic airport scenes as tech failures ripple through nationwide schedules.

The Southwest flight's departure came just before one of the most significant disruptions to US air travel in decades. At 3:54 PM ET (12:54 PM local time in Los Angeles), the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop, later describing the issue as a "temporary telecommunications outage."

While aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations, all departing flights were held on the ground until the restriction was lifted at around 8:15 PM ET. At over four hours, it was the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years and only the second since the September 11 attacks, following a January 2023 malfunction of the FAA system used to send notices to pilots.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said aging air traffic control routers had become overloaded with data, while other officials claimed that new technology being installed had overwhelmed older equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed there was no indication of a cyberattack or terrorist threat.
